Tuvaluan
Tuvaluan is a Polynesian language spoken by the 9,000 inhabitants of the nine
atolls of Tuvalu in the Central Pacific, as well as small but growing Tuvaluan
communities in Fiji, New Zealand, and Australia. This grammar is the first detailed
description of the structure of Tuvaluan, one of the least-well documented languages
of Polynesia.
While the language shares features commonly found amongst Polynesian languages,
it exhibits a number of divergent features of interest to scholars of Pacific languages,
comparative linguistics, language typology, and language universals.
Tuvaluan: A Polynesian language of the Central Pacific explores the syntax, morphology,
and phonology of the language, as well as selected features of the lexicon. It pays
particular attention to discourse and sociolinguistic factors at play in the structural
organization of the language.
Niko Besnier is Professor of Anthropology at Victoria University of Wellington,
New Zealand. He has conducted extensive field research in Polynesia, particularly
Tuvalu.

Editorial statement
Until quite recently, work on theoretical linguistics and work on language
description proceeded almost entirely in isolation from one another. Work on
theoretical linguistics, especially in syntax, concentrated primarily on English, and
its results were felt to be inapplicable to those interested in describing other
languages. Work on describing individual languages was almost deliberately
isolationist, with the development of a different framework and terminology for
each language or language group, and no feeding of the achievements of language
description into linguistic theory. Within the last few years, however, a major
rapprochement has taken place between theoretical and descriptive linguistics. In
particular, the rise of language typology and the study of language universals have
produced a large number of theoreticians who require accurate, well-formulated
descriptive data from a wide range of languages, and have shown descriptive
linguists that they can both derive benefit from and contribute to the development
of linguistic theory. Even within generative syntax, long the bastion of linguistic
anglocentrism, there is an increased interest in the relation between syntactic theory
and a wide range of language types.
For a really fruitful interaction between theoretical and descriptive linguistics,
it is essential that descriptions of different languages should be comparable. The
Questionnaire of the present series (originally published as Lingua, vol. 42 (1977),
no. 1) provides a framework for the description of a language that is (a) sufficiently
comprehensive to cover the major structures of any language that are likely to be of
theoretical interest; (b) sufficiently explicit to make cross-language comparisons a
feasible undertaking (in particular, through the detailed numbering key); and (c)
sufficiently flexible to encompass the range of variety that is found in human
language. The volumes that were published in the predecessor to the present series,
the Lingua Descriptive Studies (now available from Routledge), succeeded in bridging
the gap between theory and description: authors include both theoreticians who
are also interested in description and field-workers with an interest in theory.
The aim of the Descriptive Grammars is thus to provide descriptions of a wide
range of languages according to the format set out in the Questionnaire. Each
language will be covered in a single volume. The first priority of the series is
grammars of languages for which detailed descriptions are not at present available.
However, the series will also encompass descriptions of better-known languages
with the series framework providing more detailed descriptions of such languages
than are currently available (as with the monographs on West Greenlandic and
Kannada).
Bernard Comrie

Introduction
0.1. TUVALU
Tuvalu (formerly known as the Ellice Islands) is a chain of nine low-rising coral
atolls and islands spanning 600km in the Central Pacific, between the latitudes of
5°S and 11°S, and the longitude of 176°E and the International Dateline. The group
is situated on the outskirts of ‘Triangle’ Polynesia (i.e., the main Polynesian cultural
area minus the Polynesian enclaves in Micronesia and Melanesia). Its closest
neighbours are the Gilbert Islands (Kiribati), 350km to the North, which mark the
eastern boundary of Micronesia, and the island of Rotuma, 300km to the South.
The Tuvalu group can be subdivided geographically into a northern group,
consisting of the islands of Nanumea, Nanumaga, Niutao, and Nui
(phonemically Nuui), and a southern group, which includes Vaitupu,
Nukufetau, Funafuti (phonemically Funaafuti), Nukulaelae, and the
southernmost and smallest island of the group, Niulakita, which was not
settled permanently until the twentieth century and is used today as copra-
producing grounds by Niutao islanders.
The total land area of the nine atolls is 26km2. By any standard, the atolls
and islands are very small, the quality of their soil poor, and the land
resources that they offer very limited. Besides the indigenous coconut and
pandanus trees, the only significant food plants that grow in these
environments are swamp taro (pulaka, Cyrtosperma chamissonis) and the
more recently imported breadfruit and banana trees. Sea resources, on the
other hand, are abundant, varied and, on some islands of the group, readily
accessible. The group lies outside of the main belt of tropical westerlies, and
thus hurricanes are relatively infrequent. However, the morphology of the
atolls, where the maximum elevation above sea level is but a few feet, makes
them vulnerable to occasional storms. The atolls are relatively distant from
each other and only two (Funafuti and Nukufetau) offer safe anchorage for
sea craft. These factors, combined with limited resources, greatly restrict inter-
island communications.
Until the beginning of the twentieth century, Tuvalu remained essentially isolated
from the rest of the world (Munro 1982). Even though the Spanish explorer Mendaña
sighted Nui and Niulakita as early as 1568 and 1595 respectively, few ships called
at any of the islands of the group until recent times. Because it lies outside of the
main shipping routes and because of its lack of exploitable resources, Tuvalu was
spared, for the most part, the colonial exploitation witnessed in other parts of the
Pacific. The political and religious history of the group also contributed to its
isolation. After becoming a British protectorate in 1892, the group was amalgamated
in 1916 into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony, along with the Gilbert Islands,
Ocean Island (Baanaba), the Tokelau group, and Fanning, Washington, and

0.2. POPULATION
In 1991, there were 9043 inhabitants in Tuvalu, the majority of whom were
indigenous to the group. A break-down by island of this population figure is
provided in Table 0.1.
The population of Tuvalu is primarily of Polynesian stock. Oral traditions on
most islands affirm that they were settled either directly or indirectly from Samoa
or from an island group in the neighbourhood of Samoa (Roberts 1958). As discussed
in the next section, the linguistic characteristics of the present-day Tuvaluan dialects
indicate that its closest relatives are the so-called Samoic-Outlier languages of
Western Polynesia. Because extensive archeological field research has yet to be
conducted in Tuvalu, no dating for the settlement of the group is available, although
Bayard (1976:84) proposes speculatively a date of 300 to 500 AD, using evidence
from a variety of sources.
One atoll, Nui, is known to have received a strong input of Micronesian culture
from Kiribati (Roberts 1958, McQuarrie 1976). Gilbertese warriors invaded the atoll
in the seventeenth or eighteenth century and appeared to have subsequently
established themselves there. To date, Nui has retained strong links with Kiribati, a
fact that over eighty years of Tuvaluan and i-Kiribati political integration is likely
to have facilitated. A dialect of Gilbertese peculiar to Nui is spoken there, which

Tuvalu are also found in and around Suva (Fiji), Apia (Western Samoa), and
Auckland and Wellington (New Zealand).
0.3. TUVALUAN SOCIETY
For most intents and purposes, each individual island of Tuvalu forms a
separate society with a local island-governing structure, specific institutions,
and particular social and cultural practices. Indeed, prior to colonial
amalgamation in the late nineteenth century (which probably had little effect
on local life until well into the twentieth century), the islands and atolls were
independent entities, although they apparently sustained some contacts with
one another. However, all island communities also share many traits, and it is
on the basis of these commonalities that a sense of national identity has slowly
emerged, particularly since independence.
Following are some of the social and cultural traits that recur throughout the
group: cognatic descent with an agnatic bias; a balance between endogamy and
exogamy and between virilocality and uxorilocality with a bias for the former in
each case; an avoidance taboo between cousins of different gender which is
strongest between first cousins and gradually weakens as genealogical distance
increases; pervasive adoption, which does not preclude allegiance to blood
relatives; a complex system of land tenure based on corporate ownership by
landholding kin-based groups; the importance of exchange in the economic life;
and patterns of dual organization that pervade many aspects of social life and
culture. All atolls and islands have a chiefly system of one form or the other,
whereby a chief is elected by members of a Council of Elders over which he, or
more rarely she, presides. However, one also finds everywhere an explicitly
articulated ideology of egalitarianism, solidarity, and consensus. Frequent
conflicts arise over how these values should be implemented in particular
situations, and how they articulate with the authority of chiefs and elders. All
chiefly systems have been reinvented in recent times or have undergone major
discontinuities during the colonial period.
Subsistence agriculture and fishing still play a major role in the local
economy of islands other than Funafuti, the nation’s capital. However, money

0.4. THE TUVALUAN LANGUAGE
0.4.1. Genetic affiliations and sociolinguistic context
Native speakers of Tuvaluan refer to it as te ggana Tuuvalu ‘the Tuvaluan
language’ or more frequently and less formally as te ggana a taatou ‘our
language’ (cf. 2.1.2.1.3). Tuvaluan is one of approximately thirty members of
the Polynesian language group. Polynesian in turn is a relatively discrete
subgroup of Oceanic (or Eastern Austronesian), one of the two main branches
of the Austronesian linguistic family (as summarized in Clark 1987).
The lowest-level subgroup of Polynesian to which Tuvaluan is usually
attached is the loosely defined Samoic Outlier subgroup (Pawley 1966, 1967),
the composition of which is given in Figure 0.1.
Arguments have been proposed periodically for subgroupings that either
refine further the Samoic-Outlier proposal or provide alternatives to it. For
example, Howard (1981) groups Tuvaluan together with several Outlier
languages, namely Kapingamarangi, Nukuoro, Takuu, Nukuria, Nukumanu,
Luangiua, and Sikaiana, as well as, tentatively, Tokelauan, into a subgroup of
either Samoic-Outlier or the higher order Nuclear Polynesian, which
comprises all Polynesian languages other than Tongan and Niuean (Pawley
1966). However, these proposals have been based on equivocal evidence, in
part because descriptive materials for the relevant languages are still very
limited.
Indeed, little detailed information is available on the Outlier languages
most likely to be most Tuvaluan’s closest relatives. More information is
available on Tokelauan, a language spoken on the three atolls of Tokelau,
several hundred miles East of Tuvalu (see Map 0.1), and among Tokelauan
immigrants in New Zealand. The inhabitants of Tokelau and Tuvalu may have
similar origins and have been in sustained contact over the centuries, to the
extent that the social organizations, cultures, and languages of both groups
exhibit numerous similarities. Whether the resemblance between the two
languages is a reflection of a common historical origin or the product of
subsequent contact is difficult to gauge. The social, cultural, and linguistic
similarities between the two groups have been accentuated by the fact that
they have come under the same powerful influence of Samoan missionary-
pastors in historical times. Indeed, many borrowings from Samoan found in
Tuvaluan are also found in Tokelauan. As a result of these various prehistorical
and historical patterns of contact, the two languages are almost mutually
intelligible, and descriptions of the Tokelauan language are of particular
relevance to this work. The most detailed description of Tokelauan is Hooper
(1993), which focuses on selected aspects of the structure of the language. To

Each of the seven traditionally inhabited islands and atolls of the group where
Tuvaluan is spoken natively has its distinct dialect. The seven dialects differ from
one another mostly in the phonology (particularly suprasegmental phonology)
and lexicon, and, to a lesser extent, through the presence of a few grammatical
morphemes in some dialects that are absent or have a different form in other
dialects. The seven dialects have essentially the same syntactic structure.
Although a comprehensive study of dialectal variations has yet to be published,
one can identify a clear division between two dialect areas, one grouping Nanumea,
Nanumaga, and Niutao together, and the other Funafuti, Vaitupu, Nukufetau, and
Nukulaelae. In the Northern subgroup, Nanumea and Nanumaga probably share
more features with one another than with Niutao. No further subgrouping is evident
among the Southern dialects. The picture is greatly complicated by patterns of dialect
mixing, which may be quite ancient. Frequently, native speakers are at a loss to
identify the dialectal affiliation of particular linguistic features because they have
been borrowed across dialects. The hegemonic status of the Funafuti and Vaitupu
dialects is particularly evident: Funafuti is the seat of the national government and
Vaitupu is the location of what was until recently the only secondary school in the
group. Many Outer Islanders migrate to Funafuti in particular, where employment
opportunities are all located, and everyone in the country listens to Radio Tuvalu
which broadcasts from Funafuti. Thus all speakers of Tuvaluan are at least familiar
with, and many are bidialectal in, the Funafuti or Vaitupu dialect (the difference
between the two is minimal).
Tuvaluan has come into contact with and received a strong influence from three
languages. The influence of Gilbertese, a Micronesian language, probably goes back
the furthest in time. Like many Micronesian and Outlier Polynesian societies,
Tuvaluan society borrowed a number of important technologies from Gilbertese
society, such as coconut-sap toddy tapping and fishing magic. Along with these
technologies, a substantial body of technological vocabulary of Gilbertese origin
was incorporated into the Tuvaluan lexicon. During the colonial period (1892–1975),
Gilbertese played an important role in the political life of Tuvalu, since the seat of
the colonial administration was in the Gilbert Islands. Today, besides being spoken
natively on Nui atoll, Gilbertese is the second (and sometimes first) language of
many civil servants and other individuals who returned to Tuvalu after the two
island groups separated politically in 1975. However, its importance in Tuvaluan
daily life is rapidly decreasing.
Samoan was introduced to Tuvalu at the time of missionization. It was the
‘vernacular’ for the colonial government’s administration of the Ellice Islands until
the 1930s and that of the church before being replaced by Tuvaluan in the 1950s.
Until recently, everyone in Tuvalu was proficient in a heavily ‘Tuvaluanized’ form
of Samoan, even though many people had very little contact with native speakers
of Samoan. Samoan was acquired by reading the Samoan translation of the
Scriptures, which also served as the tool for literacy instruction. Today, knowledge
of Samoan is rapidly declining, a process which is likely to accelerate since Tuvaluan
translations of religious materials have now replaced the Samoan texts. (Religious
literature comprises the bulk of reading materials available to most Tuvaluans.)
However, Samoan has left a lasting imprint on the vocabulary, morphology, and
perhaps syntax of the language.
English is the most recent arrival on the Tuvaluan linguistic scene. In the early
years of contact and well into the twentieth century, there was little need for

0.4.2. Typological characteristics
Like most other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan has a basic verb-initial constituent
order, although it differs from most other Polynesian languages (other than Outlier
languages) in that it allows many constituent-order configurations. It is a
prepositional language, in which adjectives follow nouns, relative clauses follow
head nouns, and non-pronominal possessors follow possessed expressions.
Numerals may precede or follow the noun phrase they modify. The language
exhibits a strong bias for clauses consisting of a single noun-phrase constituent.
Various discourse and grammatical strategies enable speakers to encode reference
to a second nominal participant (if needed) without adding another nominal
constituent to the clause. Nominalization is a particularly salient process in terms
of its frequency and broad range of meaning and discourse functions.
Tuvaluan is a zero-pronominalizing language, and both subjects and direct objects
may be zero-pronominalized. Case marking follows an ergative-absolutive pattern.
While many syntactic rules refer to subject and direct-object categories, a significant
number (e.g., relativization, interrogative-word clefting, and case marking in
nominalized clauses) refer to ergative and absolutive categories. The language lacks
a passive and an antipassive. Interrogative-words generally remain in situ, although
a number of them may also appear in clefted positions. Equi-deletion is typologically
unusual in that it may be controlled by and may target both subjects and direct
objects. Raising is even more unusual, in that it may target any noun phrase in
subordinate clauses and mark it for a broad range of cases in the matrix clause. A
rule of advancement-to-possessive, which is also found in other Polynesian
languages, can extract noun phrases with a variety of grammatical functions from
relative clauses and mark them as possessive modifiers of the head noun of the
relative clause. Subject-verb agreement only occurs with some intransitive verbs,
and is marked either with infixed reduplication or by suppletion. When an
intransitive verb that allows agreement is turned into a transitive causative verb,
the causative verb agrees with the derived direct object.
A three-number distinction is marked in the pronoun system, while a simple
singular-plural contrast is encoded in noun-modifying articles. The first-person
inclusive plural pronoun is particularly salient in discourse because it helps
emphasize culturally salient values of solidary and consensus. Tuvaluan is
crosslinguistically unusual in that dual pronouns, rather than plural pronouns, are
used as honorifics. The language has a very large inventory of possessive pronouns,
the form of which is fairly predictable. A contrast is made between alienable and
inalienable possession.

There are relatively few inflectional and derivational morphological processes.
The most common morphophonemic process is reduplication, which may be internal
or external, and which can have both inflectional and derivational functions. External
reduplication may be full or partial, and is a left-to-right process.
Tuvaluan has a small phonemic inventory of fifteen or sixteen phonemes,
depending on the dialect. Only open syllables are allowed. Gemination is phonemic
for both vowels and consonants, and morphophonological patterns of compensatory
lengthening are attested. Geminated consonants may appear in any position where
ungeminated consonants appear, including word-initially. Primary stress always
fall on the penultimate vowel of the word. Intonation varies significantly from one
dialect to the other. One typologically unusual characteristic of the intonational
system is the fact that interrogative-word questions are uttered on the same
intonational contour as yes-no questions.
0.4.3. Previous descriptions
The Tuvaluan language was first mentioned in print in 1846 by Horatio Hale, the
philologist of the United States Exploring Expedition of 1838–42. In his philological
memoir, Hale provides a 120-word list of the Vaitupu dialect of Tuvaluan and the
Fakaofo dialect of Tokelauan, adding that ‘it has seemed superfluous to give separate
vocabularies for the two clusters, the words obtained at both being for the most
part alike’ (H.Hale 1846:357). Several other essays published around the beginning
of the twentieth century provided word lists of varying length and various remarks
on the language (see Besnier 1981a:xxiii–xliv for a bibliography).
There are three more substantial descriptions of the morphology and syntax of
Tuvaluan: Kennedy (1945), a phrasebook-style description of the Vaitupu dialect;
Ranby (1973), which, despite its title (‘Nanumea syntax’), is an overview of the
morphology of the Nanumea dialect; and Besnier (1981b), a pedagogical description
of the Southern dialects, with notes on dialectal variations. There are also four
attempts at lexical description: Ranby (1980), a brief lexicon of the Nanumea dialect;
Besnier (1981a), a preliminary version of a pan-dialectal dictionary currently in
progress; Noricks (1982), a lexicon based on the Niutao dialect with information on
other dialects; and Jackson (1993), a religiously oriented list mostly inspired by
previous publications. More specific aspects of the structure of various dialects
which have been the focus of descriptive work are word order and case marking
(Wang 1976, Finney 1983, Besnier 1986), zero anaphora (Besnier 1985), raising
constructions (Besnier 1988b), reported speech constructions (Besnier 1993b), and
colour terms (K.Chambers 1978). Works in anthropological linguistics and socio-
linguistics have focused on styles of everyday interactions and their socio-political
context and implications (Besnier 1989a, 1989b, 1990a, 1994a, 1994b, 1995b, 1996b)
and stylistic variation across spoken and written contexts (Besnier 1988a, 1991,
1995a).
0.4.4. Organization of the grammar and database
Like others in the series, this grammatical description follows Bernard Comrie and
Norval Smith’s 1977 Lingua descriptive questionnaire. I have chosen to deviate slightly
from the organization set by the questionnaire in cases where certain categories
could be ordered in one fashion according to formal patterns and another according
to function patterns. For example, temporal clauses which are not subordinate
clauses are still ordered under adverbial clauses in the interest of having a unified

characterization of temporality in one place. Whenever such deviations occur, I
provide ample cross-referencing.
This grammar is based partly on traditional grammatical elicitation, partly on
observations of everyday interactions over many years of field work, and partly on
a large database of texts from a wide variety of sources, representing many genres
and styles of speaking and writing. Because many examples cited were unelicited,
and because my purpose here is to provide as faithful a representation of language
structure in use, no effort was made to ‘sanitize’ the examples of sexist overtones
or religious references, although the use of such data should be understood as
implying no endorsement of any kind on my part. I made restricted use of
‘specialized’ genres, such as proverbs and lyrics of dance songs; examples drawn
from such genres are marked accordingly. I also drew as little as possible from
translated materials, despite the fact that the bulk of published writing in Tuvaluan
consists of translations. However, I have occasionally cited such materials because
they illustrate interesting patterns in stylistics or discourse, which are not to be
disregarded since they have become part of the linguistic repertoire of the speech
community. Translated examples are clearly indicated in the text.
While the examples provided herein are all from the Southern dialects
(particularly the Funafuti and Nukulaelae dialects), most of the discussion applies
to all the dialects of the group, not just because of dialect mixing, but because all
seven dialects of the group share essentially the same structure. Dialect differences
in the form of particular morphemes are indicated only for the four Southern dialects.
0.4.5. Orthography
Tuvaluan does not have a standardized orthography, and efforts to develop such a
system have not been successful to date. Most Tuvaluan writers use an orthography
loosely based on the Samoan orthography, which does not consistently mark vowel
length (phonemic in both Tuvaluan and Samoan) or consonant length (phonemic
in Tuvaluan only). Occasionally, vowel length is indicated with a macron or by
reduplicating the vowel symbol. Consonant length is sometimes indicated with an
apostrophe either preceding or following the consonant symbol, or even by
reduplicating the vowel symbol that follows the geminated consonant. Usually,
the grapheme g stands for a velar nasal, although older writers sometimes use ng.
For a fuller discussion of the various orthographic systems in use and of the politics
of standardization, the reader is referred to Besnier (1995a: xiii–xx).
The orthography used throughout this book is strictly phonemic. Vowel and
consonant gemination is marked with double letters. In the one instance where the
gemination of/t/is predictable (cf. 2.1.1.10), it is not indicated. The orthography
marks certain allomorphic variations but not others. Briefly, allomorphic variations
that consist in phonologically predictable vowel or consonant gemination are not
indicated. Allomorphic variations that consist in gemination processes conditioned
by factors other than phonology, and allomorphic variations that result in segment
alterations (be they conditioned by phonological or other factors) are indicated.
Whenever relevant, these orthographic conventions are indicated in the discussion.
When examples from other languages are cited, the orthographic conventions
follow the system used in the most accessible reference source (e.g., Milner 1966 for
Samoan and Churchward 1959 for Tongan). The orthography of Proto-Polynesian
reconstructions cited in the text is the more or less standardized system followed
by Biggs (1979) and subsequent versions of the Polynesian historical reconstruction
project at the University of Auckland (POLLEX), where *q is a glottal stop and all
other letters have their approximate IPA value.

Syntax
1.1. GENERAL FEATURES
1.1.1. Sentence-types
1.1.1.1. Direct speech and quoted speech
In Tuvaluan, quoted (or reported) speech is framed with the help of a number of
lexical and prosodic devices. These devices mark a particular stretch of discourse
as a quote in contrast to the rest of the discourse. Taken out of its discourse context,
a quoted string is indistinguishable from a nonquoted string. No lexical marker or
prosodic pattern is used exclusively to mark quoted speech.
Like many other languages, Tuvaluan has two different quoted-speech styles:
one is associated with speech purported to reproduce the exact wording of another
utterance (i.e., directly quoted speech); the other is associated with speech purported
to reproduce an earlier utterance, but which is structurally modified so that it
becomes syntactically part of the structure of the quoting context (i.e., indirectly
quoted speech).
(a) Transitions between direct speech and quoted speech Both indirectly quoted
speech and directly quoted speech are typically introduced by a speech-act verb or

(1)
Koo fai mai a Palu, “A moolii koo oti ne taamate.”

Pronominal deixis and demonstrative deixis are sensitive to transitions from

(b) Directly and indirectly quoted speech
A structural distinction is generally made between direct and indirect
quotation. However, in discourse, not all instances of direct quotation exhibit
all the features associated with directly quoted discourse; and not all indirectly
quoted discourse is marked as such. The characteristics of directly and
indirectly quoted speech described in this section are tendencies, rather than
absolute distinctions.
In informal conversation and narration, directly quoted speech is clearly
preferred over indirectly quoted speech. Indirectly quoted speech is primarily used
to express a quotation within another quotation, or to quote a communicative act
which the reporter did not witness. Furthermore, indirect quotations most
commonly consist of one-sentence, one-turn quotes; for quoted discourse that
consists of more than one sentence or turn, directly quoted speech is used.
A directly quoted string is not linked to the nonquoted discourse environment
by any subordinating or coordinating device; it is simply apposed to the non-quoted
discourse that precedes it. In contrast, an indirectly quoted string is syntactically
incorporated into the nonquoted discourse, and this is often marked
morphologically with the help of one of a number of subordinating conjunctions
described in 1.1.2.2.3, 1.1.2.2.4, and 1.1.2.2.5, the choice of which is dictated by the
type of speech act being quoted:

(c) Quoted thought
The strategies described in the previous two sections also apply to quoted thought.
The same speech-act verbs are used in the reporting of thoughts as in the reporting
of utterances, with the addition of such verbs as maafaufau ‘think’, leaka or leake
‘stuck with the idea’ (cf. 2.1.3.6.10), vvali, with the same meaning, and a metaphorical
use of the verb nofo ‘stay’ with approximately the same meaning as leaka and vvali:
(25)
Au ne vvali loa i te kelo teelaa se Ppaalagi!
I Pst stuck-with-idea indeed Cmp the blond that a Westerner
‘I would have sworn that that blond guy was a Westerner!’
There are two major differences between quoted speech and quoted thought, both
of which are tendencies rather than absolute differences. First, indirect constructions
are much more common than direct constructions in thought reporting, while the
opposite distribution applies to speech reporting. Second, linguistic action verbs
that denote thoughts are usually modified by one of the three manner demonstrative
adverbs peenei, peenaa, and peelaa ‘thus’ (cf. 2.1.2.5(d)):
(26)
Au koo maafaufau peenei, kaafai laa koo mmate koulua, kae tuumau
I Inc think thus if then Inc die you-2 but constant
te faiga teenei e llei maatou i ei.
the way this Nps good we-e-3 in Anp
‘I feel that, even after you die, the rest of us will maintain the positive
relationship that we have been enjoying.’
While these adverbs are frequent in quoted-thought constructions, their presence
is neither necessary nor sufficient for the quoted string to be interpreted as quoted
thought, since they can also appear in quoted speech constructions (cf. (a) above).
1.1.1.2. Interrogative sentences
All interrogative sentences have one characteristic in common: they are uttered on

questions, the interrogative word may remain in situ, may be moved to a preverbal
position, may be moved to a clause-initial position, or may take the form of an
equational construction. Different interrogative words vary in terms of which of
these various choices they allow.
1.1.1.2.1. Yes-no questions
1.1.1.2.1.1. Neutral yes-no questions The syntactic structure of neutral yes-no
questions is the same as that of affirmative sentences. The order of the sentential
constituents follows the same patterns, and there is no special morphological
marking on any element of the clause. For example, the following interrogative
and affirmative equivalents have exactly the same morphosyntactic structure:
(27)
E ola?
Nps alive
‘Is [it] alive?’
(28)
E ola.
Nps alive
‘[It] is alive.’
Neutral yes-no questions are distinguished from affirmative sentences through
intonation. The intonational pattern associated with neutral yes-no questions is a
steady downward contour that rises sharply on the last stressed syllable:

Affirmative sentences are never uttered with such intonational contours (cf. 3.3.4).
1.1.1.2.1.2. Leading yes-no questions Leading or biased yes-no questions are
questions in which the questioner expects a particular answer, be it affirmative or
negative (Moravcsik 1971). In Tuvaluan, they are commonly marked with the
sentence-final tag-question marker inee or nee, whether an affirmative or a negative
answer is expected. (According to some native speakers, the two forms may have
originally been dialectal variants of one another, but today both forms are used in
all dialects.) The tag-question marker is always placed at the end of the sentence.
The sentence itself has the intonation of a declarative sentence; the tag-question
marker is usually separated from the rest of the sentence by a short pause and
uttered on a significantly higher pitch level than the rest of the sentence:

‘It is a good thing that they haven’t surveyed it yet, don’t you think?’

1.1.1.2.2. Interrogative-word questions
This section covers the following two topics: the range of elements of the sentence
that can be questioned (1.1.1.2.2.1); and the behaviour of the questioned element
(1.1.1.2.2.2). For a discussion of interrogative-word questions used as exclamations
and hedges, see 1.1.1.5(b) and (d) respectively.
1.1.1.2.2.1. Elements of the sentence that can be questioned All constituents of all
clause types can be questioned, with two exceptions. First, no interrogative word
can function as a transitive verb. (Of course, any element of a transitive sentence
other than the verb can be questioned.) Second, topicalized constituents cannot be
questioned. The restriction that a topic may not be questioned may be explained
functionally: since a topicalized constituent denotes, by definition, given
information, and since interrogative-word questions are requests for new
information, they are pragmatically incompatible.

Since interrogative words do not form a separate word class, but instead behave
like the verbs, nouns, adverbs, and adjectives of which they are anaphoric (cf.
2.1.2.6), their behaviour is not distinguishable from these other categories. For
example, since all subordinating conjunctions can be followed by either a noun

subordinating conjunctions and nominal and verbal interrogative words. Thus
elements that normally appear next to a subordinating conjunction can be
questioned. Of course, the restrictions on the juxtaposition of certain subordinating
conjunctions (namely o and kee) and noun phrases (cf. 1.1.2.1.1–2) also apply to
nominal interrogative words.
Similarly, the syntactic behaviour of nominalized clauses is essentially the same

1.1.1.2.2.1.5. Interrogative-word questions and coordination All elements of nominal
and sentential coordinate structures can be questioned. In both cases, some
restrictions are imposed on the order of the coordinated elements.
 
(a) Sentence coordination
A statement and an interrogative-word question may be coordinated to one another
with the additive-adversative sentence coordinator kae ‘and, but’ (cf. 1.3.1.1). The
interrogative word may bear on one of the coordinated clauses, as in the first of the
following examples, or on any constituent of any one of the coordinated clauses:
(87)
Koulua ne olo kae aa?
you-2 Pst go and what?
‘You left and [then] what [happened]?’
(88)
Koulua ne olo ki uta kae se aa taulua fekau ne fai ei?
you-2 Pst go to bush but a what? your-2 business Pst do Anp
‘You two went to the bush, but what business did you attend to there?’
The most natural order is for the clause containing the interrogative word to follow
all other clauses in the coordinate structure. But in echo questions the interrogative
word occurs in the position of the element to be clarified in the answer:
(89)
A: Maalia ne puke nee Ioane, kae ko Moapi ne puke nee Ieelemia.

‘Ioane adopted Malia, while Ielemia adopted Moapi.’
B: Maalia ne aa kae ko Moapi ne puke nee Ieelemia?
Maalia Pst what? and Foc Moapi Pst adopt Erg Ieelemia
‘Who adopted Maalia, while Ieelemia adopted Moapi?’

1.1.1.2.2.2. Behaviour of questioned elements Different interrogative words call
for different syntactic constructions. Generally speaking, the range of syntactic
positions allowed for each particular interrogative word parallels the range of
positions accessible to lexical elements that fall into the same morphological category
as the interrogative word. (As discussed in 2.1.2.6, interrogative words are not
formally distinguishable from members of the morphological category of which
they are anaphoric.) For example, verbal interrogative words must remain in situ
because there is no verb-movement rule; in contrast, nominal interrogative words
can either occur in situ or be clefted, because noun phrases can be clefted. Table 1.1
summarizes the range of constructions accessible for each interrogative-word
question construction.
The English glosses assigned to interrogative words in this table and in the rest
of this section are approximative. For a discussion of the morphological and semantic
characteristics of each individual interrogative word, see 2.1.2.6; for a discussion of
interrogative-word question intonation, see 3.3.4.
Interrogative-word question constructions with in situ interrogative words are
discussed under (a) in the following discussion; (b) covers interrogative-word
clefting; clause-initial and clause-final interrogative words are discussed in (c); and
preverbal interrogative words in (d). The factors that determine the choice between
these various structures are described in (e).

(a) In situ interrogative words
All interrogative words may be left in the position of the constituents they question

[lit.: ‘How is it to be done?’]

1.1.1.2.2.1.1), and thus unmarked sentence-initial (topicalized) interrogative words

whose position they occupy. With a few minor exceptions (cf. 2.1.2.6), in situ

tense-aspect markers, and may be modified by any semantically and
morphologically appropriate modifier, like adjectives and adverbs.

Three interrogative word stems may be used predicatively in verbless equational
structures: the nominal interrogative word ai ‘who’, the nominal interrogative word
aa ‘what’, and the adjectival interrogative word fea ‘which’. When ai is used as
such, it is obligatorily ko-focused and takes the form kooi (cf. 2.1.2.6.1):
(115)
Kooi ttino naa?
Foc+who? the+person that
‘Who is that person?’
When aa ‘what’ occurs in equational constructions, it must be modified by an article,
most commonly an indefinite article (cf. 2.1.2.6.2(a)):
(116)
Ne aa au ika naa?
some what? your fish those
‘What [kind of] fish do you have there?’
When fea ‘which’ occurs in equational constructions, it must take the form teefea if
it refers to a singular entity or kofea if it refers to a plural entity (cf. 2.1.2.6.3(b)):
(117)
Tou faasselu teefea?
your comb where?
‘Where is your comb?’
(118)
Ou taka kofea?
your sandal where?
‘Where are your sandals?’
When there is no clear choice of a noun phrase for the second slot in the equational
construction (i.e. the slot which the interrogative word is equated with), a noun
with little or no referential loading is used, most commonly tino ‘person’ (with kooi

as a compound with the interrogative word:
(119)
Kooi ttino?
Foc+who? the+person
‘Who is it?’
(120)
Ne aa igoa?

‘What is it?’

(cf. (b) below) and when interrogative words are used as sentence fragments (cf.
2.1.2.6). Thus, in discourse, the interrogative word aa is frequently followed by mea
or igoa, and kooi by tino.2

Two nominal and one adjectival interrogative words may be found in constructions

a what? the thing Nps wish you to Anp

This last option yields the only headless relative clauses that occur with any

The analysis of clefted interrogative words as equational clauses with an embedded
relative clause is supported by six morphosyntactic parallelisms between equational
structures and the clefted interrogative-word construction on the one hand, and
between the second half of clefted constructions and relative-clause structures on
the other. First, interrogative-word clefted constructions and interrogative-word
equational constructions have the same basic morphosyntactic structure. For
example, interrogative words take the same form in both constructions, and both
constructions are available to the same interrogative words. Second, the ordering
of the interrogative word and the rest of the construction is free in clefted
constructions (although the interrogative word is commonly clause-initial). This
free ordering is also characteristic of equational structures (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)). (Because
of the tendency for the interrogative word to come first, the other half of these
constructions will hereafter be referred to as ‘the second half’ of the construction.)
Third, the second half of a clefted construction has the same morphosyntactic
structure as a relative clause. Thus the extracted noun is indexed in the rest of the
equational construction in the same way as the head noun is indexed in a relative
clause (cf. 1.1.2.3.4). Fourth, the extracted noun in the second half of a clefted
interrogative-word construction is modified by a relative pronoun (teenei, teenaa,
or teelaa, and plural equivalents). That these pronouns are relative pronouns, and
not demonstrative pronouns (which are homophonous with relative pronouns), is
evidenced by the fact that a second demonstrative may modify the extracted noun.
Elsewhere in the structure of the language, ‘double’ demonstratives are only found
as modifiers of the head of a relative clause (which justifies treating the second
demonstrative form as a relative pronoun and not a true demonstrative pronoun;
cf. 2.1.2.7.1).
Fifth, the second half of clefted constructions can undergo advancement-to-
possessive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10), as long as the extracted noun is a common noun (i.e.
advancement-to-possessive cannot take place if the extracted noun is a pronoun, a
proper noun, a relative pronoun, or a zero form). Elsewhere in the language,
advancement-to-possessive is confined to relative clause structures (cf. 1.1.2.3.10).
Finally, both interrogative-word clefting and relative-clause formation are
unbounded, i.e., they can target positions that are multiply embedded in subordinate
clauses (see 1.1.1.2.2.1.2 for examples).

On the basis of these six arguments, interrogative-word clefted constructions can be
treated as equational constructions in which an interrogative word is equated with a
noun phrase consisting of a relative clause modifying an overt or zero head noun.
Comparable analyses of interrogative-word questions have been proposed for at least
two other Polynesian languages, Niuean (Seiter 1980:106–115) and Maori (Bauer 1991),
and, further afield, for Palauan, a Western Austronesian language of Micronesia
(Georgopoulos 1991:140–181). The phenomenon is likely to be areally widespread.
In Tuvaluan, clefted interrogative-word constructions differ from equational
constructions with a relative clause in two ways: the embedded relative clause can
have an empty head, and reordering of the equated noun phrases is allowed only
if the relative clause is not headless. With ordinary relative clauses, empty heads
are generally not allowed (cf. 1.1.1.2.3.6); and there is no syntactic restriction on the
reordering of noun phrases in regular equational constructions.
Interrogative-word clefting is optional. If the in situ interrogative word is in the
absolutive case, there is a clear textual preference for the clefting strategy over the in
situ strategy. So the first of the following alternatives is preferred over the second one:
(142)
Kooi ttino koo uaa mai?
Foc+who? the+person Inc noisy Dxs
‘Who is making a noise?’
(143)
Koo uaa mai a ai?
Inc noisy Dxs Cnt who?
‘Who is making a noise?’
In all other cases, no clear pattern of textual preference is discernible.
(c)
Movement to clause-initial or clause-final position
 
The adverbial interrogative words anafea ‘when’ (past), maafea and kaafea ‘when’
(future), and aafea ‘when’ (past or future), certain prepositionally marked occurrences
of fea ‘where’, and kaiaa ‘why’ (and its allomorphs maiaa and aiaa) may be moved to
clause-initial positions. They all leave an obligatory anaphoric pronoun ei (cf.
2.1.2.1.7), which must be verb-incorporated:
(144)
Anafea koutou ne oko mai ei?
when? you-3 Pst reach Dxs Anp
‘When did you get here?’
(145)
Maafea koutou e olo ei?
when? you-3 Nps go Anp
‘When are you leaving?’
(146)
Kaiaa koe seki fano ei?
why? you Neg go why?
‘Why didn’t you go?’
An analysis of these interrogative words as being in clause-initial position, rather
than in preverbal position, is supported by the fact that, for the three temporal
interrogative words at least, nominal arguments of the verb cannot precede the
interrogative word (this test does not work for kaiaa because it can also occur in
preverbal position; cf. (d)):
(147)

you-3 when? Nps go Anp
(‘When are you leaving?’)

the locative preposition i, the directional preposition ki, or the source preposition
mai (distant source). If it moves to a clause-initial position, the preposition moves
with it and it leaves an anaphoric trace, which may be marked by a preposition or
verb-incorporated:
(150)

(151)

(152)

interrogative word remains in situ:
(153)

are stylistically marked as characteristic of rhetorical styles.
The adverbial interrogative word kaiaa ‘why’ (and its allomorphs maiaa and aiaa)
may be found in sentence-final position:
(156)

and Inc Neg go then you why?
‘And you, why is it that you are not going any more?’
Movement to this position is best described as right dislocation, since the
interrogative word is commonly separated from the rest of the sentence by a very
brief pause and a break in intonational contour (usually a rise in pitch), and since
the rest of the sentence does not have the prosodic characteristics of a complete
intonational unit.

(d) Movement to preverbal position
The adverbial interrogative word kaiaa ‘why’ (and its allomorphs maiaa and aiaa) is
the only interrogative word that may occur in preverbal position. It leaves an
obligatory anaphoric pronoun ei (cf. 2.1.2.1.7), which is frequently, but not
obligatorily, verb-incorporated:
(157)

This is the most common position for kaiaa and its allomorphs.
(e) Factors governing interrogative-word constructions
In seeking an answer to the question of what determines the position of interrogative
words in discourse, one must first recognize that a choice in position exists for a
very restricted number of interrogative words. Of the different interrogative-word
usages listed in Table 1.1, only a handful can appear in a position other than in situ.
Furthermore, in discourse, questions are typically sentence fragments, particularly
in informal spoken styles. The following exchange illustrates typical conversational
uses of interrogative words; the first two questions are part of a clarification sequence
triggered by ‘information withholding’ (Besnier 1989a), while the third is a request
for an elaboration of the original utterance:

partly by information-structure concerns. Briefly, there is an overwhelming tendency

1.1.1.2.3. Echo questions
Echo questions are requests for a clarification or verification of a previous utterance.
The previous utterance is called the stimulus of the echo construction (McCawley
1987). Various echo-question types occur in Tuvaluan, and they have the same
structure as regular questions. For example, yes-no echo questions are
indistinguishable from regular echo questions, and both positive and negative yes-
no echo questions are encountered:
(163)
K: Au see fia fano ki te fakaala.
I Neg want go to the feast
‘I don’t want to go to the feast.’
S: Koe see fia fano ki te fakaala?
you Neg want go to the feast
‘You don’t want to go to the feast?’
Structurally, a yes-no echo question is a replica or a close paraphrase of its stimulus,
except for the fact that pronominal deixis is adjusted to the change in speaker (as in
the above two examples), and for the fact that the echo question is uttered with a
rising intonational contour comparable to that of regular yes-no questions. Yes-no
echo questions are frequently used as indirect speech acts, i.e., not as a request for
clarification, but as the acknowledgement of the stimulus (see 1.1.1.5.3 for the use
of regular questions with comparable affective functions). Frequently, they open
the floor for the interlocutor to elaborate on the stimulus.
Interrogative-word echo questions of all types occur, and all elements of a
sentence that can be questioned can also be echo-questioned. Thus, for example,
the statement
(164)
Maalia ne puke nee Ioane.
Malia Pst adopt Erg Ioane
‘Ioane adopted Malia.’
may be echo-questioned with any of the following:
(165)
Maalia ne aa?
Malia Pst what?
‘What happened to Malia?’
(166)
Maalia ne puke nee ei?
Malia Pst adopt Erg who?
‘Who adopted Malia?’
(167)
Ioane ne puke a ai?
Ioane Pst adopt Cnt who?
‘Who did Ioane adopt?’
The interrogative word in echo questions is always left in situ. The same restrictions
apply to the structure of interrogative-word echo questions as to regular
interrogative-word questions. For example, the last example in the above set differs
in its basic structure from the original utterance because the echo-questioned element
occurs clause-initially in the original utterance, and unmarked interrogative words
cannot occur clause-initially (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2). Interrogative-word echo questions may

1.1.1.2.4. Answers
1.1.1.2.4.1. Answers as distinct speech acts Answers to questions are not
formally marked in any manner that distinguishes them from other speech
acts. However, the grammatical structure of a question often calls for a parallel
structure in the answer. For example, when a nominal interrogative word is
ko-clefted in an interrogative-word question (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)), there is a strong
tendency for the noun phrase that provides the information requested to be
ko-clefted as well:
(171)
F: Kooi ttino e saasaale i te auala?

‘Who is that (person) walking on the path?’

Foc Paka
‘It’s Paka.’
This pattern is only a statistical tendency, and deviations from the pattern are
attested. For example, when an interrogative-word question has the structure of an
equational construction and the interrogative word is a nominal predicate (cf.
1.1.1.2.2.2(a)), a different pattern obtains in the answer. There, the information
already specified in the question is commonly placed in clause-initial position:

1.1.1.3.1. Positive imperatives
The imperative mood for second-person imperatives is formed by deleting
obligatorily the tense-aspect-mood marker and any clause-bound preposed
constituent (cf. 2.1.3.4.3). The subject noun phrase can also be optionally deleted
from the clause. The same rule applies to intransitive and transitive clauses:
(186)
Fano (koe) kkoo!

‘Go over there, you!’
(187)
Fakalaalaa (nee koulua) oulua taliga!
Cst+open Erg you-2 your-2 ear
‘Listen carefully, (you two)!’
[lit.: ‘Open up your ears!’]
(188)
Olo (koutou) keaattea mo toku liisi!

‘Get off of my (leased) land, (you all)!’
The subject of a verb in the imperative mood appears in postverbal position when its referent
is emphasized. Other types of imperatives allow the subject of the clause to appear in other
positions (cf. 1.1.1.3.3). While tense-aspect-mood markers and clause-bound preverbal
constituents cannot appear in simple imperative clauses, preverbal adverbs can:
(189)
Toe lligi!

‘Pour [some more] again!’
So can left-dislocated noun phrases and adverbs:
(190)
Te uka teelaa, fakasolo atu!

‘That fishing line, uncoil it!’
(191)
Tino kolaa e seeai selotou taliaga, olo ki tua!

‘Those people that don’t have a pass, get out!’

boundaries of the clause differently from left-dislocated noun phrases, and can
serve as a test to distinguish between the two categories (cf. 1.11.2.1.6). Imperative

(192)

Imperative formation optionally deletes subjects of intransitive or transitive verbs,
but does not affect direct objects. (Of course, direct objects can be deleted from
imperative clauses by zero pronominalization, independently of imperative
formation.) Thus imperative formation targets subjects of intransitive and transitive
verbs as a single category, in contrast to direct objects, and provides evidence for
the nominative-accusative basis of Tuvaluan syntax.
The presence of a subject in postverbal position is less peremptory than its
absence. Thus, the first of the following examples is slightly more polite than the
second:
(193)
Vau!
come
‘Come [here]!’
(194)
Vau koe!
come you
‘[Why don’t] you come [here]!’
With certain verbs, there is a strong tendency to change the case marking of the
subject of transitive verbs from the ergative nee to the alienable benefactive maa in

which this change can take place). Compare the transitive imperative in the first
example below with the equivalent declarative in the second example:
(195)
Kai maa koe ika mo uttanu kolaa!

‘Have some of that fish and germinated coconut!’
(196)
Ne kai nee koe ika mo uttanu kolaa.

‘You had some of that fish and germinated coconut.’
While ergatively-marked imperative subjects are not ungrammatical, they are less
idiomatic than benefactively marked subjects. Direct objects retain their absolutive

Canonical imperative structures do not occur as dependent clauses in complex

used (cf. 1.1.1.3.3(a)). Occasionally, imperative structures do occur in environments

(197)

the imperative clauses.

Commands other than commands directed at small children or uttered in anger
are modified by at least one downtoner, usually aka if only one appears in the
sentence. An unmodified imperative is judged to be inappropriately peremptory
in most interactional contexts between adults. The downtoner laa (cf. 2.1.3.4.8) is
frequently used in addition to or instead of other moderating adverbs; when it is
used alone, it is less polite than aka or mua, but less peremptory than unmodified
imperatives:
(200)
Vau laa!

‘[Why don’t you] come [here]?’
The preverbal downtoner naa appears only in imperative sentences. It gives to the
command the connotation of a gentle coaxing, and frequently cooccurs with the
postverbal downtoner laa:
(201)
Naa fano laa o koukou i te mea koo poo!

combination with one another; all possible configurations of two, three, and four
adverbs are allowed. The relative ordering of aka and mua is free, but laa always
follows aka and mua:
(202)

‘[Could you possibly] come this way?’

all-purpose negator see (cf. 1.1.1.3.2 and 1.4(a)). All four adverbs can appear in other
(noncanonical) imperative constructions (cf. 1.1.1.3.3) and indirectly quoted
commands (cf. 1.1.2.2.5).

Most characteristics of second-person positive imperatives described in 1.1.1.3.1
also apply to negative imperatives. The differences between second-person negative
imperatives and equivalent positive imperatives is that the verb of the clause in the
former is marked with the imperative negator saa (or haa in the Nukulaelae dialect),

the first-person inclusive pronoun forms taa (dual) and ttou (plural), which are

1.1.1.3.3. Other means of expressing imperatives
Besides the imperative mood, a number of strategies can be exploited to express
positive and negative commands. There are also two special pronominal forms
associated exclusively with imperatives, described in 2.1.2.1.1.5.
 
(a) Subjunctive imperatives
The subjunctive mood (cf. 2.1.3.4.4, 2.1.3.4.6, and 2.1.3.4.7) can express commands

like a tense-aspect-mood marker:

(b) Statement imperatives
Commands and suggestions can be expressed with the help of constructions that
are structurally indistinguishable from equivalent declarative clauses:
(219)
Kaa fano koe ki te umaga, koo taa mai ei nee koe

(221)
Koutou e olo o nnofo i koo i tai.

‘Go and stay over there on the lagoon side!’
Statement imperatives are frequently uttered on a slightly more animated
intonational contour than the equivalent statements. They are usually (but not
obligatorily) marked for future tense with kaa (cf. 2.1.3.2.1.4), and can serve as
expressions of commands for all persons and numbers.
Related to the above pattern are imperatives which consist of two and-coordinated
clauses, the second of which describes an undesirable situation which will take
place if the situation described by the first clause takes place. Such utterances, which
have been described in other languages as having the structure of conditionals
(Lawler 1975, Van der Auwera 1986), are particularly peremptory:
(222)
Toe tasi te pati maasei, koo maalaia ei koe!

‘One more swear word and you’ll be sorry!’
[lit.: ‘One more bad word, you’ll then be doomed!’]
Any sentence-coordination strategy can be used in such indirect speech acts.
However, unmarked apposition (with or without the anaphoric ei), illustrated by
the above example, is by far the most common, perhaps because it communicates
an immediacy that reinforces the peremptoriness of the speech act. Or-coordinated

(c) Negative imperatives with oti ‘finished’
A special category of statement imperative is formed with the stative verb oti
‘finished’. The oti-imperative construction is positive in morphosyntax but negative
in meaning: it is used as a command for the interlocutor to put a stop to a particular
situation over which he or she has some degree of control. Oti-imperatives are
third-person constructions, in that the intransitive verb oti takes as subject a
nominalized verb that denotes the situation that should be ended:
(223)
Oti te tagi!

‘Enough of [your] crying!’
(224)
Naa oti mua aka laa tou ppai!
please finished please please then your insolent
‘Would [you] please stop being so insolent?’
These imperatives are very peremptory. When downtoning adverbs are used with
oti-imperatives, as in the last example above, it is usually done ironically.
(d) Negative imperatives with tapu ‘forbidden, sacred’
As described in 1.4.7(e), the verb tapu ‘forbidden, sacred’ can be used as an inherently
negative verb for all moods. Because it usually carries a strongly negative attitudinal
connotation, it is particularly well suited to express negative peremptory commands:
(225)

maneaba.’3

The verb form olo, which is the suppletive dual and plural form of fano ‘go’, takes
the form alo when it is preceded by the string taa kaa, where taa is the special
imperative form of the first-person dual personal pronoun and kaa is the future-
tense marker. The change is clearly phonologically conditioned, but this is the only
context where the form alo is attested, and the only context where such a
phonological change applies:
(226)
Taa kaa alo!
we-2-i Fut go
‘Let’s go!’

1.1.1.5. Indirect speech acts
The following discussion is by no means exhaustive, since, as discussed by Sadock
and Zwicky (1985:191–193), any sentence type can be used to achieve the
illocutionary force of any other type, a remark that probably holds for all languages.
For example, the utterance
(233)
Ee ttamaa! Koo ttoo te vaiua!
Voc the+child+Spc Inc fall the rain
‘Hey, you! It’s starting to rain!’
can have a variety of illocutionary meanings depending on the social role of the
addressee and many other aspects of the situation: addressed to a young child, it

can serve as an advice that the addressee seek shelter; addressed to a young woman,
it is a request that the addressee bring in drying laundry or salted fish, or to pull
down the woven coconut-frond screens that serve as the walls of houses; and so
forth. Indirect speech acts vary in terms of the degree to which and the way in
which they are conventionalized. This section covers only some of the more salient
conventionalized indirect speech acts, salient in terms of either their overall
frequency or their sociocultural prominence.
Various examples of indirect speech acts are discussed elsewhere in this grammar:
for the use of alternative questions to express uncertainty, see 1.1.1.2.1.3; for the use
of yes-no echo questions in acknowledging an interlocutor’s utterance, see 1.1.1.2.3;
for the use of the interrogative word fragment e aa ‘what?’ as a preannouncement,
see 2.1.2.6.2(a).
 
(a) Questions as requests, commands, and suggestions
Various question structures can be used in place of imperatives to make requests, express
commands, and offer suggestions. For example, a speaker can ask to borrow an object
by asking the prospective lender whether he or she is the owner of the object:
(234)
Tau takuu e isi?
your adze Nps exist
‘Do you have an adze [I could borrow]?’
Or the question can bear on the nature of the object:
(235)
Tau mea naa se masiasi?
your thing that a match-box
‘Can you pass me your match-box?’
[lit.: ‘Is that thing of yours a match-box?’]
Suggestions may take the form of a questioned conditional comparable to a
construction with ‘what if’ in English:
(236)
Kae aa maa tuku mua aka nee taatou te mataaupu teenaa
and what? if leave please please Erg we-3-i the question that
kee onoono atu taatou i ei fakamuli?

‘What if we leave this question [aside] so that we can come back to it
later?’

(237)
E talia nee koulua kee toe fono taatou fakavave kee fai

‘Are you [willing to] agree to meet again quickly so we can come to
some [sort of] conclusion about this matter?’
Questions about the ability on the part of the interlocutor to perform an action
(e.g., English ‘Can you pass the salt?’) do not have the status of conventionalized
indirect requests in Tuvaluan.

(241)

(c) Declarative and question structures in phatic interactions
Phatic interaction (e.g., greeting and leave-taking) is particularly rich in
conventionalized indirect speech acts. In phatic contexts, verbal interaction is in
large part formulaic, in the sense that the general gist of what is said is predictable,
although the exact form of utterances can vary. Generally speaking, two principles
are at work in such contexts: ‘show concern for the activities of others’, and ‘do not
call attention to yourself’. Underlying the first principle are phatic questions of
concern uttered when meeting or parting company with another person. For
example, when meeting someone on a path in the bush, one asks a question of the
following types:
(243)
E aa koe naa?
Nps what? you that
‘What are you up to?’

These questions are answered as if they were genuine inquiries. Interactions that
take place during leave-taking provide examples of the second principle. When
leaving a group of people, individuals are expected to announce that they are
leaving, and, for maximal politeness, sometimes provide a reason for their move or

(245)

1.1.2. Subordination
Crosslinguistically, three types of subordinate clauses are commonly
identified: (1) noun clauses (or complements), the clausal equivalent of noun
phrases; (2) adverb clauses, which share many grammatical characteristics with
adverbial phrases; and (3) relative clauses (or adjective clauses), which are noun
modifiers (Thompson and Longacre 1985:172). In Tuvaluan, the structures of
noun and adverb clauses share many characteristics. Several general patterns
of subordinate constructions can be identified, whose functions resemble the
functions of both noun clauses and adverb clauses in other languages. The
syntax of these general patterns is described in 1.1.2.1, while their function is
overviewed in 1.1.2.2 and 1.1.2.4. In terms of their formal characteristics,

other languages are associated with relative clauses in Tuvaluan.

relative clause, is described in 1.1.2.3.10. Equi-deletion and noun-phrase

1.1.2.1. General markers of subordination
Following is a description of the morphosyntactic characteristics of the six major
subordination types associated with both noun clauses and adverb clauses. The
choices in subordinate construction is determined primarily by the verb of the matrix
clause. In cases where matrix verbs can take more than one subordinate-clause
type, the different constructions carry different meanings or connotations.
The functional characteristics of the subordination types described here are
covered in 1.1.2.2 and 1.1.2.4. These sections also cover other types of subordinate
clauses, whose functional distribution is less broad than the following six types.
No syntactic or morphological feature is shared by all subordinate-clause types.
Indeed, the different types are quite disparate in structure. However, it is
noteworthy that several subordinate-clause types require that the subordinate
clause be verb-initial.
1.1.2.1.1. o-subordination
The subordinator o is used in a semantically eclectic range of subordinate
constructions, which nevertheless share a number of syntactic properties. Like other
subordinate constructions with a ‘tight’ hypotactic bond with their superordinate
clause, o-subordinate clauses always follow the superordinate clause they modify:

fakafenua].

‘We can take a look at [the principles that] island communities are based
upon.’
(256)

luga i taapola [o fai peelaa me ne kaiao].

coconuts inside coconut-leaf woven baskets and make it look like it

aspect marker. However, eligible intransitive verbs of o-subordinate clauses agree
in number with their subjects. Verbs in o-subordinate clauses can also be modified
by any preposed or postposed verb-modifying adverb and can be suffixed with a
transitive suffix:
(257)

1.1.2.1.2. kee-subordination
A subordinate clause introduced by the subjunctive subordinating conjunction kee
always follows the superordinate clause it modifies. Like o-subordinate clauses,
kee-subordinate clauses are nonfinite insofar as they allow no tense-aspect marker.
However, as with o-subordination again, eligible intransitive verbs of kee-
subordinate clauses agree in number with their subject:
(266)
Koo vau ia mo tena ika [kee kilokkilo taatou ki ei].

‘He is bringing his fish so we can take a look at it.’

olo laaua mo Kaitu]]].

should stay [here] so that he can come over so that he and Kaitu can go.’
Like o, kee can only be followed by a noun phrase if that noun phrase is part of a
subordinate equational construction. In all other cases, kee must be followed by the
verb of the subordinate clause or a preposed adverbial modifier of the verb of the
subordinate clause. However, a to-focused noun phrase can be moved to a position
preceding the conjunction kee:
(268)

‘Iaakopo ordered me to work again.’
Kee can also function as an imperative marker in simple clauses (see 1.1.1.3.3(a) for
further discussion).
O-subordination and kee-subordination share structural and semantic similarities,
and most verbs that can take o-subordinate complements can also take kee-
subordinate complements. However, there are three major differences between the
two types of subordinate clauses, which determine the choice between one or the
other in particular contexts.
(a)
When it is used as a subordinator, kee commonly implies that the primary
purpose of the situation denoted by the superordinate clause is to enable the
situation denoted by the subordinate clause to take place, or at least that the
situation denoted by the subordinate clause is contingent in one way or another
on the situation denoted by the superordinate clause:
(269)
Ne aumai nee Logo a uttanu kolaa [kee kai nee au].
Pst bring Erg Logo Cnt germinated-coconut those Sbj eat Erg I
‘Logo brought those germinated coconuts so that I could eat them.’
With o, there is no such implication. The use of o-subordination denotes
that the situations denoted by the superordinate and subordinate clauses
are temporally ordered, if the meaning of the two verbs allow such a
temporal ordering. Compare the previous example with the following:
(270)

‘Logo brought those germinated coconuts and I ate them.’

1.1.2.1.4. i-subordination
A fourth type of subordinate clause that straddles several functional categories is
associated with the subordinating morpheme i, which is homophonous and in many
ways resembles the locative preposition i. For example, when it is followed by a
personal pronoun, the subordinator takes on the form iaa or ia, following the same
patterns as the locative preposition (cf. 2.1.5.2).
(288)

‘I know that you are a Westerner.’

subordinator i is always immediately followed by a noun phrase, which may not
be marked with any other preposition or case marker (in particular, it may not be
ko-focused or ko-predicated). At first glance, i-subordinate clauses resemble
prepositional modifiers of the superordinate clauses; however, they have all
properties associated with finite clauses, and thus must be treated as subordinate
clauses.

1.1.2.1.5. Subordination by apposition
The last complementation strategy, which is associated with a restricted number of
structures, consists in apposing paratactically the subordinate clause to the
superordinate clause:

‘The fishing rods are broken from being handled carelessly by the
children.’
(291)

‘We are drenched [as the result of] having been rained [on].’

‘I’m hurt [as a result of] coconuts falling on me.’
At first glance, this construction resembles the paratactic apposition of subordinated

differ from unmarked indirect quotes in that the latter are the result of the optional
deletion of the subordinator me or i (cf. 1.1.2.2.3 and 1.1.2.2.4); in contrast, apposed
subordinate clauses cannot appear with these subordinators.
Clauses subordinated by apposition fall into three categories. One type,
illustrated by the above set of examples, denotes causes and reasons (cf.
1.1.2.4.2.4(g)). The subordinate clause in these constructions have no alternative

pseudo-ergativity (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(d)). A second type, which is further discussed in

or connotation, such as oti ‘finished’ and palele ‘depleted’:
(293)

uttanu].

(295)

1.1.2.2. Noun clauses
This section describes noun clauses in terms of the semantic characteristics of the
superordinate verbs that take noun clauses. This description follows roughly the
typological categories outlined in Noonan (1985:110–133). In the course of the
description it will be made clear that choices in subordinating strategy are lexically
governed by the verb of the superordinate clause, and that particular verbs or verb
categories can take different complement types.
1.1.2.2.1. General markers of noun clauses
There are no general markers of noun clauses that distinguish noun clauses from
adverb clauses. All subordinating strategies described in 1.1.2.1 are used for one
type of noun clause or another, and no subordinating strategy is associated
exclusively with noun clauses.
1.1.2.2.2. Types of noun clauses
Noun clauses other than indirect statements, questions, and commands fall in many
semantic classes, which are described here according to the meaning of the
superordinate verb. The type of subordination associated with each construction is
determined by the verb of the superordinate clause, and a particular verb or verb
category may sometimes allow different possibilities. The following discussion,
which is not intended to be exhaustive, provides illustrations of the various
possibilities attested.

1.1.2.2.3. Indirect statements
An indirect statement whose initial element is not a bare noun phrase is me-
subordinated (cf. 1.1.2.1.3) to its superordinate clause:
(340)

If the initial element of an indirect statement is a bare noun phrase, i-subordination
(cf. 1.1.2.1.4) is used:
(341)

‘The spirit said that she wanted to stay longer.’
An indirect statement can also be simply apposed to the superordinate clause. This
can happen as long as the first element of the indirect statement is not a noun

have undergone the deletion of the complementizer, because they always have
equivalents with an overt complementizer:

1.1.2.3. Relative clauses
Relative clauses are head-external and always follow the head noun. Relative clauses
can be either restrictive or nonrestrictive; both types exhibit essentially the same
structural characteristics. Several strategies can be used in the formation of relative
clauses. These strategies involve either the deletion of the relativized element or its
replacement with a pronoun. There are no correlative clauses (Keenan 1985:163–
168) in this language.
1.1.2.3.1. General markers of relative clauses
Relative clauses of all types share a number of structural characteristics. First, relative
clauses always follow the head noun that they modify, as illustrated through this
discussion. Second, relative clauses follow all other modifiers of the head noun; for
example, they follow postnominal possessive phrases:
(366)
Ne olo o ssala te vaka o pulisimani teelaa [e galo].
Pst go Cmp look-for the canoe of police that Nps disappear
‘They went to look for the policemen’s canoe which had disappeared.’
(367)
Pati a koe kolaa [ne fai mai] seki puli i au.

‘I have not forgotten what you told me.’
Note that a single head noun may be modified by more than one relative clause:
(368)
A ko faafine laa see iloa me ne faafine aa konaa [e
but Foc women then Neg know Cmp some women what? those Nps
toko tolu] [e mmai].
Num three Nps come
‘As for the women, [I] don’t know where the three women who are
coming are from.’
Third, relative clauses are strictly verb initial; in general, they also maintain the
basic word order VS(O)(X), as will be illustrated throughout this section. Fourth,
relative clauses are finite, and have the same syntactic and semantic features (e.g.,
marking for tense, aspect, mood, and transitivity) as their independent-clause
equivalents. In particular, subject-verb agreement can apply, even when the element
that controls agreement has been relativized:
(369)
Maatou ne mmai fakatasi mo tama a Alefaio toko lua [e
we-3-e Pst come together with children of Alefaio Num two Nps
aakkoga i Fiiti].

‘We came together with Alefaio’s two children who are studying
in Fiji.’
Fifth, a relative clause is always part of a noun-phrase constituent. Most commonly,
it appears as the modifier of the head noun; headless relative clauses are rare, as
discussed in 1.1.2.3.6. Finally, relative clauses (including headless relative clauses)
are optionally introduced by relative pronouns, which are homophonous with
demonstrative pronouns, and which become obligatory if the relative clause is used
as a sentence fragment. See 2.1.2.7 for discussion and illustrations.

1.1.2.3.2. Restrictive v. nonrestrictive relative clauses
Both restrictive and nonrestrictive relative clauses occur. Following are illustrative
nonrestrictive relative clauses:

[lit.: ‘You do not remember this eldest child of yours, whom you cannot

Nonrestrictive relative clauses have the same syntactic structure as restrictive relative

positions may be targeted and the same relativization strategies are used for both
types. Intonation does not necessarily distinguish between the two types.
Nonrestrictive relative clauses may be uttered with parenthetical intonation,
although not necessarily so. Thus, in most cases, the only factor that helps distinguish
between restrictive and nonrestrictive relative clauses is context. In particular, proper

1.1.2.3.4. Behaviour of the relativized element
There are several relativization strategies: a personal pronoun strategy, a deletion
strategy, an anaphoric pronoun strategy, and a possessive pronoun strategy. Each
of these strategies is associated with a different range of relativizing positions. With
certain positions, more than one strategy is possible, although there is always a
preferred pattern.
Because choices in relativization strategy are dictated by the grammatical function
of the relativized element (i.e., the element in the relative clause corresponding
semantically to the head noun), the range of elements that can be relativized out of
simple clauses is also discussed in this section. Relativization out of compound
and complex sentences is discussed in 1.1.2.3.7. That section also presents a summary
of positions in simple clauses which can be targeted by relativization, and a brief
discussion, with reference to Keenan and Comrie’s (1977) Noun-Phrase Accessibility
Hierarchy, of the patterns that emerge.
(a) Personal pronoun strategy
In certain cases, the relativized element can take the form of a personal pronoun.
When a personal pronoun appears in a relativized slot, it agrees in person, number,

which is illustrated below). Agreement is based on semantic factors, rather than
grammatical factors; thus, in the following, the personal pronoun in the relative clause

(379)

Pronominal traces are obligatory with relativization on possessive noun phrases
and complements of possessive verbs; they are strongly preferred with relativization

phrases (including indirect objects, middle objects, and objects of comparisons);
and they are allowed but dispreferred with relativization on subjects of intransitive
verbs and direct objects.
The subject of a transitive verb can be relativized, in which case there is a strong
preference for the relativized element to surface as an ergatively marked personal

(b) Deletion strategy
Relativization may leave an empty relativized element. As a general rule, it is not

elements that function as subjects of intransitive verbs and direct objects, since the
absolutive case is marked by the absence of a case marker. But the deletion strategy
is marginally acceptable, as mentioned in (a) above, as an alternative to the personal
pronoun strategy in relativization on subjects of transitive verbs and objects of
prepositions other than possessive markers. In all instances, the case marker or the
preposition is also deleted.

Personal-pronoun traces behave like full noun phrases. They may occur in any
postverbal position in the relative clause. The same goes for anaphoric-pronoun

[lit.: ‘That’s the man you want.’]
Similarly, relative-clause-like participial complements do not exist in Tuvaluan.
