1.1.2.3.10. Advancement-to-possessive
Relative-clause constructions are the domain of a rather unusual rule, which will
be referred to here as advancement-to-possessive (cf. Seiter 1980:97–99 on the same
process in Niuean). Advancement-to-possessive optionally extracts the subject of a
relative clause and marks it as a possessive modifier of the head of the relative
clause. Thus, for example, advancement-to-possessive extracts the subject noun
phrase Faagota from the relative clause in the first example below and turns it into
a possessively marked argument of the head noun of the relative clause, te lama,
thus yielding the second sentence:
(437)
Teenei te lama [ne sseu nee Faagota].
this the swamp-taro-plant Pst hoe Erg Fagota
‘This is the swamp-taro plant that Fagota hoed.’
(438)
Teenei te lama a Faagota [ne sseu].
this the swamp-taro-plant of Fagota Pst hoe
‘This is the swamp-taro plant that Fagota hoed.’
Advancement-to-possessive can apply to a relative clause as long as the head noun
is not already modified by a possessive modifier of any type, in which case
advancement-to-possessive is not possible:
(439)
* Teenei toku lima a te puusi [ne uu].
this my hand of the cat Pst bite
(‘This is the hand of mine that the cat bit.’)
Advancement-to-possessive is also blocked if the head of the relative clause is either
a proper name or a pronoun, since these are entities that, in normal circumstances,
do not have possessive modifiers.
Thus noun phrases that have been targeted by advancement-to-possessive
resemble closely true possessives. The output of advancement-to-possessive
frequently yield structures that are ambiguous between two readings: one that
recognizes the possessively marked noun phrase as having undergone
advancement-to-possessive, and another that recognizes it as a true possessive
modifier of the head noun and that interprets the zero-subject in the relative slot
as a zero pronoun:

1.1.2.4. Adverb clauses
1.1.2.4.1. General markers of adverb clauses
Few general statements can be made about the structure of adverb clauses as a
unified category. The only possible generalization concerns the position of an adverb

clause in reference to its superordinate clause: if the order of the two clauses is
fixed, it follows the pattern observable throughout the language, i.e., the
superordinate clause comes first and the subordinate clause second. However, the
position of adverb clauses is not always fixed, in that certain adverb-clause categories
(e.g., conditional clauses) may be either proposed or postposed to the superordinate
clause.
Many categories that are commonly encoded as adverb-clause constructions in
other languages (e.g., certain types of time clauses) are not expressed with adverb
clauses in Tuvaluan; instead, the relevant constructions are adjective or nominalized
clauses.
1.1.2.4.2. Types of adverb clauses
The following discussion categorizes adverb clauses by semantic criteria. Also
covered here, when relevant, are nonadverbial clauses that express notions typically
associated with adverb-clause constructions in other languages.
1.1.2.4.2.1. Adverb clauses denoting time Various constructions can express
temporal notions, all of which can denote past, present, or future situations. These
constructions fall into three semantic categories, which are discussed in turn: (a)
‘after’ (or sequencing) clauses, which refer to a situation that precedes in time the
situation denoted by the superordinate clause (e.g., the italicized clause in ‘After he
returned from net-fishing, he washed up’); (b) ‘before’ clauses, which refer to a situation
that follows in time the situation denoted by the superordinate clause (e.g., ‘Before
she had breakfast, she rolled up the sleeping mats’); and (c) clauses that denote
simultaneity (e.g., ‘While she was eating, he smoked his pipe’). The textual functions
of time adverbial clauses are discussed last in this section.
(a) ‘After’ clauses
Described here are eight strategies that can denote ‘after’ notions, the first six of
which are mutually exclusive for structural reasons; the remaining two can be used
in the same sentences as the other strategies.
(i) The most frequent and pragmatically and stylistically least marked way of
expressing temporal sequencing is with coordination by apposition (cf. 1.3.1.1.1),
which involves neither adverbiality nor subordination. Two or more situations that
are temporally ordered may be expressed by a sequence of independent clauses,
only the last of which has a sentence-final intonational contour. The sequencing
pattern of clauses must be iconic of the sequencing of situations:
(458)
[E taki tasi loa laa kao], [koo olo o koukkou
Nps each one indeed their-2 sour-toddy Inc go Cmp bathe
o fakamaloolloo].
Cmp in-manner-of+rest
‘[After] they’ve each had one [container of] fermented coconut toddy,
they go and wash up and have a rest.’
Clauses that are coordinate by apposition can also express simultaneity (cf. (c) below).
In sequencing clauses that are coordinated by apposition, tense-aspect-mood markers
and aspectual verbs can be exploited to convey fine distinctions in sequentiality, which
in other languages are conveyed by various morphemes (e.g., English ‘as soon as’,
‘now that’, etc.). The verb oti ‘finished’ (or one of its derivatives) is particularly frequent
in sentences denoting temporal sequencing. It either functions as the main verb of

With a preposition, in contrast, the nominalized clause may either precede the main
clause, as illustrated by the last example above, or follow it:
(469)

(c) Simultaneity
Conceptually, how two situations occur simultaneously depends on how the two
situations are perceived to take place in time. One needs to distinguish at least two
cases. In the first case, a situation is foregrounded, and usually marked for
instantaneous aspect, while the other is backgrounded, and usually marked for
continuous or progressive aspect (e.g., ‘I was sitting outside when he emerged’). In
the second case, the two situations are foregrounded in essentially the same way,
and usually have the same aspectual value (e.g., ‘He was making sennit while I was
binding lures’).
In Tuvaluan, the first type can be expressed with the same constructions as are
used for ‘after’ clauses, with the exception of the strategy that involves the anaphoric
pronoun ei, which forces a sequential reading. For example, apposed clauses can
express simultaneity:

‘[When] Niu came by [here carrying] a bunch of bananas, was he going
that way?’

must be iconic of their relative grounding: the more backgrounded clause (i.e.,
the ‘scene setting’ proposition) must precede the more foregrounded clause (i.e.,
the ‘event’ proposition). Kae-coordinated clauses can also be used to express
simultaneity; here again the order is fixed: backgrounded information first,

(a) General characteristics
In conversational discourse, conditionality may be expressed by simply apposing
the if-clause (i.e., the protasis) to the then-clause (i.e., the apodosis):7
(544)

‘Like, [if] he is hot at night, his wife stays [up] and fans [him] while

Clause coordination with kae can also be used with the same result. When
conditionality is expressed with clause apposition or coordination, the if-clause
must precede the then-clause, and is frequently ambiguous with a temporal-
sequencing reading (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.1(a)).
Conditionality is prototypically marked by one of three preverbal markers or
one of three conjunctions that are morphologically related to the preverbal markers.
The markers are kaa, the future-tense marker (cf. 2.1.3.2.1(d)); maa (or one of its
allomorphs), the precautionary-mood marker (cf. 2.1.3.4.11); and moi, the optative-
mood marker (cf. 2.1.3.4.4). The corresponding conjunctions are formed by
compounding these markers with the form fai (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hai),
derived from the verb fai ‘do, make’. The resulting forms kaafai, maafai, etc. have the
same meaning as the corresponding preverbal markers, although they occur in
different structural contexts, since one set functions as preverbal markers and the
other as conjunctions, as discussed in 2.1.3.4.2(d).
The various conditional morphemes occasionally occur in the same clause as
other semantically compatible adverb-clause conjunctions. An example with tiigaa
‘even though’ is provided in (e) below. Following is an example with auaa ‘because’
(cf. 1.1.2.4.2.4(e)):

1.1.2.5. Sequence of tenses
There is no clear constraint on sequences of tense across superordinate and
subordinate clauses comparable to the process which yields the pattern ‘I thought
you were/*are a ghost’ in English. In this respect, Tuvaluan offers an interesting
contrast to Maori, a language to which it is relatively closely related, where
Bauer (1993:74–77) finds exacting constraints on tense in complex sentences. In
Tuvaluan, the tense in a subordinate clause always refers to the time of the
situation denoted by the subordinate clause itself. Contrast the following three
sentences:
(586)
Koo muna mai [iaa ia ne fano o fai niu i motu].
Inc word Dxs Cmp he Pst go Cmp gather coconut at islet
‘He said to me that he’d gone and gathered coconuts on an islet.’
or: ‘He said that he would go and gather coconuts on an islet.’
(587)
Koo muna mai [iaa ia e fano o fai niu i motu].
Inc word Dxs Cmp he Nps go Cmp gather coconut at islet
‘He said that he was going to gather coconuts on an islet.’
(588)
Koo muna mai [iaa ia kaa fano o fai niu i motu].
Inc word Dxs Cmp he Fut go Cmp gather coconut at islet
‘He said that he was going to gather coconuts on an islet.’
or: ‘He said that he’d be going to gather coconuts on an islet.’
The complex construction which comes closest to having a constraint on tense
sequencing is apposed subordinate clauses with an aspectual verb like oti ‘finished’
or palele ‘depleted’ as superordinate verb, and which denote perfect aspect (cf.
1.1.2.2.2 and 2.1.3.3.1(d)). As discussed further in 2.1.3.3.1, the subordinate clause is
always marked for past tense in these constructions.
1.1.2.6. Equi-deletion
A deletion rule akin to equi-deletion as it has been described for better-known
languages may be triggered by a number of superordinate verbs, which form a
reasonably well-defined semantic class. Most commonly, equi-deletion is
triggered by verbs that refer to movement, either physical and metaphorical,
such as fano ‘go’ (and its plural form olo), vau ‘come’ (and its plural form aummai
or mmai), foki ‘return, come back’, eva ‘fly, jump’, sopo ‘board [a vehicle]’, saga
‘turn to, face, to turn one’s attention to’, tuu ‘stand up’, vave ‘[go, do something]
quick[ly], fast’:

I Pst go just Cmp Cst+alive my coconut-toddy
‘I just went to shave off my coconut-toddy spathes.’

Raising in Tuvaluan is typologically unusual in that it can target a much broader
range of arguments than raising rules commonly found in other languages. The
following describes the major syntactic characteristics of raising. For a more
extensive discussion of this process, and a discussion of why one is dealing with a
raising process, see Besnier (1988b).
1.1.2.7.1. Syntactic characteristics of noun-phrase raising
Tuvaluan raising is optionally controlled by a restricted number of verbs: some
aspectual verbs (e.g., kaamata ‘begin’, maasani ‘usual’, oti ‘finished’); numerals
prefixed with the multiplicative faka- (e.g., fakatolu ‘three times’, cf. 2.1.6.5.2(a)) and
the interrogative word fakafia ‘how many times’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.4(b)); some modal verbs
(e.g., kkafi ‘capable of’, mafai ‘possible’, talia ‘allow’); some affect verbs that denote
emotions, attitudes, and points of view (e.g., loto ‘desire’, see tioa ‘no wonder’, taumafai
‘try’, kaitoa ‘serve [one] right’); and a number of conjunction-like verbs which,
together with the clausal complement, form adverb clauses of various types (e.g.,
tiigaa ‘even though’, vaaganaa ‘unless’, seiloga ‘not until’, ailoga ‘probably not’). Some
raising verbs can only raise a noun phrase from a subordinate clause to the
superordinate clause in which it is directly embedded. With the raising verbs ttau
‘must’ and maua ‘be able to’, any attempt to raise a noun phrase across another
clause boundary yields ungrammatical results:
(610)
* E ttau (mo) koe [o fai mai nee ia [kee fanatu koe]].
Nps must with you Cmp tell hither Erg he Sbj go+thither you
(‘It is necessary for him to say that you should come over.’)
Other raising verbs allow raising to take place across another clause. Such is the
case of maasani ‘usual, used to’:
(611)
E maasani au [o vau ia [o ffoo]].
Nps used-to I Cmp come he Cmp massage
‘It is usual for me that he comes over to massage me.’
Verbs that allow long-distance raising include mafai ‘possible’ and a number of
aspectual verbs: tuai ‘not yet’, oti ‘finished’, etc. It is unclear why different raising
verbs should behave in different ways in this respect.
Long-distance raising is an unusual property of Tuvaluan. In English, for
example, tough-movement has this property, but not raising. The Tuvaluan
equivalents of tough-movement verbs, faigataa ‘difficult’ and faigoofie ‘easy’, also
trigger a raising-like movement. This rule does not have any of the distinctive

Noun-phrase raising can cooccur in the same sentence as a number of other
syntactic processes. In particular, it can take place in the same domain as quantifier

(613)

Noun-phrase raising can target subordinate noun phrases of any grammatical
category other than possessor and object of comparison. For example, the verb ttau
‘must’ can raise the subject of an intransitive subordinate clause:
(614)

(615)

(624)

the subordinate clause is raised to the superordinate clause. What makes the second
infelicitous is the fact that a pipe has, as an inanimate object, no volitional power,
and therefore cannot be instrumental in bringing about the state which the sentence
refers to. In contrast, in the previous example, the entity that experiences the
usualness is a human referent, and raising can apply. Raising, thus, targets whichever
noun phrase denotes the entity with the highest degree of responsibility in the
action denoted by the entire sentence, whatever grammatical role may be assigned
to that noun phrase. Responsibility differs from animacy and volition, which do
not determine whether a noun phrase can be raised (Besnier 1988b).
One consequence of the semantic constraint on Tuvaluan raising is that subjects
are by far the most frequent targets of raising (Besnier 1988b:767–773), since
subjects usually denote most responsible entities. Furthermore, the deontic modal

capability of doing something necessarily involves one highly responsible
participant, namely the participant whose capability is being commented upon.
Since raising targets such responsible participants, subjects of deontic verbs are
very likely to be targeted by the rule.
There is a correlation between the case marking assigned to raised noun phrases
in superordinate clauses and the grammatical role that it plays in the subordinate
clause from which it was raised: the more oblique the role of the noun phrase in the
subordinate clause, the more obliquely it is marked in the superordinate clause.

1.2. STRUCTURAL FEATURES
1.2.1. Internal structure of the sentence
Various types of copular sentences and comparable sentences, some of which have
verbal properties, while others do not, are treated in 1.2.1.1. Ordinary verbal
sentences are covered in 1.2.1.2; the title of that section, ‘verbal sentences’, should
not be taken to imply that all structures described in 1.2.1.1 are verbless. Adverbials
are described in 1.2.1.3.
1.2.1.1. Copular sentences
No word in the language can unequivocally be identified as a copula in the usual
sense of the term. Canonical copular sentences with nominal complements, which
I refer to as ‘equational constructions’, are built by apposing two noun phrases, as
described in 1.2.1.1.1(a). Occasionally, one of these noun phrases is a zero pronoun,
a situation that results in a clause consisting of a single overtly expressed noun
phrase. However, there are a number of verbs akin in function to copular verbs in
other languages, one of which is the existential verb, described in 1.2.1.1.1(b). There
are no copular sentences with adjective complements, as predicate adjectives are
full verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.2). The only adverbial category that can appear in copula-like
syntactic contexts is certain types of prepositional phrases that function as predicates
and share many properties with ordinary verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.3).

‘All teachers [were] Tuvaluans.’
And the following has a demonstrative pronoun in the predicate slot:
(639)

‘This [is] what we ask for.’
The other element of an equational construction can be termed the ‘subject’, in
contrast to the predicate, even though it does not share subject-like properties with
ordinary sentential subjects. This subject may also be a ko-focused definite noun
phrase, an unmarked definite noun phrase, or, more rarely, a demonstrative
pronoun. Constituents which cannot appear as either the subject or the predicate
of equational constructions are prepositional phrases, noun phrases bearing case
marking other than a and ko, adjectival phrases, and verbal clauses. Unmarked
definite noun phrases or proper noun phrases cannot function as the predicate
element of an equational construction; rather, definite or proper noun phrases must
always be marked with ko when they function as the predicate element, and this
marker in this context is best understood as a marker of predication. Thus an
equational construction cannot consist of two unmarked definite or proper noun
phrases equated to one another. Other disallowed combinations are two indefinite
noun phrases, since indefinite noun phrases can only occur as predicates, and two
demonstratives (thus ‘that’s that’ cannot be translated word for word into Tuvaluan).
In contrast, two ko-focused noun phrases can be equated to one another:
(640)
[Ko te ala o te tusi] [ko te fia sauttala mo koe i
Foc the reason of the letter Foc the want chat with you at
Amatuku naa].
Amatuku that
‘The reason for [this] letter [is] that I want to chat with you, over there
at Amatuku.’
In these constructions, one ko-marked noun phrase is focused for new information
(cf. 1.11.2.1.4), while the other is ko-marked for predication. Furthermore, the subject
of an equational construction can consist of a headless relative clause (cf. 1.1.2.3.6):
(641)
[Se lalolagi] [teenei [e oola taatou i ei]].
a world this Nps live we-3-i in Anp
‘[It is] a [worldly] world we live in.’

equational constructions, and can thus appear at the same locations and with the
same range of functions as definite noun phrases. For example, they can function

Definite noun phrases, including proper noun phrases and personal pronouns
but excluding demonstrative pronouns, can be marked with the absolutive-
contrastive marker a when they function as the subject of the equational structure,
as long as they are not already marked with ko (cf. 2.1.1.2.3 for more examples):
(644)

‘All teachers [were] Tuvaluans.’
The distribution of a, which is the only case marker that can appear in equational
constructions besides ko, is the same in equational constructions as in verbal
sentences (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1).
The difference between ko-focused definite noun phrases and indefinite noun
phrases is closely linked to the definiteness value of each possibility. The most
basic difference is that the first denote referents which the speaker assumes the
interlocutor can identify, while the second denotes referents which the speaker
assumes the interlocutor cannot identify and should not seek to identify. Thus a
predicate that denotes an identification, or a superlative characterization, or a
definition or role identification consisting of an expression that can only denote a
unique referent, will always be a ko-marked noun phrase:
(645)
[Te fafine Kilipati teenaa] [ko Maalia].
the woman Gilbert that Foc Maria
‘That Gilbertese woman [was named] Maria.’
In contrast, predicates consisting of an indefinite noun phrase identify the referent
of the subject as an element in a set or qualify it with a nonunique or nonreferential
characteristic:
(646)
[Te sukaa] [se masaki ne faatoaa iloa faaka i fenua o te
the diabetes a illness Pst just know indeed at island of the
Paasefika].

‘Diabetes [is] a sickness which has just become known in the islands of
the Pacific.’

‘That person [was] my father’s grandfather.’

To sum up, the difference between ko-focused predicates and indefinite predicates
is one of definiteness in the usual sense of the term. Significantly, it is not a difference
between definiteness, referential indefiniteness, and genericness on the one hand,
and, on the other hand, indefinite nonreferentiality, which is the contrast marked
in the morphology in other constructions (cf. 2.1.1.10–13).
It should be clear from the examples presented so far that the order of the two
elements of an equational construction does not mark their grammatical function.
The predicate element may either precede or follow the subject. The relative position
of the two elements follows roughly the same pattern as in verbal clauses (cf.
1.2.1.2.6). Briefly, constituent order marks information structure, at least as far as
constructions with definite, proper, pronominal, and demonstrative predicates are
concerned. If an indefinite predicate denotes newer information than its subject, it
is ordered after the subject; if the reverse is true, the subject comes first. Contrast
the following, bearing in mind that the reversal of syntactic role from one English
translation to the other, rendered necessary by the fact that English is a fixed word-
order language, does not represent the syntactic structure of the original sentences,
but their pragmatic structure:
(649)
[Te pelesitene muamua o te fenua nei] [ko au].

‘The first president of this island [was] me.’
(650)
[Ko au] [te pelesitene muamua o te fenua nei].

‘I [was] the first president of this island.’
As illustrated earlier, pronouns can function as elements of equational constructions.
In addition, both zero pronouns and deleted pronouns can serve as the subject of
equational constructions, which then consist only of a ko-marked noun phrase, or
of an indefinite noun phrase, or simply of a demonstrative (e.g., Teenei! ‘This one!’,
Teenaa eiloa ‘that’s it’):
(651)

‘All household heads [do].’
(652)

‘[He is] a man who quickly contradicts himself.’
Zero pronouns and deleted pronouns occur in equational constructions for the
same reasons as they do in verbal sentences. For example, they may denote a highly
topical entity, a third person singular entity which is not emphatic or contrastive,
or an inanimate entity normally not expressed with a full pronoun form. It should
be stressed that the resulting constructions are perceived as complete sentences; no
‘wording’ (to use Rumsey’s 1990 phrase) is missing from the utterance. Because
definite noun phrases which are not ko-focused cannot function as equational
predicates, an interesting contrast can be drawn between indefinite and definite
noun phrases which occur on their own. Indefinite noun phrases can function as
full utterances, since they can be interpreted as equational predicates:

(654)

An existential verb isi appears in positive existential sentences (as well as possessive
sentences; cf. 1.10.1.1). This verb behaves like any other ordinary verb, and may be
marked for the full range of tense, aspect, and mood categories, or may be marked
by any conjunction or coordinator that replaces tense, aspect, and mood markers:
(655)
Kae isi foki se mmalu faka-te-maaloo koo oti ne

‘But there is also some governmental dignity that’s been anointed onto
[him].’

‘How about our garden, are there still swamp-taro plants alive in it or
have they all died?’
The verb isi has an alternative form i ai, which is made up of the locative preposition
i and of an older form of the anaphoric pronoun ei, and which is thus formed along
the same pattern as predicative prepositional phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.3). This form is
mostly heard in oratory and other forms of formal discourse, particularly religious
discourse:
(657)
Ko te maafaufau o te tino teelaa e masaki, koo gaasolo

o see toka, koo i ai te nnumi mo te fai valevale o

ana manatu.

‘The mind of the person who is sick becomes restless, his thoughts
become tangled and confused.’
The form i ai is homophonous with the Northern Tuvaluan existential verb (the Southern
Tuvaluan innovation isi is not used in the Northern dialects), and is often encountered
in the Southern Tuvaluan spoken by native speakers of these dialects. It is also

homophonous with the existential verb in Samoan (Mosel and Hovdhaugen 1992:114)
and many other Polynesian languages. It is not clear whether the Southern form i ai is
a borrowing from Samoan, a borrowing from Northern Tuvaluan, or an archaism.
The existential verb takes as subject a noun phrase denoting the entity whose
existence is being expressed. Typically, the subject is indefinite and postverbal, since
existential forms (and the negative existential forms described in 1.4(d)) frequently
introduce new information (cf. 1.11), as illustrated in the following:
(658)
E isi ne mea koo ttau o suke.
Nps exist some thing Inc must Cmp investigate
‘There are certain things that need to be investigated.’
Existential sentences, as discussed in 2.1.1.11, are a prototypical context for
indefinitely marked noun phrases, which are otherwise rare because in other
contexts ‘definite’ articles mark both definiteness and indefinite referentiality, and
thus leave few functions for indefinite articles. However, indefinite noun phrases
are not the only possible subjects of existential verbs, as there are contexts in which
existential subjects are marked for definiteness, and occur either postverbally or
preverbally:
(659)
A suka koo isi i te sitoa.
Cnt sugar Inc exist at the store
‘Now there is sugar at the store.’
(660)
E isi ttagata teelaa ne mua mai.
Nps exist the+man that Pst come-first Dxs
‘(There is) a man (who) got here first.’
There is a subtle difference between existential sentences with definite subjects and
with indefinite subjects. Definite subjects signal that the most ‘noteworthy’ new
information in the clause is not the referent of the noun, but another element in the
clause, even if the subject does denote new information. In the first of the above
examples, what is newsworthy in the utterance is the fact that the referent of the
subject has become available. In the other clause, the most newsworthy piece of
new information is the referent of the relative clause, and not the noun itself. (See
1.10.1.1 for a discussion of definite subjects of the existential verb in possessive
constructions, which follows a similar line of argumentation.)
Both existential forms isi and i ai nominalize regularly, with either bare
nominalization or suffixal nominalization (cf. 2.1.3.5):
(661)

‘We all [can] feel that there is a happy spirit [here].’

‘If only we had bought ourselves a lamp when we had money!’
Case marking under nominalization follows regular patterns for intransitive verbs
(cf. 2.1.1.3.4). The existential verbs isi and i ai have special negative forms seeai and
seki ai, discussed in 1.4(d).
1.2.1.1.2. Copular sentences with adjectival complement

and 2.1.4).
1.2.1.1.3. Copular sentences with adverbial complement
Only one type of prepositional phrase can appear in copular contexts, and it is the
only adverbial to do so. The construction has no overt copula, and the prepositional
phrase is marked like a regular verb and behaves like one in most respects. (Thus
the prepositional phrase is a ‘complement’ only in the broadest sense of the term.)
I call these constructions ‘predicative prepositional phrases’:
(663)
Te Niivaga koo i Nanumea.
the Nivaga Inc at Nanumea
‘The M.V.Nivaga is at Nanumea.’
Predicative prepositional phrases consist principally of locative phrases marked
with the general locative preposition i (cf. 2.1.1.5.1(a)). The preposition i can also
appear as part of compound prepositions (cf. 2.2.6.1.2); these complex prepositions
can also function predicatively:
(664)
Peelaa taatou me i loto i te fono.
like we-3-i as-if in inside in the meeting
‘[It’s] as if we were part of the meeting.’
Demonstrative pronouns can appear as the object of the preposition in predicative
prepositional phrases (cf. 2.1.2.5(b)). So can the anaphoric pronoun ai (cf. 2.1.2.1.7),
in the slightly archaic form i ai of the existential verb, which, as mentioned in
1.2.1.1.1(a), is constructed like a predicative prepositional phrase.
Besides the locative preposition and complex prepositions formed from it, the
possessive prepositions a and o can also appear in predicative positions in possessive
sentences (cf. 1.10.1.2), and so can prepositional phrases formed with the benefactive
prepositions maa and moo (cf. 2.1.1.4.1(c)). In contrast, prepositional phrases with
the source preposition mai, the directional preposition ki, and the comitative
preposition mo can only take on predicative characteristics in contrastively
coordinated or negated contexts (cf. 1.3.1.3.9 and 1.4.2 respectively), of which the
following is an illustration:
(665)

maatou katoa.

‘These words are not from just me, but from us all.’

results:
(666)

we-3-e Inc to Funafuti
(‘We’re off to Funafuti.’)
As illustrated above, the subject of predicative prepositional phrases is marked
like ordinary subjects of intransitive verbs (cf. 2.1.1.2.1), and can appear either in
postverbal or preverbal position. In addition, when the preposition of the predicative
string is a compound whose second element (i.e., the object) is marked with the
locative preposition i (cf. 2.2.6.1.2), the subject can occur between the local noun

1.2.1.1.6. Miscellaneous copula-like constructions
Several verbs and constructions are semantically akin to morphemes which serve
as copulas in other languages. The following discussion surveys forms which are
not discussed elsewhere in the grammar. For other relevant constructions, see
the discussion of impersonal uses of transitive verbs like tuku ‘place’ in 1.2.1.2.1(b),
of the verb galo ‘absent’ as a negative existential in 1.4.7(f), and of various ways of
expressing ‘become’ or ‘function as’ described in 2.1.1.2.10 and 2.1.1.2.11. See also
verbal uses of nouns denoting social roles and temporal entities described in
2.2.2.1.1.
Certain verbs with very general meaning frequently appear in sentences denoting
location, existence, or role. The most salient are the intransitive verb nofo ‘stay, live,
sit’ and the transitive verb fai ‘do, make’, the former being associated principally
with human entities and the latter, which often translates as ‘be held’, with events.
These verbs carry very little meaning in contexts in which they are used as copula-
like forms, and can be viewed as dummy verb-slot ‘fillers’:
(681)

‘The meeting is in the maneaba.’

more common in the Northern dialects than in the Southern dialects. Comparable
constructions are also associated with verbs like tuku ‘place’ (cf. 1.2.1.2.1(b)) and
galo (cf. 1.4.7(f)).

an o-subordinated clausal complement (cf. 1.1.2.2.2):

1.2.1.2. Verbal sentences
1.2.1.2.1. Verbs without subjects
Any verb can appear without an overt subject. The non-occurrence of the subject
can be attributed to a variety of factors, depending on the situation. The processes
reviewed here do not affect the valency of the verb, but rather the surface realization
of the clause. The following discussion should be contrasted with that of processes
which do affect the valency of the verb, for which see 2.1.3.1.2. It is significant that
grammaticalized processes that delete subjects (i.e., categories (a) to (d) below) only
target subjects of transitive verbs. Subjects of intransitive verbs can only be deleted
by zero pronominalization (cf. (e)) or through grammatical processes affecting
grammatical relations (cf. (f)). In terms of the restricted range of processes through
which they can be deleted, subjects of intransitive verbs resemble direct objects (cf.
1.2.1.2.2). The asymmetry between subjects of intransitive and transitive verbs
exhibited here is discussed further in 2.1.1.2.2(c).
No verb in the language can appear without a subject (with one marginal
exception, discussed in 1.15.1), and dummy subjects do not exist. The absence of
dummy subjects is further discussed under (f) below.
 
(a) Agentless constructions
Verbs of all valencies may appear without an agent when this agent is generic,
unidentifiable, nonreferential, or simply not worth identifying. For example, in the
following sentence, taken from a historical narrative in which many participants
are involved in finding a contract, no subject appears:
(687)
Ne ave a te pepa teenaa ki tua i Peletaania.
Pst send Cnt the paper that to overseas in Britain
‘That piece of paper was sent overseas to Britain.’
In the narrative, any number of participants could have sent out the contract, and

the identity of the unmentioned subject is not retrievable from either the discourse
or the extralinguistic context. As in the impersonal passive construction in the
English translation, the exact identity of the unmentioned participant, or even its

The nonmention of the subject differs in semantic and pragmatic terms from

involvement of a volitional entity in placing the hammer where it was found. It

1.2.1.2.3. Indirect objects
Indirect objects are marked for case with a case marker ki (cf. 2.1.1.2.5), a cognate of
one of the two middle-object case markers (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(a)) and of the directional
preposition. There are no morphological differences between indirect object phrases
and prepositional phrases marked with ki with other syntactic and semantic
functions. For example, all occurrences of ki can take as object the anaphoric pronoun
ei (cf. 2.1.2.1.7), the preposition takes on a special suffix when it has a proper or
pronominal object, whatever its function may be (cf. 2.1.5.2 and 2.1.5.3), and it can
always be turned into a complex preposition with the local noun luga ‘top’ in formal
styles of speaking and writing, no matter what syntactic or semantic category it
denotes (cf. 2.2.6.1.2). One possible morphological difference between indirect objects
and middle objects is the fact that certain middle objects can be marked with the
case marker i, others with ki, and others with either, while indirect objects can only
appear with ki. There are no significant syntactic differences between indirect objects
on the one hand and locative and temporal obliques marked with the cognate
preposition on the other, and no differences between indirect objects and middle
objects marked with ki. For example, both indirect and middle objects (but not
oblique phrases marked with the same prepositional markers) can be marked, not
with ki, but with a cognate of the inalienable benefactive preposition moo, resulting

middle objects, and all other obliques marked with ki occur in postverbal position
only and exhibit the same free ordering with respect to other objects and verb
modifiers, with a tendency to occur after direct objects. To conclude, there is no
clear morphosyntactic argument for positing a category ‘indirect object’ in the
language. If the category is to be treated as significant, it can only be recognized on
the basis of semantic criteria.
1.2.1.2.4. Other arguments of verbs
The only other salient argument type is the so-called ‘middle object’ governed by
certain classes of verbs (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(a)). As discussed in 2.1.1.2.8(a), constructions
that take middle objects are intransitive. For a description of miscellaneous types
of objects governed by relatively restricted classes of verbs, see 2.1.1.2.8(b).
1.2.1.2.5. Combinations of arguments
All combinations of arguments are attested. In no case does the presence of a
particular type of argument in a clause require the presence of an argument of
another type.
1.2.1.2.6. Constituent order
(a) Ordering possibilities and basic order
In matrix and independent clauses, all constituent order possibilities are
grammatical, with the general restrictions that the subject of a transitive verb cannot
precede the verb if no direct object follows the verb, and that preverbal arguments
be definite. In addition, constituent order and case marking are somewhat contingent
on one another insofar as an ergatively marked noun phrase cannot appear before
the verb; if a subject precedes a transitive verb, it is left unmarked for case or is
marked with the absolutive-contrastive marker a (cf. 2.1.1.2.1).

and SV:

opposed. Left-dislocated noun phrases, whose syntax and pragmatics also differ
from preposed arguments, are discussed in 1.11.2.1.6.
When several arguments follow the verb, no matter what their case marking
may be, several tendencies predict their relative order. All other factors being equal,
first-person and second-person arguments precede third-person arguments; light
noun phrases precede heavy ones; pronominal arguments precede nonpronominal
arguments; and animate arguments precede inanimate arguments. These are only
tendencies, and in some situations one tendency may contradict another.
The order of constituents is more restricted in subordinate clauses than in matrix
or independent clauses, although some types of subordinate clause place more
restrictions on constituent order than others. Generally speaking, preposed

be followed by a nominal entity, which may be one of the constituents of the
subordinate clause (although not necessarily so since the subordinate verb can also
be nominalized and serve as the first element in the subordinate clause).
Among the various possible constituent orders (VSO, VOS, OVS, SVO), VSO
emerges as the syntactically most basic configuration. Four arguments support this
analysis. Before presenting these arguments, I will exclude the possibility that OVS
or VOS are syntactically basic, given the fact that they are typologically infrequent
as basic constituent-order configurations. (Additional evidence militating against
these possibilities will be mentioned presently.) The two remaining candidates are
therefore SVO and VSO.
First, if SVO is the basic constituent order, one needs to posit two separate
movement processes (i.e., subject preposing and direct-object postposing) in order
to account for the statistically frequent OVS variant. Only one such process (i.e.,
direct-object preposing) is needed if VSO is basic, and thus this account is more
parsimonious. Second, in cases where constituent order is restricted, namely in
subordinate clauses (setting aside the more marginal case of pseudoergative
constructions), it is always restricted to verb-initial order, suggesting that VSO is
more basic than SVO. Third, when subjects of transitive verbs are moved to preposed

the verb:

are the result of a movement process from a postverbal and preobject position to a
preverbal position. This movement process, incidentally, would be difficult to
describe parsimoniously if OVS were basic, given the fact that SOV and OSV are
not possible configurations.
Imperative clauses provide a fourth piece of evidence for positing VSO as the
syntactically basic constituent order. Imperatives are formed by deleting the tense-
aspect-mood marker preceding the verb, as well as any preposed constituent unless
it is left-dislocated (cf. 1.1.1.3.1). In particular, the subject of an imperative clause

(b) The one-constituent bias
There is a strong tendency in natural discourse for clauses to consist of a verb and
a single noun phrase, rather than a verb and two constituents. This effect, which I
term the ‘one-constituent bias’ (compare Duranti and Ochs 1990, and Ochs 1988:104–
127 on Samoan), is achieved principally by decreasing the number of arguments
that appear in transitive clauses. However, it is also achieved by ensuring that
subjectless intransitive clauses do not occur readily. A number of processes and
other grammatical characteristics are involved in this bias.
First, the agent is frequently expressed as the possessive modifier of the direct
object, as discussed in 2.1.1.2.2(c), rather than as the subject of the transitive verb.
This very frequent way of expressing agents has the effect of leaving only one
constituent in the clause, namely the direct object with its possessively marked,
agent-encoding modifier:
(725)

‘He just wore his loincloth with nothing underneath.’

the patient modified by a possessively marked noun phrase denoting the agent.

1.2.1.3. Adverbials
This section describes the general characteristics of adverbials in the context of the
clause. For a discussion of the internal structure of adverbial clauses, see 1.2.3.
1.2.1.3.1. Types of adverbials
1.2.1.3.1.1. Adverbs Adverbs form a broad and eclectic word category. Some adverbs
function as modifiers of verbs, including predicative adjectives, and attributive
verbal adjectives and adverbs. Some, like fui ‘difficult to, slow in’, saale ‘frequently’,
lookoo ‘rather’, and mai ‘hither’, can only function as such. Most adverbs that are
exclusively associated with verbs and verb-derived categories form a closed class
and have grammatical meanings that are described elsewhere in this grammar.
Others, like the intensifier loa, the downtoners laa and fua, and faka-prefixed adverbial
forms (cf. 2.2.4), can also function as modifiers of verbal and verbless clauses, or as
attributive modifiers of nouns, or both. Few generalizations can be made about
these adverbs, which form an open class. Finally, some adverbs are ‘floating’
elements that can occur at different locations in verbal and verbless clauses, whose
scope and focus vary from one situation to another. In this category fall many hedges
(e.g., kaati ‘perhaps’), pause fillers (e.g., peelaa ‘thus’), and the tag-question marker
nee (cf. 1.1.1.2.1.2).
It is noteworthy that many adverbs can also function as verbs, usually because
they are derived from verbs. In fact, adverbs are frequently difficult to distinguish
from verbs (see, for example, 2.1.3.7), and many ‘adverbial’ situations (i.e., situations
which are commonly expressed as adverbs across the world’s languages) that
involve verb-derived adverbs are preferably encoded as verbs, rather than as
adverbs. For example, the form ssoko means, as a verb, ‘joined, continuous’. As an
adverb, it denotes continuous or iterative aspect (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(g)), a function which
is clearly related through metaphorical extension to its meaning as a verb:
(736)

rather than a nominalized verb:
(742)
Koo faka-Ppaalagi mai tena leo.

‘He spoke with an English accent.’
Clearly, one is not dealing with a grammatical process here, but with a preferential
tendency underlying the language.
1.2.1.3.1.2. Prepositional phrases There are many types of prepositional phrase, which
are formed from a relatively small inventory of prepositional forms (cf. 2.1.5). The function
of various prepositional phrases is described in detail in 2.1.1.4, 2.1.1.5, and 2.1.1.6. For
further information on the internal structure of prepositional phrases, see 1.2.4.
1.2.1.3.1.3. Cases of noun phrases Superficially, cases of noun phrases are similar
in form to prepositional phrases. Most case categories (i.e., all but certain
manifestations of the absolutive case; cf. 2.1.1.2.1) are marked with preposition-
like morphemes that take as objects full noun phrases. A few morphological
processes distinguish case markers from prepositions (cf. 2.1.5), and case-marked
noun phrases differ from prepositional phrases in that they are more mobile in the
clause than the latter (cf. 1.2.1.2.5).
1.2.1.3.1.4. Adverbial clauses There are many types of adverb clause (cf. 1.1.2.4.2),
about which few, if any, structural generalizations can be drawn (cf. 1.1.2.4.1). Both
nonfinite and finite adverbial clauses occur (cf. 1.1.2.4.3).

verb, in either proposed or postposed position. Following is the order of some

superordinate clause.
1.2.1.3.3. Obligatoriness of adverbials
No adverbial is ever obligatory. Certain constructions with verbs which are
semantically associated with certain prepositional-phrase types most frequently
occur with a prepositional phrase. For example, verbs of motion most frequently
occur with a directional prepositional phrase, but even in such cases the adverbial
is not obligatory:
(748)
Koo fano (ki Niuooku).
Inc go to Niuoku
‘[He]’s going (to Niuoku [islet]).’
1.2.2. Adjective phrases
1.2.2.1. Operational definition for the adjective phrase
There are no straightforward arguments for establishing a separate category
‘adjective phrase’. Indeed, like most other morphological categories in the language,
adjectival forms are not recognizable as such when disrobed of their syntactic
context; in addition, adjectives, particularly attributive adjectives, do not move,
and thus external mobility cannot be used as a test for constituency.
All predicate adjectives function like regular verbs. Thus:
(a)
They are usually marked with any of the tense-aspect-mood markers that
may also mark verbs.
(b)
They may be modified by a full range of semantically relevant adverbial
elements.
(c)
Many agree in number with their subject like many intransitive verbs.
(d)
They occupy exactly the same location in the clause as regular verbs.
(e)
They undergo nominalization.
(f)
They control case marking like regular verbs.
A form can thus only be identified as a member of a separate class of predicate
adjectives on the basis of the fact that it is statistically more likely to appear as a
noun-modifying attributive form than canonical verbs. But even this distinction is
to a certain extent artificial because many verbs can also function as attributive
modifiers, as discussed presently. In light of the exceptionless identity between
predicate adjectives and verbs, predicative adjectives are considered to be verbs
throughout this grammar, and are not discussed further in this section.
Attributive adjectives are a little easier to establish as a separate grammatical
category, although whether or not they all form a phrasal constituent is not clear.
First, attributive adjectives can be derived from most verbs in the language, even
verbs that bear few of the semantic characteristics associated crosslinguistically

with adjectives, such as stativeness and intransitivity (e.g., gaalue ‘work’ as in taimi
gaalue ‘work time’, moe ‘sleep’ as in potu moe ‘bedroom’, ttaki ‘trawl’ as in ulu ttaki
‘trawling lure’). Second, a substantial subclass of attributive adjectives derived from
nouns cannot function as predicates (cf. 1.16.4 and 2.1.4). (As shown in the same
sections, there is also a third closed class of adjectival modifiers, which are preposed
to the noun they modify and are not treated here because they share no
characteristics with more productive types of attributive adjectives.)
Both subtypes of attributive adjectives, i.e., verbal and nominal adjectives, occur
after the noun. They cannot leave the confines of the noun phrase and still retain
their status as attributive adjectives. Verbal adjectives can be modified by many
(but not all) verb-modifying elements, like negators and postposed adverbs:
(749)
pati see aogaa
word Neg need
‘useless words’
(750)
tino vaallea kkii
person silly very
‘very silly people’
(751)
se tamaliki taua ssoko
a child argue constantly
‘a child [who is] constantly getting into arguments’
Some preposed verb-modifying elements, tense-aspect-mood markers in particular,
do not occur with attributive verbal adjectives, while others do. Whether a particular
modifier can appear in such positions is idiosyncratically determined:
(752)
te paala tai lasi atu
the kingfish quite large Dxs
‘the slightly larger kingfish’
(753)
se fafine fui fiittaa i te gaaluega
a woman difficult-to tired at the work
‘a hard-working woman’
(754)
ne tamaliki fia iinu saale
some child want drink often
‘frequently thirsty children’
Similarly, attributive nominal adjectives may be modified by many noun-modifying
elements. For example, an attributive adjective may consist of a noun and its adjective
modifier:
(755)
fale puliki llasi

‘houses [made of] large bricks’
Preposed noun-modifying elements (e.g., articles, preposed adjectives) cannot
modify attributive nominal adjectives.
1.2.2.2. Adjectives that take arguments
No adjective takes an obligatory argument. Optional arguments do occur, but only
with attributive verbal adjectives. One finds attributive verbal adjectives with
indirect objects:

(757)

‘an amazing story for children’
(758)

‘an animal useless to people’
One also finds attributive verbal adjectives with direct objects, but these must be
verb-incorporated (cf. 2.1.3.6.12):
(759)
tino fai mokopuna

‘people with grandchildren’
(760)

Direct objects which have not undergone incorporation cannot occur with attributive
verbal adjectives:
(761)
* se tagata inu te kava
a man drink the liquor
This restriction is linked in an obvious way to the fact that adjective formation
from corresponding predicates follows an ergative-absolutive pattern, in that verbal
adjectives can function as attributive modifiers of what would be the head noun of
the subject or direct object in intransitive predicative contexts, but not the subject in
transitive predicative contexts (cf. 1.16.4). The last sentence is thus ungrammatical
because the adjective modifies what would be the head noun of the subject in its
corresponding transitive predicative usage. Object incorporation is required so as
to detransitivize the adjectival predicate before it becomes an attributive modifier.
Certain attributive verbal adjectives can be modified by an ergatively marked
subject:
(762)
se tagata filifilia nee te fenua

‘a man [who is] chosen by the island community’
(763)

‘a papaw eaten by insects’

with either -(C)ia or the transitivizing suffix -gina (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(f) and 2.1.3.1.3(c)
respectively). Unsuffixed forms normally cannot appear with an ergative subject
in attributive position. Compare the suffixed form kaina ‘eaten’ in the last example
with the unsuffixed form kai ‘eat’ in the following:
(764)

1.2.2.4. Order of arguments and modifiers
The order of arguments and modifiers of attributive verbal adjectives is the same
as the order of arguments and modifiers of verbs in full clauses (cf. 1.2.1.2.6 and
1.2.1.3.2). The order of modifiers of attributive nominal adjectives is the same as
the order of arguments of nouns (cf. 1.2.5.5).

1.2.3. Adverbial phrases
1.2.3.1. Operational definition for the adverbial phrase
There is no clear argument to support establishing a distinct constituent with
adverbials as head. As shown in 1.2.1.3.1, adverbials form a very heterogeneous
structural category, one which is better defined by default than in terms of the
cohesive behaviour of its members. Hence any element which is not a noun,
pronoun, verb, adjectival modifier, or a member of a closed class of grammatical
morphemes can be considered as an adverbial, and the phrase of which the adverbial
is the head can be considered an adverbial phrase. Adverbial phrases rarely undergo
movement processes, they are not assigned any marking of any sort which could
be taken to be a symptom of adverbial constituency, and the various types of
adverbial clauses do not share any characteristic feature.
1.2.3.2. Adverbial modifiers of adverbials
Relatively few adverbials can function as modifiers of adverbials.
1.2.3.2.1. Adverbs
Adverbs can modify other adverbs, although cases of adverbs which are
unequivocally modifiers of another adverb are rare. Indeed, when two adverbs are
in the general vicinity of one another, they generally both modify the same head,
rather than modify one another. Such is the case of the following:
(772)
E vau saale eiloa ki temotou fale.
Nps come often indeed to our-3-i house
‘[She] often comes to our house.’
Even though the order of the two verb-modifying adverbs is fixed, there is little
evidence that one can be interpreted as modifying the other. Rather, the semantics
of the clause indicates that saale and eiloa both modify the verb, although no structural
argument can be presented to support this interpretation, other than the fact that
each adverb can occur without the other.
There are instances of adverbs modifying other adverbs. Modified adverbs are
clearly verb-derived, faka-prefixed adverbs being most frequent, and modifying
adverbs are generally members of the more ‘adverbial’ core of the class, i.e.,
adverbials whose form does not appear in nonadverbial contexts, and whose
meaning is highly ‘grammaticalized’, as is the case, for example, of aspectual and
modal adverbs, and intensifiers and downtoners:
(773)
E teletele fakkaokao saale.
Nps run in-manner-of+side often
‘[He] often runs sideways.’
In a context in which the above example describes someone in the habit of running
sideways whenever he runs, but not necessarily in the habit of running, the adverb
saale can be interpreted as a modifier of fakkaokao ‘sideways’, and not the verb.

A few adverbs take prepositional modifiers. These adverbs are all derived from
verbs that take the same prepositional modifiers. Following are a few examples:

Prepositional phrases cannot modify other prepositional phrases, cases of noun

constituents embedded in such constituents (e.g., noun phrases serving as the object

1.2.3.2.3. Cases of noun phrases
Cases of noun phrases do not modify adverbials.
1.2.3.2.4. Adverbial clauses
Adverbial clauses cannot modify adverbials.
1.2.3.3. Order of modifying and modified adverbials
Constructions in which adverbials modify adverbials are always head first.
1.2.3.4. Restriction of adverbial modifiers to particular adverbials
Such restrictions are discussed in 1.2.3.2.
1.2.4. Prepositional phrases
Postpositions are not attested in this language, only prepositions.
1.2.4.1. Operational definition for the prepositional phrase
Prepositional phrases are best characterized in terms of their internal structure.
Predictably, a prepositional phrase consists of a preposition and its object, where
the latter is always a noun phrase. There are relatively few distinct prepositions in
the language (cf. 2.1.5.1), and most prepositions fall unequivocally into one single

morphological class, with the caveat that there is a slightly fuzzy boundary between
prepositions and case markers on the one hand, and between certain complex
prepositions and relative clauses on the other hand (cf. 2.2.6.1.3). Thus the
prepositional phrase can be defined without much qualification as a phrase whose
head is a member of a small closed set of prepositions. Because most prepositional
phrases do not undergo movement processes, definitional arguments in terms of
mobility are not applicable.
1.2.4.2. Prepositions and their objects
A preposition cannot occur without an object, with more than one object, or with a
grammatical category other than a noun phrase (or a category that functions like a
noun phrase, e.g., a nominalized verb) as its object. Prepositions are never stranded;
when the object of a preposition is moved by a movement process like relativization,
a pronominal trace, usually the anaphoric pronoun ei (cf. 2.1.2.1.7), is always left
behind.
1.2.4.3. Modifiers of prepositions
Prepositions can only be modified by their objects. Adverbs, other prepositional
phrases, case of noun phrases, and adverbial clauses cannot modify prepositions.
The special case of complex prepositions, further described in 2.2.6.1, should be
mentioned here, although there is no clear evidence that any of these constructions
are actual cases of modified prepositions.
1.2.4.4. Prepositions that can govern more thin one case
Case is marked by the preposition itself, and thus case cannot be marked
independently of the preposition. All prepositional forms have multiple syntactic
and semantic functions, as discussed in 2.1.5.1.
1.2.5. Noun phrases
1.2.5.1. Operational definition for the noun phrase
As in many other languages, the noun phrase is the easiest constituent type to
define. First, noun phrases other than personal pronouns and proper nouns can be
identified by the fact that their first element is almost invariably an article; the only
exception is associated with the quantifier soo ‘any’, which precedes the article (cf.
2.1.6.6.4). There are four basic article forms, as discussed in 2.1.1.8.6, one of which
is a zero form, namely the definite plural article. They sometimes coalesce with or
are replaced by possessive pronouns or quantifiers, as discussed in 2.1.2.4 and 2.1.6.6
respectively.
Second, noun phrases, including phrases with a personal pronoun or proper
noun as a head, are normally marked for case, although one important case marker,
namely the absolutive case marker, appears commonly as a zero form (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1).
The only context in which noun phrases do not bear a case marker is when they
function as exclamations. Third, noun phrases always move as a block. For example,
the head of a noun phrase modified by a relative clause cannot be separated from
the relative clause. Only one syntactic process, namely conjunct splitting (cf. 1.3.1.7),
can separate various elements of a noun phrase.

1.2.5.2. Modifiers in noun phrases
Compared to other constituents, noun phrases can include a broad range of
modifiers, including adjectives, relative clauses, possessive pronouns, articles,
demonstrative adjectives, quantifiers, adverbs, prepositional phrases, intensifiers
and downtoners, and comparative and equative structures.
1.2.5.2.1. Adjectives
Adjectives from three different categories (cf. 1.16.4), two of which form open classes,
can modify the head of a noun phrase. Adjectives from the two open classes are
postposed to the noun, while adjectives from the closed class are preposed:
(779)

‘boiled germinated coconut kernels’
(780)

‘porcelain plates’
(781)

‘our last fatele dance’
1.2.5.2.2. Relative clauses
Relative clauses, which are further described in 1.1.2.3, are always postposed to the
head of the noun phrase in which they occur. They must follow all other noun
modifiers:
(782)
koutou [ne laulau atu ootou igoa]
you-3 Pst list Dxs your-3 name
‘you whose names have [just] been listed’
1.2.5.2.3. Possessive modifiers
Possessive phrases, described in 2.1.1.4.6, are postposed to head nouns, and follow
all other nonclausal modifiers in noun phrases:
(783)
te ato o te fale
the roof of the house
‘the roof of the house’
Possessive pronouns, described in 2.1.2.4, precede the noun they modify, and occur
at the same location as articles:
(784)
telotou gaaluega taaua

‘their important work’
1.2.5.2.4. Articles
Articles, as mentioned in 1.2.5.1 and further discussed in 2.1.1.8.6, are usually the
first element of the noun phrase:

1.2.5.2.5. Demonstrative adjectives
Demonstrative adjectives, described in 2.1.2.5(c), are postposed modifiers which
are ordered before certain adverbs and after others:
(787)

‘that price’
Manner demonstratives (i.e., forms on pee- described in 2.1.2.5(d)) are ordered
relatively freely in postnominal position, as illustrated in 1.2.5.5.
1.2.5.2.6. Quantifiers and numerals
As shown in 2.1.6.6, certain quantifiers are preposed modifiers, all of which except
soo ‘any’ are ordered after the article:
(788)
ne moo tii koi ttoe

‘a little tea left’
Other quantifiers occur after the noun. This category is comprised mostly of
adverbial quantifiers (i.e., quantifiers that can also function as modifiers of
verbs):
(789)

‘someone else’
(790)

old-man Nps Num few
‘a few old men’
Numerals can be either preposed or postposed to the head noun. Postposed
numerals have the structure of relative clauses, while preposed numerals behave
like morphemes denoting collective plural (cf. 1.2.5.2.10). Further discussion of the
difference between these various possibilities and of their position relative to other
noun modifiers can be found in 2.1.6.2.
1.2.5.2.7. Adverbials
Adverbial modifiers of nouns fall into two types, namely adverbs and prepositional

(although they are not commonly anchored in a single postnominal position):
(791)

passenger other also
‘other passengers as well’

(797)

‘the nicer story than your story’
Similarly, the head of a noun phrase cannot be directly marked for superlative
comparison. Rather, superlative comparison may be marked on an adjectival
modifier, or in a relative clause as in the following:
(798)
te tagata [e uke eiloa ana moa mo taki i uta nei]

‘the man with the most chickens and ducks on these shores’

(799)

‘a canoe that [sails] as fast as our canoe’
1.2.5.2.10. Others
A compounding strategy, described in 2.2.6.3.2, links together two nominal
elements with a linking morpheme -a-. Following are a few examples of such
compounds:

‘a kitten’
(801)

‘just small children’

‘an enormous house’
The resulting compounds function as nouns, with the second element as the head.
The first element varies greatly in terms of productivity and in terms of the extent
to which it alters the meaning of the head. Some are ‘adjectival’ enough to be
considered noun-phrase modifiers; they compound with a broad range of nouns
and have a highly predictable effect on the meaning of the noun. However, these
structures retain certain compound-like characteristics in that nothing can separate
the two elements, and in the sense that the first elements cannot function as
independent words.
As described in 2.1.1.8.4–5, nouns may be modified by morphemes denoting
collective plurality. These morphemes do not form a homogeneous word class:
some resemble regular compounding elements (e.g., kau ‘group [of people, fish,
etc.]’), others are compounding elements linked to the head of the noun phrase
with the linker -a- referred to in the previous paragraph (e.g., kataa- ‘school [of
trevally]’). One, namely saa, which may be preposed to proper names or to a few
common nouns to denote groups of people, functions like an article. Collective
morphemes of the first and second types are usually the last element before the
head noun, i.e., they function like regular compounding elements:
(803)
te isi avaa tuula katafa

‘the other two flocks of lesser frigate birds’
(804)
ssuaa kataa aaseu aka loa
a+other school+of trevally other indeed
‘another school of trevally altogether’
The collective saa occupies the same position as articles; see 2.1.1.8.4–5 for
examples.
1.2.5.3. Order of modifiers of the same type
Postposed nominal adjectives always precede verbal adjectives:
(805)
faafine Ppaalagi paakkaa
women Westerner thin
‘thin European women’
Only one nominal adjective, and only one verbal adjective generally modifies the
same head noun. Occasionally, a verbal adjective plays an important enough role
in the semantics of the noun phrase to form what resembles a compound with
the head noun, in which case another verbal adjective can modify the same noun,
or rather the compound made up of the noun and the first adjective. Adjectives
denoting colours, for example, may occur as the first of two adjectives in sequence:

150
Syntax
(806)

clothing white dirty
‘dirty white clothes’
Few generalizations can be drawn from such cases.
There are no restrictions on the cooccurrence of several relative clauses in a
sequence, although such occurrences are rare. Never do more than two relative
clauses modify the same head noun. When a restrictive relative clause and a
nonrestrictive relative clause occur in a sequence, the former precedes the latter:
(807)
Ko te tagata Nanumea [ne tuu i te paalota], teelaa [ne
Foc the man Nanumea Pst stand at the election that Pst
faippati taaua ki ei i ssuaa aso].

‘[He’s] the man from Nanumea who ran for election, whom we talked
about the other day.’
Except in very special circumstances (e.g., in certain nominalized constructions),
no more than one possessive modifier, be it a possessive pronoun or a possessive
phrase, can occur in the same noun phrase. Similarly, only one article is allowed in
each noun phrase. Demonstrative adjectives can cooccur with homophonous relative
pronouns, but not with one another. Quantifiers, numerals, adverbials of all types,
intensifiers and downtoners, compounding elements of the type described in
1.2.5.2.10, and collective morphemes can cooccur with one another barring semantic
incompatibility. For example, the intensifier eiloa cannot modify a head noun already
modified by the downtoner fua, since they are antonyms of one another. Similarly,
a numeral cannot cooccur with the numeral interrogative word fia, since the latter
assumes that the former is unknown information.
1.2.5.4. Inadmissible combinations of modifier types
None of the categories described in 1.2.5.2 are incompatible with one another as
entire categories; for example, while some quantifiers cannot cooccur with
numerals (e.g., naai ‘a few’), others can (e.g., isi ‘other’), and hence one cannot
state that the entire category of quantifiers and the entire category of numerals
are mutually exclusive. However, certain noun modifiers of one type cannot occur
with certain modifiers of another type for the same reasons that members of the
same categories cannot cooccur with one another, i.e., for reasons of semantic
incompatibility. For example, the singular indefinite article se and the quantifier
naai ‘a few’ clash in terms of number, and thus cannot occur simultaneously in a
noun phrase. It is very difficult to provide a full list of inadmissible combinations
since such a list would be very extensive. Furthermore, most inadmissible
combinations are not entirely ruled out, in that they form a gradient from ‘more
acceptable’ to ‘less acceptable’.
1.2.5.5. Order of the head and modifiers
The order of many modifiers is not fixed, but rather depends on semantic scope.
Examples of modifiers with variable postnominal positions are the downtoner laa
(cf. 2.1.3.4.8) and manner demonstratives (cf. 2.1.2.5(d)), which are placed after the
last element of the noun phrase marked for downtoning and manner respectively.
The following illustrate the subtle differences in meaning that different positioning
can encode:

‘a short man just like this’

‘just a short man like this’
(810)
te tagata toetoe fua laa peenei

‘a man [who’s] just short like this’

1.3. COORDINATION
1.3.1. Characteristics of coordinate structures
1.3.1.1. Sentence coordination
Strategies for coordinating sentences fall into three categories:
•
additive coordination (i.e., ‘and’-coordination),
•
additive-adversative coordination (i.e., ‘and/but’-coordination),
•
and alternative coordination (i.e., ‘or’-coordination).
Adversative coordination (i.e., ‘but’-coordination) does not form a distinct structural
category.
1.3.1.1.1. Additive sentence coordination
The only coordinating strategy that is unambiguously and exclusively additive in
meaning consists in simply apposing the clauses into an unmarked sequence. Any
number of clauses can be coordinated by apposition, and their order is not
constrained by structural or semantic factors:

152
Syntax
(814)
[E mataku i te puusi], [e mataku i kimoa], [e mataku
Nps afraid at the cat Nps afraid at rat Nps afraid
i puaka].
at pig
‘[She]’s afraid of cats, [she]’s afraid of rats, [and she]’s afraid of pigs.’
When clauses are coordinated to one another by apposition, they frequently lose
their tense-aspect-mood marker.
(815)
[Iinu mukomuko], [iinu mukomuko], [a koo
drink sweet-husk-coconut drink sweet-husk-coconut and Inc
mmai nei o iinu pia]!
come now Cmp drink beer
‘[They]’ve been drinking sweet-husked coconuts [a child’s drink] all
along, and now [they] come along and [suddenly want to] drink beer!’
Sentence coordination by apposition frequently denotes temporal sequentiality (cf.
1.1.2.4.2.1(a)(i)) or temporal simultaneity (1.1.2.4.2.1(c)). The order of clauses in such
cases must be iconic of temporality or grounding, as discussed in 1.1.2.4.2.1. When
coordination by apposition does not denote temporality, its use tends to imply that
the referents of the various clauses have equal informational prominence. The
strategy is thus ideal in cases like (814), where the main purpose of the utterance is
to convey an overall effect of inclusiveness, to which the referent of each individual
clause in the sequence contributes equally.
1.3.1.1.2. Additive-adversative sentence coordination
The coordinating conjunction kae, or its allomorphs a and ka, is used for both the
additive and adversative coordination of sentences. Whether an additive or
adversative interpretation is assigned to the construction is determined through
context. Contrast the following:
(816)
[Tino i loto i te maneapa e toko uke], [a ko te uaa]!
people in inside in the maneaba Nps Num many and Foc the noisy
‘The maneaba is full of people, and they’re making so much noise!’
(817)
[Tino i loto i te maneapa e toko timomo fua], [a ko
people in inside in the maneaba Nps Num few just but Foc
te uaa]!
the noisy
‘There are just a few people inside the maneaba, but they’re making so
much noise!’
When additiveness needs to be emphasized or disambiguated from adversativeness,
the modifier foki ‘also, as well’ is postposed to the last verb of the coordinate
construction and forces an additive reading:
(818)
Au e fakamoemoe atu [kee fakamaagalo] [kae fakapuli foki nee
I Nps hope Dxs Sbj forgive and forget also Erg
koe oku sseega katoa].
you my wrongdoings all
‘I hope that you will forgive and forget all of my wrongdoings.’
No strategy is available to emphasize adversativeness or to disambiguate it from

additiveness. This fact suggests that the adversative interpretation of kae is more
basic than its additive interpretation. This is further supported by comparative
evidence: in East Uvean, a Polynesian language in which the additive sentence
coordinator (mo) differs in form from the adversative sentence coordinator (kae),
the adversative coordinator is a cognate of Tuvaluan kae (the same seems to be true
in Niuean; cf. Seiter 1980:84–85).
The coordinating conjunction kae and its allomorphs always occur in clause-
initial position in all but the first conjunct. If the conjunct it introduces is a verbal
clause, it can only be followed by a tense-aspect marker or the focus marker ko:
(819)
[Au e fia tusi ki ei], [kae ko au e maa i telotou kaaiga].
I Nps want write to Anp but Foc I Nps shy at their-3 family
‘I want to write to her, but I feel shy [doing so] because of her family.’
Thus unmarked preposed noun phrases are not allowed in verbal clauses introduced
by kae. But kae can be followed immediately by a noun phrase if the clause it
introduces is an equational clause or a part thereof (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)):
(820)
[A ia seeai se faifeau], [kae se aoao fua].
Cnt he Neg a pastor but a lay-preacher only
‘He is not a pastor, he’s just a lay preacher.’
See also 1.3.2.1 for instances of kae immediately followed by a case-marked noun
phrase after omission of the main verb of the second clause under identity with the
main verb of the first clause of the coordinate structure.
The allomorphic variation between kae and a is phonologically conditioned.
There is a strong tendency (which is however not an obligatory pattern) for the
form a to occur before words whose initial segment is /k/, i.e., most frequently
the perfect-aspect marker koo or the focus marker ko, or, less frequently, the future-
tense marker kaa, the conditional-mood marker kaa or the conditional and temporal
conjunction kaafai, the subjunctive-mood marker kee, or the continuous aspect
marker koi:
(821)

‘When a feast is being held and you’re going to make a speech, this is

‘It’s only on Nukulaelae that it’s done that way, other islands have

‘The traditional organization will disappear, and the governmental

‘And when the celebrations are over, he doesn’t have any status any

The allomorphic variation between kae and ka is conditioned by both stylistic and
morphological factors. On the one hand, kae is preferred to ka in more formal styles
of speaking. On the other hand, there is a tendency for kae to occur when the clause
it introduces is marked for nonpast or universal tense with the marker e. In such
cases, there is a strong tendency for the tense-aspect marker e to be deleted after
kae. Occasionally, in fast speech, kae is reduced to ae.
Both independent clauses and subordinate clauses may be additively-
adversatively coordinated in the same fashion. When two (or more) subordinate
clauses are additively-adversatively coordinated, the complementizer of the second
clause may be deleted under identity with the complementizer of the first clause,
as in the first example below, or each clause may have its own complementizer, as
in the subsequent example:
(825)

Nps used-to often Cmp draw his toddy and sing his song
‘He usually sings while tending his coconut-toddy spathes.’
(826)

Additively and adversatively coordinated sentences frequently denote events that
are either simultaneous or chronologically consecutive (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.1). Whether
simultaneity or consecutiveness is at play is disambiguated through context. Certain
constructions that are encoded as coordinate structures in some languages (e.g.,
English pseudocoordination ‘go and take a bath’) are encoded as o-subordinate
constructions in Tuvaluan (cf. 1.1.2.1). For a discussion of the coordination of
questions with other sentence types, see 1.1.1.2.2.1.5. See also the discussion of
‘double’ coordination in 1.3.1.6, in which the coordinator kae becomes restricted to
additiveness. For the use of kae with the concessive conjunct ui lea, see 1.1.2.4.2.8;
with the reinforcing additive conjuncts maise and aua ‘above all’, and the reinforcing
adversative conjunct tagaai ailaa ‘lo and behold’, see 1.8.7(b). For a discussion of
and-coordinated sentences with conditional meaning and imperative illocutionary
force, see 1.1.1.3.3(b).

Alternative sentence coordination is marked with the conjunctions io, me (and its
allomorphs ma and mo) and pe (and its allomorphs pa and po):

Pst go Cmp feed his pig in bush or Nps go to the

‘whether…or’ construction:
(830)

Occasionally, me or pe (particularly the latter) is found in clause-initial position in

1.1.1.2.1.3 for a discussion.
The attested forms of the alternative coordinator are io me, io pe, me, and pe. The
morpheme io cannot be used by itself. There are syntactic, semantic, and stylistic
differences between io me/io pe and me/pe: while pe/me can introduce both elements of
a ‘whether…or’ construction, io me/pe cannot introduce the first element; io me and io
pe both place greater emphasis on the fact that an alternative between options is
being presented (much like ‘either…or’ in English); and io me and io pe are more
frequent in oratorical styles of speaking and in writing. There is no difference in
referential meaning between (io) me and (io) pe, although the latter is slightly more
archaic than the former, and hence more frequent in the speech and writing of older
speakers and in formal contexts. The morphemes me and pe are also used as markers
of conditional coordination and as complementizers in various subordinate
constructions (cf. 1.1.2.4.2). The formal similarity between markers of yes-no questions,
conditional antecedents, and complementizers used in introducing quoted questions
is crosslinguistically well attested (Sadock and Zwicky 1985:183, 186).
The allomorphic variation between me/pe, ma/pa, and mo/po is phonologically
governed: ma and pa are optionally used if the first vowel of the following word is
/a/; and mo and po are optionally used if that vowel is /o/. This allomorphy is
often not indicated in written Tuvaluan: in most written texts, me and pe are the
invariant forms of these two words (although mo sometimes appears in writing,
probably because it is homophonous with the coordinator mo).

1.3.1.3. Coordination of nonsentential elements
The morpheme most frequently used in sentential additive-adversative
coordination, kae and its allomorphs, is also used for adjective and adverb
coordination, and for the coordination of subordinate clauses. A different morpheme,
mo, is used to coordinate noun phrases, although this coordinator is also used on
occasion to coordinate verb phrases. The same morphemes are used for the
alternative coordination of all syntactic categories.
1.3.1.3.1. Additive-adversative coordination of verb phrases
Verb phrases and verbs can be coordinated with kae and its allomorphs, the same
coordinating conjunction used for sentences:
(841)
E toetoe kae pakaakaa.
Nps short and thin
‘He’s short and thin.’
There is another strategy available for additive coordination. The coordinator mo,
otherwise associated with noun-phrase coordination (cf. 1.3.1.3.3), can be used to
coordinate verbs:
(842)
E malie mo fiafia au i ei.
Nps agree and happy I at Anp
‘I agree [with it] and am happy with it.’
Verbs in subordinate clauses of various types may be coordinated with mo:
(843)
Kae e iloa nee maaua kaati koo puli mo galo maaua ia
and Nps know Erg we-2-e perhaps Inc forgotten and lost we-2-e at
koulua.
you-2
‘And we have the feeling that you two have forgotten and lost track of

The modifier foki ‘also, as well’ can be used in this construction in the same way
and for the same purpose as described in 1.3.1.1.1–2:
(844)

fakataaunuugina foki a ttou fakamoemoega.

‘We pray together to the Lord that he may bring luck and fulfilment to

Verb coordination with mo is more archaic and rarer than coordination with kae.
In particular, the expressions in which it appears tend to be conventionalized.
Their order is frequently set; for example, the coordinate pairs malie mo fiafia

The strategies used for alternative sentence coordination (cf. 1.3.1.1.3) are also used

The same strategies used for alternative sentence coordination (cf. 1.3.1.1.3) are
also used for alternative noun-phrase coordination. Alternatively coordinated noun

(863)

the additive-adversative coordination of verbs and clauses with kae:

The same strategies used for alternative sentence coordination (cf. 1.3.1.1.3) are
also used for the alternative coordination of attributive adjectives:

1.3.1.4. Coordination and accompaniment
The comitative case marker and the preposition denoting accompaniment (cf.
2.1.1.4.4) are identical to one another and to the noun-phrase coordinator, a situation
that often results in ambiguity. For example, the noun phrase marked with mo in
the following can be interpreted as either a noun phrase coordinated to the previous
noun phrase or a comitative modifier of the clause:
(887)
Ne taumafai te toeaina mo te naai tamataene konaa o
Pst try the old-man and/with the few young-man those Cmp
fakaoti te gaaluega.
Cst+finish the work
‘The old man and those few young men tried to finish the work.’ or:
‘The old man tried with those few young men to finish the work.’
In the first instance, the subject of the first verb consists of the coordinated
construction te toeaina mo te naai tamataene konaa, in which case mo is a coordinator;
alternatively, the subject of the verb is te toeaina and the noun phrase marked with
mo is a comitative modifier of the verb. Such ambiguities are common, and arise
primarily when two noun phrases, the latter of which is marked with mo, appear
contiguously in a clause. The situation is further complicated by the fact that
coordinated noun phrases can be split in certain cases (cf. 1.3.1.7), yielding one
element in preverbal position and the other in postverbal position. Compare the
above with the following:
(888)

fakaoti te gaaluega.
