‘The old man and those few young men tried to finish the work.’ or:
‘The old man tried with those few young men to finish the work.’
The same ambiguity obtains in split coordinate structures, in which the two noun
phrases are not contiguous, and the ease with which one element can appear in
preverbal position does not constitute a reliable test for distinguishing between
coordinate structures and comitative noun phrases.
However, the two constructions behave differently in a number of contexts.
First, in noun-phrase coordination where the first noun phrase is a pronoun, the
referent of this pronoun must include the referent of the noun to which the
pronoun is coordinated (cf. 2.1.2.1.18). No such requirement applies to comitative

1.3.1.5. Structural parallelism in coordinate structures
Generally speaking, few constraints on structural parallelism are imposed on
coordinate structures, but the extent to which this is true depends in part on the
type of coordination involved. The coordinator kae is normally used only for
structurally parallel structures, although it is also used in certain fixed expressions
that involve structurally disparate elements.
1.3.1.5.1. Adjectives coordinated to participial constructions
There are no participial constructions in Tuvaluan.
1.3.1.5.2. Nouns coordinated to nominalized constructions
Nominalized constructions are treated like nouns for the purpose of coordination.
They may be coordinated to other nominalized constructions, as in the first of the
following examples, or to canonical nouns, as in the second example:
(898)
Ne tai lavelave maalosi foki loa te fano llei mo solo ki

mua te gaaluega.

‘The smooth running and progress of the work was very much
hindered.’

‘his speech and [the fact that] he raised that point’
Nominalized constructions can also be coordinated to clauses, as illustrated in
1.3.1.5.4–5.
1.3.1.5.3. Adverbials coordinated to one another
Only faka-adverbs can be coordinated to one another, as shown in 1.3.1.3.7. Only
prepositional phrases of the same type can be coordinated to one another, and only
some types of prepositional phrases can be coordinated at all (cf. 1.3.1.3.9).
1.3.1.5.4–5. Clauses and verbs coordinated to one another
Clauses of any type can be coordinated to one another, and verbs can be coordinated

the superlative morphemes maise and aua, to coordinate structurally disparate
elements. These constructions are described in 1.8.7(b).
1.3.1.6. Double additive coordination
Tuvaluan has an unusual additive sentence coordinate construction in which two
clauses are either kae-coordinated or simply apposed to one another, and a particular
noun phrase in the second (or last) clause is marked with the additive noun
coordinator mo:
(913)
[Ne ttoo vaiua], [agi foki mo te matagi].

‘It rained and the wind also blew.’

frequent than cases where the two clauses are apposed to each other, I will use the
label ‘double coordination’ to refer to these constructions. When kae appears in
doubly coordinated structures, it can only have additive meaning.

mo-marked noun phrase in the second clause is contrasted with a noun phrase in
the first clause. So coordinated sentences in which there is no noun phrase in the
first clause that can contrast with the mo-marked noun phrase in the second conjunct

1.3.1.7. Split noun-phrase coordination
Under certain circumstances, the second of two additively coordinated noun phrases
can become separated from the first noun phrase. The first of the following illustrates
the resulting split-coordinate structure, and the second provides the nonsplit
equivalent:
(925)

‘Pasene and my cousin now frequently go trawling-by-rowing
[together].’

coordinated structures in which the first element is a pronoun (cf. 2.1.2.1.18).
The phrase marked with mo in split-coordinate structures is not a comitatively
marked modifier, because the latter does not have a nonsplit equivalent. Compare
the two readings of the following example, the first and most natural of which
interprets the noun phrase marked with mo as a comitative modifier of the verb,
while the second interprets it as a member of a split coordinate structure:
(927)

must be both coreferential and identical in grammatical structure and function to

The first omission process is akin to what is traditionally recognized as gapping

coordinate structure if it is identical to the main verb of the first clause:

1.3.3. Omission of elements in other coordinated constructions
1.3.3.1. Omission of elements in noun-phrase coordination
Few elements of the noun-phrase can be readily deleted in either additive or
alternative noun-phrase coordination. Adjectives can be stranded by deletion under
identity in the mo-coordination of noun phrases, as shown in 1.3.1.3.5. Otherwise,
no readily identifiable pattern can be discerned.
1.3.3.2. Omission of elements in adjective-phrase coordination
As shown in 1.2.2.1, the adjective phrase is not a well defined category in the
language. The only clear case of identity under deletion in adjective-phrase
coordination concerns prepositional modifiers. The following is a possible case:
(941)

‘an amazing and frightening story for children’
In such cases, however, it not clear that one is dealing with adjective-phrase
coordination or simply the coordination of adjectives.

1.4. NEGATION
Both sentence negation and constituent negation are marked with the same set of
negative particles, all of which precede the negated element. Negators also precede
any bound adverbs and, in sentence negation, clitic pronouns when present. In
sentence negation, the negator follows tense-aspect markers, conjunctions, and
complementizers. The negator precedes prepositions in the negation of prepositional
phrases.
As in most Polynesian languages, negators are difficult to assign to any particular
part-of-speech category. Historical evidence suggests that Proto-Polynesian negators
were verbs, whose subject was the negated sentence (Chung 1970:41–54, Clark
1976b:85–109). However, there is no compelling evidence for treating most Tuvaluan
negators as verbs. Only one negator, the existential seeai, has clear verb-like
characteristics (cf. (d) below). An analysis of negators as auxiliaries, suggested by
the crosslinguistic propensity for negators to be auxiliary verbs (Payne 1985:212–
222), receives little language-internal support, as no class of auxiliaries is identifiable
in the language (cf. 1.16.3.2).
Following is a description of the form of the four basic negators. Their function
is described in the rest of the section.
(a) see
The negator see (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hee), an irregular reflex of Proto-Samoic-
Outlier *teqe (Clark 1976b:86–87), is unmarked with respect to tense, aspect, and
mood. For example, it can be used for past or nonpast situations, and can be marked
for a variety of aspectual and modal categories:
(942)

‘Why does he not go and try out his luck?’

situation or its consequences are still relevant at the temporal reference point of the
discourse. It is often translatable as ‘not yet’:

E isi te fakamoemoega mo te manatu kee seeai se mea

peenei e toe tupu i uta nei.
thus Nps again happen in bush this
‘It is [our] hope and opinion that such a thing will not happen again on
these shores.’
The negator seeai appears as a short answer to yes-no questions bearing on the
existence of an entity, the abundance of an entity, or a possessive relationship (cf.
1.1.1.2.4.2). It also appears in negative possessive sentences (cf. 1.10.1.1) and in
idioms expressing sentence emphasis (cf. 1.11.1.3.5).
1.4.1. Sentence negation
For the purpose of negation, two different types of verbal sentence need to be
distinguished, namely those with the existential verb isi or one of its alternative
forms, and all other verbal sentences (cf. 1.4.1.1 below). As shown in 1.4.1.2, the
patterns used in negating verbless sentences resemble patterns used in negating
sentence constituents.
1.4.1.1. Verbal sentence negation
Verbal sentences other than existential sentences and possessive sentences
constructed with the existential verb can be negated with see, seki, and saa, depending
on the tense, aspect, and mood of the sentence:
(960)
Kaati koo see kkafi eiloa tena kaitaua kia Kenitii.
perhaps Inc Neg contain indeed his anger to Kennedy
‘Perhaps he could not contain his anger for Kennedy [any longer].’
(961)
Au see naa lookoo maalamalama nee au ana pati.
I Neg quite quite understand Erg I his word
‘I didn’t quite understand what he said.’

(962)

ei.

‘I don’t know where he lives.’
(963)

the other child of his Neg do then from the woman that but Pst

young woman.’
Because it is least marked semantically, see is the most common negator in natural
discourse.
Whatever the negator may be, the tense-aspect-mood marker is commonly
omitted in negative sentences, particularly when the sentence is in the nonpast or
universal tense (i.e., would be marked with e if a tense-aspect-mood marker were
present). Negative formation does not require any changes to the sentence other
than the addition of a negative particle.
The verbs (i)a and (i)o ‘to belong to’ (alienable and inalienable possession
respectively; cf. 1.10.1.2) can be negated with either see or seeai and thus behave like
verbless sentences (cf. 1.4.1.2):
(964)
E seeai/see a Nukulaelae te paalota.
Nps Neg/Neg belong-to Nukulaelae the election
‘This is not Nukulaelae’s election.’
(965)
E seeai/see io te tino sala a te tiute o
Nps Neg/Neg belong-to the person accused Cnt the duty Cmp
fakatalitonu iaa ia e see ssee.

‘It is not the duty of the accused person to show that he is innocent.’
Nominalized clauses are negated in exactly the same way as finite clauses:
(966)
E nnofo tasi fua peelaa te poouliuli mo te see iloa tonu.
Nps stay together just thus the darkness and the Neg know right
‘The lack of enlightenment and the inadequacy of one’s knowledge go
together.’
As in many other languages (Payne 1985:199–200), the scope of sentence negation
is context-dependent, insofar as the same construction can be used to negate entire
propositions, or just the verb, or particular constituents. For example, when devoid
of a discourse or real-world context, the following negative sentence has different
interpretations:
(967)
Au seki fano ki Fiiti i ttausaga koo teka.
I Neg go to Fiji in the+year Inc roll
‘I didn’t go to Fiji last year. [Rather, I stayed here.]’
or: ‘It wasn’t Fiji I went to last year.’
or: ‘It wasn’t last year that I went to Fiji.’ etc.
There is a strong pragmatic tendency for sentential constituents that are placed
after the verb to be potential targets for sentence negation, while preverbal

grammatical role may be:
(968)
A masi seki kai nee au.

[implicature: Someone ate the cabin biscuits, but it wasn’t me.]

[implicature: I did something, but eating the cabin biscuits isn’t what I

1.4.1.2. Verbless sentence negation
Two basic patterns are used in negating noun-phrase constituents of equational
constructions (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)). First, if the noun phrase to be negated is indefinite, it
is also a predicate, and it can be negated simply by preposing see or seeai:
(970)
[See se mea ttau] [teenaa].
Neg a thing proper that
‘That’s not a proper thing [to do].’
(971)
[Seeai se mea ttau] [teenaa].
Neg a thing proper that
‘That’s not a proper thing [to do].’
Second, if the noun phrase to be negated is definite, it must be ko-focused and thus
predicated, and then it can be marked with either seeai or see:
(972)
Tena taina e see/seeai ko Timo, kae ko Luka.
his sibling Nps Neg/Neg Foc Timo but Foc Luka
‘His brother is not Timo, but Luka.’
In both cases, seeai is more commonly used than see. However, prescriptively minded
native speakers of Tuvaluan state that see, rather than seeai, should be used.
1.4.2. Constituent negation
There is no constituent negation per se in Tuvaluan, in that it is not possible to
negate a constituent without first restructuring the sentence so as to give the
constituent clausal properties.
The same two basic patterns that are used in negating constituents of equational
constructions (cf. 1.4.1.2) are used for noun-phrase constituent negation in verbal
sentences. First, if the noun phrase to be negated is indefinite, it can become the
subject complement of the negative verb seeai (see is not used for this purpose):
(973)
Seeai se tino e sili.
Neg a person Nps superior
‘No one wins.’
The negation of the indefinite argument of a verbal clause turns the sentence into a
complex sentence with the following structure:

[Neg[N[S]]]
where Neg functions as the main verb of the clause and S is relativized to the negated
noun phrase. That S is a relative clause is demonstrated by the fact that it has all the
surface features of a relative clause, and by the fact that advancement-to-possessive,
a process whose domain is relative-clause constructions (cf. 1.1.2.3.10), can apply.
For example, advancement-to-possessive can derive the second of the following
sentences from the first:
(974)
E iloa nee au me e seeai se mea [e matea nee koe].
Nps know Erg I Cmp Nps Neg a thing Nps see Erg you
‘I know you can’t see a thing.’
(975)
E iloa nee au me e seeai sau mea [e matea].
Nps know Erg I Cmp Nps Neg a-your thing Nps see
Second, if the noun phrase to be negated is definite, it must be ko-focused and
moved to a clause-initial position before being preposed with either seeai or see:
(976)
Seeai ko au ne loto kee fai peenaa te kaaiga.
Neg Foc I Pst desire Sbj do thus the family
‘It was not me who wished the family to behave thus.’
As with verbless-sentence negation, seeai is more commonly used than see in noun-
phrase negation, although prescriptively minded native speakers of Tuvaluan state
that see, rather than seeai, should be used.
In addition to the above two patterns, sentence negation may be used to negate
noun-phrase constituents in verbal sentences, since the scope of negation may extend
to the noun-phrase constituents of the sentence, particularly those in postverbal
positions:
(977)
Futi kolaa seki taa nee au, kae ne taa nee
banana-tree those Neg chop-down Erg I but Pst chop-down Erg
Muna.
Muna
‘I wasn’t the one who chopped down those banana trees, Muna did it.’
This strategy is often judged to be stylistically less convoluted than noun-phrase
negation. While the following equivalent sentence is grammatical, it is stylistically
awkward:
(978)
E see ko au ne taa nee au futi kolaa, kae ko
Nps Neg Foc I Pst chop-down Erg I banana-tree those but Foc
Muna.
Muna
Noun phrases marked for the absolutive case or the ergative case can never be
negated in situ:
(979)

banana-tree those Pst chop-down Neg/Neg Erg I but Pst
taa nee Muna.

thought of as instances of predicated prepositional phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.3). This

other types of prepositional phrases (see 1.3.1.3.9 for similar patterns associated

coordinated sentences:
(980)

you Nps go Neg Ben they-3 just but Ben our-3-i children Ben
taatou katoa.

(981)

Quirkily, prepositional phrases marked with the directional preposition ki can be
negated but not coordinated (cf. 1.3.1.3.9). However, when they are negated, they

(982)
E alofa tonu ki ana mokopuna, kae see ki ana tama.

When a prepositional phrase is negated, it is much more common for the negator
to modify the verb of the clause in which the prepositional phrase appears:
(983)

katoa.

Alternatively, the noun phrase embedded in the prepositional phrase can be moved
to a clause-initial ko-focused position, where it can be negated as a regular noun-
phrase constituent:
(984)
Au ne kaitaua kiaa Teika, kae see ko Teleke.

‘I was angry at Teika, not [at] Teleke.’
Predicative adjectives are indistinguishable from regular verbs, and therefore can be
negated as verbs. Verbal attributive adjectives (cf. 1.16.4) can be negated with see:
(985)
Ioane se tagata see aakoga.
Ioane a man Neg learn
‘Ioane is an unschooled person.’
The same applies to quantifiers, which function as either predicative adjectives
(and hence verbs) or attributive verbal adjectives:

(988)

[lit.: ‘The people who went were not many.’]

(990)

Adverbs cannot be negated either. Verb-modifying adverbs are negated by negating
the entire clause:
(992)
See faipati faka-Ppaalagi, kae faka-Siaamani.

‘He is not speaking English, but German.’
One preverbal aspectual adverb, tii (or its allomorphs tuu and sii), almost always
modifies negated verbs (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(g)).
There are no inherently negative quantifiers (e.g., ‘nothing’) and adverbials (e.g.,
‘never’). Notions that are conveyed with the help of negative quantifiers and
adverbials in other languages are encoded in Tuvaluan through clausal constructions
with the existential verb seeai and indefinitely marked generic nouns like koga ‘place’,
mea ‘thing’, tino ‘person’, and taimi ‘time’:
(993)
Seeai se isi koga aka e gali peenei ei a manu.
Neg a another place in-addition Nps nice thus Anp Cnt bird
‘Nowhere is bird meat as good as here.’
(994)
Seeai ne tino i loto i telotou fale.
Neg some people in inside in their-3 house
‘There’s nobody inside their house.’
In keeping with the relative paucity of inflectional morphological processes, there
are no processes of derivational negation comparable to processes that yield forms
like ‘useless’, ‘distrust’, and ‘nonpast’ in English.

1.4.3. Multiple negatives
Most sentences in natural discourse have only one negative element. The possibility
of more than one negative element occurring in the same construction is greatly
reduced by the fact that this language does not have negative quantifiers and
adverbials. When two negators are found in the same sentence, they are usually
part of two different clauses, and one is usually a sentence negator and the other a
constituent negator. The result is always semantically positive:
(995)
Seeai se mea e see mafai nee ia o fai.
Neg a thing Nps Neg can Erg he Cmp do
‘There is nothing he can’t do.’
No instance was found in natural discourse of three or more negators in the same
sentence, and no such example was judged pragmatically acceptable or even
processable.
1.4.4. Negation of coordinated elements
The scope of negators cannot reach beyond the boundaries of a clause. When more
than one clause in a coordinate construction is negated, each clause must be negated
separately:
(996)
[See tii koukou] kae [see tii fano ki te aakoga].
Neg often bathe and Neg often go to the school
‘[He] never washes and never goes to school.’
Coordinated constituents can be negated with a single negator if constituent
coordination is used (cf. 1.3.1.3):
(997)
E see ko Ioopu mo Pule ne olo o pei tili.
Nps Neg Foc Ioopu and Pule Pst go Cmp cast fishing-net
‘It’s not Ioopu and Pule that went net-fishing.’
If only one coordinate is negated, clause coordination must be used (cf. 1.3.1.1):
(998)
E see ko Ioopu ne fano o pei tili, kae ko Pule.
Nps Neg Foc Ioopu Pst go Cmp cast fishing-net but Foc Pule
‘It’s not Ioopu, but Pule, that went net-fishing.’
In no case do the negator and the coordinator combine into a single form.
1.4.5. Negation in subordinate clauses
Negation is marked in exactly the same fashion in independent, superordinate,
and subordinate clauses. In all cases, the negator must mark the negated element
directly. In complex sentences, the subordinate clause cannot be negated by a negator
in the superordinate clause. The negation of a subordinate clause and the negation
of a superordinate clause yield different results:
(999)
E maasani o see ppusi.
Nps used-to Cmp Neg smoke
‘He is used to not smoking.’
[i.e.: ‘He is used to doing without smoking.’]
(1000)
E see maasani o ppusi.
Nps Neg used-to Cmp smoke

[i.e.: ‘He does not know how to smoke, or he is not in the habit of
smoking.’]
1.4.6. Subordinators with inherently negative meaning
Several subordinators have inherently negative meanings or implicatures. These
include the precautionary-mood marker maa and the precautionary conjunction
moo aa ‘lest’, and the conjunction manuu ‘while’.
 
(a) Precautionary-mood marker maa
The precautionary-mood marker maa (and its allomorphs mana, mane, and mani)
has an inherently negative meaning roughly equivalent in meaning (but not
stylistic markedness) to English ‘lest’ when it introduces a subordinate clause (cf.
2.1.3.4.10–11):
(1001)
Koe naa saa pati maasei iaa koe [maa maalaia].
you there Neg word bad Cmp you Prc damned
‘Don’t use swear words, lest you be damned.’
As a mood marker on verbs of independent clauses, maa marks hortatory mood,
also with an inherently negative meaning (cf. 2.1.3.2.1 (d) for further discussion):
(1002)
Ttamaliki maa too!
the+child lest fall
‘[Be careful!] The child is going to fall down!’
or: ‘Do something so that the child doesn’t fall down!’
(b) Precautionary-mood marker moo aa
The complex conjunction moo aa marks precautionary mood in subordinate clauses
(cf. 2.1.3.4.11). It is optionally preposed to the subjunctive conjunction kee (cf.
1.1.2.4.2(b)) and is followed by a tense-aspect marker, usually the nonpast universal
e or the precautionary maa:
(1003)
Laatou ne fakaffiti katoa moo aa laatou maa ppei ki te fale puipui.
they-3 Pst get-away all Prc they-3 Prc throw to the jail
‘They all scrambled away so as not to be thrown in jail.’
(1004)
Au e fano leemuu moo aa e matea nee ia au.
I Nps go quiet Prc Nps see Erg she I
‘I’m going to go quietly so as not to be seen by her.’
(c) manuu ‘while, before’
The temporal conjunction manuu ‘while, before’ expresses the fact that the event
described by the main clause should take place before the event described by the
temporal clause comes to a close (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.1(b)), and thus provides an inherently
negative temporal opposition between the referent of the main clause and the
referent of the subordinate clause:
(1005)
Naa fano laa o koukou manuu seki poo!
do go then Cmp bathe before Neg night
‘Do go and take your bath before night falls!’
(1006)
Taatou kaa olo o pei tili manuu koi laofie.
we-3-i Fut go Cmp cast fishing-net while still clear
‘Let’s go fishing while the weather is still clear.’

1.4.7. Other lexemes and constructions with negative meaning
In addition to the structures overviewed in the following, see the following sections
for a discussion of topics relevant to negativity: 2.1.1.4 (negative nonlocal semantic
functions), 2.1.3.3.1 (c) (perfect-aspect marker kai, which only appears in questions
and negative sentences); and 2.1.3.3.2.1(g) (iterative adverbs tii, tuu, and sii, which
appear most frequently in negative clauses).
(a) ikaai
The negative particle ikaai ‘no’ (or sometimes kaai in informal contexts) can only be
used in short answers to yes-no questions:
(1007)
K: Te niu teelaa ne kkati nee koutou?
the coconut-tree that Pst cut Erg you-3
‘Were you the ones that cut down that coconut tree?’
F: Ikaai. Ne kkati nee saa Toomu.
no Pst cut Erg group Toomu
‘No. Toomu and his gang cut it down.’
For a discussion of the use of ikaai and of its alternation with seeai in certain answer
types, see 1.1.1.2.4.2.
(b) see taumate ‘probably’, ailoga ‘unlikely’
The verb taumate, a borrowing from Samoan, can only be used in the negative, with
the meaning of ‘probably, it’s not unlikely’ (it can also appear as a positive adverb
in one compound, tuku taumate ‘guess wildly’. In complete sentences, it functions
as the verb of a superordinate clause, modified by the clause denoting the event
being put into question:
(1008)
E see taumate koo ne matea nee koe te vaegaa aamioga teenaa.
Nps probable Prf see erg you the kind+of behaviour that
‘You probably have witnessed this kind of behaviour.’
The hedge ailoga ‘probably not, [it’s] unlikely, [it’s] doubtful’, also a borrowing
from Samoan, can appear as the verb of the superordinate clause of complex
constructions:
(1009)
Ailoga katoa tamaliki e manuia i te sukega.
unlikely all children Nps lucky on the exam
‘The children are unlikely to all pass the exam.’
No tense-aspect-mood marker generally appears with ailoga, but when one does it
is always the universal-tense marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1.1). Ailoga can govern raising, as
shown in 1.1.2.7. For examples of the use of see taumate and ailoga in short answers
to questions, see 1.1.1.2.4.2.
(c) Negative exhortative moderator ata too
The compound ata too (probably from ata ‘properly, in moderation’ and too ‘too
[much]’) is used in imperative sentences only with the meaning of ‘don’t [act] in an
excessive manner, [act] in a moderate manner’:
(1010)
Ata too ita maalosi koe ki ttamaa, i te mea koi fooliki fua!
don’t angry strongly you to the+child because still small just
‘Don’t get too cross with that child, he is still very young!’
(d) aunoa, ausagi, ausage ‘lack, without’
The word aunoa ‘lack, without’, a borrowing from Samoan, can have a variety of

indefinite, although not obligatorily so. The subject can be a noun phrase that refers
to the entity whose nonexistence is being expressed (as in the first example below),
or to the entity that lacks the referent denoted by the object:
(1011)

‘There isn’t a soul in the maneaba.’
(1012)

‘We don’t have a single fish.’
Aunoa can also function as an attributive adjective. The object is also marked with

(1013)

(1015)

This word is much less frequent than aunoa and less well integrated into the

(e) tapu
The verb tapu, in its unmarked usage, means ‘forbidden, sacred, taboo’.11 Particularly
in informal contexts, it can be used as an inherently negative expression to convey
the fact that a particular event never takes place. In addition, the entity responsible
for the event not taking place (but not necessarily the speaker) has strong feelings
about the fact that the event should not take place. The verb that described the
event may be nominalized, in which case it functions as the subject of tapu; it may
be subordinated through apposition to the clause to tapu; or it may be marked with
maa (or one of its allomorphs) for precautionary mood:
(1018)
Kaa fano au i luga i te Niivaga, tapu te koukou, koukou

loa au i Funaafuti.

‘When I go on the M.V.Nivaga, I never take a bath, I [only] take a bath
[when I reach] Funafuti.’

you Inc forbidden you Nps again speak in inside in the maneaba
o te fenua].
of the island-community
‘You are forbidden from speaking again [publicly] in(side) the island
community’s maneaba.’
Alternatively, the subject of tapu can be a noun phrase denoting the entity which
should never materialize, modified by a possessive pronoun, as in the following:
(1020)
E tapu kkii loa sau tusi kiaa Vave.
Nps forbidden very indeed your letter to Vave
‘You are not to write to Vave.’
[lit.: ‘A letter of yours to Vave is strictly forbidden.’]

intensifying adverb kkii ‘very’:
(1021)

and Foc I in inside in our-3-e family forbidden very a-my word
e fai peelaa, “koutou paalota ki ttinoo, paalota ki ttinoo!”

1.5. ANAPHORA
The following discussion deals only with ‘free’ anaphoric phenomena, i.e., anaphoric
relationships that are not the result of a syntactic process. Thus this section does
not cover zero and pronominal anaphors associated with the movement or deletion
of a noun phrase out of particular syntactic slots: across clauses, for example, in the
formation of relative clauses (cf. 1.1.2.3) and question structures (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2),
raising (cf. 1.1.2.7), or equi-deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6); within clauses, in the formation of
imperatives (cf. 1.1.1.3) or in the movement of noun phrases to preverbal position
(cf. 1.2.1.2.6(a)).

Means of expressing anaphora include deletion, ordinary personal pronouns,
ordinary personal pronouns marked for reflexivity, one special anaphoric pronoun,
and ‘dummy’ nouns that can appear as anaphors in conversation.

Anaphora is never marked on the verb. Some intransitive verbs and causative verbs
agree in number with their subject and their direct object respectively (cf. 2.1.3.6.1),
but agreement takes place whether or not the triggering noun phrase has been
deleted from the clause (cf. 2.1.3.6.3).

1.5.1.5. Special anaphoric pronoun
The anaphoric pronoun ei, whose morphological features are discussed in 2.1.2.1.7,
has a broad range of anaphoric functions. Some of these functions are governed by
syntactic factors, while others are better described as discourse-governed. It may

function as either a bound anaphor or as a free pronoun. In each case, it refers to a
different range of referents. As a bound anaphor in such constructions as relative

person, and degree of animacy; as a free pronoun, it is anaphoric of third-person
referents, either human or nonhuman, either animate or inanimate, and usually,
but not obligatorily, singular (cf. 2.1.2.7 and cross references below). In both its

as discussed presently and further elaborated elsewhere (see below for cross

1.5.2. Domains of anaphora
Following Halliday and Hasan (1976:14–17), the terms ‘anaphoric’ and ‘cataphoric’
are used here to refer to left-to-right and right-to-left relationships between anaphors
and their antecedents respectively. Virtually all anaphor-antecedent relationships
in Tuvaluan are anaphoric.
1.5.2.1. Within the clause
The most common type of anaphoric relation within a single clause consists of
pronominal or anaphoric traces that index noun phrases that have been moved by
a grammatical process like interrogative-word movement (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2), movement
to preverbal position (cf. 1.2.1.2.6), or dislocation (cf. 1.11.2.1.6). The second most
common type consists of pronouns marked for reflexivity, discussed in 1.6. Finally,
a possessive pronoun can have an antecedent in the same clause:
(1052)

Cnt Niu Nps fan often Erg his spouse at night
‘Niui often gets fanned by hisi wife at night.’
(1053)

‘Niui often gets fanned by Savalij at night with hisi/herj new fan.’
No constraint is placed on the grammatical function of either the antecedent or the
noun phrase in which the possessive pronoun appears. However, cataphoric
relationships are not allowed with possessive pronouns, and the antecedent always
precedes the possessive pronoun, regardless of the syntactic functions of the noun
phrases. Thus the only way that the highlighted possessive pronoun in the following
example can be interpreted as coreferential with the indirect object is if the referent
is topicalized in the previous discourse, in which case the indirect object is not the
antecedent of the possessive pronoun, rather it merely has the same referent:
(1054)

Clause-internal coreferential relationships involving possessive pronouns and
possessive noun phrases are further discussed in 1.6.1.
1.5.2.2. Between coordinate structures
No special pattern of anaphora is associated with coordinate structures. Anaphoric
relationships between coordinated clauses resemble anaphoric relationships
between separate sentences. For examples, see 1.3.2.1.

expressed with zero pronouns or overt personal pronouns, or the anaphoric pronoun

pronouns and overt personal pronouns overlap to some extent, although not
completely so, as will be shown presently.

superordinate or the subordinate clause. However, patterns of coreference between

clause can have as an antecedent the subject of the superordinate clause:
(1063)
E manako te toeaina teelaai [kee ffoo nee tena mokopuna
Nps wish the old-man that Sbj massage Erg his grandchild
øi/j].
he
‘That old man wants his grandchild to massage [him].’
or: ‘That old man wants his grandchild to massage [someone else].’
(1064)

Nps wish the old-man that Sbj massage Erg his grandchild
a iai/j].
Cnt he
‘That old man wants his grandchild to massage [him].’
or: ‘That old man wants his grandchild to massage [someone else].’
However, there is a tendency to interpret the second reading of (1063), in which the
zero pronoun is not coreferential with the noun phrase in the superordinate clause,
as the most natural; while in (1064), the first reading, in which the personal pronoun
is coreferential with the noun phrase in the superordinate clause, is the most natural.
The following generalization thus emerges: zero pronouns in subordinate clauses

tend to be bound from outside the sentence, while overt personal pronouns tend to
be bound from within the subordinate clause, if the latter contains a candidate
antecedent. This tendency becomes an obligatory pattern in the case of zero
pronouns in subject position in the subordinate clause.
As shown in 1.1.2.1.2(c), the two subordinate structures I call o-subordinate and
kee-subordinate clauses respectively (with reference to the form of the
complementizer associated with each type) differ in terms of the binding patterns
they allow for zero anaphors. In o-subordinate clauses that are not subordinated to
raising verbs, one non-oblique noun phrase must be coreferential with the
superordinate clause. These patterns have consequences for the binding relations
between zero pronouns, full pronouns, and their antecedents in each case, as
illustrated in 1.1.2.1.2(c).
There is also a difference in the binding patterns associated with personal
pronouns and the anaphoric pronoun ei in complex constructions. As described in
1.5.1.5, ei appears in oblique positions in the clause, and if it refers to a human
entity it is functionally equivalent to a personal pronoun marked for oblique case.
However, in subordinate clauses that are not raising contexts, ei differs from personal
pronouns in that it cannot have an antecedent in the superordinate clause, unlike
personal pronouns, for which such an antecedent is preferred although not required.
Contrast:

‘Tutai explained to Fipej that they are angry at heri/j/k.’

constructions, the binding differences between personal and anaphoric pronouns
apply to most (but not all) subordinate constructions, including constructions with
paratactic qualities like reported speech complements, as in the above examples.
However, the restriction on the binding of ei does not apply to subordinate
constructions that are very loosely subordinated to the superordinate clause, such
as temporal or conditional clauses:
(1067)
Ioopui kaa kalaga nee au [manafai e fia faipati koe ki eii].
Iopu Fut call Erg I if Nps want speak you to Anp
‘I’ll call Iopu if you want to speak to him.’
1.5.2.4. Between different subordinate clauses
No special pattern is associated with anaphoric relationships between different
subordinate clauses, which are quite rare in natural discourse. The following is an
example of an anaphoric relationship between the direct object of an o-subordinate
clause and the indirect object of a conditional clause:

I Fut go Cmp wake-up Iopu if Nps want speak you
ki eii].

‘I’ll go and wake Iopu up if you want to speak to him.’

the most deeply embedded clause of the following sentence cannot have as an

and is thus not targeted by the binding restriction):

As in other syntactic contexts, cataphoric relationships are not allowed between
different subordinate clauses.
1.5.2.5. Between different sentences
All anaphoric strategies described in 1.5.1 can be used between different sentences.
Virtually all anaphor-antecedent relationships are anaphoric rather than cataphoric.
1.5.3. Anaphoric elements next to complementizers
The only anaphoric elements that can appear immediately after complementizers
are clitic pronouns. No restriction is placed on such occurrences, as illustrated in
2.1.2.1.1.5(a).
1.6. REFLEXIVES
The discussion in 1.6.1.4 and 1.6.2–9 covers canonical reflexive constructions, i.e.,
constructions that resemble, in structure and meaning, reflexive constructions in
other languages. When removed from their discourse context, the interpretation
of these constructions is ambiguous between a reflexive and an emphatic,
nonreflexive reading. Furthermore, they are rare in natural discourse. The
discussion in 1.6.1.5 concerns ways of circumventing reflexive constructions,
which are also the most natural ways of expressing reflexive relationships in
nonelicited discourse. For a brief discussion of causatives with reflexive meaning,
see 2.1.3.1.3(a).
1.6.1. Means of expressing reflexivity
1.6.1.1–3. Reflexive pronouns and verbal affixes
There are no special reflexive pronouns and no reflexive verbal affixes.

1.6.1.4. Other means
In their grammatically unmarked form, reflexive relations are expressed with
ordinary pronouns in target position, or a possessive pronoun if the target is
marked for possession. In addition, the postposed intensifying adverb (ei)loa often
appears as a modifier of the verb, as a modifier of the antecedent, or as a modifier
of the target:
(1070)
Ne taa eiloa nee Lusi a ia.
Pst strike indeed Erg Lusi Cnt he
‘Lusi killed himself/him.’
(1071)
Ne taa nee Lusi loa a ia.
Pst strike Erg Lusi indeed Cnt he
‘Lusi killed himself/? him.’
(1072)
Ne taa nee Lusi a ia loa.
Pst strike Erg Lusi Cnt he indeed
‘Lusi killed himself/?? him.’
Among the various forms of the intensifying adverb, loa and, in informal speech
loo, are the most common in reflexive constructions.
Because there is always the possibility that the sentence will be interpreted as a
nonreflexive sentence and loa as a straightforward intensifying adverb, the norm is
for loa to appear in at least two positions in the sentence. In addition, other emphatic
adverbs and adverbials like foki, literally ‘also’, are commonly added to reinforce
reflexive readings. Thus the following versions of the above examples are clearly
reflexive, in contrast to the earlier versions:
(1073)
Ne taa foki loa nee Lusi a ia loa.
Pst strike also indeed Erg Lusi Cnt he indeed
(1074)
Ne taa nee Lusi loa a ia loa.
Pst strike Erg Lusi indeed Cnt he indeed
If there is only one instance of loa in the clause, the reflexive reading is most
ambiguous if the adverb modifies the verb (hence the two equally idiomatic readings
of (1070)), and least ambiguous if the adverb modifies the last nominal constituent
involved in the reflexive relationship, whatever its syntactic role may be. Thus
(1072) and the following, both of which have the same meaning, are more idiomatic
as reflexive sentences rather than as nonreflexive sentences with an intensifying
adverb:
(1075)
Ne taa a Lusi nee ia loa.
Pst strike Cnt Lusi Erg he indeed
When the target is a possessive phrase, it may be expressed in one of two ways.
Least ambiguously, the target is expressed as a personal pronoun marked for
possession (cf. 2.1.2.4.5–6) and modified by loa:
(1076)
Lusi ne oko mai i te vaka o ia loa.
Lusi Pst reach Dxs in the canoe of he indeed
‘Lusii arrived in hisi/??j canoe.’
More ambiguously, the target may be expressed as a possessive pronoun and the
noun phrase it modifies may be marked with loa:

204
Syntax
(1077)
Lusi ne oko mai i tena vaka loa.
Lusi Pst reach Dxs in his canoe indeed
‘Lusii arrived in hisi/j canoe.’
However, there is doubt as to whether possessive-phrase targets of either type are
really reflexive targets, rather than simply coreferential with another noun phrase
in the clause. Indeed, antecedents and their possessive targets need not be clause-
bound and possessive targets need not follow their antecedents, and thus these
sentences are not subject to two constraints that other reflexive sentences obey (see
1.6.2 and 1.6.5 respectively for a discussion of these constraints). For example, in
the following, the possessive-pronoun target precedes the antecedent, and a
coreferential reading is still possible:
(1078)
Te aavaga a ia loa ne taa nee Losa.
the spouse of he indeed Pst strike Erg Losa
‘Heri/j husband was killed by Losai.’
In natural discourse, reflexive sentences are very rare, and situations that are
expressed as reflexive constructions in languages like English are phrased otherwise
in Tuvaluan (cf. 1.6.1.5). The only type of construction akin to reflexives commonly
encountered in natural discourse denotes actions or states that are performed or
experienced ‘by oneself’, which are expressed with a target marked with the locative
preposition i, or more rarely the directional preposition ki. When the referent of the
antecedent is singular, the verb or the target is frequently modified by the adverbial
toko tasi (loa) ‘alone, by him/herself’, made up of the human classifier toko (cf.
2.1.6.5.1(a)) and the numeral tasi ‘one’ optionally modified by the intensifier loa:
(1079)
Te loomatua koo nofo i te fale iaa ia toko tasi loa.
the old-woman Inc stay in the house at her Num one indeed
‘The old woman is by herself inside the house.’
(1080)
E kkai eiloa a laatou kiaa laatou.
Nps eat indeed Cnt they-3 to they-3
‘They eat by themselves.’
However, whether these constructions are truly reflexives or not is open to doubt.
Indeed, unlike canonical reflexive constructions (cf. 1.6.3–4), they allow the
antecedent to be expressed as a possessive modifier of the direct object:
(1081)
Ne usu tena vii iaa ia loa toko tasi loa.
Pst sing his song-of-praise at he indeed Num one indeed
‘He sang a song of praise by himself.’
1.6.1.5. Means of circumventing reflexivity
A number of constructions are used to denote situations that are expressed as
reflexive constructions in languages like English.
(a) Inherently reflexive verbs
A number of verbs have an inherently reflexive meaning, i.e., they denote situations
that are performed by an entity onto itself. Such is the case of koukou ‘wash oneself,
take a bath’, which cannot mean ‘wash [someone else]’ unless it is first transitivized
with the causative prefix faka- (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)):

(1082)
Tamaliki ne koukkou i te tooga o te vaiua.
child Pst wash-oneself in the fall+Nom of the rain
‘The children washed themselves in the rain.’
(b) Causative prefixation
Some verbs acquire inherently reflexive meanings when marked for causativity
with the prefix faka- (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)). In these situations, the causative form of a
verb X can be understood as meaning ‘causing to X oneself’:
(1083)
A Tetuki koo fakasausau.
Cnt Tetuki Inc Cst+perfume
‘Tetuki is perfuming [herself]/is being perfumed/? is perfuming
[someone].’
The target need not be expressed overtly. If it is not, as in (1083), the sentence is
potentially ambiguous in two ways. First, the overt noun phrase can be interpreted
as the direct object of the verb and the sentence as having a zero pronoun as subject;
such is the case of the first alternative reading of (1083). Second, the overt noun
phrase can be interpreted as the subject and the sentence as having a zero pronoun
as direct object; such is the case of the second alternative reading of (1083). The
reflexive reading can be disambiguated by adding an overt target and intensifying
adverbs:
(1084)
A Tetuki koo fakasausau loa nee ia a ia loa.
Cnt Tetuki Inc Cst+perfume indeed Erg she Cnt she indeed
‘Tetuki is perfuming herself/* is being perfumed/* is perfuming
[someone].’
One-argument constructions are most naturally interpreted as reflexive when the
argument is proposed; when the argument is postposed, both reflexive and
nonreflexive interpretations are equally idiomatic.
Most inherently reflexive causative verbs also have nonreflexive causative uses,
while a few do not. The verb fakasausau does:
(1085)
A Tetuki koo fakasausau nee ana tama.
Cnt Tetuki Inc Cst+perfume Erg her children
‘Tetuki is being perfumed by her children.’
In contrast, fakamate, literally ‘cause to die’ and with the idiomatic meaning of
‘commit suicide’, cannot be used as a transitive nonreflexive verb or as a transitive
reflexive verb with an overt target:
(1086)
A Lusi ne fakamate.
Cnt Lusi Pst Cst+die
‘Lusi killed [himself]/* Lusi was killed.’
(1087)
* A Lusi ne fakamate nee tino / nee ia a ia loa.
Cnt Lusi Pst Cst+die Erg person Erg he Cnt he indeed
(‘Lusi was killed by people/by himself.’)
The verb fakamate is thus further down the path towards relexicalization than more
ordinary causatives (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)).
Whether or not they can also be used transitively, most reflexive causative verbs
are intransitive. For example, their absolutively marked argument can be advanced-
to-possessive, a process which only subjects can undergo (cf. 1.1.2.3.10), and since
the absolutive case marks subjects of intransitive verbs or direct objects, this

(1088)

‘It was in eighty-one that Lusi killed himself.’
(1089)

A few causative verbs can have an inherently reflexive interpretation, but are also
transitive. One such case is fakamaa ‘put (someone, oneself) to shame’. Derived
from the intransitive maa ‘ashamed’, the use of which is illustrated in (1090), this
causative form can have one of two interpretations, as shown in (1091):
(1090)

I Inc ashamed
‘I am ashamed.’
(1091)
Au koo fakamaa nee toku taina.
I Inc Cst+ashamed Erg my sibling
‘My brother is making me ashamed [of myself].’
or: ‘My brother is making me ashamed [of him, of someone else].’
The reflexive interpretation of (1091) is more pragmatically acceptable than its
nonreflexive interpretation.
Whether a causative form is obligatorily or potentially transitive or not does not
depend in any clear sense on the type of root from which the causative verb is
derived. Causative verbs that are derived from nouns (e.g., fakasausau ‘perfume’,
from the noun sausau ‘perfume’) allow both reflexive and transitive usages.
However, verb-derived causative verbs are idiosyncratic. For example, fakamate
‘kill oneself’, derived from the intransitive verb mate ‘die’, is obligatorily intransitive,
but fakataapea ‘set adrift’, from the intransitive root taapea ‘adrift’, can be used either
as an intransitive reflexive or a transitive nonreflexive verb:12
(1092)
A Lusi koo fano o fakataapea.
Cnt Lusi Inc go Cmp Cst+adrift
‘Lusi went to set himself adrift.’

A Lusi koo fakataapea nee te fenua.

‘Lusi was set adrift by the island community.’

(1094)

I Fut go Cmp Cst+rest
‘I am going to take a rest.’
(1095)

Inc Cst+appear Dxs now a illness new
‘A new illness is rearing its head.’

1.6.2. Clause-boundedness of reflexivity
The following discussion concerns only canonical reflexive constructions. In simple
and coordinate sentences, the antecedent and the target of a reflexive relationship
must be in the same clause. Thus, in the following coordinate construction, the
reflexive target must be coreferential with Vave, and cannot refer to Lusi:
(1102)
[Lusi ne taua mo Vave] kae [taa loa nee Vave a ia
Lusi Pst fight with Vave and strike indeed Erg Vave Cnt he
loa].
indeed
‘Lusii had an argument with Vave and Vave killed himself/*himi.’
Similarly, in complex clauses, the antecedent and the target must be in the same
clause. In the following, the target can only be coreferential with Vave:
(1103)
Lusi e manako [kee taa loa nee Vave a ia loa].
Lusi Nps wish Sbj strike indeed Erg Vave Cnt he indeed
‘Lusii wants Vave to kill himself /*himi.’

illustrates a reflexive in a me-subordinate construction (cf. 1.1.2.1.3) and (1105) a
reflexive in a relative clause. In each case, the antecedent can only be the noun

1.6.3–4. Constraints on the antecedent
Subjects of either intransitive or transitive verbs can function as antecedents, and
are virtually the only grammatical category that can do so. In most examples
provided so far, the antecedents are subjects of transitive verbs. Following is an
example of the subject of an intransitive verb functioning as an antecedent:
(1106)
Tamaafine, maatou e maannako ki ne gatu moo maatou
young-woman we-3-e Nps want to some clothing Ben we-3-e
loa!
indeed
‘Young women, we want some clothes for ourselves!’
In one restricted context, a direct object can function as the antecedent. This can
only occur if the target is the subject of the clause:
(1107)
Ne taa loa a Vave nee ia loa.
Pst strike indeed Cnt Vave Erg he indeed
‘Vave killed himself.’
The antecedent may be a full noun phrase or a pronoun, as illustrated by all reflexive
examples provided so far. It can also be a zero pronoun, although a zero pronoun
can only function as reflexive antecedent if its referent is highly topical in the
discourse. For example, the following reflexive sentence can function as the answer
to a question such as ‘Who did Lusi kill?’ or ‘What did Lusi do to himself?’, but
would probably not occur in isolation:
(1108)
Ne taa loa ø a ia loa.
Pst strike indeed he Cnt he indeed
‘He killed himself.’
The antecedent cannot be expressed as the possessive modifier of the direct object,
in the same manner that the subject of nonreflexive transitive clauses is commonly
expressed (cf. 2.1.1.2.2(c)). Thus Niu in the following cannot be interpreted as the
antecedent of the indirect object:
(1109)
Ne lafo loa te tusi a Niu kiaa ia loa.
Pst mail indeed the letter of Niu to he indeed
‘Niui’s letter was sent to himj.’
(* ‘Niu mailed the letter to himself.’)

Antecedents are very frequently topicalized or ko-focused. As discussed in 1.11 and
1.12, both processes normally leave a pronominal trace in the original location of
the noun phrase if the latter is the subject of a transitive clause, and do not leave a
trace if the noun phrase is the subject of an intransitive verb or a direct object. In
reflexive constructions, this pattern is slightly different, in that the trace is obligatory
if the moved noun phrase is the subject of a transitive verb. Thus (1110) has a reflexive
reading because the trace is present, but (1111) cannot be reflexive because the trace
is absent:
(1110)
A Niu ne taa nee in a ia loa.
Cnt Niu Pst strike Erg he Cnt he indeed
‘Niu killed himself.’
(1111)
A Niu ne taa a ia loa.
Cnt Niu Pst strike Cnt he indeed
‘Niui indeed killed himj.’
If the antecedent is the subject of an intransitive verb or a direct object and it is
moved, it frequently leaves an absolutively marked pronominal trace. Sentences in
which it does not are less likely to be interpreted as reflexive constructions and are
less pragmatically acceptable as such. Compare:
(1112)
A Niu e alofa fua a ia kiaa ia loa.
Cnt Niu Nps feel-empathy just Cnt he to he indeed
‘Niu only empathizes with himself.’
(1113)
A Niu e alofa fua kiaa ia loa.
Cnt Niu Nps feel-empathy just to he indeed
‘Niu only empathizes with him.’
(? ‘Niu only empathizes with himself.’)
The pattern differs from nonreflexive sentences, where moved subjects of intransitive
verbs and direct objects do not leave a pronominal trace.
Another salient difference between reflexive and nonreflexive sentences is that
in the former the antecedent cannot be an interrogative word. Thus, if an
interrogative word appears in the position of an antecedent, the target cannot be
interpreted as being coreferential with it:
(1114)
Ne taa nee ai a ia loa?
Pst strike Erg who? Cnt he indeed
‘Whoi killed himj?’
(* ‘Who killed himself?’)
If the antecedent is to be questioned, an alternative questioning strategy must be
used, such as interrogative-word clefting (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)):
(1115)
[Kooi] [ttino [ne taa nee ia a ia loa]]?
who? the+person Pst strike Erg he Cnt he indeed
‘Who killed himself?’
Antecedents may be deleted in imperative sentences in the same manner that
preverbal elements are deleted in imperative nonreflexive sentences (cf. 1.1.1.3):
(1116)
Taa a koe loa!
strike Cnt you indeed
‘Kill yourself!’

Vave Inc go Cmp strike Erg he Cmp he indeed
‘Vave has gone to kill himself.’

noun phrase has been raised to the superordinate clause. The unraised equivalent
is provided in the second example:
(1118)

‘Vave must kill himself.’

‘Vave must kill himself.’
Raising leaves an optional pronominal trace in nonreflexive subordinate clauses

1.6.5. Constraints on the target
The target may have a much wider variety of syntactic functions than the antecedent.
Most commonly, it is the direct object of the clause; many examples have already
been provided in the above discussion (e.g., sentence (1119)). Alternatively, an
indirect object, middle object, or other obliquely-marked argument of the verb can
function as the target (cf. examples (1106), (1109), and (1112)). The only type of
modifiers of direct objects and oblique arguments that can be coreferential with an
antecedent are possessive modifiers (cf. (1076) and (1077)); however, as discussed
earlier, the resulting relationships are not true reflexives. No reflexive relationships
could be elicited in copular constructions or in subject- or object-complements.
The target must follow the antecedent in a linear fashion. This requirement
applies whether the antecedent is a subject or a direct object (cf. (1107)). Thus the
following cannot be given reflexive interpretations:
(1120)
Ne taa loa nee ia a Vave loa.
Pst strike indeed Erg he Cnt Vave indeed
‘Hei killed Vavej.’
(* ‘Vave killed himself.’)
(1121)
Ne taa loa a ia nee Vave loa.
Pst strike indeed Cnt he Erg Vave indeed
‘Vavei killed himj.’
(* ‘Vave killed himself.’)
Targets are always overt pronouns. Unlike antecedents, they cannot appear as zero
pronouns. In the following, the direct object and indirect object respectively are not
overt, and the sentences cannot have a reflexive interpretation:
(1122)
Ne taa loa nee ia ø loa.
Pst strike indeed Erg he he indeed
‘Hei killed [himj].’

1.6.6. Reflexivity in nominalized clauses
Nominalization and the changes that it brings about in the clause do not affect
reflexivity in any way. Reflexive relations follow the same patterns in nominalized
clauses as they do in ordinary clauses. In particular, the antecedent and the target
must be part of the same nominalized clause:
(1126)

nominalized clauses retain some clausal properties even though they function as
noun phrases in many other respects, since the modifiers of ordinary noun phrases
can function as reflexive targets.
1.6.7. Reflexive relations in ordinary noun phrases
Coreferential relationships may exist between different noun-phrase modifiers, as
in the following, in which the possessive modifier and the ‘about’ modifier refer to
the same referent:
(1127)

and target. Thus, in the following version of the previous example, the two modifiers
cannot be interpreted as coreferential:
(1128)

1.6.8. Reflexive structures without overt antecedent
Antecedents can be non-overt only if they are zero pronouns, which can happen
only under specific circumstances (cf. 1.6.3–4), or if they are deleted in imperative
constructions, or raised or equi-deleted from subordinate clauses. See 1.6.3–4 for
details.
1.6.9. Other uses of reflexive forms
The pronoun forms that are used as reflexive targets are ordinary personal pronouns,
which can have the full range of pronominal functions in other contexts. The adverb
loa and its allomorphs is an intensifier in nonreflexive sentences.
1.7. RECIPROCALS
The discussion in 1.7.1.3 covers the marking of canonical reciprocal constructions,
i.e., constructions that resemble, in structure and meaning, reciprocal constructions
in other languages. The discussion in 1.7.1.4 concerns uses of quantifiers that
have reciprocal connotations and that often cooccur with other means of expressing
reciprocal relationships. Section 1.7.1.5 discusses a verb that has strong reciprocal
connotations and is the most common way of expressing reciprocality. Sections
1.7.2 to 1.7.9 deal with reciprocal relationships independently of the strategy used
to mark reciprocality. For a brief discussion of inherently reciprocal verb forms
and causatives with reciprocal meaning, see 2.1.3.1.2(d) and 2.1.3.1.3(a)
respectively.
1.7.1. Means of expressing reciprocality
1.7.1.1–2. Reciprocal pronouns
There are no special reciprocal pronouns.
1.7.1.3. Verbal affixes
Many verbs can take a semiproductive reciprocal circumfix, fe-?-(C)aki, where X
stands for the root of the verb and C is a consonant specific to each verb root (some
verb roots take no consonant):
(1129)
Koo fetoolaki fuaa taki mo fuaa moa.
Inc Rcp+locate+Rcp egg+of duck and egg+of chicken
‘The duck’s eggs and the chicken’s eggs are switched around.’
(1130)
Laaua e femaasaloaki saale mo tena aavaga.
they-2 Nps Rcp+jealous+Rcp often with his spouse
‘He and his wife are constantly jealous of one another.’
(1131)
Vave mo Niu ne fesuiaki laa gatu.
Vave and Niu Pst Rcp+change+Rcp their-2 shirt
‘Vave and Niu have exchanged shirts.’
The morphology of the circumfix is discussed in 2.1.3.1.4 and 2.1.3.6.9. Verbs that
do not allow circumfixation can be marked for reciprocality by one of the means
described in 1.7.1.4 and 1.7.1.5.
In some cases, the circumfix appears not on the verb, but on a verb-derived
adverb modifying the verb. Sometimes the adverb is further marked with the
adverb-producing prefix faka- (cf. 2.2.4) and sometimes not:

(1132)
Laaua e nnofo fakafesaagai.

‘They are sitting opposite each other.’
(1133)
Tamaliki koo mmoe feuufaki.
child Inc sleep tête-bèche
‘The children are sleeping tête-bèche to one another.’
1.7.1.4. Quantifiers
Reciprocality can also be marked on the nominal arguments of the verb, with the
help of the quantifiers (s)suaa- ‘one, (an)other’ and isi ‘one, other’ (cf. 2.1.6.6.3(c)
and (d)), which must occur in two separate noun phrases (and never more than
two) in the same clause to have reciprocal meaning. However, these quantifiers do
not necessarily give a reciprocal interpretation to the clause:
(1134)
Koi fai vaa ssuaa maaloo ki ssuaa maaloo.
still have poor-relationship a+other state to a+other state
‘These states are still in conflict with one another.’
or: ‘One state is still in conflict with the other state.’
Because of its ambiguity, this reciprocal strategy almost always appears in tandem
with another way of marking reciprocality, i.e., the use of a circumfixed verb (cf.
1.7.1.3) or the marking of the verb with fakatau (cf. 1.7.1.5), or both:
(1135)
Ne fefaiaki ssuaa fafine mo ssuaa fafine.
Pst Rcp+say+Rcp a+other woman and a+other woman
‘The women argued with one another.’
(1136)
Koo fakatau faippati ssuaa tino ki ssuaa tino.
Inc compete talk+Agr a+other person to a+other person
‘People are speaking to one another.’
(1137)
Koo fakatau fetuliaki te isi puusi mo te isi puusi.
Inc compete Rcp+chase+Rcp the other cat and the other cat
‘The cats are chasing one another.’
Sentences in which reciprocality is marked by more than one means do not have
nonreciprocal interpretations.
Reciprocal sentences with quantifiers can differ slightly in meaning from
sentences in which reciprocality is marked with fakatau (cf. 1.7.1.5):
(1138)
Koo faipati ssuaa tino mo ssuaa tino.
Inc speak a+other person and a+other person
‘People are speaking to one another [either at the same time or taking
turns].’
(1139)
Koo fakatau faippati tino.
Inc compete speak person
‘People are speaking to one another [at the same time].’
1.7.1.5. Lexical means
Reciprocality can be expressed by proposing the verb with the word fakatau, whose

literal meaning as a full verb is ‘compete, exchange’. As a verb, the word is relatively
common in everyday discourse, because it has culturally-salient connotations of
exchange, competition, and binary social organization, all of which are central to
social life in Tuvalu (see the Introduction to this grammar).
The verb fakatau is much more productive as a marker of reciprocality than the
reciprocal circumfix. Expressions with fakatau are best analysed as verb series (cf.
2.1.3.7). The interpretation of sentences in which fakatau appears as the sole potential
marker of reciprocality is always ambiguous: in addition to denoting reciprocality,
such sentences can also have a literal interpretation (i.e., ‘compete, exchange’), or a
metaphorical interpretation denoting plurality, repetition, or back-and-forth motion:
(1140)
Tamaliki koo fakatau koukkou.
child Inc compete bathe+Agr
‘The children are washing each other.’
or: ‘The children are holding a washing-up competition.’
or: ‘The children are washing themselves over and over again.’
However, many verbs lend themselves better to one reading than the others. With
verbs denoting situations that are commonly associated with competitive efforts,
fakatau is normally interpreted in its literal sense:
(1141)
Tamaliki koo fakatau ttele.
child Inc compete run+Agr
‘The children are having a race.’
In contexts which could involve neither competition nor reciprocality, fakatau is
usually interpreted as referring to repetition or plurality:
(1142)

‘The chickens are pecking away at their food.’
With other verbs, a reciprocal interpretation of fakatau is pragmatically most natural.
Such is the case of fesoasoani ‘help’, which frequently appears with fakatau in natural
discourse:
(1143)

‘Please let us try and help one another so that this disease disappears.’

(1144)

‘The children are chasing one another.’
As illustrated in example (1137), all three strategies may also be used in the same
clause.
Whatever meaning fakatau may have, the verb that is serialized to it may agree
in number with the agreement-controlling noun phrase in the clause, if it is an
agreeing verb. This is illustrated in sentences (1140), (1141), and (1142) above. In

1.7.2. Clause-boundedness of reciprocality
Whatever strategy is used to mark reciprocality, a reciprocal relationship can exist
only between noun phrases that are in the same clause. In the following sentence,
a reciprocal relationship cannot exist between the subject of the superordinate clause
and the oblique noun phrase in the subordinate clause:
(1145)

tino.

‘One person wants [him] and the other person to be jealous of each
other.’
(* ‘One wants the other to be jealous of each other.’)
The zero pronoun in the subordinate clause cannot be coreferential with the subject
of the superordinate clause because zero pronouns in subordinate clauses cannot
be coreferential with zero pronouns in superordinate clauses (cf. 1.5.2.3). Thus, in
the only possible interpretation of this sentence, the zero subject of the subordinate
clause is not coreferential with the subject of the superordinate clause, and the
impossibility of a reciprocal relationship between the subject of the superordinate
clause and the oblique modifier of the subordinate clause is demonstrated.
1.7.3–5. Constraints on the antecedent and target
Whatever strategy is used to mark reciprocality, the antecedent of the reciprocal
relationship must be the subject of the clause or its referent must be included in the
referent of the subject of the clause. Subjects of both intransitive and transitive
verbs can function as antecedents. The former case is illustrated by all examples
provided so far. The latter case is illustrated by the following:
(1146)
Koo fakatau tuli nee te isi tino te isi tino.
Inc compete chase Erg the other person the other person
‘They are chasing one another.’
In many cases, the antecedent and the target of a reciprocal construction are
denoted by a single noun phrase with plural meaning, which refers to both the
agent and the patient of the reciprocal situation, as illustrated in examples (1130),
(1132), and (1133). This noun phrase may be a coordinate structure made up of
two noun phrases (and occasionally more than two), as in (1147) below. When the
first noun phrase is a nonsingular pronoun, the referent of the second noun phrase
is usually included in the referent of the pronoun as in (1148) below, a pattern
that applies to nonreciprocal contexts (cf. 2.1.2.1.18). Furthermore, the coordinate
structure can be split like ordinary coordinate noun phrases (cf. 1.3.1.7), as in
(1149):
(1147)
Vave mo Niu koo fetuliaki.
Vave and Niu Pst Rcp+chase+Rcp
‘Vave and Niu are chasing one another.’

Reciprocal targets cannot be equi-deleted, raised, or questioned.
1.7.6. Reciprocality in nominalized clauses
Nominalization and the changes that it brings about in the clause do not affect
reflexivity in any way. Reflexive relations follow the same patterns in nominalized
clauses as they do in ordinary clauses.
1.7.7. Reciprocal relations in ordinary noun phrases
No instance of reciprocality within ordinary noun phrases was found in natural
discourse or could be elicited.
1.7.8. Reciprocal structures without overt antecedent
Antecedents can be non-overt only if they are zero pronouns, as illustrated in
1.7.3–5.
1.7.9. Other uses of reciprocal forms
Circumfixed forms may denote repeated or interactive situations involving more
than one entity, which are often close in meaning to reciprocal situations, but not
actually reciprocal; illustrations are provided in 2.1.3.1.4. Reciprocality is only one
of the several meanings of the verb fakatau, and probably a nonbasic meaning; see
1.7.1.5 for illustrations of its other meanings and of the possible ambiguities which
may arise from its polysemy. The split quantifiers isi and suaa- appear as true
quantifiers in many other contexts, for which see 2.1.6.6.3(c) and (d).
1.8. COMPARISON
There are two principal means of expressing comparison, which are discussed in
1.8.1 to 1.8.5. Correlative comparison can also be expressed in two ways, and these
are described in 1.8.6. 1.8.7 treats various means of expressing superlative
comparison. For a discussion of the marking of comparison and degrees of quality
on adjectives, see 2.1.4.4 and 2.1.4.5. The same topics in reference to adverbs are
treated in 2.1.7.1 and 2.1.7.2. Also relevant is the discussion of the marking of objects
of comparison in 2.1.1.2.6.
1.8.1. Means of expressing comparison
(a) Deictic adverbs and locative prepositions
Comparison may be expressed with the help of one of the deictic adverbs described
in 2.1.3.6.10. The position and grammatical behaviour of these adverbs when used
as markers of comparison is the same as when they function as deictic adverbs. In
comparative clauses, the deictic is postposed to the word that denotes the parameter
of comparison (i.e., the verb or attributive adjective). Of the four deictics mai ‘hither’,
atu ‘thither’, aka ‘up’, and ifo ‘down’, atu is by far the most common and semantically
least marked in comparative constructions:
(1155)
E lasi atu taku ono ne ffuti.
Nps big Dxs my barracuda Pst pull
‘The barracuda I caught is bigger.’

Syntax
(1156)
E uke atu laa a manafa o Silo i manafa o Tito.
Nps many Dxs then Cnt land of Silo at land of Tito
‘Silo has more land than Tito.’
(1157)
Toku tagata nei e sana atu loa iaa koe.
your man this Nps spear-fish Dxs indeed at you
‘This guy is more of a spear-fisherman than you are.’
The three remaining adverbs can also function as markers of comparison. The deictic
mai is used when the comparison denotes or connotes the fact that the entity being
compared is closer to the point of reference of the discourse than the entity forming
the standard of comparison. This ‘greater proximity’ is not necessarily the most
important aspect of the comparison, and it can be defined either literally or
metaphorically, according to the same parameters described in 2.1.3.6.10 for the
deictic uses of these adverbs:
(1158)
Koo pili mai a Oolataga i loo o Niuooku.
Inc near Dxs Cnt Olataga at compared of Niuoku
‘Olataga Islet is closer [to here] than Niuoku Islet.’
The deictic aka ‘up’ may be used when the comparison denotes or connotes an
increase or a greater quantity, height, etc. of some sort, while ifo ‘down’ appears
when the comparison involves a decrease or a lower quantity, height, etc. of a literal
or metaphorical nature. Again, comparative uses of aka and ifo resemble semantically
their deictic uses:
(1159)
E uke aka eiloo a tino Nanumea i loo o tino
Nps many up indeed Cnt person Nanumea at compared of person
Niutao.

‘Nanumea Islanders are more numerous than Niutao Islanders.’
(1160)
E maalalo ifo te taipola i te sefe.

‘The table is lower down than the larder.’
Whenever mai, aka, and ifo appear in comparative constructions, atu is always a
possible alternative.
The standard of comparison, which is always optional (witness (1155)), may be
a noun phrase or a nominalized clause, and it is marked with the locative preposition
i. As shown in 2.1.1.2.6, this preposition forms the basis of a complex comparative
preposition formed with the comparative particle loo, a borrowing from Samoan.
The comparative particle is sandwiched between the locative i to the left and, to the
right, either another locative i, the inalienable possessive marker o, or, in casual
speech, the noun phrase denoting the standard of comparison. These various

be added to qualify the parameter of comparison:
(1161)

Constructions with sentential standards of comparison are very rare in discourse.
These constructions are more idiomatically expressed with the alternative
comparative construction described in (b) below.
Taken out of a discourse context, many comparative structures are semantically
ambiguous. Indeed, in most cases, the deictic adverb can potentially be given a
noncomparative deictic interpretation, and the locatively marked object can be given
one of the many other meanings that locatively marked prepositional phrases can
carry. For example, note the two possible interpretations of the following sentence:
(1164)
Koo sua aka eiloa ttai i aso kolaa.

or: ‘In those days the high tide was higher [than these days].’
Comparative constructions can be disambiguated by using one of the complex forms
of the comparative use of the locative preposition, namely i loo i, i loo o, or i loo. The
morpheme loo can only be followed by a noun phrase referring to a standard of
comparison (cf. 2.1.1.2.6), and it thus disambiguates the entire construction.
However, it does not disambiguate between different possible comparative
interpretations of the same sentence, as discussed in 2.1.1.2.6. Of course, in most
discourse contexts, ambiguities between a comparative interpretation and other
interpretations rarely arise.
Another way of disambiguating comparative interpretations from other
interpretations is to use as the sentence verb a lexeme with the general meaning of
‘large’ or ‘small’, e.g., lasi ‘large’, maaluga ‘high’, or fooliki ‘small’, or the Samoan
borrowings sili and silia ‘exceed’ (the two forms have the same meaning in Tuvaluan).
The entity being compared, the parameter of comparison, and the standard of
comparison can be expressed in one of two ways. In one, the subject of the verb
refers to the entity being compared, the parameter of comparison is expressed as a
locatively marked nominalized clause, and the standard of comparison is provided
in another locatively marked modifier:
(1165)
Koo maaluga atu koe i tou taina i te aava ki ei.
Inc high Dxs you at your sibling at the respect to Anp
‘You respect him more than your brother [does].’
In the other construction, the parameter of comparison is nominalized and functions
as the subject of the verb, the entity being compared is encoded as the subject of the
nominalized clause referring to the parameter of comparison, and the standard of
comparison is expressed as a locative phrase:
(1166)
Koo maaluga atu te aava o koe ki ei i tou taina.
Inc high Dxs the respect of you to Anp at your sibling

(b) Coordinated comparative clauses
Alternatively, comparison can be expressed by coordinating two clauses, the verbs
of which are antonyms or otherwise contrastive in meaning. The first clause contains
a noun phrase that refers to the entity being compared, and the second clause
contains a noun phrase that refers to the standard of comparison. The two noun
phrases usually have the same syntactic and semantic role in their respective clauses,
and the standard of comparison is commonly marked for contrastiveness or focus
or both:
(1167)
Ne poa maalosi telotou vaka, a ko temotou vaka seki
Pst catch-fish strongly their-3 canoe but Foc our-3-e canoe Neg
poa maalosi.
catch-fish strongly
‘Their canoe caught more fish than ours.’
[lit.: ‘Their canoe was very lucky, but our canoe was not very lucky.’]
Either additive coordination by apposition (cf. 1.3.1.1.1) or additive-adversative
coordination with kae or one of its allomorphs (cf. 1.3.1.1.2) can be used in these
constructions. This strategy works well when the parameter of comparison can be
expressed with an antonymic pair or otherwise contrasted lexically (e.g., poa ‘catch
fish’ v. its negation, matua ‘old’ v. maalosi ‘healthy’). It is particularly appropriate
when the entity being compared and the object of comparison are sentential
elements, rather than noun phrases. For example, compare (1162) above with the
following equivalent sentence, which is pragmatically better formed:
(1168)
E loa te tulamu, kae lauliki te sefe.
Nps long the drum but narrow the larder
‘The drum is taller than the larder is wide.’
[lit.: ‘The drum is tall, the larder is narrow.’]
These constructions have all the syntactic and semantic characteristics of coordinated
clauses. They are always ambiguous between a simple contrastive and non-
comparative interpretation and a comparative interpretation. Generally speaking,
the more structural and semantic parallelism there is between the two clauses, the
more likely they are to be interpreted as a comparative construction. For example,
the structural and semantic differences between the two clauses are reduced to a
minimum in the following sentence, and as a result the sentence is normally
interpreted as a comparative construction, unless the context indicates otherwise:
(1169)
Koo maattua tino konei, a koo foolliki tino kolaa.
Inc old person these but Inc young person those
‘These people are older than those people.’
1.8.2–4. Omission under identity in comparative constructions
Most constructions in which comparison is expressed with a deictic adverb and the
standard of comparison is expressed with a locative preposition (cf. 1.8.1(a)) are
monoclausal constructions. They can only be biclausal when the standard of
comparison is a nominalized clause, which occurs rarely. When it does, as in
examples (1162) and (1163), there is no evidence of any systematic process of
omission of elements under identity with the superordinate clause. Rather, the
nominalized clause consists of the constituents most essential to its interpretation

Syntax
221
as a standard of comparison. Indeed, the longer the nominalized clause, the less
idiomatic it is. However, no grammatical statement can be produced to predict
what must be deleted or what must not.
Coordinated comparative clauses of the type described in 1.8.1(b) usually consist
entirely of constituents that are not coreferential. Any ‘peripheral’ materials, i.e.,
constituents that are not essential to the comparison such as a prepositional phrase,
can be deleted. However, peripheral materials are infrequent because these
constructions generally consist only of the most essential constituents. This bare-
bone tendency helps to highlight the comparative contrast and thus to minimize
the possibility that the construction will be interpreted as something other than a
comparison.
1.8.5. Differences between comparative structures
The difference between the two comparative structures is principally a matter of
style (the former being more formal than the latter), as well as potential ambiguity,
in that deictic adverbs and prepositional standards of comparison are less
ambiguously comparative than coordinated comparative clauses. There is no clear
contrast between the expression of comparison with a comparative particle plus
reduced comparative clause and the expression of comparison with a preposition
plus standard of comparison.
1.8.6. Correlative comparison
Correlative comparison can be expressed in one of two ways. One consists of a
conditional-temporal construction marked with the conditional conjunctions kaafai

1.8.7. Superlative comparison
Superlative comparison (e.g., She is the best mat-weaver of all women of this island) can
be expressed in several ways, some of which are inherently ambiguous while others
are not.
(a) Unmarked constructions
Superlative comparison is most simply, but also most ambiguously, expressed with no
marking whatsoever. Whenever an entity is singled out among other entities as being
associated with a gradable characteristic, the resulting construction can be interpreted
as a superlative construction if this interpretation is appropriate to the context:

1.9. EQUATIVES
Equatives can be expressed in one of two ways. The first makes use of demonstrative
forms that function either as an adverbial modifier of the verb or as the main verb
of the clause. The second employs one of several verbs that denote similarity or
identity between the referents of nominal constituents.
1.9.1. Means of expressing equatives
(a) Demonstrative verbs and adverbs
Equatives may be expressed with the help of demonstrative forms in pee-, namely
peenei ‘thus’ (near speaker), peenaa ‘thus’ (near the interlocutor), peelaa ‘thus’
(away from speaker and interlocutor), which are also used in adverbial clauses
of manner (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.2). The meaning and form of these demonstratives are
discussed in 2.1.2.5(c).
Demonstratives in pee- can take two types of object that differ in meaning,
grammatical structure, and overt marking. Objects marked with the comitative
preposition mo denote the standard of realis equation; objects marked with the
complementizer me (or its phonologically-conditioned allomorphs ma and mo) are
predicates, and they denote the standard of irrealis equation.

takes as a subject the noun phrase referring to the entity being equated and as an

The only biclausal constructions with equative meaning are constructions with
predicative objects. Generally speaking, noun phrases that are identical in the main

always on the subject of the superordinate clause (cf. 1.9.1(a)).
1.9.5. Differences between equative structures
Equative constructions can take either a comparative clause or a prepositionally-
marked standard of comparison. The difference between the two types of object is
such that full clauses denote irrealis equative standards while noun phrases denote
realis equative standards.
1.10. POSSESSION
Sentences that express possession fall into three broad types. The first is structurally
identical to existential sentences, the second is structurally unique, and the third
makes use of a variety of verbs that in other contexts denote attributes, acquisitions,
or locations. The contrast between alienable and inalienable possession is marked
only in the first two types. Possessive sentences of all types also encode all semantic
categories regularly associated with verbal clauses.
1.10.1. Possessive sentences 1.10.1.1. Possessive sentences with existential verbs
The most unmarked way of expressing possession is by using the positive existential
verb isi or its alternative form (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b)), or the negative existential verb seeai
or its alternative forms (cf. 1.4(d)), with a noun modified by a possessor as subject.
These structures cannot denote anything other than possession. The possessor can
be either a possessive noun phrase or a possessive pronoun. The noun it modifies
denotes the possessed entity, and the possessive relationship is marked for the
appropriate possessive class:
(1205)

Inc exist a kingfish of they-3
‘They already have one kingfish.’
(1206)

‘They have no empathy for poor people.’

modifier, the subject, or as the possessive modifier of another noun phrase in the
clause:

1.10.1.3. Miscellaneous verbs denoting possession

possessive relationship has, at some stage in the past, been initiated by the
possessor. It is thus particularly suitable to express alienable possession (cf.

for alienability and inalienability:

clothing, adornments, and kinship ties:

direct object have nonincorporated equivalents, in contrast to the equivalent
construction in Niuean (Seiter 1980:75–78).
Finally, the verb nofo ‘stay, live’ may denote possession. In possessive contexts,
it usually implies that the possessive relationship is temporary, illegal, or
anomalous in one fashion or another. Thus it is common in reference to loans,
leases, and thefts:
