1.10.2. Alienable and inalienable possession
Nonsentential possessive relationships are marked for possessive class based on a
semantic contrast that resembles the marking of alienability and inalienability in
languages where these categories are attested (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1). Alienability and
inalienability are also marked in most possessive sentences. In possessive sentences
with existential verbs (cf. 1.10.1.1), alienability is encoded in the possessive modifiers
of the subject; compare saku ‘my’ (alienable) in the first example below with soku
‘my’ (inalienable) in the second:
(1231)
Koo isi saku mooto foou.
Inc exist a-my outboard-engine new
‘I have a new outboard engine.’
(1232)
Koo isi soku tili foou.
Inc exist a-my fishing-net new
‘I have a new fishing net.’
The two possessive verb forms (i)a and (i)o (cf. 1.10.1.2) denote alienable and
inalienable possession respectively:
(1233)
E iaaku te mooto foou teenaa.
Nps belong-to+me the outboard-engine new that
‘That new outboard engine is mine.’
(1234)
E iooku te tili foou teenaa.
Nps belong-to+me the fishing-net new that
‘That new fishing net is mine.’
With the possessive verb maua (cf. 1.10.1.3), alienability and inalienability can only
be marked if the agent is expressed as a possessive modifier of the possessed noun
phrase:
(1235)
Koo maua taku mooto foou.
Inc have my outboard-engine new
‘I have a new outboard engine.’
(1236)
Koo maua toku tili foou.
Inc have my fishing-net new
‘I have a new fishing net.’

With fai, the direct object is marked for alienability and inalienability as long as it is
not verb-incorporated:
(1237)
E fai aavaga a laatou.

‘They have spouses.’
(1238)

‘They have grandchildren.’
Since fai as a possessive verb is used for bodily attributes, clothing, and adornments,
and kin categories, most of which are inalienably possessed (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1), its direct
objects are more commonly marked for alienable possession than inalienable
possession. Finally, with possessive uses of nofo ‘stay, live’, possessive class cannot
be marked.
1.10.3–5. Other categories associated with possession
No other semantic feature of possession is encoded in any of the above constructions
(but note the implicature of possessive uses of nofo ‘stay’ described in 1.10.1.3).
Because possessive sentences of all types behave like regular verbal sentences in
most respects, they can be regularly marked for all semantic categories associated
with ordinary verbal sentences (e.g., tense, aspect, and mood).
1.11. EMPHASIS
Various related categories, including informational stress, new-information focus,
and the focus of yes-no questions, can be understood to fall under the general
rubric ‘emphasis’, both from a crosslinguistic perspective and for the purpose of
the description of Tuvaluan grammar. Indeed, these various categories are all
expressed by the same means, which consist of several formally heterogeneous
morphemes and constructions. The distinction between sentence emphasis and
constituent emphasis is not clearly marked, in that the same morphemes and
constructions can mark one or the other. In many instances, whether a particular
constituent or the entire sentence is emphasized is a matter of context rather than
linguistic form.
1.11.1. Sentence emphasis
1.11.1.1–2. Contradictory v. noncontradictory emphasis
There is no distinction between contradictory and noncontradictory sentence
emphasis. Both can be marked in a variety of ways that include movement processes,
lexical items, and particular constructions associated with emphasis. The discussion
of superlative comparison in 1.8.7 presents further relevant materials.
1.11.1.3. Means of expressing sentence emphasis
1.11.1.3.1. Intonation and stress
Various intonation contours and other suprasegmental tools can be exploited for
different purposes, including the marking of sentence emphasis. For example, a
switch to high falsetto often denotes surprise and indignation, in addition to
emphasis. A deliberate style of delivery, in which vowels are drawn out, the

nongeminate consonant that precedes the stressed vowel of a word is geminated,
the overall tempo is slow, and voice volume high, is coloured with affect, in that
the speaker often comes across as self-assertive and often displeased while using
this style of delivery. However, the primary function of these strategies is not
sentence emphasis, but rather the marking of affect. Since high affect itself is
generally salient pragmatically, the sentence is emphasized as a consequence.
1.11.1.3.2. Noun-phrase focusing
Sentence emphasis can be marked by moving one argument of the verb to preverbal
position and marking it with the preposed morpheme ko. As discussed in 1.11.2.1.4,
ko-focusing generally marks a noun phrase for new-information focus, i.e., it marks
constituent emphasis; however, in many situations, the scope of the emphasis is
the entire sentence, even though what is formally marked for emphasis is a noun
phrase. In the following example, the ko-focused noun phrase does not refer to
new information since its referent is introduced in the immediately preceding clause
or sentence. Rather, the emphasized category is the entire sentence:
(1239)
[from a discussion of whether different organizations, including village
moieties, should pay for the use of the maneaba]
Au e maafaufau peelaa kee see ttogi a ituuala, mo ko
I Nps think thus Sbj Neg pay Cnt village-side because Foc

‘I think that village sides should not pay, because they are subdivisions

Therefore, in my view, village sides should not pay.’
It is in these contexts that one frequently finds ko-focused first- and second-person
pronouns, which are not focused as a means of marking them for new information
(since first- and second-person referents are quintessentially given information in
most interactional contexts), but rather as a means of emphasizing the entire
sentence:
(1240)
Ko taatou kee fesoasoani taatou ki tino maattiva.

‘We should come to the help of poor people.’
Sentence emphasis is frequently marked by an idiomatic structure that consists of
the following sequence: an optional left-dislocated noun phrase (cf. 1.11.2.1.6) that
denotes the subject of the sentence; a ko-focused personal pronoun coreferential
with the left-dislocated noun phrase if there is one, and modified by a form of the
intensifier eiloa, usually loo; and finally the verb, marked with the inceptive-aspect
marker koo:
(1241)
Ko ia loo koo fano mo te sili i te valea.
Foc he indeed Inc go with the superior at the stupid
‘When it comes to stupidity, he wins it all.’

These structures are very common in natural discourse.
1.11.1.3.3. Nominalization and focusing of the verb
A sentence can be emphasized by nominalizing the verb and ko-focusing it:
(1242)
Ko te paleleega eiloa teenei o aku paka.
Foc the deplete+Nom indeed this of my tobacco
‘This is the last of my tobacco.’
This strategy is reminiscent of the propensity for exclamatory sentences to be
expressed as nominalized sentences (cf. 1.1.1.4), and of the expression of correlative
comparison with the same structure (cf. 1.8.6). Nominalized and ko-focused verbs
are often modified by intensifying adverbs in these constructions; note the
appearance of eiloa in both the above examples.
1.11.1.3.4. Intensifying adverbs
Various intensifying adverbs can be added to the verb to emphasize the entire
sentence. Among these adverbs figures the ubiquitous intensifier eiloa or one
of its allomorphs (ailoa, ailoo, eiloo, loa, or loo), which modifies principally
verbs, but also nouns, verb and noun modifiers, and even certain conjunctions
(e.g., 1.1.2.4.2.8) to mark either sentence or constituent emphasis. Several
intensifying adverbs of different types can be used concurrently in the same
phrase:
(1243)
Tou tagata naa, se Ppaalagi foki eiloa maa saasaale.

‘That guy, [he looks] exactly [like] a white man when he walks.’

1.11.1.3.5. Miscellaneous constructions
Emphasis can be expressed with a grab-bag of idiomatic constructions. One
construction takes as a main verb either oko, the literal meaning of which is
‘reach’, or the Samoan borrowing ese, which has no independent meaning in

old-fashioned, but constructions with oko are very frequent in natural
discourse. The verb is always marked with the inchoative aspect marker koo.
The subject of these verbs can be a nominalized clause:

1.11.2. Constituent emphasis
1.11.2.1. Means of expressing constituent emphasis
1.11.2.1.1. Intonation and stress
There is a general tendency for emphasized constituents to be given greater
suprasegmental prominence than the rest of the sentence. This prominence can be
achieved through a variety of heterogeneous means that cannot be described in an
integrated fashion: intonation peaks, increased voice volume, switches to falsetto,

prolongation of vowels, etc. However, suprasegmental phenomena alone cannot
mark constituent emphasis, and should be viewed as the consequence, rather than
the primary marking, of constituent emphasis.
1.11.2.1.2. Intensifying adverbs
Intensifying adverbs can modify noun phrases or verbs to mark either constituent
or sentence emphasis (cf. 1.11.1.3.4). Following are illustrations of intensifying
adverbs as noun modifiers:
(1256)
Teenei loo tou toe aso e vau ei koe kkonei!
this indeed your last day Nps come Nps you to+here
‘This is the very last time you come here!’
(1257)
Ttele atu naa maatou i te mata eeloo o te ava.

‘We ran to the very mouth of the boat passage.’
When the noun is modified by both an attributive adjective and an intensifying
adverb, the target of the emphasis may be either the adjective or the entire noun
phrase:
(1258)
Se maattugaa puusi lasi eeloa.

‘[It’s] a cat that is very large indeed.’
or: ‘[It is] indeed a very large cat.’
1.11.2.1.3. Movement
Noun phrase movement to unmarked sentence-initial position denotes topic, rather
than emphasis (cf. 1.12.1.2). If a noun phrase is moved to sentence-initial position
and marked with ko, it denotes new information (cf. 1.11.2.1.4). Noun phrases do
not move to any other position in the sentence. Verbs, adjectives, and adverbials do
not move at all, although some adverbials can be left-dislocated (cf. 1.11.2.1.6).
1.11.2.1.4. Ko-focusing
What I call ‘ko-focusing’ throughout this grammar is actually several different but
related constructions and processes with similar surface representations. The two
most important are the following: the predication of a noun phrase by proposing it
with the grammatical morpheme ko, which is described in 1.2.1.1.1(a); and the
marking of a sentence-initial noun phrase with ko. The ubiquitous marker ko also
appears, either optionally or obligatorily, in a variety of contexts where its pragmatic
or syntactic functions may or may not be transparently related to predication or the
marking of new information: indirectly-quoted speech (cf. 1.1.1.1(b)); several
question structures, particularly with ai ‘who?’ (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(a)-(c)); answers (cf.
1.1.1.2.4.1); subjunctive subordination (cf. 1.1.2.1.2); subordination with me (cf.
1.1.2.1.3); certain types of after-clauses (1.1.2.4.2.1(a)(i)); purpose clauses with ko te
mea (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.3(a)); because-clauses with ona or auaa, and apposed because-clauses
(cf. 1.1.2.4.2.4(d)-(f)); concession clauses with seiloga (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.8); the marking of
exclusion (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.8 and 2.1.1.4.26); alternative sentence or noun-phrase
coordination (cf. 1.3.1.1.3 and 1.3.1.3.4); gapping (cf. 1.3.2); sentence negation (cf.
1.4 and 1.4.1.2); constituent negation (cf. 1.4.2); the marking of reflexive antecedents
(cf. 1.6.3–4); certain correlative comparative structures (cf. 1.8.6); certain emphatic

marking of qualification (cf. 2.1.1.4.31). Noun phrases that are raised from a
subordinate to a superordinate clause of a complex sentence can also be marked for
case with ko (cf. 1.1.2.7). In all circumstances, ko replaces all other case markers. The
following discussion is only concerned with certain predicative uses of ko and with
its uses as a marker of new-information focus.
The situation is further complicated by the fact that predicative ko also appears
in a construction that resembles clefting in other languages, in which the ko-marked
predicated noun phrase is in sentence-initial position, and is equated to a headless
relative clause:
(1259)
[Ko Nukulasi loa] [[ne ttapa mai kia au]].

‘It was Nukulasi who called out to me.’
The structural differences between clefted and sentence-initial ko-marked noun
phrases can be subtle because, in many instances, the two have exactly the same
surface realization. However, there are several differences between the two types.
Clefted structures are equational constructions, and the second element of the
equation is a relative clause. Thus if a relative demonstrative form (cf. 2.1.2.7) appears
after the ko-marked noun phrase, the latter is likely to be clefted rather than sentence-
initial:
(1260)
Ko Leenese fua teelaa ne faipati aka.
Foc Lenese just that Pst speak up
‘It was just Lenese that spoke up.’
However, this test is not fool-proof because what looks like a relative pronoun can
also be a demonstrative, as the two categories are homophonous. Furthermore,
since relative clauses cannot be marked for certain tense, aspect, and mood
categories, such as subjunctive, the ko-marked noun phrase in the following
sentences cannot be clefted:
(1261)
Ko taatou kee fesoasoani taatou ki tino maattiva.
Foc we-3-e Sbj help we-3-e to person poor
‘We should come to the help of poor people.’
(1262)
Ko ttaimi kee fakaffonu.

‘[We] should ensure that [our] time is filled up.’
Clefted and sentence-initial ko-marked noun phrases have different pragmatic
functions. Clefted noun phrases commonly single out one option or aspect of a
referent out of several possible options. Clefting thus has a contrastive value,
whether the contrast is explicit or implicit. Observe how the discourse context
preceding the ko-marked clefted noun phrase establishes or implies a contrast in
the following:

kaimanako po ko te kaisanosano. Maatou mo Faiva mo Telava,

it can target both subjects and direct objects. It derives (1267) from (1268):
(1267)

1.11.2.1.5. Pseudoclefting
The only construction that resembles structurally pseudocleft constructions in other
languages is a clause in which the main verb is the existential verb isi (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b))
or its negative counterpart seeai (cf. 1.4(d)), and in which the noun phrase is modified
by a relative clause providing the rest of the sentence:
(1270)
E isi ttagata teelaa ne mua mai.

‘(There is) a man (who) got here first.’
From a structural standpoint, there is nothing special to remark about this
construction; in particular, the distinction between regular existential verbs with
definite and indefinite subjects as discussed in 1.2.1.1.1(b) also applies here. From a
pragmatic standpoint, the construction provides a means of introducing a participant
in the discourse, which establishes both its existence and its topical relevance for
the subsequent discourse.
1.11.2.1.6. Right- and left-dislocation
Right-dislocation is very rare and, in most cases, the right-dislocated material is an
afterthought or an elaboration of the information provided in the main body of the
sentence:
(1271)
I koo laa, seei ne mea peenei, peelaa, ne iti.

‘Over there, there is nothing like this, like, electricity.’
(1272)
Aalo maatou i suaa taimi, vau ei maatou, maatou mo Eeuta

mo Laipe.

‘We were rowing another time, [and] we were coming back, [there was]
Euta, Laipe, and me.’
(1273)
Mmoe katoa laatou i koo, i te fale o saa Vave.

‘They are all sleeping over there, at Vave’s house.’
However, see 1.1.1.2.2.2(c) for a discussion of the special case of the right-dislocation
of the interrogative word kaiaa ‘why?’.
Left-dislocation is more frequent and better established as a syntactic category
than right-dislocation, and it targets most common locative and temporal
prepositional phrases marked with the locative preposition i or the source
preposition mai. The preposition is never stranded and moves with the noun phrase.
Generally, no pronominal or anaphoric trace appears in the main body of the
sentence:

(1275)

Prepositional phrases whose head is the directional preposition ki generally do not
dislocate. However, when ki takes on a meaning other than directionality, left-
dislocation is possible:
(1276)
Kae ki mea tau tupe, koo fiittaa toku maafaufau.

‘But when it comes to money, I worry a lot.’

(1277)

Arguments of the verb and nontemporal nonlocative modifiers can also be left-
dislocated. If the dislocated noun phrase is the subject of an intransitive verb or a
direct object, a pronominal copy of the noun phrase is left behind in the main body
of the sentence:
(1278)
Maatou nei, koo vaaivvai eeloo maatou i te aalo.

‘Us here, we are exhausted from rowing.’
If the dislocated noun phrase is the subject of a transitive verb or an oblique
argument, a case-marked overt pronominal or anaphoric copy is left behind in the
main body of the sentence:
(1279)

the team this Prf Cst+bad Erg they-3 the government of
ttou atu fenua.

‘A small kingfish, [there] take a look at it!’
(1281)

‘[During] fatele dancing in Kiribati, people often [start] shaking [with

When the object of the locative preposition i is left-dislocated, the anaphoric pronoun
ei may be regularly incorporated into the verb (cf. 2.1.3.6.12):
(1282)

te mea e mmae saale ei tou tinae.

‘The cloudy deposit at the bottom of the sour toddy container, that’s
what gives you a stomach ache.’
Left-dislocation thus distinguishes between prepositional phrases marked with i
that denote locations and prepositional phrases marked with the same
preposition that have nonlocative meaning: the former dislocate with the
preposition, while the dislocation of the latter strands the preposition and gives
it an anaphoric pronoun as its object (which can be verb-incorporated in turn).
It is sometimes difficult to distinguish between left-dislocated and
topicalized arguments of the verb (cf. 1.12.1), because the patterns of pronoun
stranding are roughly the same in both situations, and because a pause is not
always identifiable between the left-dislocated material and the rest of the
sentence. (In writing, most Tuvaluans use punctuation idiosyncratically and
sporadically, and thus ambiguity arises in writing as well.) However, several
factors can disambiguate the two categories. First, the formation of imperatives
discriminates between left-dislocated constituents and preverbal constituents
by allowing the former but not the latter (cf. 1.1.1.3.1). Second, tense-aspect-
mood markers are readily deleted in clauses with a left-dislocated noun
phrase, as illustrated in (1277) and (1279). Third, left-dislocation can apply to
oblique noun phrases and in fact applies primarily to certain types of obliques,
whereas movement to preverbal position cannot (cf. 1.12.2.2). Finally, a left-
dislocated element can occur in the same sentence as a preverbal noun phrase,
particularly if the former is a temporal or locative prepositional phrase. In
such situations, the left-dislocated element always precedes the preverbal
noun phrase, as illustrated in (1274). In contrast, two noun phrases cannot be
topicalized in the same sentence (cf. 1.2.1.2.6(a)).
Left-dislocation is comparatively rare in natural discourse with noun
phrases other than locative and temporal noun phrases. It has both emphatic
and focusing functions, in that a left-dislocated noun phrase usually denotes a
scene-setting entity that provides a perspective from which what follows can
be interpreted, and that also frequently represents new information. The rest
of the sentence generally elaborates on some aspect of the referent of the
dislocated noun phrase. Given this discourse function, it is not surprising to
find locatives and temporals as primary targets for left-dislocation, since place
and time are typical elements in scene-setting. Left-dislocation is also one
means of handling heavy noun phrases (cf. 1.13).
1.11.2.1.7. Contrastive case-marking
As discussed in 2.1.1.2.1.1, the case marker a can mark optionally any noun

complicated distribution, and does not always have a significant functional
load. However, when it is optional and does not serve as a gap-filler (cf.

1.11.2.1.8. Possible combinations
Many markers of emphasis of various kinds can cooccur with one another, either
within the same noun phrase or as markers of different elements in the same
sentence. Only a couple of examples will be given here, because many illustrations
have already been provided in the foregoing.
Intensifying adverbs can cooccur with all other emphasis-marking devices,
within either the same noun phrase or the same sentence. The marker ko is in
complementary distribution with the contrastive marker a, but either one can mark
left-dislocated noun phrases that are not already marked with a preposition.
Following is an example of a dislocated noun phrase marked with a:

laaua foki loa konaa koo fakagaalue i mea tau iti.

were the ones that had been put to work on the power [generator].’
1.11.2.2. Elements that can be emphasized by various means
1.11.2.2.1. Constituent types
Intensifying adverbs can mark either noun phrases or verbs. The morphemes ko
and a, whatever their precise function, can only mark noun phrases, including

nominalized verbs. Clefting, pseudoclefting, and dislocation can only target noun
phrases and, in the case of dislocation, certain adverbials, as elaborated upon in
1.11.2.1.6. Verb emphasis and sentence emphasis are not distinguishable from one
another: the same emphatic structure can be understood as emphasizing the verb
only or the entire sentence, and only context can disambiguate the two cases. For
the emphasis of attributive adjectives, see 1.11.2.1.2. Predicative adjectives, as usual,
behave like verbs.
1.11.2.2.2. Constituent functions
For the purpose of emphasis, no distinction is made between the constituents of
main, subordinate, and coordinate clauses. For example, the constituent of a
subordinate clause can be ko-fronted to sentence-initial position:
(1288)
A ko faafine laa see iloa me ne faafine aa kolaa e
but Foc women then Neg know Cmp some women what? those Nps
toko tolu e mmai.

‘As for the women, [no one] knows where the three women who’re
coming are from.’
Some emphasis-marking devices treat different types of constituents differently
according to their grammatical function, as discussed in 1.11.2.1. As illustrated in
1.11.2.1.8, different constituents can be emphasized in the same clause or sentence.
No specific restriction exists as to which or how many constituents can be
emphasized at the same time.
1.11.2.2.3. Morphological processes accompanying dislocation
Left-dislocation can leave a pronominal or nominal copy of the dislocated noun
phrase; see 1.11.2.1.6 for discussion.
1.11.3. Focus of yes-no questions
The same means of marking emphasis in declarative sentences are also used to
mark the focus of yes-no questions, as long as the pragmatic function of each method
is appropriate. Among the various means of marking emphasis, ko-clefting stands
out as the least ambiguous way to mark the focus of yes-no questions in elicited
contexts. Observe, for example, the following neutral yes-no question, whose focus
is evenly distributed over the entire sentence:
(1289)
Te tusi teenei ne ave nee Vave kia Mele i te vaka taluai?
the letter this Pst send Erg Vave to Mele on the ship last
‘Did Vave send this letter to Mele on the last ship?’
The above contrasts with the following versions, in which a different nominal
element is ko-focused:
(1290)
Ko te tusi teenei ne ave nee Vave kia Mele i te vaka taluai?

‘Was it this letter that Vave sent to Mele on the last ship?’
(1291)
Ko Vave ne ave nee ia te tusi teenei kia Mele i te vaka taluai?
Foc Vave Pst send Erg he the letter this to Mele on the ship last
‘Was it Vave who sent this letter to Mele on the last ship?’

1.12. TOPIC
This section assumes a classic definition of sentence topic as the constituent
identifying what the sentence is about, as opposed to a discourse topic, a proposition
that denotes the ‘question of immediate concern’ for the discourse (Keenan and
Schieffelin 1976:380). However, attention will be paid to discourse factors that
condition sentence topics.
1.12.1. Means of expressing sentence topic
As in all languages, topic in Tuvaluan can be expressed in a variety of ways that
differ from one another in the extent to which they are grammaticalized and
conventionalized. By far the most grammaticalized and common means of marking
topic is the movement of a noun phrase to preverbal position, where it is left
unmarked for case or marked optionally with the contrastive-absolutive marker a
(cf. 1.11.2.1.7 and 2.1.1.2.1.1). The preverbal noun phrases in the following are
provided with their discourse environments to illustrate how the topicality of the
referent of the noun phrase may be established in the preceding discourse (in the
case of (1294)), or may be utilized in the ensuing discourse (in the case of (1295)):
(1294)
E fai mai kiaa ia me teefea te mea teelaa e faittali
Nps say Dxs to he Cmp where? the thing that Nps wait-for
laatou ki ei. Ana muna, te mea teenaa koo leva loa ne
they-3 to Anp his word the thing that Inc long-time indeed Pst
ave nee ia ki te failautusi.
send Erg he to the secretary
‘[He] asks him where was that thing they were waiting for. He answers
[that] he had sent out that thing to the secretary a long time ago.’
(1295)
Te faanau saa tamaa nei ne lau aka nee maaua, e
the children group guy this Pst count up Erg we-2-e Nps
tinogafulu ma ttoko tasi.
ten and the+Num one
‘We’ve counted how many children there were in what’s-his-name’s
family, [there are] eleven [of them].’
Needless to say, topicality can also be established in the extralinguistic context,
rather than the discourse.
Whether topicalization should be characterized as movement to preverbal or
sentence-initial position is debatable, because no linguistic material can occur before
the verb of a clause other than topicalized noun phrases and peripheral elements
like left-dislocated phrases. However, since topicalized noun phrases always follow
left-dislocated noun phrases when they cooccur in the same sentence (cf. 1.11.2.1.6),
the former can be assumed to be preverbal rather than sentence-initial.

Topicalized noun phrases cannot be indefinite, a restriction that follows from
the fact that they represent given information. Movement to preverbal position can
affect the degree of specificity of a noun phrase. In preverbal position, noun phrases
tend to be specific as well as definite, while definite noun phrases can be either
specific or nonspecific in postverbal position:
(1296)
E ppoi atu fua nei laatou, te uaeelesi koo oko mai.
Nps surprised Dxs just now they-3 the telegram Inc reach Dxs
‘Then they were surprised by the [already mentioned] telegram.’
(1297)
E ppoi atu fua nei laatou, koo oko mai te uaeelesi.
Nps surprised Dxs just now they-3 Inc reach Dxs the telegram.
‘Then they were surprised by a [not necessarily already mentioned]
telegram.’
Also following from the fact that preverbal noun phrases are topics, first- and second-
person pronouns and proper nouns occur in preverbal position more frequently
than in postverbal position, and more commonly than nonproper third-person
referential expressions, since first-person, second-person, and proper entities are
prime candidates for topicality:
(1298)
Au nei koo ttalo eiloo ko temotou failautusi kee naa tapale.
I this Inc pray indeed Foc our-3-e secretary Sbj please remove
‘I am praying that our secretary will be dismissed.’
(1299)
Maiema mo Mele ne olo ki fafo o olo ki tua.
Maiema and Mele Pst go to outside Cmp go to back
‘Maiema and Mele have left [the house] on their way to the oceanside
[of the village].’
Movement to preverbal position represents the only clear means of marking topics
with morphosyntactic tools. Preverbal noun phrases are frequent in natural
discourse, and have relatively weak pragmatic value. In other words, a preverbal
noun phrase need not be emphatically topical to be placed in preverbal position,
and a noun phrase that has not been topicalized can still be high in topicality.
Topicalization may compete with other priorities in discourse, and these other
priorities frequently prevent topicalization from applying to noun phrases that are
nevertheless high in topicality. The immediate result of the weak pragmatic value
of topicalization is that word order in Tuvaluan can be characterized as relatively
free (cf 1.2.1.2.6(a)).
Preverbal noun phrases should be distinguished from left-dislocated noun
phrases, which they frequently resemble, but which they differ from in several
respects (cf. 1.11.2.1.6).
1.12.2. Elements that can be topicalized
1.12.2.1. Constituent types
Movement to sentence-initial position can target noun phrases and no other
constituent type.
1.12.2.2. Constituent functions
Topicalization can apply to subjects of intransitive or transitive verbs and
to direct objects. Oblique arguments, including middle objects, cannot

move to preverbal position. In contrast, they can be ko-focused (cf.
1.11.2.1.4) or left-dislocated (cf. 1.11.2.1.6), but the pragmatic functions of
these processes are different from topicalization. Eligible arguments of
main, subordinate, and coordinate clauses can all be topicalized, but only
one argument per sentence can.
1.12.2.3. Morphological processes accompanying movement
As shown in 1.2.1.2.6(a), topicalized subjects of transitive verbs leave a pronominal
copy in their original position after the verb. This copy is not obligatory, but is
preferred. An optional pronominal copy can also be left when the subject of an
intransitive verb or a direct object is topicalized. This copy adds some emphasis to
the topicalized constituent:
(1300)
Koe see alofa koe moo tou tuagaene.
you Neg feel-empathy you Ben your sibling
‘You have no empathy for your sister.’
These patterns are very similar to those that apply to the movement of interrogative
words (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2) and the ko-focusing of noun phrases (cf. 1.11.2.1.4).
1.13. HEAVY SHIFT
There is no clear evidence of noun phrases being moved solely on account of their
weight, in part because the order of arguments and modifiers in the sentence is
relatively free. As discussed briefly in 1.2.1.2.6(a), heavy arguments of the verb
usually follow oblique modifiers. The scope of this remark can be expanded as
follows: all other factors being equal, there is a tendency for arguments and modifiers
to be ordered from least heavy to most heavy in postverbal position, a principle
that appears to apply to many other languages, including English (cf. Quirk et al.
1985:1361–1362). Of course, defining precisely what enters into the definition of
weight (e.g., syntactic complexity, length in words, pragmatic prominence) is an
empirical question beyond the scope of this work.
Besides left-to-right ordering, left-dislocation (cf. 1.11.2.1.6) can come in handy
in preventing potential processing problems caused by heavy noun phrases; in
left-dislocated position, heavy noun phrases can be isolated from the rest of the
sentence and thus processed separately.
1.14. OTHER MOVEMENT PROCESSES
Discussed here are two processes that affect one quantifier, katoa ‘all, other’ (cf.
2.1.6.6.2(a)). This quantifier may be moved, within the same clause, from a
noun phrase to the verb of which the noun phrase is an argument or modifier.
This process, which is referred to as quantifier float, is discussed in 1.14.1.
Furthermore, katoa can be moved from a noun phrase in a subordinate clause
to the verb complex of the corresponding superordinate clause; this process,
described in 1.14.2, is referred to as quantifier raising in this grammar, in that it
bears some conceptual similarities to noun-phrase raising (the phrase is given
a different meaning here from that given to it in certain formal syntactic
frameworks).
Noun-phrase raising, whose domain is the subordinate clause, is discussed under
subordination (cf. 1.1.2.7).

1.14.1. Quantifier float
Quantifier float is a process that extracts the quantifier katoa from the structural
confines of the noun phrase it modifies and postposes it to the main verb of the
clause, deriving (1302) from (1301) for example:
(1301)
A loomaattua katoa koo fiaffia.
Cnt old-women all Inc happy
‘All the old women are happy.’
(1302)
A loomaattua koo fiaffia katoa.
Cnt old-women Inc happy all
‘The old women are all happy.’
Quantifier float can take place with any verb and in any clause type, including
nominalized clauses:
(1303)
Ne ppoi laatou i te lagonaaga katoa nee laatou te tala
Pst surprised they-3 on the hear+Nom all Erg they-3 the story
teenaa.

‘They were surprised when they all heard that story.’
The quantifier katoa may have a variety of meanings in different contexts (cf.
2.1.6.6.2(a)). Its occurrences that are targeted by quantifier float mean either ‘all’, as
illustrated above, or ‘all other(s)’:
(1304)
A te maneapa e ttala mai eiloo nee te ulu o te
Cnt the maneaba Nps open Dxs indeed Erg the head of the
fenua. Teelaa laa, koo faippati katoa ei a tino.

‘The maneaba is opened by the chief himself. Once this is done, all
other people [may] speak.’
Quantifier float can only be launched from plural noun phrases, a convenient
restriction which will be used here to identify the origin of a floated quantifier.
Not all verb-modifying occurrences of katoa are the result of quantifier float (or
quantifier raising; cf. 1.14.2). Indeed, in the following sentences, the quantifier cannot
have floated from any nominal argument of the verb:
(1305)
Koo too poouli katoa.
Inc too dark all
‘It’s far too dark.’
(1306)
Ne kai fakafaa katoa i te aso nei.

‘[She] ate all of four times today.’
Many verb-modifying occurrences of katoa are not quantifiers, but intensifiers, with
the rough meaning of ‘completely, very (much)’, as illustrated in the last two
examples. That katoa in the following sentence is not a quantifier is demonstrated
by the fact that the only nominal entity in the sentence it could have quantified is
not quantifiable:
(1307)
Koo maa katoa te maasina.
Inc full all the moon
‘The moon is completely full.’

(1315)

1.14.2. Quantifier raising
The process referred to here as ‘quantifier raising’ is the optional movement of the
quantifier katoa from a noun phrase in a subordinate clause to the verb of the
superordinate clause in which the subordinate clause is embedded. It maps the
first of the following sentences onto the second:
(1326)
Koo oti [ne oko olotou vaka katoa ki uta].
Inc finished Pst reach their-3 canoe all to land
‘All their canoes have landed.’
(1327)
Koo oti katoa [ne oko olotou vaka ki uta].
Inc finished all Pst reach their-3 canoe to land
‘Their canoes have all landed.’
Quantifier raising can take place in a variety of subordinate constructions, including
apposed subordinate clauses denoting aspectual notions, as illustrated by the above
examples and by the following:
(1328)
Koo palele katoa [ne kai nee ia ttou ika].
Inc depleted all Pst eat Erg he our-3-i fish
‘He’s eaten all of our fish.’
Quantifier raising can also apply to o-subordinate clauses and kee-subordinate
clauses whose superordinate verbs can trigger noun-phrase raising (cf. 1.1.2.7):
(1329)
E iloa katoa [o kkake tamataene Tuuvalu].
Nps know all Cmp climb young-man Tuvalu
‘Tuvaluan young men can all climb [trees].’
(1330)
E mafai katoa [o kaitaua au kia laatou].
Nps can all Cmp angry I to they-3
‘I can get angry at them all.’
(1331)
Koo pili katoa [o maua nee laatou telotou peeofuga].
Inc near all Cmp get Dxs they-3 their pay
‘They are about to get paid.’
Quantifier raising cannot apply to subordinate clauses that cannot also trigger noun-
phrase raising:
(1332)
* Koo pakia katoa au [ne ttoo nee niu kolaa].
Inc wounded all I Pst fall Erg coconut those
(‘I got hurt because all those coconuts fell on me.’)
However, quantifier and noun-phrase raising are independent processes, in that
one can take place without the other. In all of the above grammatical examples,
quantifier raising has applied, but noun-phrase raising hasn’t. The following
example demonstrates that a quantifier can be raised out of one noun phrase, while
another noun phrase undergoes noun-phrase raising:

1.15. MINOR SENTENCE TYPES
A number of constructions exhibit characteristics that distinguish them from more
common constructions in the language. In this category fall structures with the
hedge ailoga ‘unlikely’ (cf. 1.4.7(b)) and a variety of verbs that occur frequently or
exclusively in the negative (cf. 1.4.7(b) and (h), and 1.11.1.3.5). The following
provides a nonexhaustive sampling of minor sentence types not covered elsewhere
in the grammar.
1.15.1. Sentences without arguments or with restricted arguments
In 1.2.1.2.1, I assert that no verb appears exclusively without a subject. One
possible exception is mata, a verb-like lexeme which appears only in direct
questions (i.e., not in indirectly-reported contexts, not in noninterrogative

questions), which translates roughly as ‘[do you] reckon, [do you] expect, [what
do you] think’:
(1338)
Mata e lele koe maafea?
reckon Nps fly you when?
‘When do [you] think you’re going to fly off?’
(1339)
E mata e ttoo vaiua maataeao?
Nps reckon Nps fall rain-shower tomorrow
‘Do [you] reckon it’s going to rain tomorrow?’
(1340)
Koo mata e fia ana tausaga?
Inc reckon Nps how-many? his year
‘How old do [you] think she is?’
This verb is a borrowing from Samoan, although in that language it has the broader
meaning of ‘look like, seem’ and its syntactic behaviour does not appear to be
idiosyncratic (Mosel and Hovdhaugen 1992:598–599). In Tuvaluan, mata never appears
with an overt subject, but its subject is always implied to be a second-person entity. It
sometimes appears with a tense-aspect-mood marker (either e or koo), but more
frequently without one. It does not undergo morphosyntactic processes regularly
associated with verbs, such as nominalization and causative formation. It takes a
sentential complement, which is subordinated to it by apposition (cf. 1.1.2.1.5).
Another verb with an unusual syntactic behaviour is kaittoa (or, more rarely,
kaitoa) ‘serve X right’. This verb never takes a tense-aspect-mood marker. It generally
appears without an overt subject. It can occur alone as an exclamation, or it can be
modified by a kee-subordinated clause:
(1341)
Kaittoa kee naa mate!
serve-right Sbj then die
‘Serves [him] right that he die.’
However, kaittoa can control noun-phrase raising (cf. 1.1.2.7), and the raised noun
phrase can be marked as the subject of an intransitive verb as in the following, or
alternatively can receive comitative case marking or be ko-focused:
(1342)
Kaittoa tou fafine kee naa laoa i te ivi!
serve-right your woman Sbj then choke on the bone
‘[It will] serve that woman right if she chokes on a bone.’
The verb toikia ‘lucky X’, of unknown origin, is used in exclamatory clauses only
with a postposed subject and no tense-aspect-mood marker. It is often used
ironically:
(1343)

‘Lucky you, no one else turned out to be as smart as the two of you!’
(1344)

‘Your conceit will get you a long way!’

1.15.2. Superlative expressions
Two superlative words, namely maaffaga (or maafaga, sometimes ffaaga or faaga) and
maattuga (or maatuga, maattua, or maatua) can govern several types of construction.
First, these words can be modified by an indefinite noun phrase denoting the entity
being marked as superlative, which may or may not be modified by an adjective
denoting the superlative parameter. If no parameter is indicated, one can assume
that size is the relevant parameter:
(1345)
Maattuga eiloa se puusi te puusi teenaa!
superlative indeed a cat the cat that
‘What an enormous cat!’
(1346)
Maaffaga se tamaliki valea!
superlative a child stupid
‘What a stupid child!’
These constructions resemble equational structures, but the structure of the predicate
does not conform to any recognizable pattern. Second, the superlative words can
take a possessive modifier marked for inalienable possession and denoting the
entity being marked as superlative:
(1347)
Maattuga eiloa o puusi te puusi teenaa!
superlative indeed of cat the cat that
(1348)
Maaffaga o tamaliki valea!
superlative of child stupid
In this construction, the possessively marked noun phrase lacks an article, an
idiosyncratic feature only found in this construction. Third, the superlative word
can take the compounding particle -a- (cf. 2.2.6.3.2) and form a nominal compound
with the noun that denotes the entity being marked as superlative:
(1349)
Maattugaa puusi eiloa te puusi teenaa!
superlative+of cat indeed the cat that
(1350)
Maaffagaa tamaliki valea!
superlative+of child stupid
These various constructions appear most commonly as interjections, and they have
the status of clauses. However, the nominal compound version illustrated by the
last examples can function as ordinary noun phrases:
(1351)

Pst see Erg we-3-e the superlative+of cat Inc walk at
ttua fenua.
the+back island
‘We saw an enormous cat walking on the oceanside of the island.’
Different dialects may allow a different range of possibilities for the various forms
of the superlative words.
1.16. WORD CLASSES
As in other Polynesian languages (cf. Bauer 1993:254), word classes in Tuvaluan
cannot generally be described in terms of their internal structure. Indeed, taken out
of their syntactic context, most words cannot be assigned to a particular class,

Syntax
257
because the limited inflectional morphology fails to provide formal markers of word-
class affiliation, in the same way that gendered endings help identify nouns in
languages like Spanish, for example. However, lexical words do not belong to any
word class indiscriminately, and Tuvaluan and other Polynesian languages do have
lexical classes, despite claims made by some authors (e.g., Biggs 1973:50 for Maori,
Tchekhoff 1979 for Tongan). Lexical classes are defined on the basis of structural,
semantic, and distributional factors.
1.16.1. Noun
The greatest difficulties in defining word classes arise in distinguishing between
the two open word classes, nouns and verbs. (Special problems also arise in
defining adjectives, although these are of a different nature, as discussed in
1.16.4.) Indeed, as is commonly pointed out for Polynesian languages in general,
words that denote nominal entities (i.e., ‘nominals’) can occur as verbs, and vice
versa. In the following, the italicised nominals are syntactically verbs:
(1352)
A Fiiti e mauga?
Cnt Fiji Nps mountain
‘Is Fiji mountainous?’
(1353)
A Peletaania koi ulu eiloa ki te fafine.
Cnt Britain still head indeed to the woman
‘Britain[’s government] is still headed by a woman.’
(1354)
Tou tagata ne paasika mai i ttafataeao.
your man Pst bicycle Dxs in the+morning
‘That guy rode here on his bike this morning.’
(1355)
E feituu Nukulaelae.
Nps side Nukulaelae
‘He is part-Nukulaelae.’
(1356)
Tino Naaluu e pausi ki sitoa Saina.
person Nauru Nps suitcase to store China
‘Nauruans use Chinese stores as if they were their suitcases.’
(1357)
Maatou e Assaa i Amatuku.
we-3-e Nps Sunday at Amatuku
‘We are going [to spend] Sunday on Amatuku Islet.’
However, the apparent freedom with which nominals can be treated as verbs and
vice versa does not mean that the distinction between noun and verb is irrelevant
to the language. Indeed, each word in the language has one basic word-class
membership. For example, the italicised words in the above examples are nouns in
their most basic forms, and their occurrence in verbal morphosyntactic frames is
marked. Markedness is based on several criteria:
(a)
The meaning of the word is often less specific when it is used as a noun than when
it occurs as a verb. For example, the word feituu as a noun means ‘side, half, slice,
lineage’, but when it is used as a verb, as in (1355), it has the more restricted meaning
of ‘related on one side of one’s family [to a particular descent group]’.
(b) The meaning of the verb is often predictable from the meaning of the
noun, but the reverse is not true. In examples (1353), (1354), and (1356),
the nominal X acquires the meaning ‘use as an X’ when embedded in a

verbal frame. The meaning of the noun cannot be derived from the
meaning of the verb.
(c)
Native speakers are much more likely to provide the nominal meaning of
the verb than its verbal meaning in both monolingual elicitation and
translation exercises. For example, native speakers will always gloss paasika
as ‘bicycle’ in elicitation, even though they may also concede when pressed
that the word can also be given the meaning of ‘use as a bicycle, ride a bicycle’,
as in (1354).
(d) Nominals used as verbs are often subject to structural restrictions that are
not imposed on their nominal uses. For example, pausi ‘suitcase’ in (1356)
must be modified by a prepositional phrase denoting the entity being used
as a suitcase. (Indeed, many nouns can function as verbs in this syntactic-
semantic frame.)
(e)
Nominals in a semantic field may differ from one another in terms of their
propensity to be used as verbs. For example, Assaa ‘Sunday’ is the only noun
referring to a day of the week that can be used verbally, as in (1357). The semantic
field ‘days of the week’ is thus complete in the noun category but deficient in
the verb category (see 2.2.2.1 for additional examples).
(f)
The nominal occurs as a noun with much greater frequency than as a verb in
natural discourse.
Besides the semantic, morphosyntactic, and distributional criteria that distinguish
nouns from verbs, one simple morphological criterion can be applied to identify
nouns or noun-like words (e.g., nominalized verbs) in specific morphosyntactic
contexts. Nouns other than most proper nouns (but see 2.1.1.10.5–6) are preposed
with an article or a modifier in complementary distribution with articles, and may
be modified by a noun-modifying demonstrative form (cf. 2.1.2.5). While this
criterion is useful in specific morphosyntactic contexts and probably works better
in Tuvaluan than in other Polynesian languages (compare Bauer 1993:254–256 on
Maori), it is of little use in assigning decontextualized words to the nominal class.
1.16.2. Pronoun
Personal pronouns form a well-defined closed class (cf. 2.1.2.1.10), to which the
anaphoric form ei (cf. 2.1.2.1.7) and the affective form kita (cf. 2.1.2.1.12) can be
added as peripheral members. Possessive pronouns form a large but nevertheless
closed paradigm (cf. 2.1.2.4.3), and can be defined internally in terms of the
semantic categories that they encode (cf. 2.1.2.4.2), and externally in terms of their
syntagmatic behaviour (e.g., they are in complementary distribution with articles).
Demonstratives define a closed formal class but do not form a well-defined word
class: some demonstrative forms behave like pronouns, others like verbs and
adjectives, and others like adverbs. However, demonstrative pronouns and
demonstrative verbs display syntagmatic peculiarities that indicate that they are
not fully-fledged members of these word classes. Relative forms are formally
identical to demonstrative adjectives and pronouns and behave like them,
although they can cooccur with other demonstratives while other demonstratives
do not cooccur with one another (cf. 1.1.2.3.1 and 2.1.2.7).
1.16.3. Verb 1.16.3.1. Lexical verb
It is more difficult to define verbs as distinct from nouns than the reverse because
all verbs other than the most marginal can nominalize without undergoing any
changes in form, and as such acquire the morphosyntactic behaviour of nouns.

However, as discussed in 2.1.3.5(a), nominalized verbs differ from canonical nouns
in several respects, and these differences motivate separating nominalized verbs
from canonical nouns, and thus separating verbs from nouns.
From a syntagmatic standpoint, a broad operational definition for the word
class ‘verb’ may consist of three criteria:
(a)
To be a verb, a word must be able to be preceded by the universal-tense
marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1.1) except when it occurs in a verb series (cf.
2.1.3.7). However, this condition is not sufficient because some words
that clearly do not function as full verbs can take e (but not other tense-
aspect-mood markers), such as certain occurrences of the negators see
and seki, which otherwise do not behave like verbs (cf. 1.4(a)-(b)). Nor is
the condition necessary because certain lexemes behave like verbs in
certain respects although they cannot be marked by any tense-aspect-
mood marker, including e; such is the case of kaittoa ‘serve X right’ (cf.
1.15.1), as well as constructions with itiiti (cf. 2.1.3.4.16) and the
compounds moo mea and muu mea (cf. 2.1.6.6.3(b)), which denote nearly
realized situations.
(b) A verb must be able to undergo bare nominalization (cf. 2.1.3.5(a)). Suffixal
nominalization does not provide a good test, because some verbs, like
possessive verbs and heavy verbal strings like predicative prepositional
phrases, do not take the nominalizing suffix for reasons other than their lack
of verbal qualities.
(c)
A verb must be able to appear with one nominal argument. While there are
many instances of verbs without subject or direct object in natural discourse
(cf. 1.2.1.2.1 and 1.2.1.2.2), all verbs can appear with a nominal argument, with
the exception of the marginal cases discussed in 1.15.1.
1.16.3.2. Auxiliary
Crosslinguistically, auxiliaries commonly mark such categories as the tense,
aspect, mood, or voice of the verb with which they are associated (Schachter
1985:41), and often attract number, person, and gender agreement, if these
categories are marked in the language. Very few of these tell-tale categories are
productively marked in Tuvaluan, which makes it difficult to argue for or against
an analysis of negators as auxiliaries. While tense-aspect-mood markers precede
negators (cf. 1.4), it is difficult, if not impossible, to decide whether they mark
primarily the verb or the negator. Two of the negators contrast solely in terms of
tense and aspect (unmarked see v. past-perfect seki), while the third negator is used
only in the imperative mood (saa). Since tense, aspect, and mood can also be
marked elsewhere in the sentence, it is not accurate to say that the primary role of
the negator is to mark these categories. Yet the three negators see, seki, and saa form
the one closed word class that comes closest to being classifiable as an auxiliary
class in Tuvaluan.
Another candidate for inclusion in the category ‘auxiliary’ is the desiderative fia
(cf 2.1.3.4.15). Seiter (1980:10) treats its Niuean cognate as an auxiliary, on account
of the fact that it ‘qualif[ies] the reality of the situation described by the main verb’.
In Tuvaluan, there is no structural motivation for treating fia as an auxiliary, and
while Seiter’s remark on the semantics of the Niuean cognate can also apply to
Tuvaluan fia, it represents a weak argument for establishing a separate auxiliary
class. Finally, a number of words denoting aspectual or modal categories can
function either as adverbs or as superordinate verbs, and their adverbial uses

resemble auxiliaries; such is the case of the iterative maasani (literally ‘used to’, cf.
2.1.3.3.2.1(g)), gaasolo ‘become’, and fui ‘hardly, with difficulty, by taking a long

1.16.4. Adjective
The nature of the category ‘adjective’ is a proverbially thorny issue crosslinguistically
(Dixon 1982, Thompson 1989). Tuvaluan does not have a unified adjectival category,
but instead has three classes of adjective. One has verbal properties and is the most
open class; the second has nominal properties and is less open; and the third and
most restricted constitutes a residual class. The first two classes are further discussed
in 2.1.4.
1.16.4.1. Verbal adjective
Verbal adjectives are ‘verb-like’ because they can function as predicates, and they
can also always be used as attributive modifiers of nouns. Verbal adjectives can
only be distinguished from verbs on a semantic basis: verbal adjectives characterize
some property of the referent of a noun (Dixon 1982). No structural criteria clearly
demarcate the boundary between the two categories. For instance, the ability to
take on an attributive function is not an exclusive property of verbal adjectives,
since it also characterizes many verbs:
(1358)
se tagata kkau
a man swim
‘a good swimmer (of a man)’
Similarly, gradability is not possible with some verbal adjectives (cf. 2.1.4.5), and
thus does not provide a good discriminating criterion. Furthermore, some verbs
can be used in comparative constructions (cf. 2.1.4.4), so comparison is not an
exclusive property of verbal adjectives. Thus the boundary between verbal adjectives
and verbs is blurred at best.
In attributive contexts, a variety of syntactic and semantic relationships may
exist between the adjective and the noun it modifies. The modified noun may
correspond to the subject of the intransitive verb from which the adjective is derived:
(1359)
ne vai mmoko
some water cold
‘some cold water’
(1360)
ko fakalavelave ttupu o te olaga
Foc problem happen of the life
‘life’s problems’
It may correspond to its direct object:
(1361)
uttanu saka
germinated-coconut-kernel boil
‘boiled germinated coconut kernels’
(1362)
laakau kaina
plant eaten
‘edible plants’
It may also correspond to a variety of instrumental modifiers:

‘my sports shoes’

or to a temporal or locative modifier:
(1365)

Many verbal adjectives specialize in particular relationships with the nouns they

that correspond to subjects in predicate contexts (e.g., te tagata saka ‘a good dancer
of a man’) or to instruments (e.g., te titi saka ‘a dancing skirt’).
The noun modified by an attributive verbal adjective cannot correspond to the
subject of the transitive predicate that corresponds to the adjective. This does not
mean that transitive verbs cannot serve as attributive adjectives. However, in order
for a transitive verb form to function as such and modify the agentive noun, it must
have an intransitive form. For example, kake ‘climb’, can be used either intransitively
or transitively, and thus can function as an attributive adjective:
(1368)
se tagata kake

‘an excellent climber of a man’
In contrast, the verb puke ‘grab’ is not readily used as an intransitive verb, and it
does not fare well as an attributive adjective modifying its agent:
(1369)

(‘a child [who] grabs [things]’)
(The above is grammatical if puke is given its alternative meaning of ‘adopt’, and if
the child is understood as corresponding to the direct object of the verb in the
equivalent predicative construction.)
In theory, all verbs can be used adjectivally, but some lend themselves better
to being used as adjectives than others. For example, it is difficult to imagine
what the existential verb isi and its negative form seeai would mean as attributive

biographic’, are much more common in attributive than in predicative frames.
These idiosyncratic patterns cannot be predicted from the formal or semantic
characteristics of the word.

1.16.4.2. Nominal adjective
Nominal adjectives are homophonous with and identical in meaning to nouns,
and denote nongradable notions. They are thus not subject to comparison or to the
expression of degrees of quality (cf. 2.1.4.4 and 2.1.4.5). They can only occur as
attributive modifiers of nouns:
(1370)
te loomatua Ppaalagi
the old-woman Westerner
‘the elderly white woman’
(1371)
tifa fatu mo ipu kilaasi
plate stone and cup glass
‘porcelain plates and glass cups’
(1372)
ne nofoga mootokaa
some seat car
‘some car seats’
Although many nouns can function as nominal adjectives, not all do, and whether
particular nouns do or not is idiosyncratically determined.
1.16.4.3. Other adjective
There remains a handful of adjectives and comparable modifiers that do not
fall into either of the categories described in 1.16.4.1 and 1.16.4.2. Most
prominent is a very small class of modifiers that are preposed to nouns, rather
than postposed like other adjectives. In this category fall toe ‘last, remaining’
(which can also take on a superlative meaning, as shown in 1.11.1.3.5), the
diminutive intensifier lee (cf. 1.4.7(g)), matua ‘original, canonical,
unadulterated’, and the Samoan borrowings maatai and uluai ‘first’ (the latter
is only used in high rhetoric):
(1373)
Teenaa eiloo tena maatai pati ne iloa o fai, ko te pati

maasei.

‘That was the very first word he was able to utter, a swear word.’
(1374)

‘This is our last fatele tonight.’
(1375)
Koe e kai ki te matua ika io mo ko te kaapa ika?

‘Do you want to have fresh fish or canned fish?’
To the above should be added miscellaneous types of modifiers preposed to
nouns, namely nouns with collective meaning (cf. 2.1.6.5.1) and an eclectic set
of quantifiers (cf. 2.1.6.6.3). These are adjectival forms insofar as they have an
attributive function, although they share little else with verbal and nominal
adjectives. Finally, one productive compounding process described in 2.2.6.3.3
generates verbal noun-adjective compounds, which can in turn be used
attributively.

1.16.5. Preposition and case marker
Both case markers and prepositions form closed classes (cf. 2.1.1 and 2.1.5.1),
but the boundary between them is difficult to determine precisely because a
number of forms function as both prepositions and case markers (and
ambiguously so in certain contexts), and because they occupy the same
positions in the phrase, where they are in complementary distribution (with
one minor exception discussed in 2.2.6.1.1). The two basic case markers, the
ergative and pseudoergative nee and the optional contrastive-absolutive a,
are the least ambiguous: they clearly differ from other grammatical
morphemes in that they function solely as markers of case relations. The
three basic prepositions, locative i, directional ki, and source mai, take a
prefix -(a)a when their object falls in certain categories, as discussed in 2.1.5.2
and 2.1.5.3, and this morphological peculiarity places them in a class of their
own. However, they take the same suffix when they are used as case
markers, and thus suffixation is not a good discriminating criterion. The
same three prepositions can also take another, more archaic, suffix -te under
the same conditions, but three other grammatical morphemes may also take
this suffix, albeit more rarely: the alienable possessive a, the inalienable
possessive o, and the comitative mo. Finally, both case marking and
prepositional uses of i, ki, and mai can be the basis for the formation of
complex prepositions (cf. 2.2.6.1.2).
1.16.6. Numeral, quantifier, and interrogative word
Numerals do not form a separate word class. Rather, they function like verbal
adjectives (cf. 2.1.6.1 to 2.1.6.5). Quantifiers do not form a separate word class
either, nor do they behave in a homogeneous fashion: one finds in their ranks
adverbs, verbs, affixes, and articles. For further discussion, see 2.1.6.6. The
same can be said of interrogative words, some of which behave like nouns,
and others like verbs or adverbs; their morphological classification is
discussed in 2.1.2.6.

2.1. INFLECTION
Like other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan tends to encode syntactic and semantic
information onto isolated morphological categories, rather than onto bound affixes,
morphophonemic alternations, clitics, or derivational processes. For example, the
syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases are generally expressed with the
help of prepositional morphemes. Apart from number agreement in some verbs
and adjectives, very few processes modify the form of lexemes, be they nouns or
members of other word classes. The consequence of this tendency is that there are
very few form-internal criteria whereby members of various word classes can be
distinguished (cf. 1.16).
2.1.1. Noun inflection
2.1.1.1. Means of marking syntactic and semantic functions
As noted above, information on the syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases
is primarily encoded by prepositions and particles that function like prepositions.
In addition, word order plays a minor role in marking syntactic and semantic
functions (cf. 1.2.1.2.6). Indeed, certain prepositions are lost when their objects occur
in certain syntactic positions, but their syntactic and semantic function is retrievable
from their position in the sentence. However, the marking of syntactic and semantic
functions is not the primary role of word order, but rather an incidental function.
First and foremost, word order marks information structure (cf. 1.12.1).
A summary of prepositions and preposition-like markers that encode the
syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases, along with cross-references to
their various uses, is provided in 2.1.5.1.
2.1.1.2. Syntactic functions
Attention is drawn to processes discussed elsewhere in this grammar that affect
the morphological marking of syntactic functions as well as, in some cases, these
syntactic functions themselves. These include: advancement-to-possessive (cf.
1.1.2.3.10); noun-phrase raising (cf. 1.1.2.7); nominalisations (cf. 2.1.1.3.4); and
‘double’ additive coordinated constructions (cf. 1.3.1.6). In the following discussion,
I refer to tests for transitivity, which are summarized in 2.1.3.1.
2.1.1.2.1. Subject of intransitive verb
The same marking strategies are used for agentive and nonagentive subjects of
intransitive verbs. Subjects of intransitive verbs are marked in the same way as

direct objects in transitive clauses (cf. 2.1.1.2.4). See 2.1.1.2.2 for further discussion.
For a discussion of case-marking patterns associated with the arguments of
pseudoergative constructions, see 2.1.3.1.3(d).
2.1.1.2.1.1. Agentive subject of intransitive verb All agentive subjects of intransitive
verbs (with the exception of the third-person singular pronoun in certain positions,
as discussed below) can be marked with a zero case marker, no matter where in the
clause the noun phrase occurs, and whether the noun phrase is a full noun phrase
or a pronoun (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.3 for illustrations of the latter case):
(1376)
Koi tele ø tena gafa.
still run his genealogy
‘He still has descendants.’
(1377)
ø te gaaluega teelaa e see ttogi.
the work that Nps Neg pay
‘That work doesn’t pay [anything].’
The one exception to this pattern is the nonzero form of the third-person pronoun
(cf. 2.1.2.1.1.1–2) and in situ interrogative words that function as subjects of
intransitive verbs (cf. 2.1.2.6).
Definite agentive subjects of intransitive verbs can be marked with the preposed
case marker a, glossed throughout this description as an ‘contrastive-absolutive’
marker. For example, the following are roughly equivalent in meaning to sentences
(1376) and (1377) respectively:
(1378)
Koi tele a tena gafa.
still run Cnt his genealogy
‘He still has descendants.’
(1379)
A te gaaluega teelaa e see ttogi.
Cnt the work that Nps Neg pay
‘That work doesn’t pay [anything].’
The marker a may appear in all contexts in which a definite argument of the verb is
left unmarked for case, whatever the syntactic and semantic functions of the noun
phrase. In many cases, it has a contrastive function, as illustrated in 1.11.2.1.7. Even
though it is uniformly glossed as a contrastive marker for convenience in this
description, a does not always mark information structure and, in many instances,
it has a very low functional load. Indeed, it tends to appear as a ‘filler’ whenever a
definite noun phrase lacks an overt article and a case marker or preposition. Since
both the plural definite article and the absolutive case marker are zero forms, a
noun phrase appears with no article or case marker when it is definite, plural, and
in the absolutive case, or when it occurs in preverbal position, where noun phrases
are not marked for case (cf. 1.2.1.2.6 and 1.12.1):
(1380)
Kae kesekkese a tala.
but different Cnt story
‘But there are different [versions of] the story.’
(1381)
A pou o te fale e tofu loo mo tino.
Cnt post of the house Nps each-have indeed with person
‘Each post in the house belongs to someone.’
Animacy has no effect on the likelihood that the noun phrase will be marked with
a, but definiteness does: a cannot mark indefinite noun phrases. The marker is

(1382)

Furthermore, a is frequent with personal pronouns in absolutive or unmarked case

(au is the only pronoun with /a/ in initial position). The marker is not ungrammatical
with au, but it is rare. This phenomenon clearly has a phonological basis, in that au
also triggers the apocope of certain morphemes in a in other contexts (cf. 2.1.2.1.1).
In most instances, a is optional and its presence is not conditioned by morpho-
syntactic factors. The only contexts in which a is obligatory are when the overt
form of the third-person singular pronoun receives either the absolutive case or is
unmarked for case, and does not immediately follow the verb (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.1–2),
and when an in situ interrogative word functions as the subject of an intransitive
verb (cf. 2.1.2.6). Both instances involve noun phrases marked by neither a case
marker nor an article, and thus they can be viewed as the grammaticalization of the
preference pattern described earlier. In no case can a ever appear in addition to
another case marker or preposition. The marker must not be confused with the
form of the additive-adversative conjunction with which it is homophonous (cf.
1.3.1.1.1–2), which can be preposed to certain prepositions.
Subjects of middle constructions (cf. 1.2.1.2.4 and 2.1.1.2.8) receive the same case-
marking pattern as agentive subjects of intransitive clauses:
(1384)

(1385)

‘I just heard the news.’
The case-marking pattern described in this section, i.e., the alternation of a zero
case marker with a, is also characteristic of direct objects (cf. 2.1.1.2.4). Following
traditional nomenclature (Comrie 1978, Dixon 1994), I refer to this category as the
absolutive case. I investigate the extent to which the absolutive case reflects a
significant syntactic category in 2.1.1.2.2.
For a discussion of pseudoergative constructions, in which the subject of certain
intransitive verbs is marked for the ergative case, see 2.1.3.1.3(d).
2.1.1.2.1.2. Nonagentive subject of intransitive verb In most cases, no distinction
is made between agentive and nonagentive subjects of intransitive verbs. The case-
marking patterns described in 2.1.1.2.1.1 also apply to nonagentive subjects.
With several categories of intransitive verbs that take nonagentive subjects,
interesting patterns emerge. First, a number of verbs that denote ‘bringing’, ‘taking’,

these verbs, the noun phrase that receives absolutive-case marking is often the
patient, while the agent is marked for the oblique case with the comitative
preposition mo. Second, in the category which I label ‘experience verbs’, the
absolutively marked noun phrase is again the patient, while the agent or experiencer
is marked obliquely with the locative preposition i. Of course, in all these cases,
which noun phrase functions as the syntactic subject of the verb is an empirical
question, which is addressed in the following.
 
(a) Subject of ‘bringing’ verb and subject of possessive clause  
Several verbs of motion can appear in constructions that denote ‘bringing’ and
‘taking’. In these constructions, the agent is marked as an oblique argument with
the comitative preposition mo and the patient is marked for the absolutive case:
(1386)
Oku kope koo fano mo ia ki tai.
my luggage Inc go with he to sea
‘He took my luggage to the ship.’
The verbs fano, literally ‘go’, vau ‘come’, and tele ‘run’ are the most common in this
frame, but many other verbs of motion and verbs denoting motion-like situations
can also appear in the construction: ttolo ‘crawl’, kkefu ‘fast’, and tipa ‘stroll’. In
these constructions, fano usually means ‘take’, vau ‘bring’, and tele and similar verbs
‘steal’. The construction is the most idiomatic way of referring to bringing, taking,
and related situations. When the patient is an animate entity, the verb is often
semantically ambiguous:
(1387)
Teleke koo fano mo ia ki tai.
Teleke Inc go with he to sea
‘He took Teleke to the ship.’
or: ‘Teleke went with him to the ship.’
Thus sentences with animate patients do not provide good test cases for the
investigation of the syntactic structure of these constructions.
The verb nofo ‘stay, live’ can also appear in the same type of construction, in
which case it takes on a possessive meaning, commonly associated with temporary
possession (cf. 1.10.1.4):
(1388)
Ana mea koo nofo katoa mo au.
his thing Inc stay all with I
‘I’ve got all his belongings.’
The same construction is also used to denote situations in which one entity
encounters another, particularly if the encounter is metaphorical (e.g., ‘encountering
difficulties’):
(1389)
Ne fepaki te afaa mo te vaka kaakoo.
Pst collide the westerlies with the ship cargo
‘The cargo ship ran into strong westerlies.’
Verbs that fall into this category include fepaki ‘collide, run into, meet in contest’
and its alternative form feipaki, poko ‘strike’, and the Samoan borrowings feagai ‘face,
up against’ and fetaui ‘meet’ (and their reciprocal causative forms fakafeagai and
fakafetaui; cf. 1.6.1.5(b)). All verbs that fall into this last category can also take objects
marked with the directional preposition ki rather than the comitative preposition
mo; thus (1389) is equivalent in meaning to (1390):

‘split’ (cf. 1.3.1.7), which they resemble. Indeed, for most constructions of the type

under discussion.
Second, constructions of the type under discussion have alternative forms in
which case marking is switched around into a less exotic pattern, i.e., in which the

(1394)

an experience verb in predicate position. In experience clauses, one participant,

The label ‘experience clause’ is not to be taken to imply that all clauses denoting
physical, emotional, and mental experiences fall into this category. Many verbs
denoting experiences of various types are transitive or middle verbs (cf. 2.1.1.2.8),
and never govern the case-marking patterns described here. However, utterances
denoting sensory, emotional, and other physical and mental experiences are
frequently expressed with such constructions, as discussed presently, and all
constructions of this type denote sensory, emotional, and other physical and mental
experiences.
Which noun phrase functions as the subject in experience clauses? An answer to
this question can be sought by submitting these clauses to various tests. Only certain
tests can be applied to experience clauses. For example, imperative formation, which
discriminates subjects from other noun phrases (cf. 1.1.1.3), cannot apply here
because experience verbs do not occur in imperative contexts. Similarly, no
experience verb appears to undergo subject-verb number agreement, so this test
cannot be applied to determine which noun phrase controls agreement. In addition,
embedding experience clauses in complex constructions to which equi-deletion
applies only yields pragmatically-awkward results.
Oblique arguments of experience verbs are identical in behaviour to other
prepositional phrases headed by the locative i. For example, when they are third-
person pronouns, they can take the anaphoric form ei (cf. 2.1.2.1.7):

(1432)

[lit.: ‘This is the thing that is felt in the hearts of men.]

denoted by experience verbs (i.e., sensation, feelings, emotions, and other types of

liver). Similar patterns of ethnopsychological understanding have been reported
elsewhere in Polynesia (e.g., Levy (1984) on Tahiti, Shore (1982:173) on Samoa) and
in many other societies in Oceania and elsewhere in the world (Talmy 1985:111).
Thus the fact that experiencers can be, and often are, encoded as locatively marked
obliques in experience clauses is related to a certain view of what an experience
represents. However, not all feelings and sensations are viewed as having an
experiencer-external basis; remembering, for example, is not talked about in the
same terms as forgetting. Significantly, masaua and manatua ‘remember’ cannot

The third problematic construction consists of sentences in which an absolutively

noun phrase denotes a cause or an agent:
(1437)
Ttou fenua ne puapuagaatia i tino Ppaalagi.

‘Our team was defeated by their team.’
In Polynesian linguistics, the locatively marked noun phrase in these constructions
has traditionally been referred to as the ‘stative agent’ (e.g., Chung 1978:28–30,

locatively marked noun phrase is not necessarily an agent. Indeed, the referent of
the locatively marked noun phrase can be inanimate, and can thus be better
described as a cause:
(1440)
Tino koo fiittaa i te pakamaiota.
person Inc tired at the toddy-caramel-ball
‘People are tired of [eating] balls of caramelized toddy and grated
coconut.’
(1441)
Kaati kaa fiaffia koulua i taku gaaluega.

‘You will probably be happy with my work.’

This description captures well the semantic function of animate arguments in

the following example in which the actions of the ‘initiator’ can be interpreted as

[i.e., ‘because he is very gifted, because he is an inspiration for others

However, the descriptor ‘initiator’ identifies accurately the fact that the participant
is not necessarily involved as a responsible, active, and volitional entity in the
situation denoted by the clause (i.e., it can be low in agency). This characteristic is
particularly important when the verb can be used transitively. For example, compare
(1443) above with the following transitive clause:
(1444)

‘He [himself] can do everything.’
In the transitive clause, the referent must be interpreted as being responsible for
the situation denoted by the clause, through its direct actions, for example. However,
in Tuvaluan at least, ‘initiator’ is not felicitous when the locatively marked argument

A general description of this construction in Tuvaluan would characterize the
locatively marked participant as an entity that brings about, directly or indirectly,
volitionally or nonvolitionally, the situation denoted by the clause. In addition, the
referent of the locatively marked participant is frequently targeted or affected either
by the situation or by its direct consequences. For example, the actions resulting
from the feelings denoted by the following clause can only be directed at the referent
of the locatively marked participant:
(1445)

‘Tolu is ashamed of his brother.’

2.1.1.2.2. Subject of transitive verb
Several case-marking strategies are associated with subjects of transitive verbs. The
most basic is the ergative case, which does not distinguish between agentive and
nonagentive subjects, but upon which certain semantic restrictions are imposed.
Its morphology is covered in (a) and its affective value is described in (b). The
subject of a transitive verb is frequently expressed as the possessive modifier of the
direct object, as discussed in (c), and, in certain constructions described in (d), as a
benefactive phrase. The discussion in (e) delineates the implications of the previous
subsections for an understanding of ergativity as a morphological and syntactic
category in Tuvaluan.
Other sections of relevance to the topics covered here are the discussions of
clitic pronouns (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5(a)), of restrictions on the agentive argument of
causative verbs (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)), and of the transitivizing suffix (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(c)).
 
(a) Ergative case marking  
Subjects of transitive verbs are commonly marked with the ergative case marker
nee, which is obligatory when the noun phrase is postverbal:
(1465)
Toko uke tino ne ave nee vaka kaisoa.
Num many person Pst send Erg ship steal
‘Many people were stolen by slave ships.’
(1466)
E see iloa foki nee tino taumua o tauloto fakallei.
Nps Neg know also Erg person former Cmp study properly
‘People in the olden days also did not know how to study properly.’
The marker is optionally reduced in form to ne when the following word consists
of more than two morae. This predictable alternation is not indicated in the
orthography used here. The marker can be followed by any article, noun, or
preposed noun modifier, with the exception of the plural indefinite article ne, with
which it is nearly homophonous:
(1467)
* Ne sau mai nee ne tino.
Pst carry Dxs Erg some person
(‘Some people carried [her] here.’)
When the subject of a transitive verb is indefinite and plural, its article is simply
dropped, and the noun phrase then becomes homophonous with its definite plural
counterpart, since the plural definite article is a zero form:
(1468)
Ne sau mai nee tino.
Pst carry Dxs Erg person
‘Some people carried [her] here.’
No restriction applies to the sequencing of nee with the singular indefinite article
se, the plural definite article (a zero form), or the coalesced form of the indefinite
plural article niisi ‘some, other’. Thus the above restriction clearly has a phonological
motivation. The ergative case marker nee is an irregular reflex of the Proto-Polynesian
case marker *e; the regular reflex e is found in the three Northern dialects and is
occasionally heard in the Southern dialects, particularly in religious discourse.
When the subject of a transitive verb occurs in preverbal position, it is left
unmarked for case, or it is marked with the absolutive-contrastive case marker a
(cf. 1.2.1.2.6). However, there is a strong tendency for preverbal subjects to be indexed
by a personal pronoun in postverbal position, usually immediately after the verb

(b) Affective value of the ergative case  
Although no morphological distinction is made between agentive and nonagentive
subjects of transitive verbs, ergative case marking is constrained by a number of
semantic restrictions. While the morphological category ‘ergative’ is strongly
associated with the syntactic category ‘subject of transitive verb’, the ergative case
may mark categories other than subjects of transitive verbs and some subjects of
transitive verbs are not marked ergatively.
In the majority of cases, the ergative case marks a personal pronoun, whether it
functions as the index of a moved noun phrase or a full pronoun. When it marks
full noun phrases, these are typically definite and specific. However, indefinite
and nonspecific noun phrases are not grammatically excluded from ergatively-
marked argument slots:
(1471)
Fakanofonofoga kolaa e faigataa o fakassee nee se tino.
resolution those Nps difficult Cmp Cst+wrong Erg a person
‘It is difficult for someone to dispute these resolutions.’
The propensity for personal pronouns and definite noun phrases to be marked
ergatively is symptomatic of the fact that the ergative case has strong affective
connotations. An ergatively marked noun phrase commonly refers to an entity that
is centrally involved in bringing about the situation denoted by the clause. It is thus
not surprising that pronouns, i.e., animate entities which are high in topicality, should
be so commonly marked with the ergative case, and that definite noun phrases should
be much more common than indefinite noun phrases in ergative slots.
The above remark characterizes a case category, and not the syntactic category
‘subject of a transitive verb’ or the semantic category ‘agent’. First, the subjects of
many transitive verbs are not marked with the ergative case. Subjects of transitive
verbs may be zero pronominalized (cf. 1.2.1.2.1(d)), in which case they do not appear
at all in the clause and thus obviously receive no case marking:
(1472)
Te moa ne kaisoa.
the chicken Pst steal
‘A chicken got stolen.’
Subjects of transitive verbs can also be expressed in such a way that they will not
receive ergative case marking. For example, they can be expressed as a possessive

the verb has a reported speech complement or not and whether the speech is
reported directly or indirectly have no effect on case marking. In the following
