connotation is a negative one. In particular, ergatively marked subjects are common
with speech-act sentences that denote socially inappropriate verbal behaviour.
Again, the same notion of responsibility and involvement characterizes the
difference between ergatively marked noun phrases and their alternatives.
To summarize, agents may be marked in ways other than with the ergative case,
and the ergative case is used to mark categories other than subjects of transitive
verbs. While many ergatively marked noun phrases denote agentive subjects of
transitive verbs, the case category ‘ergative’ denotes something other than the
syntactic category ‘subject of transitive verb’ or the semantic category ‘agent’.
Observations of cases in which these various categories do not overlap suggest
that the ergative case typically denotes the high level of responsibility and
involvement of referents of noun phrases it marks. When these characteristics are
either absent or unimportant, agents are expressed with means other than the
ergative case. Thus the characteristic value of the ergative case is an affective one.
 
(c) Agent of transitive verb expressed as possessive modifier of direct object  
The agent of a transitive verb can be expressed as the possessive modifier of the
direct object (compare Duranti and Ochs 1990 on Samoan). For example, the
possessive modifier in the following is most naturally interpreted as referring to
the agent of the sentence:
(1478)
Ne kkati telotou niu.
Pst cut their-3 coconut-tree
‘They cut down the coconut tree.’
Unlike the agent of an equivalent transitive clause with two overt arguments, the
possessive agent is not ascribed a high degree of responsibility in the situation
described by the clause. Compare the previous sentence with the following:
(1479)
Ne kkati nee laatou te niu.
Pst cut Erg they-3 the coconut-tree
‘They were the ones who cut down the coconut tree.’
Structures with possessively-marked agents are very common in discourse. They
bear some resemblance to relative clauses that have undergone advancement-to-
possessive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10), although, as will be shown presently, they differ from
these structures in important ways.
For an agent to be expressed as a possessive modifier of the direct object, both
the agent and patient must denote entities that can potentially be in a possessor—

(e) Ergativity as a morphological and syntactic phenomenon  
When faced with an ergative-absolutive system, the grammarian must ascertain
the extent to which the morphological categories ‘absolutive’ and ‘ergative’ reflect
syntactically significant categories, i.e., whether ergativity is a morphological
phenomenon superposed on a syntactic structure based on a nominative-accusative
pattern, or whether the categories of ergative and absolutive are also recognized as
syntactic categories in the structure of the language (Dixon 1994:143–181).
Several processes provide evidence that Tuvaluan syntax is based on a
nominative-accusative system. Among such processes are: advancement-to-
possessive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10), which applies equally to subjects of intransitive and
transitive verbs and no other category; noun-phrase deletion associated with
imperative formation (cf. 1.1.1.3.1), which also constrains preverbal subjects in both
intransitive and transitive clauses; the referential constraint that rules out the
coreference of the zero subject of a subordinate clause, be it intransitive or transitive,
and the subject of the superordinate clause (cf. 1.5.2.3); and causative formation (cf.
2.1.3.1.3(a)), in which underlying subjects of both intransitive and transitive verbs
become direct objects in causative clauses. Equi-deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6) allows all
superordinate subjects to control the deletion of subordinate subjects, although, as
will be discussed presently, subjects of intransitive and transitive verbs do not behave
as a unified category when equi-deletion targets direct objects. One process, direct-
object incorporation (cf. 2.1.3.6.12), refers to direct objects as a category distinct
from subjects of intransitive verbs, and hence argues against the syntactic
significance of a category ‘absolutive’ in the syntax of the language.
In contrast, there are arguments for recognizing ergative and absolutive
categories as being of syntactic significance. All syntactic processes involving
movements and traces refer to subjects of intransitive verbs and direct objects as

movement (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)), relative clause formation (1.1.2.3.7(a)), and clefting

clauses usually move to preverbal position without leaving a pronominal trace,
while subjects of transitive verbs usually leave an ergatively marked trace (cf.
1.2.1.2.6(a) and 1.12.2.3). These trace patterns are not absolute rules, but tendencies.
Similarly, nominalization affects subjects of transitive verbs in one way, and
subjects of intransitive verbs and direct objects in another way (cf. 2.1.1.3.4). Clitic
pronouns, when they can occur, can only function as subjects of transitive verbs
(cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5). And what is called here ‘causative inversion’ (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)) affects
causees in causative constructions that are derived from subjects of transitive

Equi-deletion in which the direct object of the superordinate clause is deleted
(cf. 1.1.2.6) refers to subjects of intransitive and transitive verbs as distinct categories,
with the subject of an intransitive verb being more alike (but not identical to) the
direct object than the subject of a transitive verb. The extent to which this process
may be usefully taken as evidence for either syntactic accusativity or syntactic
ergativity is unclear.
Finally, one finds a battery of semantic and derivational processes that refer to
the subject of an intransitive verb and the direct object as a unified category. Among
these figure: suffixation with -goofie ‘readily’ and -gataa ‘not readily’ (cf. 2.2.2.2.2);
prefixation with the potential prefix ma- (cf. 2.1.3.4.7); prefixation with the stativizing
prefix ma- (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(e)); and V-gaa-N compounding (cf. 2.2.6.3.2). The
interpretation of desiderative clauses (cf. 2.1.3.4.15) is also based on an ergative-
absolutive pattern, although this is only a tendency rather than an absolute pattern.
Similar ergatively based phenomena are found in all languages, including languages
with nominative-accusative syntactic systems (Dixon 1994:18–21), but their
prevalence in Tuvaluan is noteworthy.
The characteristic commonly referred to as the ‘dispensibility’ of arguments,
which is sometimes invoked in discussions of ergativity (e.g., Biggs 1974 for
Polynesian languages) yields equivocal patterns in Tuvaluan. As shown in 1.2.1.2.1
and 1.2.1.2.2, there are many different ways in which subject and object arguments
of verbs can be ‘dispensed with’ or omitted, and it is not clear that one pattern
should be given greater weight than the other. However, it is significant that
most processes affecting subjects described in 1.2.1.2.1 ((a)-(d) in particular) refer
to subjects of transitive verbs only, and thus treat this category as distinct from
both subjects of intransitive verbs and direct objects. Furthermore, one notes that
certain structures, described in 1.2.1.2.5(b) as being part of a ‘scheme’ to prevent
the proliferation of clauses with two arguments, only apply to the category subject
of transitive verb: such is the case of the fact that the subject of a transitive verb
can be expressed as a possessive modifier of the direct object (cf. (d) below).
However, these should not be construed as syntactic processes in the usual sense
of the term, and their implication for the syntax of grammatical relations is not
clear.
The general conclusion one can draw from the above discussion is that, while
Tuvaluan does not have an ergative-absolutive syntax, it exhibits a strong ergative-
absolutive syntactic undercurrent. Certainly all processes traditionally taken to be
‘superficial’ or ‘postcyclic’ follow an ergative-absolutive pattern. What is also
interesting is that most processes that are typically taken to be ‘major’, ‘deeper’,
‘cyclic’, or ‘term-creating’ (depending on the theoretical framework), namely raising,
object incorporation, quantifier float, and equi-deletion, either cannot be used as

2.1.1.2.6. Object of comparison
Objects of comparison in canonical comparative constructions (i.e., as described in

The object of equative constructions of various types can be marked with the

constructions in 1.9.1. Other verbs with equative connotations, e.g., tofu ‘each have’,
also take objects marked with mo. See 2.1.1.2.8(b) for other constructions with the
same marker.
In addition to the above, verbal and adverbial demonstrative forms in pee- can
take predicative objects marked with the complementizer me or one of its allomorphs
when these refer to irrealis comparisons or equations (cf. 1.9.1(a)). Because only
indefinite noun phrases can function as predicates (i.e., as one half of an equational
construction), equative objects marked with me must be indefinite.
2.1.1.2.8. Other objects governed by verbs
The following discussion is divided into two parts. The first describes middle objects,
associated with certain categories of verbs. The discussion focuses in particular on
whether the constructions in which middle objects occur are transitive or not. The
second part of this section deals with several miscellaneous categories of objects,
each of which is associated with a relatively small class of verbs. Several minor
categories of objects are described elsewhere; objects of ‘bring’ and ‘take’
constructions, which are marked with the comitative preposition mo (cf.
2.1.1.2.1.2(a)); objects of experience verbs (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.2(b)); and objects of cause-
target verbs (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.2(c)).
 
(a) Middle objects  
In addition to the object categories described so far is what has traditionally been
referred to as ‘middle objects’ in Polynesian linguistics. A middle object is the
nonsubject argument of a middle verb, which forms a semantically defined class of
verb. In the Polynesian languages in which they are attested, middle verbs commonly
include verbs of perception (e.g., ‘see’, ‘hear’), verbs denoting emotions and other

psychological processes (e.g., ‘love’, ‘want’, ‘know’), and miscellaneous verbs that
take animate or human objects (e.g., ‘meet’, ‘help’). This description adequately
captures the characteristics of the class in Tuvaluan, with a few significant caveats.
First, many verbs that denote cognitive processes other than emotions (e.g., cognitive
perception) are not middle but transitive, such as iloa ‘know’, manatua and masaua
‘remember’, and tauloto ‘memorize, study’. Second, only verbs denoting voluntary
sensory perception are middle verbs (i.e., fakalogo ‘listen’, kilo ‘look’, onoono ‘watch’,
ssogi ‘smell voluntarily’, ttami ‘taste voluntarily’, and patele ‘touch voluntarily’), while
verbs denoting involuntary sensory perception (i.e., logo and lagona ‘perceive, hear,
taste involuntarily, feel’, matea and lavea ‘see’, ssogi ‘smell involuntarily’) govern either
experiencer or transitive case marking, as illustrated by the following minimal pair
with logo ‘hear’, the first sentence of which is ergative, the second middle:
(1520)
Teelaa laa, logo nee te faifeau te tala teenaa.
thus hear Erg the pastor the news that
‘So the pastor heard the news.’
(1521)
Teelaa laa, logo te tala teenaa ki te faifeau.
thus hear the news that to the pastor
‘So the news reached the pastor.’
Third, it is indeed the case that many semantically unclassifiable middle verbs take
animate objects, either preferentially or obligatorily (e.g., fesoasoani ‘help’, aasi ‘visit’,
tautali ‘follow’, faittali ‘wait for’). However, many verbs that frequently or always
take animate objects are transitive, rather than middle (e.g., taki ‘lead’, uga ‘send [a
person]’, ttuli ‘chase’). Thus it is imprecise to characterize the ‘miscellaneous’ class
of middle verbs as verbs that take animate objects. Furthermore, many
‘miscellaneous’ middle verbs can take animate or inanimate objects:
(1522)
E fesoasoani saale ki tena maatua.
Nps help often to her mother
‘[She] frequently helps her mother.’
(1523)
E fesoasoani saale ki te gaaluega o te kaaiga.
Nps help often to the work of the family
‘[She] frequently helps [with] the work of the family.’
In short, middle-verb status is lexically defined and cannot be characterized with a
precise semantic criterion.
Middle objects are marked with the directional preposition ki or the locative
preposition i. Which preposition is used is lexically determined by the verb. A
majority of middle verbs take middle objects marked with ki:
(1524)
E manako ki te lima seeleni.
Nps wish to the five shilling
‘[He] wants the five shillings.’
(1525)
Kiloko fua laa ki pateta konei!
look+Dxs just then to sweet-potato these
‘Just take a look at these sweet potatoes!’
A few verbs take objects marked with the locative preposition i:
(1526)
Tino katoa koo inoino i te kaaiga teelaa.
person all Inc hate at the family that
‘Everyone dislikes that family.’

A number of middle verbs can take objects marked with either preposition. In such
cases there is a subtle semantic difference between ki and i: directionally marked
middle objects generally denote more dynamic and telic situations than locatively
marked middle objects:
(1527)
Au e ppoki saale ki pulisimani.
I Nps afraid often at police
‘I always get scared of the police.’
(1528)
Au e ppoki saale i pulisimani.
I Nps afraid often at police
‘I always get scared [when] the police [is around].’
Middle objects marked with i are often superficially similar to cause-target
participants (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.2(c)). Such is the case of (1528), in which the locative
argument could be interpreted as a cause-target. However, there is a slight semantic
difference between the middle objects and cause-targets. Cause-target participants
are generally less affected, sometimes less directly affected, by the situation denoted
by the clause than homophonous middle objects. Thus, if the locatively marked
participant in (1528) is a middle object, the feeling of fear must be aimed directly at
the police, but this is not necessarily so if the participant is given a cause-target
interpretation.
Like indirect objects (cf. 2.1.1.2.5), ki-marked middle objects are interchangeable
with the inalienable benefactive preposition moo with many verbs (cf. 2.1.1.4.1),
particularly if the middle object refers to an animate entity:
(1529)
Au e maafaufau saale moo tamaliki.
I Nps think often Ben children
‘I frequently think of the children.’
The difference between middle objects marked with the benefactive preposition
and middle objects marked with the directional preposition is similar to the
difference between benefactively marked indirect objects and directionally marked
indirect objects (cf. 2.1.1.2.5). The benefactive preposition gives to the middle object
the connotation that it is affected, usually in a favourable manner, by the situation
denoted by the clause, or that it is the intended owner of an entity produced in
that situation. For example, a likely connotation of the last example above is that
the worrying is for the welfare of the children, and thus that the children can
potentially benefit from it. Compare the following, which does not have such a
connotation:
(1530)
Au e maafaufau saale ki tamaliki.
I Nps think often to children
‘I frequently think of the children.’
Middle-object marking with the locative preposition is not interchangeable with
the benefactive preposition.
Many verbs can alternatively function as middle verbs or govern other case
patterns, each case being associated with different valency patterns. For example,
maalamalama ‘understand’ is alternatively a middle, transitive, or experience verb,
while poko ‘strike’ can be a middle, ‘bring’/‘take’, or experience verb. For further
examples and discussion of the differences in meaning between these various uses,
see 2.1.3.1.2(c).

Middle clauses can be tested for transitivity in several ways.15 First, the behaviour
of their subject can be contrasted with that of subjects of intransitive and transitive
verbs to see which they resemble most. Second, middle objects can be contrasted
with direct objects on the one hand and obliques on the other. Third, the clause
itself can be tested against processes that discriminate between intransitive and
transitive structures.
First, subjects of intransitive and middle verbs behave in a similar fashion in
causative formation (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)). For example, the verb patele ‘touch’ takes a ki-
marked object in noncausative contexts, as shown in the following example:
(1531)
Te tamaliki teenei ne patele ki te moolii kasa.
the child this Pst touch to the pressure-lamp
‘This child touched the pressure lamp.’
When a middle clause like (1531) is turned into a causative, the subject becomes the
direct object and the middle object remains untouched:
(1532)
Te tamaliki teenei ne fakapatele nee au ki te moolii kasa.
the child this Pst Cst+touch Erg I to the pressure-lamp
‘I made this child touch the pressure lamp.’
Superficially, structures like the above resemble both a causative construction
derived from an intransitive clause with a prepositional participant, and a causative
construction derived from a transitive clause. However, if causative inversion, a
process which applies to all transitive-derived causatives (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)), is applied
to this sentence, the result is ungrammatical (or grammatical but with the different
meaning of ‘I made the pressure lamp touch this child’):
(1533)
* Te moolii kasa ne fakapatele nee au ki te tamaliki teenei.
the pressure-lamp Pst Cst+touch Erg I to the child this
Thus causative inversion treats subjects of middle clauses like subjects of intransi
tive clauses. So do relativization and other movement processes akin to relativization
(e.g., interrogative-word movement, clefting, and movement to preverbal position).
When a middle clause is relativized on its subject, the deletion strategy applies (cf.
1.1.2.3.4(b)):
(1534)
Teenaa ttamaliki [ne patele ki te moolii kasa].
that the+child Pst touch to the pressure-lamp
‘That’s the child who touched the pressure lamp.’
Second, middle objects can be contrasted with canonical direct objects on the one
hand and oblique participants on the other. From a morphological perspective

marking or may acquire an inalienable possession marker, while the middle object
remains unchanged (cf. 2.1.1.3.4). Thus the morphological behaviour of both

respectively:
(1542)

‘When Reverend Murray looked for those papers, he didn’t find them.’
(1543)

‘When Reverend Murray looked for those papers, he didn’t find them.’
As noted in 2.1.1.3.4.5(d), direct objects of nominalized transitive verbs may take
on case marking similar to that of locatively marked middle objects in a particular
set of circumstances. However, the situation in which this can happen is very
restricted, and such cases only allow the locative preposition i, which is less
common than ki as a middle-object marker. Thus the partial resemblance between
middle clauses and these cases of nominalized transitive clauses is due to
homophony.
Middle objects are thus oblique and middle clauses are intransitive. One small
subtype of middle objects, namely objects of desiderative verbs, undergo verb
incorporation (cf. 2.1.3.6.12), and thus resemble direct objects. However, other types
of obliques also undergo incorporation, and thus the pattern is inconclusive,
particularly in the light of the fact that it concerns only a very small subset of middle
objects.
It is difficult to distinguish middle objects from obliques other than semantically.
Even semantic criteria are sometimes problematic. One possible avenue would
invoke the fact that middle objects are more central or indispensable in the clause
than obliques. However, a middle object is not more indispensable to a middle
verb than a directional participant to a verb of motion or a locative participant to a
verb like nofo ‘stay, live’. One wonders whether there is any argument for treating
middle objects as a separate category, other than the fact that many of them must be
translated as direct objects in Western languages.
 
(b) Miscellaneous object categories  
A variety of verbs, most of which cannot be characterized as forming a well-defined
semantic class, take object-like participants marked with such prepositions as the
directional ki, the locative i, the comitative mo, and the inalienable class benefactive
moo. Which of these various possibilities is allowed is determined idiosyncratically
by the verb. Many verbs allow for more than one possibility, sometimes (but not
always) with subtle semantic differences between the various possibilities. For
example, the verb iku ‘end up, conclude’ can take a directionally marked object if
the object denotes a goal, either literally or metaphorically, or a comitatively marked
object in other cases. Compare the paraphrased translations of the following two
sentences, which attempt to capture these connotational differences:
(1544)
Temotou gaaluega ne iku ki te manuia.
our-3-e work Pst end to the luck
‘Our work ended so that we gained good fortune out of it.’
(1545)
Temotou gaaluega ne iku mo te manuia.
our-3-e work Pst end with the luck
‘Our work ended, and its end was characterized by good fortune.’
No identifiable semantic contrast is associated with some other alternations:

2.1.1.2.9. Complement of copular construction
In terms of case marking, complements of equational constructions (other than
demonstrative pronouns) are not distinguished from the subject of complement
constructions (cf. 2.1.1.2.3), and the same range of case markers can appear in both:
the zero form of the absolutive case marker; the absolutive-contrastive marker a,
whose appearance is governed by the same patterns as in intransitive clauses; and
ko-focusing. For examples and discussion, see 1.2.1.1.1(a). The only other type of
copular constructions with a complement are predicative prepositional phrases (cf.
1.2.1.1.1(c)). Trivially, the complement in these constructions is marked with the
appropriate preposition.

The complement of this verb is left unmarked for case, and cannot take an article or

For additional examples of adjectives with object, see 2.1.1.1 and 2.1.4.
2.1.1.2.13. Agent in passive and impersonal constructions
There are no passive, pseudopassive, or antipassive constructions (cf. 2.1.3.1.1).
Impersonal constructions are expressed either with a non-overt agent or a generic
agent marked in the same fashion as any other agent (cf. 1.2.1.2). The morphological
behaviour of arguments in impersonal constructions does not differ from the
behaviour of arguments in any other construction.
2.1.1.2.14. Topic
As discussed in 1.12, 2.1.1.2.1, 2.1.1.2.2, and 2.1.1.2.4, arguments that occur in
preverbal position because of their topicality are marked either with the zero form
of the absolutive case or with the absolutive-contrastive marker a.
2.1.1.2.15. Emphasized element
The most important markers of emphasis are the focus marker ko and the absolutive-
contrastive marker a, which are discussed in 1.11, along with minor marking devices
associated with emphasis.
2.1.1.3. Syntactic functions with nonfinite verbs
The only constructions that do not exhibit the same range of case-marking features
as finite clauses are nominalized clauses, which fall into two different categories.
2.1.1.3.1. Syntactic functions in absolute constructions
Absolute constructions (e.g., John being a fool) do not exist.
2.1.1.3.2. Syntactic functions in infinitive clauses
There is only one type of infinitive clause, namely the o-subordinated clauses
described in 1.1.2.1.1, which are infinitive insofar as their verbs cannot be assigned

clauses is exactly the same as in finite clauses.
2.1.1.3.3. Syntactic functions with gerund forms
As described in 2.1.3.5, gerund forms and nominalized forms are not clearly
distinguished from one another. Each of the two types of nominalized clauses
corresponds to both gerunds and nominalisations in other languages.
2.1.1.3.4. Syntactic functions with nominalized verbs
The marking of syntactic functions in nominalized clauses may differ in a rather
complex manner from the patterns described in 2.1.1.2. All case-marking patterns
described in this section apply to both ‘bare’ and suffixal nominalized clauses (cf.
2.1.3.5).
The first general difference between syntactic participants in finite and
nominalized clauses is the fact that, unlike their counterparts in finite clauses, the
participants in nominalized clauses must all follow the verb if they are not
pronominal. If they are pronominal, they can be expressed as preposed possessive
pronouns, with some restrictions, as described in the following.
Before turning to the details of case marking in nominalized constructions, it is
important to note that confusion may arise with respect to several features of
nominalized constructions because of homophony or near-homophony among
various grammatical morphemes. As shown presently, arguments of nominalized
verbs may take on case-marking patterns similar to those that apply to finite clauses,
or they may take on possessive prepositions. It is important to distinguish between
the contrastive marker a, which in both finite and nominalized contexts may mark
noun phrases in the absolutive case (cf. 2.1.1.2.1 and 2.1.1.2.4), and the alienable
possessive preposition a (cf. 2.1.1.4.6). Thus the morpheme a in the following
sentence is not a possessive marker because the nominalized verb cannot be marked
with an alienable possessive pronoun:
(1571)
Kaati kaa see lasi te faipatigina a taatou ki mataaupu konei.

‘Perhaps we shall not speak too long about these topics.’
(1572)

my speak+Trn to subject these
(‘my speaking about these topics’)
Furthermore, many nominalized verbs, both unsuffixed and suffixed, either
resemble closely or have the same form as nouns to which they are etymologically
related and often very close in meaning (cf. 2.1.3.5). For example, the unsuffixed
nominalized form of the verb aavaga ‘marry’ is homophonous with the noun aavaga
‘spouse’. Yet these two words take on different case-marking patterns when
associated with possessively marked modifiers. The possessor of the noun aavaga
is usually marked for alienable possession by a (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1), while the nominalized
verb aavaga, as an intransitive verb, may take a subject marked by o for inalienable
possession (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.1):
(1573)

2.1.1.3.4.1. Subject of nominalized intransitive verbs Two patterns are associated
with subjects of nominalized intransitive verbs, including nominalized middle verbs.
 
(a) Finite case marking  
The case marking of the subject noun phrase may remain unchanged under
nominalization. Thus, as in finite intransitive clauses (cf. 2.1.1.2.1), the subject of an
intransitive verb may be marked with the zero form of the absolutive case marker
or with the absolutive-contrastive marker a. This strategy is less common than the
alternative strategy described in (b) below. It is particularly unidiomatic (but not
ungrammatical) if the subject of the nominalized verb is a pronoun:
(1579)
?? Koo lavea nee au te faigaattaa (a) laaua.
Inc see Erg I the difficult Cnt they-2
‘I [can] see how difficult they both [are].’
 
(b) Possessive marking  
More commonly, the subject of a nominalized intransitive verb is marked for
inalienable possession. If it is a full noun phrase or a pronoun, it is marked with the
possessive preposition o (cf. 2.1.1.4.6):
(1580)
Koo oko loa te agi o te matagi i te fakamataku.
Inc reach indeed the blow of the wind in the Cst+fear
‘The blowing of the wind is very scary.’

‘I [can] see how difficult they both [are].’

as a preposed possessive pronoun (cf. 2.1.2.4) modifying the nominalized verb:
(1582)
Koo lavea nee au telaa faigaattaa.
Inc see Erg I their-2 difficult
While inalienable possession marking is most common, a few intransitive verbs
require that their subject be marked for alienable possession if they are marked for
possession:
(1583)

‘He told me the story when I arrived.’
(1584)

‘The swamp-taro pudding no longer tastes nice when I eat it.’
The type of possessive marking required is determined by the verb. With some
verbs, like inu ‘drink’, the subject can be marked for either alienable or inalienable
possession, although there usually is some preference for one over the other (in
this case, alienable possession):
(1585)

‘It is not good for us to drink water that has not been boiled.’
The choice in possessive class reflects in very rough terms the amount of agency
involved in the situation denoted by the clause. For example, fano ‘go’ presupposes
more agency on the part of the referent of its subject than moe ‘sleep’, and thus the
subject of the former takes alienable possessive marking and the latter inalienable
possessive marking. In contrast, when fano appears in a ‘taking’ construction in
which the patient is expressed as the subject and the agent as a comitatively marked
modifier (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1(a)), the subject can only be marked for inalienable possession:
(1586)

for alienable possession even though it is low in agency:

I Pst hurt at my fall+Nom
In fact, which of the two possessive classes must be used is determined more or
less idiosyncratically by the verb.

2.1.1.2.1) is treated like subjects of ordinary intransitive clauses, a reflection of the

2.1.1.3.4.3. Subject of nominalized transitive verb Subjects of transitive nominalized
verbs are most commonly marked for the ergative case, and thus nominalization
does not affect their case marking. If they are pronominal and under certain
conditions, they may also be expressed with a possessive pronoun of the alienable
class. Each of these two possibilities is reviewed here in turn. Postverbal subjects of
transitive nominalized verbs cannot be possessively marked, whether or not they
be pronominal, whether or not a direct object is present in the nominalized clause,
and whatever case marking is assigned to the direct object:
(1591)
* te ssalaaga a/o toku taina (o/i) tena aavaga i te vao
the search+Nom of/of my sibling of/at his spouse in the bush
(‘my brother’s search for his spouse in the bush’)
The case marking of subjects of nominalized transitive verbs is sensitive to the case
marking of the direct object under certain circumstances. A summary of grammatical
and ungrammatical case-marking patterns in transitive clauses is provided in
2.1.1.3.4.4(e).
 
(a) Finite case marking  
Subjects of transitive nominalized verbs may be marked for the ergative case
with nee:
(1592)
Te kalagaaga nee koe au seki lagona nee au.
the hear+Nom Erg you I Neg hear Erg I
‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’
This strategy is allowed whether the nominalized clause has an overt direct object
(as in the above examples) or not:
(1593)
Te kalagaaga nee koe seki lagona nee au.
the hear+Nom Erg you Neg hear Erg I
‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called [him].’
When the direct object of the nominalized verb is marked for the absolutive case
(cf. 2.1.1.3.4.4(a)), the linear order of the two noun phrases follows the same patterns
as in finite clauses (cf. 1.2.1.2.5). When the direct object of the nominalized verb is
marked with a possessive preposition, the linear order of the two noun phrases is

(b) Alienable possessive pronoun  
If the subject of a nominalized transitive verb is a personal pronoun, it may be
expressed as a possessive pronoun of the alienable class, preposed to the
nominalized verb. Compare (1592) with the following:
(1594)

your hear+Nom I Neg hear Erg I
‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’
This strategy is allowed in four cases. First, it is allowed if the direct object is overt
and marked for the absolutive case, as illustrated in the above examples. Second,
the strategy is allowed if the direct object takes middle-object marking, a possibility
discussed in 2.1.1.3.4.4(c):
(1595)
Tau kalagaaga i au seki lagona nee au.
your hear+Nom at I Neg hear Erg I
Nominalized transitive constructions in which the subject is expressed as a
possessive pronoun are the only nominalized constructions in which the direct
object may be marked as a middle object (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.4(d)). It is also the most
idiomatic of all four alternatives. Third, the pronominal subject of a transitive
nominalized verb may be expressed as a possessive pronoun if the direct object is
marked with the inalienable possessive preposition o (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.4(c)); the resulting
construction is less idiomatic than the previous two, but not ungrammatical, and
in this respect Tuvaluan contrasts with many other Polynesian languages, where
two possessively marked arguments cannot appear in the same nominalized clause
(Clark 1981:71):
(1596)

your hear+Nom of I Neg hear Erg I
Finally, pronominal subjects may be expressed with a possessive pronoun if the
direct object is not expressed overtly in the nominalized clause:
(1597)
Tau kalagaaga seki lagona nee au.
your hear+Nom Neg hear Erg I
‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called [him].’

like ordinary intransitive clauses, and their arguments are case-marked according
to the patterns described in 2.1.1.3.4.1:
(1598)
Au koo puapuagaatia i te seeai (o) neaku sene.
I Inc suffer in the Neg of my cent
‘I suffer from not having any money.’
Similarly, predicative prepositional phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(c) and 1.10.1.2) behave like
ordinary intransitive verbs under nominalization:
(1599)

2.1.1.3.4.5. Direct object of nominalized verb Four case-marking patterns are
associated with direct objects of nominalized verbs, many of which are sensitive to
the case marking of the subject of the clause. This section closes with a summary of
case-marking possibilities for subjects and direct objects in transitive nominalized
clauses (cf. (e) below).
(a) Finite case marking
Direct objects of nominalized verbs may be case-marked in the same fashion as
they are case-marked in finite clauses, i.e., for the absolutive case. Illustrations are
provided in 2.1.1.3.4.3(a) and in example (1594). This strategy is possible no matter

is present or not in the clause. It is unidiomatic but not ungrammatical if the subject
is expressed with a possessive pronoun (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.3(b)).
(b) Inalienable possessive pronoun  
The pronominal direct object of a nominalized verb may be expressed as a possessive
pronoun of the inalienable class preposed to the nominalized verb:
(1600)

‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’

by a possessive pronoun referring to the subject of the clause (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.2(b)).
 
(c) Inalienable possessive noun phrase  
The direct object of a nominalized verb may alternatively be marked for inalienable
possession with the preposition o:
(1601)

The unusual distribution of this case-marking pattern and its preferred status
suggests that a grammatical filter blocks certain case-marking patterns. Indeed,
middle-object marking is a preferred alternative to the cooccurrence in the same
clause of, on the one hand, a possessive pronoun (the subject) and an absolutively-
marked modifier (the direct object), and, on the other hand, a possessive pronoun
(the subject) and a possessive noun-phrase modifier (the direct object). Neither of
these alternative configurations is ungrammatical, although they are both perceived
as lacking in idiomaticity and elegance. The cooccurrence of two possessive
modifiers in the latter configuration is unique, because in all other circumstances
only one possessive modifier is allowed (cf. 2.1.1.4.6 and 2.1.2.4.5–6). That the former
configuration is less than idiomatic undoubtedly results from the fact that it
expresses the subject with a less referential strategy than the direct object, a state of
affairs which is universally marked (Hopper and Thompson 1980).
I have assumed here that the marker i is indeed the middle-object marker i.
However, this preposition also marks many other syntactic and semantic functions
(cf. 2.1.5.1 for a complete list). Whether or not the preposition i in nominalized
clauses is truly a middle-object marker cannot be ascertained, because middle objects
are not syntactically distinguishable from obliques (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(a)), and Seiter

accusative marking’ (in reference to the fact that middle objects in Niuean have
direct-object properties). Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that middle objecthood is
marked with both the case markers ki (homophonous with the directional
preposition) and i, whereas only i can appear as a direct-object marker in
nominalized clauses. This distribution suggests that the two categories are not
exactly the same (despite the expedient terminology I have adopted here), a point
whose significance is discussed in 2.1.1.2.8(a).

2.1.1.4. Nonlocal semantic functions
Each of the following sections comprises three subsections. The first describes

first two syntactic positions. The third position is the most ‘deficient’, in that many
semantic functions cannot be expressed with a predicative construction.
Negative functions (e.g., negative instrumental, negative quality) can always be

2.1.1.4.1. Benefactive
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Benefactive noun phrases are marked with the benefactive prepositions maa and
moo when they function as adverbial elements in a clause. The first form can be
roughly characterized as an alienable benefactive marker and the second as an
inalienable benefactive marker, according to the criteria described in 2.1.1.4.6.1.
Thus when the referent of the benefactive phrase is the recipient of an entity, and
when the ensuing possessive relationship would be marked for alienable possession
in a possessive phrase or clause, the alienable benefactive preposition is used:
(1614)
Koo maua nee koe o lafo mai ne tusi maa maatou.

‘You can [afford to] send letters to us.’

process may result in a possessive relationship of the inalienable type. For example,
when the referent of the benefactive phrase is the recipient of a canoe, inalienable
benefactive marking is obligatory because vaka ‘canoe’ is an inalienably possessed

The first-person singular pronoun coalesces with the benefactive prepositions maa
and moo, as shown in 2.1.2.1.20. To be noted here is the formal resemblance between
the alienable possessive and benefactive markers on the one hand (a and maa
respectively) and between the inalienable possessive and benefactive markers on
the other (o and moo respectively).
However, the marking of alienability and inalienability in benefactive phrases
is much less strict than in possessive phrases. In particular, when the benefactive
relationship does not result in a possessive relationship, the inalienable marker
moo is often used across the board:

Nps wish Foc the lawyer of person Sbj stand Ben he
‘He wants the people’s lawyer to defend him.’

E seeai se tino ia taatou e ola moo ia eiloo.

the inalienable marker is often used even if the resulting possessive relationship is

Thus the inalienable benefactive preposition is more frequent than its alienable
alternative. In other Polynesian languages (e.g., Tongan), the contrast between
alienable and inalienable benefactives is not as loose as in Tuvaluan, which suggests
that the contrast is in the process of disappearing in the latter. However, the form
of the alienable preposition is not disappearing because it has functions other than
the marking of benefactive functions (for cross-references, see 2.1.5.1).
 
(b) Attributive element in a noun phrase  
Benefactive phrases functioning as attributive elements in noun phrases are also
marked with maa and moo. Here again, the inalienable form is more frequent than
the alienable form:
(1620)
Konei laa tala moo taatou i ttaimi nei.
these then news Ben we-3-i at the+time this
‘This is the news (for our benefit) for the time being.’
Possessive modifiers of noun phrases can also have benefactive functions. For a
benefactive to be expressed as a possessor, the benefactive relationship must result
in a possessive relationship:
(1621)
Kaa fano koe ki te umaga, koo taa mai ei nee koe
Fut go you to the taro-swamp Inc strike Dxs Anp Erg you
ttamaa kaauli a Mele.
the+small young-taro-swamp of Mele
‘When you go to the taro swamp, dig up a small swamp-taro corm for
Mele.’
The alienable-inalienable contrast is strictly marked in all possessive phrases with
benefactive meaning, as for regular possessive contexts.
 
(c) Complement of copular construction  
Benefactive phrases marked with maa or moo can function as copular elements. The
internal structure of predicated benefactive phrases does not differ from other
manifestations of benefactive phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.3):
(1622)
Te kkaiga fiafia teenei e moo taatou katoa.
the meal happy this Nps Ben we-3-i all
‘This meal is for all of us.’
Predicative possessive clauses (cf. 1.10.1.2) can denote benefactive functions:
(1623)
E iaa Mele eiloo ttamaa kaauli teenei.
Nps belong-to Mele indeed the+small young-taro-swamp this
‘This small swamp-taro corm is for Mele.’

and moo can be negated (cf. 1.4.2):

Koe e fano, see moo laatou fua, kae moo ttou faanau, moo
you Nps go Neg Ben they-3 just but Ben our-3-i children Ben
taatou katoa.

2.1.1.4.2. Source
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Source as a nonlocal semantic function is not distinguished formally from source
as a local function (‘motion from’). The least marked way of denoting source is
with the general locative preposition i:
(1626)
Te fuaa taki teenei ne maua i te taki a saa Iokapeta.
the egg+of duck this Pst get at the duck of group Iokapeta
‘[I] got this duck’s egg from Iokapeta’s family’s duck.’
Alternatively, source can be denoted by the preposition mai, which can be used
instead of i or in addition to it (yielding the complex preposition mai i). This
preposition generally denotes a source if the situation denoted by the clause is
somehow oriented towards the point of reference of the discourse (cf. 2.1.1.5.1(a)
and (c) for further discussion). In many cases, the difference in meaning between i
and mai or mai i is of an affective nature, and in most cases either preposition can be
used without there being a difference in grammaticality:
(1627)
Koo ola manuia mai tena masaki.
Inc alive lucky from his illness
‘[She] has recovered from her illness.’
(1628)
Ne maua foki nee au taku tusi mai i te ulu o te
Pst get also Erg I my letter from from the head of the
maaloo.
government
‘I also got a letter from the prime minister.’
When a source also has instrumental functions, instrumental marking can be used
instead of source (cf. 2.1.1.4.3). Both patterns are equally acceptable and frequent,
and they both provide slightly different connotations to the role of the referent of
the prepositional phrase:
(1629)
Te moolii ne utu i/ki te fagu kalasini teenaa.
the lamp Pst fill from/with the bottle kerosene that
‘[I] filled the lamp from/with that bottle of kerosene.’
 
(b) Attributive element in a noun phrase  
All phrases described in (a) above can also function as attributive elements in noun
phrases:
(1630)
Teenaa foki ttala ia Evotia.
that also the+story from Evotia
‘That’s also what Evotia said.’
[lit.: ‘That’s also the story from Evotia.’]
Like benefactive functions (cf. 2.1.1.4.1), source can also be marked with possessive
modifiers in noun phrases. Both possessive prepositions and possessive pronouns
can be used to mark source, and marking a source with a possessive does not imply
that the entity was obtained with the consent or through the agency of the source:

(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
The instrumental function is primarily denoted by the preposition ki, which in
other circumstances denotes direction:
(1637)
Maatou e kini saale nee ia ki te pate kilikiti.
we-3-e Nps strike often Erg he with the bat cricket
‘He’d commonly beat us up with a cricket bat.’
The same preposition can denote ‘abstract’ instruments, which are sometimes
difficult to distinguish from manner phrases:
(1638)

Pst try Cmp Cst+bad I with their-3 word
‘They tried to destroy my [reputation] by talking.’
[lit.: ‘X tried to make me bad with their words.’]

Instruments marked with this preposition must denote entities that are centrally
involved in the situation denoted by the clause. Thus ki cannot be used to mean
‘with the help of’ (this notion is expressed paraphrastically with the verb fakaaogaa
‘make use of’). This also means that ki can be used to connote that a situation could
not take place without the referent of the object of the preposition.
Two transitive verbs, kiki ‘eat as accompaniment to protein food’ and ppeke ‘eat
with a sauce, dunk’ (cf. 5.1.4.2), take both a direct object and an instrumental modifier.
What is interesting about both verbs is that their direct object and instrumental
modifier can be swapped. Thus the following pairs describe the same situation:
(1639)
Koo ppeke taku pulaka ki te kapeni.
Inc dunk my swamp-taro with the coconut-toddy-sauce
‘I’m dunking swamp taro in caramelized coconut-toddy sauce.’
(1640)
Koo ppeke taku kapeni ki te pulaka.
Inc dunk my coconut-toddy-sauce with the swamp-taro
‘I’m using caramelized coconut-toddy sauce to dunk swamp taro.’
A similar type of inversion is also attested in causative constructions derived from
transitive clauses (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)).
(b-c) Attributive element in a noun phrase and complement of copular
construction
Instrumental phrases with ki cannot appear as attributive elements of noun phrases
and cannot be predicated. To express instrumental notions as attributes or predicates,
a paraphrase is used, such as a clause with the verb fakaaogaa ‘make use of’, which
can be relativized and function as a noun modifier.
2.1.1.4.3.1. Negative instrumental Negative instrumental functions may be
expressed with aunoa or, less commonly, ausagi ‘lack, without’ (and ausage, an
alternative form of ausagi), verbal forms borrowed from Samoan that can function
either as verbs or as complex prepositions (cf. 1.4.7(d)). These forms usually have
emphatic connotations, often translated as ‘without a single X’ or a comparable
expression, and must be followed by an indefinite noun phrase optionally marked
by the comitative preposition mo:
(1641)
E aunoa mo se fao a te faaiteega o fale taumua.
Nps lack with a nail Cnt the build+Nom of house before
‘Houses in the olden days were built without a single nail.’
The words aunoa and ausagi are verbs, and thus can appear in relative clauses and
as adjective modifiers of nouns:
(1642)
Vaegaa gaaluega teenaa aunoa mo se mea fai gaaluega, se
kind+of work that lack with a thing do work a
gaaluega fiittaa fua.

‘This kind of work without a single tool is tiresome work.’
2.1.1.4.4. Comitative
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
The comitative preposition mo is used to introduce comitative modifiers of
clauses:

‘[She] is staying with people whom she knows.’
Comitative noun phrases are often superficially identical to coordinated noun
phrases because the comitative preposition is homophonous with the additive
coordinator, and ambiguities arise in many cases. However, there are structural
and semantic differences between cases in which mo is used as a noun-phrase
coordinator and cases in which it functions as a comitative marker for adverbial
modifiers of clauses. For further discussion, see 1.3.1.4 and 1.3.1.7.
 
(b) Attributive element in a noun phrase  
Comitative phrases that function as attributive modifiers in noun phrases are marked
in the same fashion as comitative clause modifiers: (1644) Koo fai te fono mo tino
kolaa ne mmai i te vaka. Inc do the meeting with person those Pst come on the ship
‘A meeting with the people who arrived on the ship is being held.’
 
(c) Complement of copular construction  
Comitative functions cannot be expressed as complements of copular constructions.
2.1.1.4.4.1. Negative comitative The only way to express negative comitative
functions is with the negative verbs, complex prepositions, and adjectival modifiers
aunoa and ausagi described in 2.1.1.4.3.1. However, only emphatic negative comitative
notions can be thus expressed, and since aunoa and ausagi take an indefinite noun
phrase as object, they cannot take proper names or pronouns as objects. When they
denote a comitative notion, phrases or clauses with aunoa and ausagi frequently
have the meaning of ‘without anyone’, ‘without anything’, etc.:
(1645)
Au ne fano ki motu aunoa mo se tino.
I Pst go to islet lack with a person
‘I went to the islets without anyone.’
2.1.1.4.5. Circumstance
The same constructions can denote circumstance, quality, and manner. The following
discussion presents examples of all three categories.
 
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
The least marked way of denoting circumstance, quality, and manner is with the
comitative preposition mo:
(1646)
Ne ttala nee au tau tusi mo te fiafia lasi.
Pst decipher Erg I your letter with the happy large
‘I read your letter with great joy.’
The use of mo to mark circumstance, quality, or manner always implies that the
situation denoted by the verb and that denoted by the prepositional phrase occur
simultaneously:
(1647)
E kai mo te maakona.
Nps eat with the satiated
‘[She]’s eating even though she’s already had enough.’
(* ‘[She]’s eating until she’s had enough.’)

Furthermore, mo-marked prepositional phrases generally denote a circumstance,
quality, or manner that affects in a substantial fashion the general tenor of the
situation denoted by the verb (e.g., its moral evaluation, its general ‘intensity’, etc.).
This may be the reason why verbs like vave ‘quick’ and fiittaa ‘tired’ can be
nominalized and function as mo-marked adverbials, but not their respective
antonyms tuai ‘slow’ and maalosi ‘healthy, energetic’.
In some contexts, circumstance, quality, and manner can be expressed with the
locative preposition i:
(1648)
Te masaki teenaa e kaamata eiloa i te ssana.
the illness that Nps start indeed at the diarrhoea
‘That illness begins with diarrhoea.’
Semantically related to circumstance, quality, and manner are noun phrases denoting
standards of comparison or quality. This category is associated in particular with
superlative expressions and expressions of intensity that consist of a conventionally
metaphorical superlative verb, such as tafasili ‘superior’, oko ‘reach’, and the negative
existential seeai (cf. 1.11.1.3.5). In these constructions, the standard of comparison
or quality is expressed with a noun phrase marked with the locative preposition i:
(1649)
E sili te gogo i te gali maa ssunu.
Nps superior the brown-noddy at the nice Prc roast
‘Brown noddies are best roasted.’
The same category is also attested in constructions which do not strictly fit the
patterns illustrated above:
(1650)
Ko ia loo koo fano mo te sili i te valea.
Foc he indeed Inc go with the superior at the stupid
‘When it comes to stupidity, he wins it all.’
See also 2.1.1.2.6 for a discussion of standards of comparison, which are marked in
a similar manner.

and manner:

2.1.1.4.6. Possessive
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Possessives cannot function as adverbial elements of a clause.
 
(b) Attributive element in a noun phrase  
The possessive modifier of a noun is postposed to the noun it modifies and
introduced with a possessive preposition a or o, which denote alienable and
inalienable possession respectively (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1):
(1657)
Ko te fakatonuga a te taupuleega.
Foc the order of the council-of-elders
‘[These] are the orders of the Council of Elders.’
(1658)
Ko te failautusi o te taupuleega.
Foc the secretary of the council-of-elders
‘[He] is the secretary of the Council of Elders.’
The possessive prepositions have allomorphs aa and oo, which appear when they
are followed by a word (other than an article or other grammatical morpheme) of
two morae or less. In the orthography used in this grammar, this predictable
allomorphy is not indicated.
Possessive modifiers are generally ordered after adjectives and before
prepositional phrases, relative clauses, noun complements, and any heavy modifier
of the head noun. Not more than one possessive modifier may modify the same
head noun, including possessive pronouns (cf. 2.1.2.4.5–6).
 
(c) Complement of copular construction  
For a discussion of predicative possessive phrases, see 1.10.1.2.
2.1.1.4.6.1. Alienable v. inalienable possession The possessive prepositions a and
o mark alienable and inalienable possession respectively. The marking of alienability
and inalienability is obligatory in all possessive relationships, as well as all syntactic
categories that make used of possessive markers (e.g., the marking of case on the
arguments of nominalized verbs; cf. 2.1.1.3), with the exception of advancement-
to-possessive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10). It is also obligatorily encoded in possessive predicates
(cf. 1.10.1.2) and, optionally so, in benefactive constructions (cf. 2.1.1.4.1).
‘Alienability’ here is used as a language-specific category, in that it is defined in
a specific, occasionally idiosyncratic, fashion. It is customary in Polynesian
linguistics to refer to alienable possession as ‘A-class possession’, and to inalienable

possession as ‘O-class possession’, in reference to the phonological form of
possessive morphemes associated with each possessive class, so as to avoid any
confusion which may potentially arise from the use of the terms ‘alienable’ and
‘inalienable’.17 I opt for the more traditional terms ‘alienable’ and ‘inalienable’ here
because they are more intelligible to an audience not necessarily familiar with the
areal literature.
Generally speaking, alienable possession is used for most material belongings,
objects and attributes that can be acquired or lost (including food, drink, animals
kept or hunted for food, and the enclosures in which animals are kept), objects and
attributes that depend directly on the possessor for their existence or well-being,
physical actions and movements, and verbal acts (including the languages one
speaks). Inalienable possession is used for parts of a whole (e.g., body parts), objects
and attributes that are intimately bound to the possessor and on which the possessor
depends for its existence or well-being (e.g., one’s health, one’s origin), immutable
objects that are normally acquired through inheritance (e.g., dwellings, landholding
units, gardens, wells), objects which are worn as clothing or adornment (including
flower crowns, perfumes, etc.), objects that are used in close contact to the body
(e.g., bedding, mats, bathing water), and most emotions and sensations.

is the referent’s sibling, sibling set, or kin group. However, toe ‘child’ (with
affectionate connotation) receives inalienable possession marking. Terms for kin-
group categories to which one belongs, from which one descends, and of which
one is the ancestor are all inalienably possessed: kaaiga ‘family’, mata kaaiga or pui
kaaiga ‘clan’, tupuga ‘ancestry’, gafa ‘genealogy, descent, ancestry’, fakatelega
and fakasologa ‘descent’. The noun fanauga ‘children issued from the same parents,
sibling set’ is alienably possessed if the possessor is a parent, and inalienably
possessed if the possessor is a member of the sibling set.
It should be clear from the above description that possessive classes are not
gender categories or Bantu-style noun classes. Rather, possessive classes are best
analysed as characteristics of possessive relationships, even though all nouns that
can be marked for possession have an unmarked association with either alienable
or inalienable possession. The best generalization of the assignment of possessive
classes to particular possessive relationships is identical to that described insightfully
by Wilson (1976) for Hawaiian: when the possessor controls the initiation of the
possessive relationship, the relationship will be marked for alienability; otherwise,
the relationship will be marked for inalienability. This generalization is maximally
predictive, and allows one to posit only a handful of exceptions. For example, it
provides an elegant account of possessive-class assignment with kinship terms.
The generalization predicts that if a kinship term refers to a kinship relationship
whose initiation the possessor exerts some control over, the term will be marked
for alienable possession. The only two terms that refer to such categories are tama
‘child’ and aavaga ‘spouse’, which are indeed marked for alienable possession, while
all other terms are marked for inalienable possession.
In a handful of cases, one needs to identify a further dimension to possessive-
class assignment. Indeed, inalienable possession appears in some contexts to be
affectively more charged than alienable possession. This additional parameter
allows one to account for the variation between alienable and inalienable
possession of aavaga ‘spouse’, and the inalienable possession of the affectively-

2.1.1.4.9. Quantity
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Quantities can occur as adverbial elements in clauses when they denote a unit of
measure (‘by the pound’), a quantifiable or quantified standard (‘for ten cents’), or
a way of measuring (‘in length’) applicable to the situation denoted by the clause.
The first two categories, i.e., units of measure and quantifiable standard, are marked
in the same manner as instrumentals, i.e., with the preposition ki:
(1666)
A ika koo ttogi ki te pauna.
Cnt fish Inc sell to the pound
‘Fish is being sold by the pound.’
The third category, standard of measure, is marked with the locative preposition i:
(1667)
Te paala nei e sefulu pauna i te mmafa.
the kingfish this Nps ten pound at the heavy
‘This kingfish is ten pounds (heavy).’
(1668)
A ika koo ttogi ki te ono sefulu sene i te pauna.
Cnt fish Inc sell to the six ten cent at the pound
‘Fish is being sold for sixty-five cents per pound.’
 
20 Alienability is the only semantic distinction marked on possession in Tuvaluan. In closely
related Oceanic languages, such as Fijian, additional possessive categories are used with edible
and drinkable possessions, a system which can be reconstructed for languages ancestral to
Proto-Polynesian. Remnants of these two classes are identifiable in several Polynesian
languages (e.g., Tongan and Rennellese), in which drinkables and edibles are marked for
inalienable possession, contrary to the predictions of the general rule (Wilson 1982:26–30). In
Tuvaluan, no traces of these classes remain; both edible and drinkable possessions are marked
for alienability.

(1671)

(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
The marking of adverbial elements denoting material is the same as that of adverbial
elements denoting instrumental notions (cf. 2.1.1.4.3):
(1672)

‘My canoe is going to be made of kanava wood.’

(1673)

‘[It’s] a canoe [made of] kanava wood.’
 
(c) Complement of copular construction  
Material cannot be expressed predicatively. Constructions of the type described in
(a) above are used.

However, emphatic constructions with aunoa and ausagi (cf. 2.1.1.4.3.1) may be used
with objects denoting material if this material can also be seen as an instrument,
i.e., if it is not an essential material, or if it is only one of many other possible types
of material:
(1674)
Temotou fale e taa aunoa mo se puliki.
our-3-e house Nps build lack with a brick
‘We are building our house without a single brick.’
If this condition is not met, the result is not acceptable:
(1675)

2.1.1.4.12. Cause
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Many of the constructions associated with clauses denoting causes can also be used
to mark noun phrases that denote causes and semantically related notions (e.g.,
motivations, reasons). Several of these are described in 1.1.2.4.2.4 as taking
predicative noun phrases. Note in particular the use of the Samoan borrowings ona
and talu, which frequently introduce nominal elements denoting causes (cf.
1.1.2.4.2.1(a) and 1.1.2.4.2.1(c)).
Several additional constructions can express causes. As discussed in 2.1.1.2.1.2(c),
adverbial elements that denote causes can also be expressed in cause-target
constructions as prepositional phrases marked with the locative preposition i. This
preposition is in fact the least-marked way of denoting causes, and can appear in a
very broad range of constructions, namely any construction in which the verb does
not take a causal object:
(1676)
Koo faanoanoa tena loto i taaga o ana mokopuna.
Inc sad her heart at action of her grandchild
‘She is depressed by her grandchildren’s behaviour.’
(1677)
Te paala e tasi ne sao ia Aaifoou.
the kingfish Nps one Pst escape at Aifou
‘One kingfish got away because of Aifou.’
With certain verbs (but not all), causes can also be marked with mai or mai i, a
feature that indicates that the cause-marking preposition i is identical not to the
locative preposition but to the source preposition (cf. 2.1.1.4.2):
(1678)
Toku masaki ne maafua i/mai te kai valea i te
my sickness Pst originate from/from the eat stupid at the
faaipoipoga.

‘My being sick stems from eating thoughtlessly at the wedding.’

cases, case marking is determined idiosyncratically by the verb. Thus verbs that
take an argument bearing the meaning of ‘on account of often require that the
cause be marked with the inalienable benefactive preposition moo:
(1679)
Koo fakatooese atu moo te fakamafuliiga fakavave

teenaa.

2.1.1.4.13. Purpose
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Purpose may be marked with the same morphological categories as benefactives
(cf. 2.1.1.4.2). The following illustrates the use of the benefactive preposition moo
and the directional preposition ki to indicate purpose:
(1681)
Au nei koo fakatokatoka moo/ki te fono a te Paalamene.
I this Inc get-ready Ben/to the meeting of the parliament
‘I am getting ready for the parliamentary session.’
Which preposition may be used depends on the verb. Some verbs allow either, as
illustrated by the above.
 
(b) Attributive element in a noun phrase  
Both moo and ki can mark purpose:
(1682)
Te polokalame moo aso llasi e peenaa.
the programme Ben day big Nps thus
‘Here is the programme for the Christmas season.’
(1683)
Seki ai se fakatonuga ki te gaaluega kaa fai.
Neg exist a order to the work Fut do
‘No order [has been issued] about the work to be accomplished.’
 
(c) Complement of copular construction  
Only moo prepositional phrases can function as predicates denoting purpose:
(1684)

Nps Ben you your spouse and Ben your spouse you
‘You [should be dedicated] to your wife, and your wife [should be
dedicated] to you.’

2.1.1.4.15. Reference
 
(a) Adverbial element in a clause  
Reference may be expressed in a number of ways, the most basic of which are
prepositional phrases marked with either the directional preposition ki or the
inalienable benefactive preposition moo. Following is an example of ki as a marker
of reference:
(1685)
See iloa kiaa koe, a ko au e fakattau peenaa.
Neg know about you but Foc I Nps opine thus
‘I don’t know about you, but that’s what I think.’
The following is an example of a prepositional modifier marked with moo:
(1686)
Ana muna ki te kaaiga kee saa manavasee moo ia.
his word to the family Sbj Neg fear Ben he
‘He tells the family not to worry about him.’
There is little difference in meaning between ki and moo, although moo is perhaps
slightly more formal than ki. Occasionally, reference is marked with the
preposition i:
(1687)
Moi fakailoa mai i te ota, peenei laa koo ttunu neaku
if Cst+know Dxs at the raw-fish thus then Inc cook some-my
laisi.
rice
‘If you had let me know [that there was] raw fish, I’d have cooked
some rice.’
However, the reference phrase in these situations is best analysed not as a
prepositional phrase but as an abbreviated existential clause, in which case i is not
an instance of the locative preposition but of the complementizer i.
Complex prepositions denoting reference can be formed from either ki or moo.
Either preposition can combine with the noun uiga ‘meaning, reason’ used as a
verb and marked with the universal tense-aspect-mood marker e, yielding e uiga ki
or e uiga moo, which are equivalent in meaning:
(1688)
Au seki faipati eiloa e uiga moo te feituu teenaa.
I Neg speak indeed Nps mean Ben the aspect that
‘I said nothing about that aspect [of things].’
As illustrated in (b) below, e uiga ki and e uiga moo are frequently used as attributive
elements in noun phrases. Of the two forms, the first is less common than the
second. Another complex preposition associated with the reference function consists
of the universal tense-aspect-mood marker e, the verb tusa ‘concern, regard’
(etymologically related to ttusa ‘equal, amount to’; cf. 1.9.1(b)), and the comitative
preposition mo or the directional preposition ki, which are the object markers
associated with regular verbal uses of tusa:
(1689)
E teenaa te koga e tali atu ei au e tusa mo
Nps that the side Nps answer Dxs Anp I Nps concern with
tau faipatiiga.

‘This is what I tell you in answer to what you said.’

Only positive partitive notions can be marked. No special marking is associated

2.1.1.4.19.1. Partitive numeral The marking of partitive functions in numeral expressions
is always optional. Indeed, regular numeral expressions of all types described in 2.1.6
can be interpreted as having a partitive meaning in the appropriate context:
(1702)

or: ‘Two of the young men came and helped me.’

(1703)

Nps Num two from young-man Nps come Cmp help Dxs to I
‘Two of the young men came and helped me.’
(1704)

replaced by the inalienable possessive marker o. Compare the last example above

(1705)

2.1.1.5. Local semantic functions
(a) General remarks
The following discussion focuses principally on adverbial elements that denote
local semantic functions. The structure of local semantic functions in other positions
is easily derived from adverbial positions. Unless otherwise indicated, attributive
elements in a noun phrase are identical to adverbial modifiers (some examples are
provided in this section). Furthermore, as shown in 1.2.1.1.1, many prepositional-
phrase types can function as predicates. Predicative prepositional phrases marked
with i or with complex prepositions formed with i (i.e., whose first element is the
locative preposition) are by far the most common and idiomatic. However, no
prepositional phrase marked with the prepositions ki or mai or compounds formed
from either of them ever appears in predicative position. There is no grammaticalized
way of expressing direction predicatively. Whenever the following discussion
focuses on prepositions other than i, mai, and ki, or whenever nonprepositional
constructions are discussed, the range of positions available to these structures is
discussed explicitly.
It is frequently difficult to distinguish, formally or otherwise, canonical local
functions, metaphorical local functions, and syntactic functions that resemble local
functions in form or meaning (e.g., nonlocal source v. motion from). For example,
the local prepositions ki and i in the following denote abstract entities, which are
marked in exactly the same way as nonabstract location:
(1733)

‘Civilization is always improving.’
(1734)

‘You are right on that account.’

discussed once, namely under ‘general’ local functions (cf. 2.1.1.5.1). The reason
for this is that the same forms are used for all types of local functions. For example,
in the following examples, the same preposition ki denotes motion to a general

of the verb (as in the case of ulu ‘enter’) or alternatively on the dynamics of the

Ambiguity rarely arises. As will be shown presently, cases of potential ambiguity
can be circumvented by using complex prepositions.
As discussed in 2.1.1.5.1, the semantic distinction between the various simple
prepositions is not well captured by the categories ‘at rest’, ‘motion to’, ‘motion
from’, and ‘motion past’. For example, rather than a distinction between ‘at rest’
and ‘motion from’, simple prepositions encode a distinction between, on the one
hand, general location or source and, on the other hand, location or source oriented
towards the point of reference of the discourse. The contrast between ‘motion to’
on the one hand and ‘at rest’ and ‘motion from’ on the other hand is more clearly
formalized, although the directional prepositions can appear in situations that could
be described as ‘at rest’. The category ‘motion past’ is never marked formally.

made up of one of the three simple prepositions and a noun from a closed semantic
class. Their formation and syntax are discussed in 2.2.6.1.2. The nouns that appear

described in 2.1.1.5.2–29, but with what will be called here ‘fixed framework’ uses

in relative terms, speakers of the language more commonly express location relative
to fixed points and fixed directions. The same complex prepositions can be used

In their fixed framework uses, the local nouns from which complex prepositions

can mark the object of the local noun tua ‘outside’ in complex prepositions:
(1779)
Ttou moa koo ttoo katoa ki tua mo te paa moa.

‘All the chickens have gotten out of the chicken coop.’
Furthermore, the adverb keaattea ‘away’ with an object marked with mo can float in
the clause, and thus behave like a prepositional phrase (cf. 2.1.1.5.4).
(d) Motion past
There is no formal marking of motion past. The notion is denoted in the same way
as either motion to or motion from, depending on the direction of the motion.
Alternatively, motion past can be expressed with the complex preposition associated
with lateral motion (cf. 2.1.1.5.11) or with the verb fakaseke ‘[sort of] miss, cause
[oneself] to miss’, which takes an object marked with mo (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(b)):
(1780)
Ne fakaseke eiloo mo te maneapa i tena saasaalemaiiga.

‘He walked past the maneaba on his way here.’
Worthy of mention are uses of the causative prefix faka- with proper place names to
mean ‘via, by way of’. The resulting lexemes are postposed or are floating adverbs
that modify the entire clause:
(1781)
Te Niivaga ne ui mai faka-Nukufetau.
the Nivaga Pst go-through Dxs in-manner-of+Nukufetau
‘The M.V.Nivaga came via Nukufetau.’

2.1.1.5.2. Proximate
There is no formal marking of proximal location or motion. Proximity is expressed
with the verb pili ‘close, near’, and its causative (and usually reduplicated) form
fakapilipili ‘[move] near [to, from, etc.]’:
(1782)

‘I haven’t come near that person.’
The verb pili can serialize (cf. 2.1.3.7) with verbs denoting location at rest, but not
motion:
(1783)

‘Our home is close to the church.’
(1784)

(‘I am going near the church.’)
In the last case, fakapilipili can be used as an adverb:

‘I am going near the church.’
2.1.1.5.3. Interior
Interior location is denoted with complex prepositions formed with loto ‘middle,
heart’:
(1786)
Konei ana fakaasiga ne fai i loto i te fono.

‘This is what he revealed at the meeting.’
(1787)

‘[They] should all come to the central part of the maneaba.’
2.1.1.5.4. Exterior
Exterior location can be expressed in a number of ways. The least marked is with
complex prepositions formed with tua ‘outside’:

‘The spade was left outside the kitchen hut.’
(1789)
Atuli aka tamaliki konaa ki tua o te fale!

‘Please tell those kids to get out of the house!’

2.1.1.5.12. Lateral-contact
Lateral-contact location is not marked in any specific manner.
2.1.1.5.13–16. Citerior and citerior-contact, ulterior and ulterior-contact
Both citerior and ulterior locations (and corresponding contact locations) are marked
similarly. Complex prepositions with mua ‘front’ (cf. 2.1.1.5.5) and tua ‘back’ (cf.
2.1.1.5.6) can denote citerior and ulterior locations respectively, while tafa ‘side’ (cf.
2.1.1.5.11) can denote either citerior or ulterior locations. These local nouns must be
modified by the deictic adverbs mai if they denote a citerior location and atu if they
denote an ulterior location (cf. 2.1.3.6.10):
(1805)

‘the house on this side of the maneaba’

2.1.1.5.17. Medial (two entities)
Medial location between two entities is most frequently described
paraphrastically:
(1808)
Au e sagasaga i loto i te maneapa, Teleke e nofo i oku

tafa, a ko Tevasa teenei i toku feituu kkoo.

Alternatively, medial location may be expressed with a prepositional
construction that resembles a complex preposition but in fact is not one. In this
construction, the word vaa ‘gap’ in the singular is the head of the noun phrase
functioning as the object of the preposition, and takes an inalienable
possessive modifier denoting the reference of the location (i.e., entities on each
side of the location):
(1809)
Au ne sagasaga i te vaa o Tevasa mo Teleke.
I Pst sit in the gap of Tevasa and Teleke
‘I sat between Tevasa and Teleke.’
This construction differs from complex prepositions in two ways. First, the noun
vaa is always in the singular, whereas local nouns in complex prepositions are always
in the plural; second, the reference of the location can only be marked as a possessive
modifier of vaa ‘gap’, whereas in complex prepositions they can be marked as either
possessive or locative modifiers (cf. 2.2.6.1.2(a)). Thus vaa probably keeps its literal
meaning in constructions denoting medial location, which are thus closer in meaning
to ‘in the gap between’ than ‘between’.

2.1.1.6. Location in time
2.1.1.6.1. General
Prepositions that denote location in time are identical in form and, with a few
exceptions, meaning to prepositions that denote physical location (cf. 2.1.1.5). Thus
the most general way of referring to points in time at rest (i.e., without movement
in time), as well as to temporal sources, is with i:
(1816)
Te Leo o Tuuvalu e ppono saale i te iva.
the voice of Tuvalu Nps close often at the nine
‘Radio Tuvalu is off the air at nine.’
The preposition mai denotes points in time and temporal sources that are somehow
oriented towards the point of reference of the discourse. This is the case, for example,
of points in time that denote the beginning of a situation which is still current at the
temporal point of reference of the discourse, or the first occurrence in the future of
an iterative situation:
(1817)
Teelaa e iloa nee au ne maafua mai i te vaai taimi teenaa.

‘That’s how I know that [it] originated in that period of time.’
(1818)
mai mua loo, i te kaamataaga o te lalolagi

‘very early on, when the world began’
As with location in space (cf. 2.1.1.5(c)), mai is obligatory when the end point of
temporal motion is specified within the same clause:
(1819)

‘from that year until this year’

movement in time are not marked with ki. However, this preposition does denote
movement in time:
(1820)

‘It’s coming up to two hours.’
(1821)

‘There won’t be a single ship till next year.’

For this purpose, a prepositional modifier is added to the temporal expression:

‘[The bell for] evening prayer strikes at 6:30 every day.’

the noun that refers to the temporal category, and marking it optionally with the
adverb katoa ‘all, every’ (this modifier is obligatory with aso ‘day’):
(1849)

‘Let’s cast the fishing net every evening.’
(1850)

‘[He] trawls every day.’

months is pluralized to mark frequentativeness, the proper suffix -a(a) regularly
attached to prepositions becomes optional, an indication that they lose proper-noun

2.1.1.6.3. Punctual-future
Points in the future may be denoted in one of two ways. First, the preposed quantifier
suaa ‘other’ (cf. 2.1.6.6.3(c)) modifies temporal terms of all types, either by itself, in
which case it means ‘next’, or in conjunction with preposed attributive numerals:
(1852)
E oko mai i ssuaa vaaiaso eiloa.

‘[It]’ll be here next week.’
(1853)
i te suaa Assaa
in the other Sunday
‘next Sunday, the following Sunday’
(1854)

‘[It]’ll be held again in three years.’
Although expressions with both suaa and a numeral are grammatical, they are
stylistically contrived. Of relevance here are the expressions taeao (aka) ‘tomorrow’,
taeao atu or te aso atu ‘the day after tomorrow’, and other temporal expressions
discussed in 2.1.3.2.1(d).
Second, the clause maa vau,22 literally, ‘[which] will come’ (or sometimes such
alternatives as koo pili mai ‘[which] is near’) can modify terms referring to any point
in time ‘larger’ than a day. When a numeral is present in the temporal expression
(e.g., ‘in three years’), the construction takes the form of an ordinal construction of
the nominalized predicate type (cf. 2.1.6.4.1):
(1855)
i te Assaa maa vau
at the Sunday Prc come
‘next Sunday, the following Sunday’
(1856)
E toe fai i te tolu o tausaga maa vau.
Nps again do at the three of year Prc come
‘[It]’ll be held again in three years.’
The two strategies cannot be combined in the same phrase. The words vaaiaso ‘week’,
maasina ‘month’, and tausaga ‘year’ can also be modified with the attributive adjective
foou ‘new’, in alternation with other possibilities, to denote ‘next’. The resulting
noun phrase behaves like an ordinary temporal modifier.
Several adverbs denoting points in the future are formed with an unproductive
prefix maa-, e.g., maataeao ‘tomorrow’ (cf. taeao ‘morning’), maanei ‘in a moment’,
derived from nei ‘now’ (cf. 2.1.2.5(d)), maafiafi ‘this afternoon or early evening’ (cf.
afiafi ‘afternoon or early evening’), and maapoo ‘tonight’ (from poo ‘night’). The prefix
also appears in the future interrogative word maafea ‘when?’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.3(d)), and
may be related to the tense-aspect-mood marker maa that appears in maa vau ‘next’

2.1.1.6.4. Punctual-Past
Expressions that denote points in time in the past have the same structure as the
second of the punctual-future constructions described in 2.1.1.6.3. The temporal
expression is most frequently modified by the relative clauses koo teka or koo tea
‘[which] has passed’ (tea is a Samoan borrowing, teka is the cognate autochthonous
form), or koo fano ‘[which] has gone’ or, optionally, its suppletive plural form koo

or the past tense form ne fano ‘[which] went’. The verb in the relative clause is
sometimes modified by a temporal adverb like nei ‘now’ or atu ‘away’. The same
construction can be used for time expressions of all types except periods of the day:
(1857)

‘He came here two hours ago.’

interrogative root fea it forms the past tense interrogative word anafea ‘when’ (cf.
2.1.2.6.3(d)). It also appears in the compound anagataa ‘long lasting’, formed from—
gataa ‘not readily’ (cf. 2.2.2.2.2); and the adverb analeva ‘quite a while ago’ (from
leva ‘long time’), which is only used as a short answer to questions with anafea
‘when’; anamua ‘a long time ago’ (from mua ‘before’); and the fossilized form anaafi
‘yesterday’, which occasionally becomes annafi. Corresponding to ana- is a prefix
maa- with future meaning (cf. 2.1.1.6.3), although anapoo ‘last night’ is only attested
in the Northern dialects (the Southern dialects have i te poo, literally ‘in the night’),
while maapoo is attested in Southern Tuvaluan.
2.1.1.6.5. Duration
Duration with countable temporal units can be marked with a numeral verb
denoting the time that the situation lasts, whose subject is a nominalized clause
denoting the durative situation:
(1860)
Koo lima ana aso i tena gaaluega foou.
Inc five his day at his job new
‘He’s been at his new job for five days.’
A number of forms other than numerals can also function as the predicate, such as
kaatoa ‘whole, complete’:
(1861)
Koo kaatoa nei toku maasina i konei.
Inc whole now my month at here
‘I have been here a month.’

Anterior-duration expressions are complex structures that consist of the verb oko

modifier denoting the temporal expression:
(1867)

(1868)

(1869)

‘There won’t be a ship till next month.’
