2.1.1.6.12–13. Point in period (past and future)
Points in a period, whether past or future, are generally not distinguished formally
from general temporal location, duration, anterior-duration, and posterior-duration.
In most cases, the tense-aspect marking and the general meaning of the sentence
indicate when a time expression refers to a point in a period rather than to another
time concept. For example, a clause marked for iterative punctual aspect can only
denote points in a period:
(1879)
A te Niivaga kaa fakalua mai kee oko kia Teesema.

‘The M.V.Nivaga will [call] twice here until December.’
When the reference period is expressed with a prepositional phrase, the fact that
the sentence refers to a point in a period can be stressed with the use of complex
prepositions formed with loto ‘centre’ (cf. 2.1.1.5.18):
(1880)

not exclusively associated with points in a period.
2.1.1.7. Double case marking
Double case marking does not occur. Noun phrases that have several syntactic or
semantic functions can only carry overt marking for one of these functions. As a
result, there are occasions in which potential ambiguities exist. Instances of such

2.1.1.8. Number
A distinction between singular and plural noun phrases is marked obligatorily
with the help of preposed articles, which also mark definiteness and specificity
(cf. 2.1.1.10–13). This binary distinction contrasts with the three-way singular-
dual-plural distinction marked in personal and possessive pronouns (cf.
2.1.2.1.4). When a noun is modified by a possessive pronoun, the form of the
possessive pronoun coalesces with that of the article (cf. 2.1.2.4); thus, in what
follows, statements about articles also apply to possessive pronouns unless
otherwise indicated.
This discussion focuses principally on nouns, rather than nominalized verbs.
Although nominalized verbs are marked with the same article forms as nouns, and
are thus marked for number, they differ from nouns in several respects. For example,
they most commonly take a singular definite article regardless of number or
definiteness considerations, and they can also undergo number agreement with
their underlying subject (cf 2.1.3.5).
For a discussion of number marking on direct objects that have undergone object
incorporation, see 2.1.3.6.12. For a discussion of number marking on nouns modified
by numerals, see 2.1.6.
2.1.1.8.1. Number categories
Two number categories are distinguished in nouns, namely singular and plural
(or, more accurately, ‘nonsingular’, since ‘plural’ here differs from the category
‘plural’ in pronouns). For example, the first member of each of the following pairs
is marked for singular number and the second for plural number:
(1881)
te aso fakamanatu
the day Cst+remember
‘the commemorative day’
(1882)
aso fakamanatu
day Cst+remember
‘the commemorative days’
(1883)
te tausaga teelaa
the year that
‘that year’
(1884)
tausaga kolaa
year those
‘those years’
All noun types are marked for the same number categories.
2.1.1.8.2. Obligatoriness of number marking
Number marking is obligatory. No noun phrase is ever ambiguously singular or
plural. However, number marking is not always based on semantic criteria. For
example, some noun phrases marked for singular number denote semantically
plural entities. For example, nouns that refer to groups, such as kaaiga ‘family’, fono

singular number, even though they are treated by other number-sensitive processes
as plural expressions:

collective notions, such as kau ‘shoal [of fish], group [of humans]’, tuula ‘flock [of

Certain nouns or noun classes are inherently plural or preferably plural. First, the

directions. The most important are mua ‘front’, tua ‘back’, luga ‘top’, lalo ‘bottom’,
loto ‘centre’, fafo (or fofo) ‘outside’, and tafa ‘side’, as well as fale ‘settlement’, gaaloto

locations and directions, a feature which can be simply explained as a consequence
of their plural number, since plurality is marked with a zero article (cf. 2.1.1.8.6).
That they are plural nouns is attested by the following: when they are marked with
a possessive pronoun, the plural form of the pronoun is obligatory. Thus the plural
oku ‘my’ must be used in the following, and the singular toku ‘my’ cannot:
(1893)

‘at my side’
Thus, rather than establishing a separate class of locative nouns on account of the
fact that they lack articles, as is commonly done for other Polynesian languages,
they can simply be posited as obligatorily plural. Indeed, this is not an unusual
characteristic in the language, as members of other semantic classes are obligatorily
or preferably plural, such as terms referring to ‘areal’ parts of the body. For example,
fatafata ‘chest area’, mata ‘area around the eyes’, isu ‘area around the nose’, gutu
‘area around the mouth’, and tua ‘back area’ are all commonly used in the plural;
when they appear in the singular, they lose their ‘areal’ meaning and refer to specific
body parts.
In addition, most nouns that refer to mass or ‘uncountable’ entities are least
marked in the plural. Objects and concepts like suka ‘sugar’, tai ‘sea water’, sameni
‘cement’, vaiua ‘rain’, fattili ‘thunder’, maafaufauga ‘thought’, tuaa ‘ancestry’, aamioga
‘behaviour’, uiga ‘personality’, maalosi ‘vitality’, taimi ‘time’, and koga ‘place’ are all
regularly denoted by plural noun phrases. These are not obligatorily plural nouns
in the same sense as locative nouns are, because they can also appear in the singular.
Mass nouns, for example, are marked for the singular number when they refer to a
generic notion. For example, suka ‘sugar’ is in the plural in the first of the following
examples because it refers to a nongeneric entity, and in the singular in the second
example because it refers to a generic entity:
(1894)

‘There is no more sugar at the store.’

‘Sugar is an energy food.’

2.1.1.8.3. Miscellaneous means of marking number in nouns
Besides being encoded in the form of the articles, number can also be indicated
on nouns by lengthening either one or two segments of the word. This
alternative strategy is restricted to three nouns, but it is obligatory. The three
nouns in question are tagata ‘man’, whose plural form is taagata; fafine
‘woman’, plural form faafine; and loomatua ‘old woman’ (a borrowing from
Samoan ‘olomatua, whose first two segments have been idiosyncratically
metathesized), plural form loomaattua. The plural forms of the first two in the
list differ from the plural forms of the etymologically related verbs tagata
‘male’ and fafine ‘female’, namely taaggata and faaffine respectively.
Furthermore, tagata and fafine may each take on one of two singular forms
when prefixed with faka- ‘in the manner of’ (cf. 2.2.4.1), each with a distinct
meaning: fakatagata and fakafafine (plural forms fakataagata and fakafaafine) mean
‘[act like a] gender-inverted person’ (e.g., by cross-dressing, acting
effeminately or in a mannish manner; see Besnier 1994c); and the forms

2.1.1.8.4–5. Collective and distributive plurals
There is no systematic formal difference between collective plurals and distributive
plurals. However, collective plurality is a significant semantic category in the lexicon.
First, certain nouns that are consistently marked for singular number are
inherently collective; such is the case of kaaiga ‘family members’, fanauga ‘children
issued from the same parents, sibling set’, and fenua ‘island community’. These
nouns can be modified by plural demonstratives, they trigger number agreement
like plural nouns (cf. 2.1.3.6.5(b)), and they can be enumerated. These are features
that demonstrate that they refer to collective plural entities:
(1900)
E toko fia toutou fanauga?
Nps Num how-many? your-3 siblings
‘How many siblings are there in your family?’
Inherently collective nouns also have noncollective uses: for example, kaaiga can
mean ‘family’, fanauga ‘litter’, and fenua ‘island, atoll, country’, all of which are
noncollective entities. When they have noncollective referents, they behave like
any other noun with respect to number marking and agreement.
Second, certain compounding morphemes can give eligible nouns a collective
meaning. Like nouns with inherently collective meaning, these compounds are
always marked with singular articles. The compounding morphemes in question
are semantically specialized. A typical example is kau, which, when preposed to
a nominal descriptor or modified by an attributive adjective, refers to the group
of persons that meet the description, be it the entire set of possible referents or a
subset of it:
(1901)
Koo kau ki te kau tteke.
Inc join to the group oppose
‘[He] has joined the opposition.’
The same word has several other referents with related meaning, the most ‘collective’
of which denotes the multiplicity of the referent of the noun to which it is preposed:
(1902)
Seeai se kau namu peelaa mo te namu i te koga teelaa!
Neg a group mosquito thus with the mosquito at the place that
‘That place is infected with mosquitos!’
The word vai can also be used with the same meaning (e.g., te vai tino ‘a crowd of
people’).

akau, laga, and gutu ‘shoal of pelagic fish, trevally, or dolphins’ (manu, literally ‘bird’,

taken as the expedient representative of the group for the context at hand. Although
the ties that bind the member of the group together can be tenuous and temporary,
expressions with saa can also refer to socially significant units like families or

family or household (matai):

2.1.1.8.6. Means of marking number
Number is marked with preposed articles, which also mark definiteness and related
categories (cf. 2.1.1.10–13). The article paradigm is provided in Table 2.2. The form
of the singular indefinite article in the Nukulaelae dialect is he. The indefinite plural
article has an alternative form ni, which is its unmarked form in the Northern dialects
of Tuvaluan. This form is occasionally heard in Southern Tuvaluan as an independent
morpheme, although it is marked as an interdialectal borrowing. However, it
appears obligatorily in the formation of the bimorphemic quantifier niisi (cf.
2.1.6.6.3(d)).
The absence of an overt article can be interpreted as a marker of definite plurality.
With nouns of certain grammatical functions, the empty article slot is frequently
filled with the absolutive-contrastive case marker a (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1). All articles
coalesce with possessive pronominal forms, which thus mark nouns for number in
the same manner as articles (cf. 2.1.2.4.3). Possessive pronouns are syntagmatically
incompatible with articles.
The definite singular article te has an interesting phonological effect on any
word that follows it whose first segment is /t/ (as first described in detail by Milner
1958). What follows te is usually the head of the noun phrase, although it is
sometimes a preposed nominal modifier such as toe ‘last’, toko ‘numeral marker for
humans’, tau ‘pair [of kin categories]’. Whatever comes immediately after te, if its
initial segment is /t/, it is obligatorily geminated, a predictable effect that is not
indicated in the orthography used in this work. Following is the IPA phonetic
representation of one such instance:
(1908)
te titi [te t?iti]
the dancing-skirt
‘the dancing skirt’
Compare the form of the same word when it is preceded by the singular indefinite
article se and the plural definite zero form:
(1909)
se titi [se titi]
a dancing-skirt
‘a dancing skirt’
(1910)
titi [titi]
dancing-skirt
‘dancing skirts’
In addition, the singular definite article can coalesce with words whose initial
segment is /t/, in which case the article loses its vowel and simply becomes a
geminating prefix. Word-initial geminate dental stops that result from this process

even when it is not in a grammatical context that calls for an article (cf. 2.1.1.10.5–
6(a)). Variants of the above processes are also attested in various Polynesian Outlier

A comparable, though considerably more restricted, process is observable with
the singular indefinite article se. When the word that follows this article has the
phoneme /s/ in initial position, the article may coalesce with the noun in the same
way as the singular definite article does. Thus se saamala ‘a hammer’ may appear as
ssaamala. The presence of the full form of the indefinite article before words
beginning in /s/ never triggers the gemination of the word-initial segment. In
most cases, this process is a fast speech phenomenon characteristic of very informal
contexts, and does not have the same grammaticalized status as the variations in
the form of the singular definite article. It appears to have become grammaticalized
only with the quantifier suaa- ‘other’ (cf. 2.1.6.6.3), whose most frequent form is
ssuaa-. This form can be analysed as having a coalesced singular indefinite article
in word-initial position.
2.1.1.8.7. Number marking with foreign words
Borrowed nouns fall into different nondiscrete types. On the one hand, some
borrowed nouns have been integrated into the vocabulary of the language: their
phonological shape has been adapted to conform to the phonological structure of

donor language is never used except when code-switching; they are known to all
competent monolingual speakers; and their meaning sometimes diverges from
their meaning in the donor language. Such is the case of nouns like faatele ‘fatele
dance’, faamasino ‘judge’, and tuupulaga ‘generation’ (borrowed from Samoan
fa’atele, fa’amasino, and tu¯pulaga); ikalaoi ‘choice-quality swamp-taro corm’, kaleve
‘coconut toddy’, and tuukauano ‘spade’ (borrowed from Gilbertese ikaraoi, karewe,
tuukawano); and suka ‘sugar’, sene ‘cent’, and fooleni ‘parade’ (borrowed from
English, the last from ‘fall in’). These borrowings are marked for number in the
same way as noun of autochthonous origin. On the other hand, one finds
borrowings whose phonological shape is not adapted to the phonological structure
of the language, which are not standardized as fully-fledged members of the
lexicon of the language, and whose use depends on the speaker’s knowledge of
the donor language. In some cases, such words may retain number marking from
the donor language. Whether they do or not depends on the speaker’s fluency in
the donor language.
Integrated and unintegrated borrowings are extremes on a continuum. Generally
speaking, borrowings become more integrated as time goes on, and their currency
increases; borrowings from English lose their native number marking early in this
process, and the singular form quickly becomes the only form used.
2.1.1.9. Classes and genders
There are no classes or gender categories in the language. As shown in 2.1.1.4.6.1,
the alienable-inalienable contrast identified in possessive structures should not be
analysed as a gender-like phenomenon, because it has a clear semantic basis, because
the categories it defines are not mutually exclusive, and because it is only relevant
to one specific type of structure.
Unlike certain other Oceanic languages (e.g., Palauan, Kilivila), Polynesian
languages do not have classifier systems, and Tuvaluan is no exception. Certain
inflectional and derivational morphemes resemble classifiers, such as the collective
morphemes described in 2.1.1.8.5, some of the specialized numeral forms identified
in 2.1.6.3, the numeral modifiers described in 2.1.6.5.2, and some of the quantifiers
discussed in 2.1.6.6.3. However, their use is restricted to certain parts of the lexicon
and is not intrinsically linked to enumeration, and hence they should not be
considered as classifiers in the usual sense of the term.
2.1.1.10. Definiteness
Definiteness is marked by the same articles that mark number. Even though I refer
to ‘definite articles’ and ‘indefinite articles’ throughout this grammar and gloss
these articles ‘the’ and ‘a’ (or ‘some’ in the case of the plural indefinite form) in
interlinear translations, the semantics of these morphemes is complex. In particular,
the significant contrast is not a definite-indefinite contrast, but one involving
definiteness, referentiality, and genericness. This section must be consulted in
conjunction with the discussion of indefiniteness (2.1.1.11), referentiality (2.1.1.12),
and genericness (2.1.1.13).
2.1.1.10.1. Means of marking definiteness
Definiteness is one of the categories marked by the two definite articles, the singular
form te and the zero plural form (cf. 2.1.1.8.6). For example, the first of the following
is marked for definiteness, and the second for indefiniteness:

2.1.1.10.2. Obligatoriness of definiteness marking
All nonproper nouns must appear with an article (although this article may be a
zero form in the case of the indefinite plural article), and all articles are marked for
definiteness. Hence definiteness is obligatorily marked on nouns.
2.1.1.10.3–4. Definiteness and spatial orientation
The spatial relationship between referents and participants in the speech act does
not affect the form of definiteness.
2.1.1.10.5–6. Definiteness and nominal categories  
(a) Proper nouns and pronouns
Generally speaking, proper nouns and personal pronouns are not marked for
definiteness, even when they function as the head of a nonrestrictive relative
clause (cf. 1.1.2.3.2). However, this statement must be qualified in a number
of ways.
First, a sizeable number of place names in Tuvalu appear with an
obligatory singular definite article te. Many are derived from common nouns
denoting environmental features, both natural and artificial: Te Puka literally
‘the puka tree (Pisonia grandis)’, Te Fale ‘the settlement’, Te Fatu o Manu ‘the
rock of the birds’, and Te Aasaga Loa ‘the long sandbank’. Others are not
recognizable descriptors (e.g., Te Afaatule). When the head noun begins with
the segment/t/, the coalesced form of the singular definite article is
normally used (e.g., Ttumuiloto). These places names never appear without
the article te and cannot take any other article. The article is thus part and
parcel of the place name.
Second, the place name Tuuvalu ‘Tuvalu’ (literally, ‘the eight customs’) always
appears with a coalesced singular definite article, which is not indicated in the
orthography used here (cf. 2.1.1.8.6). Indeed, the first consonant of the word is
always a geminate; that this geminate is caused by the coalescence of an article can
be ascertained by the etymology of the word (te ‘the’, tuu ‘tradition’, and valu ‘eight’).
The name can also appear preceded by the full form of the singular definite article
when it is used as a noun, yielding the less common but perfectly acceptable form
Te Tuuvalu. In this respect, the word does not differ from other definite singular
nouns with the segment/t/in word-initial position, which can appear with either
a geminated initial segment or a geminated initial segment and the full form of the
article (cf. 2.1.1.8.6).
The word differs from other place names described in the previous
paragraph in that it may function in ways other than as a place name, where in
normal contexts articles do not appear. For example, it can function as an
attributive adjective:

2.1.1.11. Indefiniteness
Indefiniteness is obligatorily marked with indefinite articles.
2.1.1.11.1. Means of marking indefiniteness
The two indefinite articles se and ne (cf. 2.1.1.8.6) mark indefiniteness as well as
nonreferentiality. For contrastive examples of each, see 2.1.1.8.1 and 2.1.1.10.1. For
a discussion of the fact that indefinite nouns are frequently nonreferential, see
2.1.1.12.

2.1.1.11.2. Obligatoriness of indefiniteness marking
Indefinite articles appear in one of two contexts: as markers of nonreferential
indefiniteness and in a number of grammatical constructions that are
conventionally associated with indefinitely-marked noun phrases. The
former case is discussed in 2.1.1.12. The following discussion focuses on the
latter case.
Indefinite noun phrases appear most frequently as the subject of positive
and negative existential verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b) and 1.4(d) respectively),
including existential verbs that denote possession (cf. 1.10.1.1), and as an
element of equational constructions (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)), including interrogative
equational constructions (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)). The reason why these grammatical
functions are associated with indefiniteness is simple, given the definition of
indefiniteness as an information category used when the speaker-writer
assumes that his or her interlocutor is not able to identify the referent of the
noun phrase (Chafe 1976). Since both existential and equational constructions
commonly serve to identify and qualify new nominal referents, they are
canonical contexts for indefiniteness. Note that indefinitely marked noun
phrases in such contexts can refer to either specific or nonspecific entities.
Furthermore, in some grammatically conditioned contexts, the indefinitely
marked noun phrase may alternatively be marked with a definite article. Such
is the case, for example, of existential constructions that function as possessive
clauses, where the alternation between indefiniteness and definiteness results
in subtle differences in information structure (cf. 1.10.1.1). However,
indefiniteness is more frequent than definiteness in these contexts.
In addition, indefiniteness is preferred when the noun phrase appears with
certain quantifiers, in particular isi ‘other’, suaa- ‘other’, soo ‘any’ (cf. 2.1.6.6),
and when it is the object of the irrealis equative construction peenei me, peenaa
me, peelaa me (cf. 1.9.1(a)). These morphemes and constructions are commonly
associated with nonreferential entities, which explains the preponderance of

2.1.1.11.3–4. Indefiniteness and spatial orientation
The spatial relationship between referents and participants in the speech act does
not affect the form of definiteness.
2.1.1.11.5–6. Definiteness and nominal categories
Plural nouns are marked for indefiniteness in the same general fashion as singular
nouns, although with different morphemes, as shown above. Mass nouns are for
the most part plural (cf. 2.1.1.8.2), and they are marked for indefiniteness in the
same way as regular plural nouns.
2.1.1.12. Referentiality
Referentiality is a significant category, but it is not associated with distinct
morphemes. Rather, it is a secondary function of markers of definiteness.
2.1.1.12.1. Means of marking referentiality
There are two ways of marking nonreferentiality: one is productive, and the other
is restricted to a small class of nouns.

mentioned in the same stretch of discourse, or that it is located at or associated

Final-vowel gemination has functions other than the marking of
nonreferentiality. First, certain ‘local nouns’ optionally undergo final-vowel
gemination in contexts where they are used as independent fixed framework
locative expressions (cf. 2.1.1.5(d)), that is, not as part of complex prepositions
(cf. 2.1.1.5(c)). The following local nouns can undergo this process: tua ‘back
part of the village’, mua ‘front part of the village’, namo ‘lagoon(ward)’, uta
‘land(ward)’, and fale ‘towards the settlement’. Other terms are excluded either
because of their phonological structure (e.g., tai ‘lagoon(ward)’, the antonym
of uta, ends in a high vowel), or because of the unproductive nature of the
process. The difference in meaning between regular and geminated forms of
local nouns is rather insignificant. Geminated forms tend to connote greater
distance, either physical or metaphorical, between the point of reference of the
discourse and the referent of the local noun. Regular and geminated forms do
not differ from one another in terms of referentiality in the usual sense of the
term, although it is noteworthy that local nouns denote very general locations
and directions, and thus are inherently less than fully referential.
Second, proper names that are marked with the preposed collective
morpheme saa (or haa in the Nukulaelae dialect) optionally undergo final-
vowel gemination, as discussed in 2.1.1.8.4–5, unless they already end in a
geminate vowel. These cases differ from final-vowel gemination with dummy
and local nouns, as proper names ending in a high vowel can undergo final-
vowel gemination (e.g., saa Peetelii ‘Peteli and her group’, saa Mauu ‘Mau and
his group’). Similarly, noun phrases with tama ‘what’s-his-name, what’s-her-
name’ and toko lua ‘those two’ as head, which have other unusual
characteristics, can also undergo final-vowel gemination, and in certain cases
must do so (cf. 2.1.1.8.4–5, 2.1.6.5.1(a)). Final-vowel gemination carries no
identifiable meaning in these cases, and there is no semantic or pragmatic
difference between nongeminated and geminated equivalents when both are
possible. It clearly does not mark nonreferentiality, since these expressions
always refer to specific individuals or groups of individuals.
Final-vowel gemination is not a productive process, and an integrated
characterization of its various uses should not be sought. In a significant
number of cases, it denotes both nonreferentiality and distance or lack of
relevance to the discourse context. In other cases, it does not have an
identifiable function.
2.1.1.12.2. Obligatoriness of referentiality marking
The marking of nonreferentiality is obligatory in equational and existential
constructions, since only referential noun phrases can appear in these contexts.
Similarly, the marking of nonreferentiality is obligatory in other indefinite noun
phrases insofar that these are always nonreferential. The marking of
nonreferentiality with final-vowel gemination is never obligatory.
2.1.1.12.3–4. Referentiality and nominal categories
Both plural and mass nouns are marked for referentiality in the same general fashion
as singular nouns, although with different morphemes, as shown above.
2.1.1.13. Genericness
Genericness is a significant category insofar as generic noun phrases can only be
marked with definite articles.

2.1.1.13.2. Obligatoriness of genericness marking
Indefinite articles cannot be used to mark genericness, and thus the category can
be considered to be obligatory.
2.1.1.14. Obviation
Obviation, the marking of the relative importance of actors in discourse, is not
marked. Relative importance is marked on a clause-by-clause basis with the same
strategies as those used for ordinary pragmatic salience (cf. 1.11 and 1.12).
2.1.2. Pronouns
Tuvaluan has clearly identifiable classes of personal pronouns, possessive pronouns,
demonstrative pronouns, and relative pronouns. There are no separate forms of
reflexive or reciprocal pronouns. Also covered in this section are nonpronominal
demonstrative forms (2.1.2.5), which share semantic characteristics with
demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative words, most of which are not
pronominal (2.1.2.6).
Overt personal and possessive pronouns (i.e., forms other than zero
pronouns) generally refer to human entities or, marginally, nonhuman animate
entities. This tendency does not apply to pronominal traces associated with

2.1.2.1.1.5. Reduced pronouns Reduced forms of personal pronouns are used in three
restricted contexts: as subject clitics of verbs suffixed with the transitivizing suffix -
gina; as subject clitics following the complementizer moo; and, in the second-person

from other Polynesian languages such as Samoan and Tongan, where reduced clitic
pronouns are much more ubiquitous, in terms of both their overall statistical frequency
and the range of constructions in which they appear. For discussions of the alternative
forms of the first-person singular pronoun, see 1.10.1, 2.1.2.1.20, and 2.1.2.4.5–6.

transitive suffix (which has several forms), and they are particularly frequent in
negative clauses with an epistemic verb, although not restricted to these contexts:
(1949)

‘I hid the clothes-pegs.’

2.1.2.1.3. Inclusion v. exclusion
The distinction between inclusion and exclusion is morphologically encoded in the
pronoun paradigm for both nonsingular numbers in the first person only. The first-

is no pronoun form with ‘general’ reference, i.e., unspecified with respect to inclusion
or exclusion, and the choice between an inclusive or exclusive form is obligatory.

2.1.2.1.4. Number
A three-way distinction between singular, dual, and plural referents is encoded
obligatorily in the morphology of both personal and possessive pronouns. This is a
more elaborate distinction than the singular-plural distinction marked on ordinary
noun phrases (cf. 2.1.1.8).
2.1.2.1.4.1. Number distinction in pronouns Personal and possessive pronouns of
all persons are marked for one of three number categories: singular, dual, or plural.
In the first person, both inclusive and exclusive forms exist in the dual and plural.
Following is an example of the number contrast in the second person:
(1976)
Koe/koulua/koutou e fano maataeao.

‘You/you (two)/you (three) are leaving tomorrow.’
2.1.2.1.4.2. Obligatoriness of number The number distinction is obligatory for all
persons and for both inclusive and exclusive reference.
2.1.2.1.4.3–4. Overlaps between number categories There are no overlaps between
number distinctions, other than in the honorific use of the dual number (cf.
2.1.2.1.12). In socially-unmarked usage, the dual number is always used to refer to
two entities, and two entities can only be referred to pronominally with dual
pronouns. Similarly, the plural number always refers to three or more entities.
In natural discourse, care is always taken to choose pronoun forms that refer to
the most inclusive and broadest range of referents. For example, if an individual
performs a task in the presence of other individuals, the activity is described as
having been performed by everyone present, even when the witnessing parties
play no active role in the performance of the activity, and plural pronouns are used.
Thus if three people go angling in a canoe with fishing gear for only one person,
they will describe the activity as follows:
(1977)
Maatou ne olo o maattau i tua.
we-3-e Pst go Cmp angle at outside
‘We (three) went angling outside the reef.’
A fuller description of the expedition might then detail the division of labour, but
the overall activity will be considered, through pronoun choice and otherwise, to
have been performed by every adult present, including inactive parties. Again,
these patterns are consistent with the concern prevalent throughout Tuvaluan society
(and many other Polynesian societies) with sharing, partaking, and including (cf.
2.1.2.1.3). From a Tuvaluan perspective, the act of ratified witnessing (taapuaki) is
qualitatively on a par with the actual performance of a task in terms of its importance.

2.1.2.1.6. Proximity distinctions in personal pronouns
Different degrees of proximity to the participants in the speech act are not marked
in personal-pronoun morphology. However, personal pronouns may be modified
by demonstrative pronouns that may specify some sort of proximity (usually
metaphorical), as discussed and illustrated in 2.1.2.5 and 2.1.2.7.
2.1.2.1.7. Anaphoric pronoun
Like its cognates in other Polynesian languages (Chapin 1974), the anaphoric
pronoun ei has a wide range of uses. Its form is invariant, although it optionally
takes the form ai when it follows a word whose last segment is /a/:
(1982)
Teenei te fenua ne ola aka ai.
this the island Pst alive Dxs Anp
‘This is the island where [he] grew up.’
The allomorph ai also appears in one form of the existential verb (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b))
and in several forms of the negative existential verb (cf. 1.4(d)). The anaphoric
pronoun also coalesces with several other morphemes in the formation of the
intensifying adverb eiloa and its allomorphs.
The anaphoric pronoun occurs in a wide variety of contexts. It is a bound anaphor
in certain contexts, and behaves as a free pronoun in other contexts. As a bound
anaphor, ei can refer to antecedents of any person and number. For example, it may
refer to a third-person plural antecedent (1983) or to a second-person singular
antecedent (1984):
(1983)

‘Those are the suitable people I’ve thought about.’
(1984)

‘[He] is just angry at you, to whom I said that you should not go.’

above examples, or to inanimate entities:

animate or inanimate, and which are usually (but not obligatorily) singular. As a
free pronoun again, ei does not necessarily refer to nominal entities; as illustrated

2.1.2.1.8–9. Gender, class, and other categories in pronouns

2.1.2.1.12. Social and affective distinctions in pronouns
(a) Affective first- and second-person pronoun
One form, kita, has pronominal characteristics, although it does not always function
as a pronoun in the ordinary sense of the term. It is stylistically and affectively
marked. It may refer to either a first- or second-person singular entity. In the latter
case, it is used either independently like any other free personal pronoun, or in
postposed apposition to the regular free second-person pronoun koe:
(1994)
A kita koo see mafai o puli i toku loto.
Cnt you Inc Neg can Cmp forgotten in my heart
‘[I] will never forget dearest you in my heart.’
(1995)
E alofa au kiaa koe kita.
Nps feel-empathy I to you you
‘I feel affection for dear little you.’
If it refers to a first-person singular entity, kita must be modified by the short form
of the first-person demonstrative nei (cf. 2.1.2.5):
(1996)
A kita nei koo see too te moe i poo.
Cnt I this Inc Neg fall the sleep at night
‘Poor old me cannot fall asleep at night.’
Kita sometimes modifies an ordinary possessive pronoun of the first or second
person, in which case it appears at the end of the entire phrase modified by the
possessive pronoun:
(1997)
Toku nuku kita e see mafai o puli i aku.
my home-island I Nps Neg can Cmp forgotten at I
‘I will never forget my home island.’
The use of kita is highly specialized, and the form is rare in everyday discourse.
First, it serves as a strongly affective index, connoting feelings of affection and
empathy (alofa) when it refers to a second-person entity or to one’s home island.
Alternatively, when it refers to the first person, it connotes feelings of helpless-
ness, vulnerability, and self-abasement (fakaalofa, i.e., feelings that bring about
feelings of alofa in others). Second, it is stylistically marked, in that it is mostly used
in courting contexts, particularly love letters and love songs, or when talking or
singing about one’s home island. Its affective meaning and stylistic specialization
are obviously related. The form has cognates in other Polynesian languages; in
languages like Tongan and Samoan, the cognate forms are in considerably wider
use than in Tuvaluan.24

crosslinguistically unusual, in that it is much more common for pronouns of the
highest number to encode social status (Head 1978:157–158). However, it is attested

namely Tikopia, and the non-Polynesian Oceanic language Mota.
(c) Miscellaneous honorifics
Several honorific nouns may be used instead of pronouns, and, optionally, in
combination with other nominal descriptors. The most common is mmalu ‘respect,
honour’, which may be used, along with proper or common modifiers, as an
alternative to second- or third-person pronouns with the meaning of ‘honourable,
excellency, exalted’. It may function as a verb, in which case the specifier is encoded
as a subject. Alternatively, it may function as a noun modified by a possessive noun
phrase or pronoun of the inalienable class or a locative prepositional phrase. As a
noun, it can also be apposed with a descriptive noun phrase. Modifiers of mmalu
follow ordinary usage, so that second-person forms are used when addressing the
referent and third-person forms are used when referring to third parties. When
pronominal, the possessive modifier is marked for singular, dual, or plural number

an entity of any number:

Compared to other languages of Western Polynesia, Tuvaluan has relatively few
terms and expressions associated with power differentials. Contrast, for example,
the restricted inventory described here with the elaborate honorific codes found in
Samoan (Duranti 1992, Milner 1961) and Tongan (Philips 1991). The comparable
paucity of honorific forms and usages must be understood in the context of the
meaning of hierarchy in Tuvaluan society. At the same time that the socio-political
organization of the islands of Tuvalu is stratified, and this stratification is deemed
desirable by the inhabitants, much emphasis is placed on egalitarianism, particularly
at the ideological level (Besnier 1996a). Indeed, the convergence of these different
propensities makes Tuvalu one of the least stratified societies in Polynesia, along
with other atoll societies. The dearth of honorific terms (and the foreign origin of
many of the terms that do exist) can thus be seen as a reflection of the ideology of
equality that permeates the speech community. In fact, the few honorific forms that
are found in the language are better understood as indexes of genre and situation,
rather than as honorifics in the more usual sense of the term.

Of course, only forms that are semantically compatible occur in such constructions.
Excluded are coordinate sequences in which the referents of the coordinate noun
phrases cannot be included in the referent of the initial pronoun, although such
constructions are grammatical if they are interpreted as disjointly coordinated
structures:

‘they and I’
(* ‘they, including me’)
Because it can only refer to the speaker-writer and his or her interlocutor to the
exclusion of any other party, the first-person dual pronoun cannot occur as the first
element of inclusively coordinated constructions. Thus the following two
constructions are not felicitous (although not ungrammatical):

(‘you and I’)

(2030)

‘Moeava, Tevasa, and me.’
(In disjointly coordinate constructions, the constituent order is free, and politeness
does not dictate that first-person entities be mentioned last.) Disjointly coordinated
constructions place greater emphasis on distributionality, while inclusively
coordinated constructions stress the unity of the referent. Disjointly coordinated
constructions are particularly frequent in religious discourse, which is heavily
influenced by English. Their particularly ubiquitous nature in religious genres may
also stem from the importance of repetition and parallelism in these genres (Besnier

2.1.2.1.19. Secondary pronoun system
There is no secondary pronominal system in which it is possible to specify in greater
detail the composition of nonsingular combinations of persons.
2.1.2.1.20. Case marking of pronouns
All pronouns may be marked for case as if they were ordinary noun phrases, as
illustrated in 2.1.2.1.1. In several contexts, an alternative form of the first-person
singular personal pronoun appears.
First, after the benefactive case markers maa (alienable) or moo (inalienable), the
first-person singular pronoun takes on the form -ku, which coalesces with the case
marker, yielding the forms maaku and mooku. The same form also appears when it
is preceded by the purpose conjunct moo (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.3(a)). The Northern dialects
also have an alternative form -u for the second-person singular personal pronoun,
which is not attested in the Southern dialects.
Second, in the Nukulaelae dialect only, the first-person singular personal pronoun
optionally takes on the form aku when it follows the prepositions i (location, etc.),
ki (direction, etc.), or mai (source, etc.), regardless of their grammatical or semantic
function:
(2035)
Ko ia loo koo kaitaua mai ki aku.
Foc he indeed Inc angry Dxs to me
‘She’s very angry at me.’
The form aku is also the unmarked first-person form, regardless of case marking, in

1.10.1.2) and when it is used as a possessively marked postposed modifier (cf.
2.1.2.4.5–6).
Six prepositions and case markers take on special suffixed forms when their
object is a personal pronoun: i (location, etc.), ki (direction, etc.), mai (source, etc.),
mo (comitative, etc.), a (alienable possession, etc.), and o (inalienable possession,
etc.). The same forms are also used when these morphemes mark proper nouns.
For further discussion and illustrations, see 2.1.5.3.
2.1.2.2. Reflexive pronouns
As discussed in 1.6, there are no special reflexive-pronoun forms. Personal-pronoun
forms (other than the zero form of the third-person singular) serve as reflexive
pronouns, particularly when they are modified by the intensifying adverb loa, which
marks emphasis and discourse prominence in other contexts. The formal similarity
between reflexive and emphatic pronouns is not an uncommon phenomenon
crosslinguistically, and it is even attested in some dialects of English (cf. Baker
1995).
2.1.2.3. Reciprocal pronouns
There are no reciprocal pronoun forms, as shown in 1.7.
2.1.2.4. Possessive pronouns
Possessive pronouns are a particularly important morphological category: they are
relatively numerous, and they occur frequently in discourse because their
grammatical functions extend beyond simply marking pronominal possession.
2.1.2.4.1. Possessive pronouns as a morphological category
Like most other Oceanic languages, Tuvaluan has a large inventory of possessive-
pronoun forms, which encode a broad spectrum of semantic information. Possessive-
pronouns are incompatible with articles, because their forms include reduced
articles, as shown in the following discussion. They are also in paradigmatic
complementary distribution with noun modifiers that are incompatible with articles
(cf. 2.1.6.6).
2.1.2.4.2. Semantic categories in possessive-pronoun morphology
Five semantic categories are marked in possessive pronouns: the alienability of the
possessive relationship; the number of the possessor; the person of the possessor;
the number of possessed entity; and the definiteness of the possessed entity.
However, only a few forms encode information from all five categories.
(a) Possessive class
The alienability or inalienability of the possessive relationship is marked obligatorily
in the form of possessive pronouns in the first- and second-person singular and
optionally in the form of possessive pronouns in the third-person singular. In
addition, in the Nukulaelae dialect only, alienability is also marked in the forms of
the second-person dual and plural possessive pronouns. For example, in the first-
person singular, the definite singular possessed possessive-pronoun form is taku
for alienable possession and toku for inalienable possession:

the same as for nonpronominal possession (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1).
(b) Number of possessor
Because the forms of possessive pronouns are derived from personal-pronoun forms
(cf. 2.1.2.4.3), they obligatorily encode the singular-dual-plural contrast in the
number of the possessor. For example, the forms of the third-person singular

groups of people), the most encompassing number category is usually encoded in
the possessive pronoun, as is the case for personal pronouns (cf. 2.1.2.1.4.3–4):
(2041)

such as dwellings and ancestry. Thus Tuvaluan will rarely speak of toku kaaiga ‘my

2.1.2.4.3. Possessive-pronoun paradigm
Possessive-pronoun forms are constructed more or less regularly from three
elements. First, articles in full or reduced form, depending on the person and
possessor number; four article forms can appear, corresponding to the definite
singular article te (in reduced form, t), indefinite singular se (in reduced form, s)
definite plural ø, and indefinite plural ne (in reduced form, n). Second, a marker of
possessive class, either a for alienable possession or o for inalienable possession,
which is homophonous with the corresponding possessive preposition (cf. 2.1.1.4.6),
and which only surfaces in some forms. Third, a reduced form of the personal
pronoun from the paradigm provided in Table 2.7.
The alternative forms in the second-person dual and plural cells are dialectal
variants. In the dual, -lua is characteristic of the Funafuti and Nukufetau dialects, -
luu of the Vaitupu dialect, and -ulua of the Nukulaelae dialect; in the plural, -ootou
is the Funafuti, Vaitupu, and Nukufetau form, and -outou the Nukulaelae form.
The possessive-pronoun paradigm for the Funafuti dialect only (which is used

In most cases, the difference between the two strategies is very subtle. It is less

These possessive forms have contrastive affective functions. The first-person
possessive forms have connotations of positive affect, and thus commonly
appear in utterances denoting or connoting such emotions as alofa ‘empathy’
towards the referent. In contrast, second-person forms convey negative affect,
and surface in contexts where the referent is being scorned, derided, or
otherwise presented in a less than flattering light (see Besnier 1989a and 1990a
for a discussion of the use of these forms in gossip). In these constructions, the
first person is then associated with positive feelings and the second person
with feelings from which one distances oneself. When they appear in these
constructions, demonstrative pronouns do not necessarily agree in deixis with
the possessive pronoun and do not necessarily have affective meaning, even
though demonstrative forms are often used in expressing affect in other
contexts (cf. 2.1.2.5.1(d)). For example, in example (2067), the second-person
possessive pronoun connotes negative affect, while the first-person
demonstrative pronoun form nei denotes the physical or social proximity of
the referent to the speaker, and has no affective value. The expressions toku
tagata, tou fafine, etc. do not always denote affect, and in some contexts tou
tagata may mean literally ‘your man’, in which case possession refers to a
kinship affiliation or a friendship tie.

2.1.2.4.7–11. Reflexive, reciprocal, emphatic, and adjectival possessive pronouns
There are no reflexive or reciprocal forms of possessive pronouns. Unlike other
Polynesian languages (e.g., Tongan, Samoan, East Uvean), Tuvaluan does not have
adjectival forms for possessive pronouns with emphatic and affective meaning,
although possessively marked personal pronouns (including the special first-person
singular forms) provide emphasis for the marking of possession, as described in
2.1.2.4.5–6. Personal pronouns may also be used predicatively in possessive verb
constructions, as shown in 1.10.1.2.
2.1.2.5. Demonstrative pronouns and other demonstrative forms
The discussion presented in this section applies to canonical demonstrative
pronouns, as well as forms related in structure or function to demonstrative
pronouns. For terminological convenience, I will use the term ‘demonstrative
pronoun’ to refer to canonical demonstrative pronouns only, and ‘demonstrative’
to all forms that resemble demonstrative pronouns, including but not restricted to
canonical demonstrative pronouns.
Most demonstratives consist of two bound morphemes. The first morpheme
(tee-, ko-, pee-, or ø) provides information about morphological class and syntactic
function, while the second morpheme (nei, naa, or laa, or the question form fea
discussed in 2.1.2.6.3(b)) provides a deictic value. The discussion that immediately
follows focuses on the former, and the latter is described in 2.1.2.5.1. Occasional
reference will be made here to ‘first-person’ forms (i.e., forms in nei), ‘second-person’
forms (i.e., forms in naa), and ‘third-person’ forms (i.e., forms in laa); these labels
are fully explicated in 2.1.2.5.1.

2.1.2.5.1. Semantic categories associated with demonstratives
For each demonstrative category, several semantic parameters distinguish the
meaning of the different forms: location in space, location in time, textual reference,
and affective distance, as well as combinations of these. These parameters concern
principally the semantic differences among the bound morphemes nei, naa, and laa,
which constitute the second element of most demonstrative forms. The following
discussion applies to canonical demonstrative pronouns, locative nouns,
demonstrative adjectives, relative pronouns, demonstrative adverbs, demonstrative
verbs, and demonstrative discourse conjuncts. There are a few exceptions and
qualifications to the general patterns described presently, the result of certain forms
having acquired specialized meanings; these are discussed in the previous section.
Demonstrative forms are rich in indexicality, in that they may invoke different types
of meaning in different contexts, and particular instances of their use are often
ambiguous between various readings.
(a) Location in space
Location in space is the most basic semantic parameter that distinguishes
semantically among nei, naa, and laa forms. It is based on a contrast among locations
in the general vicinity of the speaker (nei forms), the general vicinity of the
interlocutor (naa forms), and away from both the speaker and the interlocutor (laa
forms):
(2111)
te pausi teenei/teenaa/teelaa

‘this/that suitcase [near me]/[near you]/[away from both you and me]’
It is on the basis of these basic semantic values that I refer to forms in nei as ‘first
person’, forms in naa as ‘second person’, and forms in laa as ‘third person’. No
distinction in relative distance (e.g., contact v. closeness), relative location (e.g.,
inside v. outside), or visibility (e.g., visible v. invisible) is relevant.
If a location can be equally characterized as being in the vicinity of the speaker
and of the interlocutor, first-person forms are used, unless parameters other than
location in space (e.g., possession, see below) apply:
(2112)

‘this house in which we both are located’

First- and second-person demonstrative forms frequently carry affective

that they feel an affective affinity towards a particular entity. Such is the case in the

referents in different contexts, or ambiguous referents in specific contexts. The
potential ambiguity between different possible affective readings of the same form

2.1.2.5.4. Number marking in demonstratives
Demonstrative pronouns, the long forms of demonstrative adjectives, and relative
pronouns are marked for number. Forms in tee- are singular and forms in ko- are
plural:

‘this matter’
(2142)

‘these matters’
Number marking follows the same singular-plural contrast as is marked in noun
phrases (cf. 2.1.1.8). Locative pronouns, the short forms of demonstrative adjectives,
manner demonstratives, and demonstrative discourse conjuncts are not marked
for number. For example, the same short forms are used for both singular and
plural referents in the following:
(2143)
te mataaupu nei
the matter this
(2144)
mataaupu nei
matter these

In other cases, only plural demonstrative forms can appear. When nouns are

2.1.2.5.5. Class and gender in demonstratives
Demonstrative pronouns are not marked for either class or gender, which are not
significant categories in the grammar of Tuvaluan.

2.1.2.5.6. Case marking of demonstratives
Demonstratives other than locative pronouns are never marked for case. If a
particular syntactic context calls for a demonstrative form to appear in a case-marked
or prepositionally marked phrase, a ‘dummy’ noun (e.g., tino ‘person’, koga ‘place’,
mea ‘thing’, feituu ‘aspect’) is used as the head of the phrase, which can then be
modified by a demonstrative adjective:
(2151)
Au see faipati ki te feituu teenaa.
I Neg speak to the aspect that
‘I am not talking about that (aspect).’
The locative pronouns konei, konaa, kolaa, and koo are always marked with a
preposition (cf. 2.1.2.5(b)). These forms optionally coalesce with the directional
preposition ki to yield the forms kkonei, kkonaa, kkolaa, and kkoo:
(2152)
Aku muna nei ma kaa vau au kkonei, koo llei.
my word this Cmp Fut come I to+here Inc good
‘I thought that when I got here, [it]’d improve.’
(2153)
Moo mea atu kkoo.
little thing Dxs to+there
‘[Make a little room by] moving down that way.’
2.1.2.5.7. Other grammatical categories marked in demonstratives
No other grammatical category is marked in the form of demonstratives.
2.1.2.5.8. Adjectival uses of demonstratives

2.1.2.6. Interrogative words
There are only four interrogative-word roots, each of which can be attached to
a variety of prefixes and case markers to form morphologically-complex
interrogative words. In the following discussion, simple and derived forms are
treated together under the base form. Two morphologically complex
interrogative words are derived through a productive derivational process,
namely faka-prefixation; the derivational morphology utilized in deriving
other complex interrogative words is unproductive.
Interrogative words do not form a special morphological class. Instead, they
behave like other preforms of different morphological categories. Some are
anaphors for nominal entities, in the sense that their morphosyntactic
behaviour is the same as that of a noun (e.g., they receive case marking and
take articles); others are proverbs, in that they are marked and behave like
verbs (e.g., they are marked for tense, aspect, and mood, and they may be
modified by adverbs); still others are adverbials and adjectives. Generally
speaking, interrogative words are not readily distinguishable in terms of their
syntactic behaviour from members of the morphological categories of which
they are anaphors.

with each interrogative word, simple and complex (the English glosses

The basic form of the interrogative word is ai (from Proto-Polynesian *hai). The form
oi is used if the interrogative word is preceded by a grammatical morpheme whose
final vowel is /o/ (e.g., o ‘of’, mo ‘with, and’). When the interrogative word is marked
with the focus marker ko, the two morphemes coalesce. The result is written as one
word in the orthography used in this grammar, and in the orthographic system used
by most native writers. The allomorphic change to oi is obligatory in informal spoken
discourse. Occasionally, in oratorical contexts, the forms mo ai, o ai, ko ai, etc. are heard,
particularly in religious discourse. These are Northern Tuvaluan forms, and are
connotatively marked in the Southern dialects. (Their appearance in religious discourse
may be caused by the fact that they resemble the Samoan form ai, which is invariant.)
The form ei is used following grammatical morphemes whose final segment is /e/
(principally the ergative case marker nee). It is only characteristic of conversational
discourse. In contrast to allomorphic variation between ai and oi, the form ei is optional.

receives case marking. Prepositions that take on the suffix -a(a) when marking proper

2.1.2.6.3. fea
The base form of the interrogative word fea ‘where?, which?’ is discussed in (a).
The complex forms teefea and kofea ‘where?’ are discussed under (b), peefea ‘how?’
under (c), and the temporal anafea, maafea, and aafea under (d).
(a) Base form
The interrogative word fea (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hee) has two meanings. Used
as a noun, it refers to locations:
(2196)
Koe e fano ki fea?
you Nps go to where?
‘Where are you going?’
(2197)
Mai fea tou fou?
from where? your flower-crown
‘Where did you get your flower crown?’
(2198)
Au uu ne puke i fea?
your coconut-crab Pst grab in where?
‘Where did you get these coconut crabs?’
Location may be a metaphorical notion, as in the following:
(2199)
Koe e tuu i fea i te paalota?
you Nps stand at where? in the election
‘Where do you stand as far as the elections are concerned?’
Used as an adjective, fea indicates that the question concerns a choice, like English
‘which’:
(2200)
Kae ne gatu laa foki fea e manako koe ki ei?
and some clothes then also which? Nps wish you to Anp
‘And which types of clothes do you want now?’
(2201)
Te aso lima fea e fai ei te paalota?
the day five which? Nps do Anp the election
‘Which Friday is the election going to be held on?’
The interrogative word can therefore function as either a noun or an adjective. As a
noun, it behaves like a locative noun, i.e., it is marked as a plural definite noun
with a zero article. It may be marked by prepositions. Because of its meaning, fea as
a noun is most commonly marked with the locative preposition i, the directional
preposition ki, or the source preposition mai. Used as a sentence fragment, fea must
be marked by a preposition:
(2202)
I fea?
at where?
‘Where?’
For a discussion of the demonstrative short forms nei and naa, which are closely
related in function to some of the uses of fea, see 2.1.2.5(c) and 2.1.2.5(d).
(b) teefea, kofea
Like fea, teefea and kofea are used in questions about locations or choices. Unlike the
base form of the interrogative word, they function as nominal predicates; teefea (in
the Nukulaelae dialect, teehee) is the singular form, kofea (in the Nukulaelae dialect,
kohee) the plural form:

closely related in morphosyntactic behaviour. Neither teefea nor kofea can be
marked by articles or case markers. When they are used as sentence fragments,
teefea and kofea are unmarked, although they may be modified by postposed

(2206)

present many parallels to those of teefea and kofea.
(c) peefea
The interrogative word peefea (in the Nukulaelae dialect, peehee) is used to form
questions about the manner in which an event takes place:
(2207)

‘How do [you] light that lamp of yours?’

of a particular entity:
(2208)

‘What does she look like?’
[lit.: ‘How-are her features?’]

[i.e.: ‘Provide a description of his character or looks.’]

and postverbal arguments of the verb and other adverbial modifiers is not fixed,
although there is a tendency for the interrogative word to precede arguments of
the verb and other adverbials. When it is used as a sentence fragment, peefea is
unmarked, although it may be modified by postposed adverbs of various types:

(d) anafea, maafea, aafea
These three interrogative words (in the Nukulaelae dialect, the first two are anahee
and maahee respectively) are all used in questions about time. They differ from one
another as follows: anafea is used for past events; maafea for future events; and aafea
for both:
(2211)
Koutou ne oko mai anafea?
you-3 Pst reach Dxs when?
‘When did you get here?’
(2212)
E fakaoti maafea te maasina?
Nps Cst+end when? the month

Aafea ne mmai ei koutou?
when? Pst come Anp you-3
‘When did you get here?’
(2214)
Koutou e olo aafea?
you-3 Nps go when?
‘When are you leaving?’
All three interrogative words call for answers that consist of time expressions other
than precise times of the day; questions about clock time must be posed with fia (cf.
2.1.2.6.4(a)).
Anafea, maafea, and aafea function as adverbs. When they occur postverbally,
their ordering with respect to postverbal modifiers and arguments of the verb is
flexible, although it is stylistically most felicitous for the interrogative word to
precede other elements. Like other adverbial interrogative words, anafea, maafea,
and aafea may be placed in clause-initial position in both nonquoted questions and
quoted questions. In indirectly quoted environments, they must be ko-focused, as
required by the complementizer me:
(2215)

Nps Neg know Erg I Cmp Foc when? Nps go Anp we-3-e
‘I don’t know when we’re going.’

quote strings without a quoting frame:
(2216)

Foc when? Pst come Anp you
‘When did you come?’

although they may be modified by postposed adverbs of various types:
(2217)

2.1.2.7. Relative pronouns and other relative words
2.1.2.7.1. Relative pronouns
Relative clauses are optionally introduced by relative pronouns that are formally
identical to demonstrative adjectives. Although relative pronouns are most often
adjectival modifiers of the head noun, they become full pronouns in one context
(see 2.1.2.7.1.1 below).
The three singular forms, with their canonical meanings, are teenei ‘in the vicinity
of the speaker’, teenaa ‘in the vicinity of the interlocutor’, and teelaa ‘away from the
speaker and interlocutor’; the three corresponding plural forms are konei, konaa,
and kolaa (see 2.1.2.5.1 and 2.1.2.7.1.3–7 for a more precise characterization of the
differences between nei, naa, and laa forms):
(2238)

taafaoga a te lalolagi teenei [e fai i konei i ssuaa tausaga].

‘We’re very busy preparing for the Olympic Games that will be held
here next year.’
(2239)

(2240)

we-3-e Nps stay together with my sibling young this Nps
aavaga mo ttagata Tokelau].

2.1.2.7.1.1. Restrictive, nonrestrictive, and headless relative pronouns The same
optional relative pronouns are used in restrictive and nonrestrictive relative clauses.
Their use in restrictive relative clauses is illustrated above. Examples of relative
pronouns in nonrestrictive relative clauses are presented in 1.1.2.3.2. Relative
pronouns can also modify headless relative clauses. As discussed in 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)
and 1.1.2.3.6, they are obligatory in one type of headless relative clause,
ungrammatical in another type, and optional in a third type.
2.1.2.7.1.2. Number marking on relative pronouns Like the demonstrative adjectives
with which they are homophonous (cf. 2.1.2.5.4), relative pronouns are marked for

and kolaa are dual or plural. Relative pronouns agree in number with the head of
the relative clause, which indicates that they are primarily modifiers of the head,
rather than arguments of the relative clause.

demonstratives (cf. 2.1.2.5.1). For example, when the head noun of the relative clause
is a personal pronoun, the relative pronoun usually agrees in deixis with the head.

2.1.3. Verb morphology
2.1.3.1. Voice and valency
Tuvaluan lacks a passive construction. However, a number of processes have a
syntactic effect comparable to that of passivization, in that they decrease the valency
of verbs, or have the opposite effect, namely to increase valency. These processes
are described in 2.1.3.1.2–2.1.3.1.4.
Throughout this grammar, I invoke the term ‘transitivity test’ to refer to processes
and other features of the morphology and syntax of the language that discriminate,
in one fashion or another, between transitive and intransitive constructions. A typical
transitivity test consists of a grammatical process that can take place in a transitive
clause but not in an intransitive clause. These processes and features often do not

438
Morphology
yield the same results in particular grammatical contexts, i.e., a particular
construction may ‘pass’ one transitivity test but not another. This state of affairs is
common in all languages, and is clearly related to the fact that transitivity must be
understood not as a binary opposition, but as a set of nondiscrete parameters
involving not just verb morphology but many other features of the clause, including
tense and aspect, the obligatory or optional presence of arguments of the verb and
their number, the dynamics of the situation denoted by the clause, and the pragmatic
function of the clause in the discourse context in which it appears (Hopper and
Thompson 1980). Thus a particular construction, and a particular instance of this
construction, may behave as a transitive clause according to certain parameters but
not others, and discrepant results across transitivity tests can be expected to be the
norm rather than the exception.
Because Tuvaluan has ergative-absolutive morphology, many transitivity tests
are also useful as tests for the category ‘subject’. The existence and importance of
this category is always potentially problematic in ergative-absolutive languages,
in that subjects of transitive and intransitive verbs receive different morphological
marking, which raises the question as to whether they are different syntactic
categories or not. Elsewhere in this work, I make use of transitivity tests to address
this question (see in particular 2.1.1.2.1 and 2.1.1.2.2).
The following can be listed as transitivity tests that refer to the entire clause or
to the arguments of the clause and their morphosyntactic behaviour (this is not a
complete list): case marking in relative clauses and interrogative-word questions
in which the interrogative word does not appear in situ (cf. 1.1.2.3.4 and 1.1.1.2.2.2
respectively); case marking and general behaviour when the verb is prefixed with
faka- (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)); the possible appearance of a clitic pronoun when the clause is
moo-subordinated, which only intransitive clauses allow (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5); and the
ability of the clause to undergo -gina suffixation, which is passed by all transitives
but only some intransitives (cf. 2.1.3.1.3).
Transitivity tests that refer specifically to the subject of the clause, and thus help
distinguish subjects from nonsubjects, include: advancement-to-possessive in
clauses where the only argument is marked for the absolutive case, which indicates
that the clause is intransitive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10); whether the noun phrase can control
object equi-deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6); whether the subject can trigger verb agreement,
which indicates that the clause is intransitive (cf. 2.1.3.6.1); and the formation of
imperatives (cf. 1.1.1.3 and 2.1.3.4.3). Transitivity tests that refer specifically to the
direct object of the clause, and thus help distinguish direct objects from other
categories, include: the ability to undergo incorporation (cf. 2.1.3.6.1); the ability to
undergo causative inversion (2.1.3.1.3(a)); and the ability to be targeted by equi-
deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6).
2.1.3.1.1. Passive
Nothing in the morphosyntactic structure of the language can be identified as a
voice contrast in the usual sense of the term. Verb morphology is not marked for a
passive or antipassive category, and there is no evidence of passive or antipassive
processes (cf. 2.1.1.2.8). A variety of morphosyntactic processes have semantic and
pragmatic functions equivalent to that of passivization in other languages, such as
the marking of informational prominence of nonagentive arguments, the semantic
‘reorientation’ of the verb towards nonsubject arguments, and the possibility for
certain nominal participants to remain unmentioned (for discussions of these and
other crosslinguistic functions of passives, see Weiner and Labov 1983, Shibatani
1985, Thompson 1987, and others). Some of these processes are described in the

that pervades natural discourse.
2.1.3.1.2. Valency-decreasing processes
The valency of a verb can be affected in a number of ways. This section reviews
verb forms that may occur in constructions with different valency. Valency can be
affected by the presence or absence of a subject (cf. (a) below), the presence or
absence of a direct object (cf. (b)), different case-marking patterns (cf. (c)), and the
ability of certain verbs to take on an inherently reciprocal meaning (cf. (d)). Another
morphological process that decreases valency is described in 2.1.3.1.4.
The grammatical features described in this section are properties of verbs as
lexemes. Verbs do not fall into classes that are easily identifiable in terms of their
internal structure or their semantics. In certain cases, it is not clear whether forms
with different valency should be considered different manifestations of the same
lexeme or homophonous lexemes. For example, the verb kai ‘eat’ can appear in
transitive, intransitive, and middle constructions. In each case, it takes on a slightly
different meaning, as shown presently. Is it the same lexical item throughout, or
should its various manifestations be considered to be separate words? One
characteristic of this verb supports the first analysis: when the direct object of the
transitive verb kai is incorporated into the verb (cf. 2.1.3.6.12), the verb agrees in
number with its subject, a property of intransitive and middle manifestations of kai.
Hence there is a structural link between intransitive, middle, and transitive forms.
Furthermore, in the case of certain verbs, it is not clear whether the least marked
form is its transitive or intransitive manifestation. For example, the verb uku ‘dive
(for recreation or food-gathering)’ is a verb of type (b) below; in natural discourse,
it is most frequent as an intransitive verb, but it may take on transitive morphosyntax
and take as direct object a noun that refers to any edible marine species that one
commonly gathers by diving (e.g., in the Funafuti dialect, kalea ‘spider shell’).
Because its direct object must be selected from a semantically restricted range, and
because it is considerably less frequent in discourse, the transitive uses of the verb
are more marked than the intransitive uses. The opposite is true of the transitive
verb ggali ‘gnaw’, which, in its intransitive manifestations, acquires the more
specialized meaning of ‘gnawed at by a driving pain’. Thus the patterns described
below should not necessarily be considered to derive intransitive verbs from
transitive verbs, rather than the opposite. (Compare the following with an example
of a process that clearly derives a marked transitive construction from an unmarked
intransitive, such as the formation of pseudoergatives, as described in 2.1.3.1.3(d).)
(a) Nonmention of a subject
A number of verbs can appear in either transitive or intransitive constructions,
such that the argument realized as the direct object in the transitive construction
corresponds to the subject in the intransitive construction:
(2257)
Te gaaluega kaa kaamata nee taatou.
the work Fut start Erg we-3-i
‘We are going to start the work.’

The fact that the argument in the second sentence can undergo advancement-to-

demonstrates that it is the subject of the clause, and, since it is marked for the
absolutive case, that the clause is intransitive:
(2259)

Verbs that conform to this pattern are numerous and do not form a definable class.
In many cases, a slight difference in meaning exists between transitive and
intransitive uses of the same verb. For example, the verb sulu as a transitive verb
has as its most basic meaning ‘sheath, insert’:
(2260)
Taku naifi kaa sulu nee au i te vaa o atooga.
my knife Fut sheath Erg I in the gap of thatching-segment
‘I am going to sheath my knife in between the thatching segments.’
As an intransitive verb, the same verb acquires a variety of meanings, the most
basic of which is ‘dive head first, disappear into’:
(2261)
Te puaka koo sulu ki loto i te vao gasu.
the pig Inc disappear to middle in the bush saltbush
‘The pig has disappeared into the saltbush grove.’
In the latter contexts, sulu also becomes an agreeing verb, which provides further
evidence for its intransitive status (cf. 2.1.3.6.1).
The above phenomenon should be distinguished from the various processes
that delete the subject of transitive verbs, which are overviewed in 1.2.1.2.1.
(b) Nonmention of a direct object
Many verbs can appear in clauses that differ in valency such that the subject of
transitive uses of the verb corresponds to the subject of its intransitive uses. Compare:
(2262)
Teika koo faitau nee ia tena tusi ne aumai.
Teika Inc read Erg he his book Pst bring
‘Teika is reading the letter he received.’
(2263)
Teika koo faitau.
Teika Inc read
‘Teika is reading.’
Verbs that fall in this category are more numerous than verbs that fall in the
previously described category. The one-argument version of these verbs is
intransitive because many undergo subject agreement, an exclusive feature of
intransitive verbs (cf. 2.1.3.6.1). Compare the invariable form ota ‘eat raw’ in
the first of the following sentences with the plural form oota in the second
sentence:
(2264)
Maatou ne ota nee maatou taku atu ne ffuti i te afiafi.
we-3-e Pst eat-raw Erg we-2-e my bonito Pst pull in the evening
‘Last night we had raw the bonito I caught.’

Other terms referring to ingestion and related activities follow this pattern, including
kai ‘eat, eat (something)’, inu ‘drink, drink (something)’, and ppusi ‘smoke, smoke

which can either affect the agent or another party, e.g., fakalanu ‘rinse oneself, rinse

homogeneous semantic category: kaisoa ‘steal, steal (something)’, kalaga ‘call, call
(someone)’, aakai ‘request, request (something)’, ssili ‘ask, ask (something)’. Generally
speaking, the intransitive use of these verbs has a more general and atelic meaning
than their transitive uses, a fact which is derivable from the difference in valency
(cf. Hopper and Thompson 1980).
Again, verbs that fall in this category do not form a well-defined category either
semantically or syntactically, and membership of this category must be specified in
the lexicon. Certain notions that can be expected to fall into this pattern on the
basis of crosslinguistic evidence are encoded in the lexicon as two separate lexemes,
each of which is associated with a different valency. For example, the intransitive
mmuni ‘hide’ bears no relation to the transitive ffuna ‘hide (something)’. Certain
verbs also can only become transitive when marked with the causative prefix faka-
; witness koukou ‘bathe’ and fakkoukou ‘bathe (someone)’.
The patterns described above are to be distinguished from discourse-governed
processes overviewed in 1.2.1.2.2, which delete the direct object of a verb.
(c)
Variation between experience, middle, ‘bring’/‘take’, cause-target, and
transitive constructions
A number of verbs can appear alternatively in middle constructions (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(a)),
experience constructions (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.2(b)), ‘bring’/‘take’ constructions (cf.
2.1.1.2.1.2(a)), and transitive constructions, or a subset of these possibilities. In this
category fall verbs like kai ‘eat’, inu ‘drink’, ssala ‘search’, maalamalama ‘understand’,
tausi ‘care for’. Compare the following, in which tausi is used alternatively as a
middle verb (with ki) and a transitive verb (without the preposition):
(2266)
Te taulasiga e see saga o tausi (ki) olotou tamana
the majority Nps Neg pay-attention Cmp care to their-3 father
mo olotou maatua.
and their-3 mother
‘The majority don’t pay much attention to taking care of their parents.’
Generally speaking, middle verbs denote atelic situations, which affect the object
less completely than situations denoted by the corresponding transitive
constructions, and they favour a partitive perspective on the object. The following
illustrates this contrast:
(2267)
Maatou ne inu nee maatou a pii i tau taapola.
we-3-e Pst drink Erg we-3-e Cnt drinking-coconut in your basket
‘We drank up the drinking nuts that were in your basket.’

(d) Formation of inherently reciprocal constructions
Certain verbs can occur in either intransitive constructions in which the subject
refers to all participants, or in transitive constructions in which the participants are
referred to disjointly by the subject and direct object. In the intransitive construction,
the subject can be a coordinated construction or a noun phrase with a plural referent,
as in the second of the following:
(2270)
Koo ffusu nee Peetaia ttamataene Nanumea!
Inc fight Erg Petaia the+young-man Nanumea
‘Petaia is fighting a young Nanumean!’
(2271)
Peetaia mo ttamataene Nanumea koo ffusu!
Petaia and the+young-man Nanumea Inc fight
‘Petaia and a young Nanumean are fighting!’
Coordinated subjects are often split (cf. 1.3.1.7):
(2272)
Peetaia koo ffusu mo ttamataene Nanumea!

If one of the coordinated noun phrases is a pronoun, the referent of the pronoun
normally includes the referent of the other noun phrase, as it would in any other
construction (cf. 2.1.2.1.18), whether the coordinate construction is split or not.

intransitive version in (2274) and in the intransitive version with a split coordinate

(2273)

I Pst kiss Erg I the+person that in down in the taro-swamp
‘I kissed that person down in the taro swamp.’
(2274)
Maaua mo ttino teenaa ne ssogi i lalo i te umaga.
we-2-e and the+person that Pst kiss in down in the taro-swamp

in intransitive and transitive constructions. For example, llou means ‘force’ as a
transitive verb; as an inherently reciprocal intransitive verb, it has the more specific
meaning of ‘arm-wrestle’.
(e) Stativizing prefix ma-
The prefix ma-, whose cognates in other Polynesian languages have traditionally been
referred to as ‘stativizing’ prefixes, decreases the valency of the verb. It is attached to the
root form of verbs, i.e., the basic form of the lexeme, stripped of reduplicated elements

443
and any other bound morpheme. Thus ma- may be affixed to verbal roots that otherwise
can only appear in reduplicated form; for example, malemu ‘drowned’ is related to llemu
‘drown (something)’, which does not have a nonreduplicated form. Furthermore, in a
few cases, the unprefixed form does not exist in the contemporary language; for example,
the forms makui ‘sprained’ and makeke ‘hard’ are attested, but there are no forms *kui and
*keke with related meanings. The prefix has several unproductive and uncommon
allomorphs, namely ga-(e.g., gaofe ‘crooked’, from ofe ‘bend (something)’), pa- (e.g., palele
‘depleted’ from lele ‘fly off’), and ta- (e.g., talave ‘delayed’ from lave ‘stuck’). Because verbs
prefixed with the alloforms are idiosyncratically related in meaning to the unprefixed
forms, the alternative versions of the prefix are best analysed as having fossilized with
the root to which they are attached.
In its basic form, the stativizing prefix ma- is moderately productive. It cannot
be prefixed to borrowings, but it can be prefixed to a wide range of verbs. It is
treated as an integral part of the word by infixal reduplication (cf. 3.4.5.2.2), and
prefixed forms can serve as input for other processes of morphological
compounding, causative prefixation in particular (e.g., fakamakosu ‘cause to be
disturbed’ from makosu ‘disturbed’ from kosu ‘disturb’), as will be discussed
presently. Although there are a few instances where prefixed forms have acquired
more specialized meanings than unprefixed forms (e.g., maeva ‘migrate’ from eva
‘fly’, matilo ‘shine’ from ttilo ‘look admiringly’), the meanings of most prefixed and
unprefixed forms are related to one another in a regular and predictable manner.
The prefix may be attached to either intransitive or transitive verbs, although it
is most common with transitive verbs. The resulting form denotes a nondynamic,
continuous, and atelic situation. The label ‘nondynamic’ must be qualified to a
certain extent, as some forms are used to denote dynamic situations; in some cases,
the dynamic usage is more frequent than the nondynamic usage. For example,
makalo ‘propelled’ is frequently given the dynamic meaning of ‘move swiftly, rush’,
and malapa ‘flashed’ the dynamic meaning of ‘flash’:
(2276)
Koutou e maakkalo ki fea?
you-3 Nps propelled to where?
‘Where are you all rushing?’
(2277)
Koo malapa te uila.
Inc flashed the lightning
‘There is lightning.’
The prefix also implies that this situation is the result of a dynamic situation, usually
the situation denoted by the unprefixed form of the verb if there is one, with the
referent of the argument of the prefixed verb corresponding to the patient of the
unprefixed verb or a comparable participant with low agentivity. For example,
compare the following pairs:
(2278)
Te mataloa ne ttala nee au.
the door Pst open Erg I
‘I opened the door.’
(2279)
Te mataloa koo matala.
the door Inc open
‘The door is open.’
[implicature: because it has been opened by someone]
(2280)
Ne llemu nee ia te puusi.
Pst drown Erg he the cat
‘He drowned the cat.’

(2286)

(2288)
