(f) Suffix -(C)ia
The unproductive morpheme -(C)ia can be suffixed to verb roots and affect their
valency in a complex manner. Cognates of the suffix are found in most, perhaps
all Polynesian languages, where their form and meaning have been the subject
of an extensive literature. The meaning of this suffix differs from one language
to another in the Polynesian family, and many of these differences are still
poorly understood.
Before characterizing the form and meaning of the suffix, it is important to
note that many Samoan words with cognates of this suffix have been borrowed
into the Tuvaluan lexicon (e.g., aafaaina ‘(not) matter’, afaatia ‘caught in a storm’,
amuia ‘blessed’, fakataasia ‘assembled’, inosia ‘ostracized’, lausia ‘counted’,
maafatia ‘worried’, maalaia ‘doomed’, maataulia ‘recognizable’, motusia ‘of a
relationship, broken’, puapuagaatia ‘distressed’, taagisia ‘mourned’, taulia
‘prized’, tiigaaina ‘in pain’, vaaoia ‘rejected’). These forms were borrowed as
unitary lexical items, and did not undergo suffixation after borrowing. They
must be carefully distinguished from manifestations of the suffix in
autochthonous words, as they differ in form and function from Tuvaluan
suffixed forms, as discussed presently. The situation is further complicated by
the fact that, corresponding to many suffixed forms borrowed from Samoan,
one also finds unsuffixed forms of Samoan origin (e.g., inoino ‘abhor’ v. inosia,
puapuagaa ‘distressful’ v. puapuagaatia) as well as unsuffixed Tuvaluan cognates
of borrowed Samoan suffixed forms (e.g., tagi ‘cry’ v. tagisia, vvao ‘prevent’ v.
vaoia). To add to the potential confusion, many suffixed borrowings have been
so thoroughly incorporated into the lexicon in everyday usage that many
speakers of Tuvaluan do not recognise these forms as borrowings.
The first segment of the suffix is a consonant, which may be realized as f, g, m, s,
or t, or ø. It may also surface as n, but in this case the vocalic segment i metathesizes
with the consonant, so that the resulting suffix is -ina and not *-nia, and the segment
i is deleted if the verb root ends in i. (There is an alternative analysis of the form of
this allomorph, which will be discussed presently.) Furthermore, a suffix -a can
appear with certain roots and have the same semantic and syntactic characteristics
as -(C)ia, and thus must be considered to be one of its allomorphs. A historical
explanation of the shape of this allomorph will be offered presently. The form -a of
the suffix should not be confused with a homophonous suffix which has a variety
of derivational functions; this is discussed in 2.2.2.1.2.
The suffix -a also appears obligatorily in a small number of verbs that refer to
perceptive experiences of various kinds: lavea and matea ‘see’, lagona ‘hear, feel’, the
archaic logona ‘feel tired’, and iloa ‘know’ (to which should be added several
borrowings from Samoan, e.g., masaua ‘remember’). None of these words surfaces
in root form. These instances of -a do not share the characteristics of other
manifestations of the suffix, and they should be considered to have fused with the
root. Indeed, unlike all other -(C)ia suffixed forms, these verbs can be further suffixed
with the transitivizing suffix -gina (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(d)), and they can take clitic pronouns
(cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5). They are not discussed further here.
The complete list of allomorphs of the suffix reads as follows: -fia, -gia, -mia, -
(i)na, -sia, -tia, -ia, and -a. The allomorph -lia appears in a number of words

Some suffixed forms have the identification of an agent or cause ‘built into’ their

The suffix exhibits some of the properties associated with passives in other
languages: it topicalizes or otherwise highlights a patientive participant; it
deemphasizes the agent (as will be shown presently); and it casts an affectively
charged light onto the situation (compare the affective passive voice in Japanese, as
described by Howard and Niyekawa-Howard 1976). However, -(C)ia is not a
passivizing suffix because it simply lacks the regularity and many of the syntactic
properties of passives (cf. Siewierska 1984). For example, it does not consistently
detransitivize verbs, as discussed below.27
While some -(C)ia forms commonly appear in resultive and perfective contexts,
neither aspectual category is an important feature of -(C)ia suffixation. Indeed, all
suffixed forms can appear in imperfective sentences:

Because of its low productivity, the suffix is best described as a derivational
morpheme. It is treated here with other valency-affecting processes because it does
have an identifiable (if complex) effect on the valency of the clause, and because of
its importance in Polynesian comparative linguistics.
2.1.3.1.3. Valency-increasing processes
This section covers the following valency-increasing processes: the formation of
causative verbs with the productive causative prefix faka-, discussed in (a); the
formation of causatives with the verb fai ‘do, make’, described in (b); suffixation
with the productive transitivizer -gina, described in (c); and pseudoergative
constructions, discussed under (d).
(a) Causatives with faka-
Causativity is expressed with the help of a productive prefix faka-, which is affixed
to verbs of all valencies. The prefix has many other functions, several of which are
conceptually related to causativity (see 2.2.2 and 2.2.4, for example). Following is
an example of the derivation of a causative from an intransitive verb:
(2328)
Temotou paa moa koo lasi.
our-3-e coop chicken Inc large
‘Our chicken coop is large.’
(2329)
Temotou paa moa koo fakalasi nee maatou.
our-3-e coop chicken Inc Cst+large Erg we-3-e
‘We are enlarging our chicken coop.’

Not all verbs can be prefixed with faka-. The process is most productive with
intransitive verbs including middle verbs, although many common intransitive
verbs like fano ‘go’ and vau ‘come’ cannot be faka-prefixed. The number of transitive
verbs that can be prefixed is more restricted. A handful of transitive verbs, like kai

can be made causative with the verb fai ‘make’ (cf. (b) below). In a handful of cases,
the prefix can be attached to a string made up of the negative verb see (cf. 1.4(a))
and the verb being negated; thus one finds faka-see-aogaa ‘treat as useless, render
useless’ (cf. aogaa ‘useful’), faka-see-talitonu ‘dismiss’ (cf. talitonu ‘believe’), and faka-
see-aamanaia ‘depreciate’ (cf. aamanaia ‘treasure, esteem’). For some unknown reason,
all such cases fall into the same semantic field of devaluing activities. The prefix
can be attached to borrowings; for example, from puapuagaatia ‘distressed’, a
borrowing from Samoan, can be derived fakapuapuagaatia ‘distress (someone)’, and
the suffixation of leevolo ‘level’, a borrowing from English, yields the form fakaleevolo
‘level (something)’.
The prefix faka- has two allomorphs. When it is prefixed to a verb with k as an
initial segment, the prefix is reduced to fak-, as in fakkoukou ‘make (someone) take a
bath, bathe (someone)’, from koukou ‘wash up, bathe’. The other allomorph, faa-, is
found in causative forms borrowed from Samoan (e.g., faauu ‘nurse’, faaina
‘illuminate’, faaopoopo ‘add’). Some borrowed forms have retained their causative
meaning, while others have not. Members of the first category do not differ in
behaviour from causative forms of autochthonous origin. The prefix faka- cannot
be attached to a word already affixed with faka- even when the latter has a non-
causative meaning. However, it may be attached to Samoan borrowings in faa-that
do not have causative meaning (e.g., fakafaanoanoa ‘sadden’ from faanoanoa ‘sad’).
Even after noncausative uses of faka- are set aside, not all forms prefixed with faka-
are causative in the strict sense of the word. Many faka-prefixed forms resemble causatives
but diverge from canonical causatives in their semantic and morphosyntactic behaviour.
Some are relexicalized causative forms; for example, the verb matala ‘open’ can be
causativized as fakamatala ‘open (something)’. But there is another form, homophonous
with the causative fakamatala, which bears the metaphorically related meaning of ‘explain,
clarify’. However, the latter form cannot be considered to be derived from matala ‘open’
because the unprefixed verb cannot be used with the meaning of ‘explained, clarified’,
and should be analysed as having undergone relexicalization. The form fakamatala
‘explain’ is thus a word which is separate from and homophonous with fakamatala ‘open’,
even though it may have originally been a metaphorical extension of the latter. Further
evidence for analysing these two forms as separate words is provided by the fact that
relexicalized forms are subject to different agreement processes from canonical causatives,

Ditransitive verbs do not undergo faka-causative formation. Causative verbs differ
from other transitive verbs in one significant respect, namely the fact that many
can undergo number agreement, which no noncausative transitive verb does.
Agreement with causative verbs is sometimes controlled by the direct object,
sometimes by the subject; for further details, see 2.1.3.6.1–6 and 2.1.3.6.12(a).
It is noteworthy that faka-causative formation treats the subject of intransitive
and transitive verbs as the same category, in that both become the direct object of
the causative verb. The above patterns also verify Comrie’s (1978) hypothesis to
the effect that causees occupy the highest position on the Noun Phrase Accessibility
Hierarchy (cf. 1.1.2.3.7) not already occupied by another argument of the verb.
Causative verbs derived from transitive verbs can undergo an unusual process
whereby the causee is demoted to the oblique position occupied by the former
direct object of the noncausative sentence, which then comes to occupy the position
left empty by the demotion, i.e., that of the direct object. No other changes take
place in the clause. This process is optional, and it derives sentence (2358) from
sentence (2357), which is in turn derived from the noncausative sentence (2356):
(2356)

‘I remembered what you told me.’

I call ‘causative inversion’. Thus sentence (2354) has the following alternative form,

prominence assumed by the causee and giving greater informational prominence
to the referent of the noun phrase moved to direct-object position, which can then
be easily (and often is) topicalized. The awkward English translations of the above
sentences are an attempt to render the informational structure of the resulting
construction with the passive voice.

(b) Causatives with fai ‘do, make’
Causativity can also be expressed with the verb fai ‘make, do’. In contrast to faka-
prefixation, this strategy does not affect the valency of the clause. It is an alternative
to faka-prefixation in that it can be used instead of the latter with any prefixable
verb; it is also complementary to faka-suffixation in that it is the only causative
strategy available for verbs that cannot be prefixed with faka-; and it is supplementary
to it in that the two strategies are occasionally used simultaneously.
Causatives with fai are complex sentences with fai as the superordinate verb,
which can be translated in this context as ‘intend to, cause to, make it so that’, and
either an o-subordinated or subjunctively subordinated clause denoting the situation
to be made causative:
(2371)
Kaati koo fai [o gata te tusi].
perhaps Inc make Cmp end the letter
‘[This] letter is about to end.’
(2372)
Laatou e fai [kee ttoo laatou i te malaga].
they-3 Nps make Sbj include they-3 in the journey
‘They are trying to get included in the journey.’
The contrast between o-subordinated and subjunctively subordinated complements
of fai has the same characteristics as the same contrast in other contexts (cf. 1.1.2.1.2):
subjunctive subordination implies a more contingent, less assured situation than
o-subordination; the subject and the direct object of the o-subordinated complement
are potential targets of subject- or object-controlled equi-deletion, whereas the
arguments of the subjunctive clause are not (cf. 1.1.2.6); and the o-complement places
certain coreference requirements between the arguments of the superordinate and
subordinate clauses, whereas the subjunctive complement doesn’t.
Causatives with fai are particularly useful with verbs that cannot be faka-prefixed

(c) Transitivizing suffixation
What I refer to as the ‘transitivizing suffix’ is a morpheme -gina, with two additional
allomorphs -gia and -ga, whose function is more complex than simply increasing
the valency of verbs. One of the forms of -(C)ia, namely -gia (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(f)), is
homophonous with the form -gia of the transitivizing suffix; the two homophonous

suffixes are easily distinguished from one another in that one has alternative forms
-gina and -ga while the other does not.
The three forms of the transitivizing suffix, -gina, -gia, and -ga, originate from
three different dialect areas: -gina is a Northern Tuvaluan form, -gia was probably
the original form in the Funafuti and Vaitupu dialects, and -ga that of the suffix in
the Nukufetau and Nukulaelae dialects. Today, all three forms are in current use
throughout Southern Tuvalu. The form -ga has retained its marked dialectal
characteristics, but not -gina and -gia; in fact, -gina is more common today than -gia,
which is mostly characteristic of language use by older individuals. In the following
discussion, -gina will be assumed to be the base form.
The suffix cannot be attached to roots already suffixed with -(C)ia (2.1.3.1.2(f)),
except if these are borrowings from Samoan like puapuagaatia ‘distressed’, which
are treated like ordinary unsuffixed verbs:
(2380)

‘[He] was persecuted because of his beliefs.’
The suffix -gina is very productive, and few verbs disallow it. It can be affixed to
borrowings from English of relatively recent import, such as fitipoolo ‘(play) football’,
tisikasi ‘discuss’, and poloo ‘borrow’:

‘He is just playing around with you.’

as illustrated in 2.1.3.6.12. Suffixed forms can undergo other morphological processes
associated with verbs, such as nominalization, both suffixal (cf. 2.1.3.5(b)) and bare
nominalization:
(2382)

to many, although not all, intransitive verbs:

(d) Pseudoergative constructions
Another syntactic phenomenon with clear implications for the valency of the verb
is the formation of what I have called elsewhere ‘pseudoergative constructions’
(Besnier 1986:254–255). Most pseudoergative constructions consist of a canonically
intransitive verb, i.e., a verb which can only be intransitive in other contexts, with
an obligatory ergatively marked postposed argument that denotes an entity which
is highly involved in bringing about the situation denoted by the sentence as a
responsible entity. The situation denoted by the clause often has strong negative
connotations:
(2407)
A papa ne mimi nee te puusi.
Cnt mats Pst urinate Erg the cat
‘The cat urinated all over the mats.’
(2408)
Ne pati maasei nee ia te fenua.
Pst word bad Erg he the island-community
‘He swore at the island community.’
As illustrated in the above sentences, there is often a second argument in the
pseudoergative construction, which denotes an entity affected by the situation.
Typically, this argument is preposed to the verb, as shown in sentence (2407),
although it may also occur in postposed position, as in (2408) and the following:
(2409)
E kata nee Faiva a pati a Tepope e ssee.
Nps laugh Erg Faiva Cnt word of Tepope Nps wrong
‘Faiva makes fun of Tepope’s verbal mistakes.’
The second argument is marked for the absolutive case. It must follow the ergatively
marked argument, so that the following alternatives to (2408) and (2409), in which
the ergative argument follows the absolutive argument, are ungrammatical:
(2410)
* Ne pati maasei te fenua nee ia.
Pst word bad the island-community Erg he
(2411)
* E kata a pati a Tepope e ssee nee Faiva.
Nps laugh Cnt word of Tepope Nps wrong Erg Faiva
The absolutively marked argument of a pseudoergative construction is dispensable,
in contrast to the ergatively marked noun phrase, as will be shown presently. The
ergatively marked argument corresponds to the subject of the verb in regular
intransitive manifestations. Compare (2407) and (2408) above with the following
intransitive constructions:
(2412)
Te puusi koo mimi.
the cat Inc urinate
‘The cat is urinating.’
(2413)
A ia ne pati maasei.
Cnt he Pst word bad
‘He swore.’

The ergative argument can undergo advancement-to-possessive from a relative
clause, and thus behaves like a regular subject (cf. 1.1.2.3.10). This process derives
sentence (2414) from (2415):
(2414)
Teenei te mata a te see [ne mimi].
this the eye of the toddy-bug Pst urinate
‘This is the eye which the toddy bug urinated into.’
(2415)
Teenei te mata [ne mimi nee te see].
this the eye Pst urinate Erg the toddy-bug
In contrast to the absolutive argument, the ergative argument is neither dispensable
nor readily movable in pseudoergative constructions. For example, it cannot be
zero-pronominalized:
(2416)
* Ne pati maasei te fenua.
Pst word bad the island-community
(‘[He] swore at the island community.’)
Movement to preverbal position, ko-clefting, and left-dislocation of the ergatively
marked noun phrase all yield marginally acceptable sentences. Ergative arguments
can be advanced-to-possessive, as illustrated above, or relativized, although they
rarely are in discourse. Its canonical position is postverbal, where it is always marked
for the ergative case.
Pseudoergative clauses are frequently either accompanied by a subordinate
clause or are themselves subordinated to another clause. This other clause commonly
denotes the result of the negative situation denoted by the pseudoergative clause,
or otherwise reinforces or explains the affective markedness of the latter. In example
(2417), the pseudoergative clause is the superordinate clause, while it functions as
the subordinate clause in (2418):
(2417)
Koulua ne laauga nee Faiva [ia koulua seki olo ki te
you-2 Pst make-speech Erg Faiva because you-2 Neg go to the
fakaala].
feast
‘Faiva made a [derogatory] speech about you because you did not show
up at the feast.’
(2418)
Koo tele Peeteli [me ne paakalaga nee maatou].
Inc run Peteli because Pst shout Erg we-3-e
‘Peteli ran away because we tried to shout her down.’
One subordinating strategy frequently applied to pseudoergative clauses is
subordination by apposition (cf. 1.1.2.1.5):
(2419)
A ttama nei koo tai lagia [ne too nee te niu i tena
Cnt the+guy this Inc a-little simpleton Pst fall Erg the coconut in his
tamalikiiga].
child+Nom
‘That guy is a little off his rocker because a coconut fell on him when
he was a child.’
Some verbs acquire specialized meanings in pseudoergative constructions. Such is
the case of tagi ‘cry, complain’, which, when it is a pseudoergative verb, usually has
the meaning of ‘lodge a legal complaint’:

On occasion, a canonically transitive verb can be used pseudoergatively. In such
cases, the ergatively marked argument is the same as the subject of the regular
transitive manifestation of the verb, but the ‘affected’ argument must differ from
the direct object of the corresponding transitive verb. For example, compare the
pseudoergative use of tii ‘throw down, fetch down’ in (2421) with its regular
transitive use in (2422):
(2421)
Te kaapa ne tii nee Tafia ki te
the corrugated-iron Pst throw-down Erg Tafia with the
pii.
drinking-coconut
‘Tafia [damaged] the corrugated iron sheet [by] throwing down a
drinking coconut [onto it].’
(2422)
Te pii ne tii nee Tafia ki luga i te
the drinking-coconut Pst throw-down Erg Tafia to top on the
kaapa.
corrugated-iron
‘Tafia threw down a drinking coconut onto the corrugated iron sheet.’
Instances of the above type are rare. Pseudoergative constructions derived from
transitive verbs have the same semantic and syntactic characteristics as regular
pseudoergative clauses.
Pseudoergative constructions have both transitive and intransitive properties.
With regular intransitive verbs they share the ability to undergo number agreement,
which is controlled by the pseudoergatively marked argument:
(2423)
Toku mata ne mmimi nee see.
my eye Pst urinate+Agr Erg toddy-bug
‘Toddy bugs have urinated into my eye.’
Pseudoergative verbs undergo agreement if the verb also does so in its regular
intransitive uses. However, agreement in pseudoergative constructions is not
grammatical for all native speakers. Generally speaking, younger speakers allow
agreement to take place but not older speakers.
Pseudoergative verbs behave like transitive verbs in most other respects. First,
and most obviously, they take an ergatively marked subject which retains its ergative
case marking when nominalized, as other subjects of transitive verbs do:
(2424)
i te mimiiga nee te see toku mata
at the urinate+Nom Erg the toddy-bug my eye
‘when a toddy bug urinated into my eye’
When suffixed with the transitivizing -gina (cf. (c) above), the ergatively marked
argument can be expressed with a clitic pronoun, indicating that pseudoergative
verbs behave like regular transitive verbs:
(2425)
Palele fale o tino ne ana tekaaga i te ao.
depleted house of person Pst she stroll+Trn at the daytime
‘She’s visited everyone else’s house today.’

2.1.3.1.4. Reflexive and reciprocal verb forms
There are no special reflexive forms of verbs. Reciprocal forms of many verbs can
be derived by attaching to the root a circumfix fe-/-(C)aki, whose morphology is
described in 2.1.3.6.9. The circumfix may be attached to verbs of all valencies. First,
it may be affixed to intransitive verbs, as the following basic and derived sentence
pair attests:
(2427)
Au ne kiinau mo temotou pule.
I Pst argue and our-3-e boss
‘The boss and I had an argument.’
(2428)
Ne fekiinauaki maaua mo temotou pule.
Pst Rcp+argue+Rcp we-2-e and our-3-e boss
‘The boss and I argued with each other.’
The circumfix can also form reciprocal forms of verbs with indirect objects and
middle verbs:
(2429)
Au ne kata ki toku taina.
I Pst laugh to my sibling
‘I laughed at my brother.’
(2430)
Maaua mo toku taina ne fekataaki.
we-2-e and my sibling Pst Rcp+laugh+Rcp
‘My brother and I laughed at one another.’
Circumfixation can also derive reciprocal forms of transitive verbs:
(2431)
Niu koo tuli nee Tevasa.
Niu Inc chase Erg Tevasa
‘Tevasa is chasing Niu.’
(2432)
Koo fetuliaki Niu mo Tevasa.
Inc Rcp+chase+Rcp Niu and Tevasa
‘Tevasa and Niu are chasing one another.’
The subject of reciprocal verbs of all types may be an additively coordinated phrase,
as in (2432). It may also be a nonsingular pronoun, to which an inclusively
coordinated noun phrase (cf. 2.1.2.1.18) is frequently attached, as in (2428) and (2430).
In all reciprocal sentences, coordinated elements in subject position, be they regularly
or inclusively coordinated, can be ‘split’, as in any other sentence with coordinated
noun phrases as subject (cf. 1.3.1.7).
Most circumfixed verb forms are intransitive, as evidenced by several of their
characteristics. First, their subject is always marked for the absolutive case, and the
verb cannot take an ergatively marked argument; hence case marking treats the clause
as intransitive. Second, the subject of a circumfixed verb follows case-marking patterns
associated with subjects of intransitive verbs when the clause is relativized or
nominalized. For example, the noun phrase can be marked for inalienable possession
when the verb is nominalized (cf. 2.1.1.3.4), and it relativizes by deletion (cf. 1.1.2.3):
(2433)
te femaasaloakiiga o Niu mo Tevasa
the Rcp+distrust+Rcp+Nom of Niu and Tevasa
‘when Niu and Tevasa distrusted one another’

(2434)
Konaa eiloa tino [e femaasaloaki].
those indeed person Nps Rcp+distrust+Rcp
‘Those are the people who distrust one another.’
Finally, reciprocal verb forms may appear in moo-subordinated clauses with clitic
pronouns, which, as shown in 1.1.2.4.2.3(a), must be intransitive:
(2435)
Aumai aka te kaapa koukou [momaa felanulanuaki].
bring please the can bathe Cmp+we-2-e Rcp+rinse+Rcp
‘Please bring me the bath can so that the two of us can rinse one another.’
Thus most reciprocal verbs are intransitive. However, a small number of circumfixed
verbs are transitive; such is the case of fesuiaki ‘exchange’, from sui ‘change (one’s
clothes, etc.)’, which can take an ergatively marked subject and an absolutively
marked direct object, and behave like a transitive verb in all respects:
(2436)
Ne fesuiaki nee laaua laa gatu.
Pst Rcp+change+Rcp Erg they-2 their-2 shirt
‘Vave and Niu have exchanged shirts.’
The direct object of transitive circumfixed verbs never denotes the reciprocal target,
but refers to another participant in the situation.
Reciprocal circumfixation makes the verb ineligible for number agreement with
its subject, even when the root form of the verb from which the reciprocal form is
derived is an agreeing verb (cf. 2.1.3.6). For example, the root form of the verb kata
‘laugh’ agrees in number with its subject (plural form kkata), but its circumfixed
form fekataaki ‘laugh at one another’ is invariable.
The circumfix fe-/-(C)aki is not exclusively associated with the formation of
reciprocal forms of verbs. Indeed, many circumfixed forms denote repeated or
interactive situations that involve more than one entity, which are often close in
meaning to reciprocal situations, but not reciprocal in the strict sense of the term.
Witness the use of fetoloaki ‘(of a large group of humans or animals) to move in all
directions’ (cf. tolo ‘crawl’) and femateaki ‘die like flies’ (cf. mate ‘die’):
(2437)
A kaipea koo fetoloaki i te mataafaga.
Cnt land-crab Inc Rcp+crawl+Rcp on the beach
‘Crabs are crawling all over the beach.’
(2438)
Tino koo femateaki i ttau laa.
people Inc Rcp+die+Rcp because-of the+season sun
‘People are dying like flies because of the drought.’
Other examples of such forms are fefokiaki ‘(of several individuals) go back and
forth’ (cf. foki ‘return’), feiitaki ‘very close together’ (cf. ii ‘tightly woven’), fenumiaki
‘(of several objects) all tangled up’ (cf. nnumi ‘tangled’), and feteleaki ‘(of several
individuals) run all over the place’ (cf. tele ‘run’). Some forms, like fefaiaki ‘to argue
(with one another)’ (cf. fai ‘say’), may be used in reciprocal contexts, although not
obligatorily so.
Reciprocality can also be marked with the verb fakatau, whose literal meaning is
‘compete, exchange’ see 1.7.1.5 for discussion.
2.1.3.2. Tense
Tense is primarily denoted by preverbal particles traditionally called ‘tense-aspect
markers’ or, more accurately, ‘tense-aspect-mood markers’ in Polynesian linguistics,
which also function as markers of verbal finiteness. The general category will be

Morphology
473
referred to here as ‘tense-aspect-mood markers’, and the terms ‘tense marker’, ‘aspect
marker’, and ‘mood marker’ will be used in cases where the marker has a clearly
identifiable primary function. These morphemes are linearly ordered before any
other proposed verb-modifying element, including preposed adverbs and clitic
pronouns. Full constituents (e.g., noun phrases) cannot be placed between the tense-
aspect-mood marker and the verb.
The tense-aspect-mood marker is frequently deleted in discourse, in a variety of
situations. First, it is deleted when the location in time of a particular situation is
clear from either the discourse or the extralinguistic context. Such is the case of the
second sentence of the following discourse fragment, which does not have an overt
tense-aspect-mood marker because these categories are clearly the same as those of
the previous sentence:
(2439)
Ia, koo fai aka ttaaofi o ssuaa tino, peelaa, ‘ko ttino
so Inc do Dxs the+opinion of a+other person thus Foc the+person
teelaa.’ Fai ssuaa taaofi o ttino peelaa, ‘Ko ttino
that do a+other opinion of the+person thus Foc the+person
teelaa’.
that
‘So, one person voices an opinion, “that person”. Another person voices
an opinion, “that person”.’
Second, tense-aspect-mood markers are frequently deleted when several consecutive
clauses denote temporally ordered situations. For example, a clause that denotes a
situation which provides the temporal setting for another situation often appears
without a tense-aspect-mood marker:
(2440)
Ia, oko mai te maaloo, a koo fakanofo ei a nofoga o
so reach Dxs the government and Inc Cst+stay Anp Cnt chair of
te maaloo.
the government
‘So, the government arrives, and [it] establishes governmental
positions.’
Similarly, clauses that denote situations which succeed one another and are marked
for roughly similar tense, aspect, and mood categories frequently lose their tense-
aspect-mood marker. In some cases, only some clauses lose their markers (cf. example
(2441)), while in others (e.g., (2442)) all clauses appear without an overt marker:
(2441)
Vau laa kkonei, koo ssala ei ki sefe tusi o te lotu, see
come then to+here Inc search Anp to box book of the church Neg
maua.
get
‘[He] came here, looked [for it] in the church’s book boxes, and didn’t
find [it].’
(2442)
Ia, nofo mai laa i ei, fano Laapana keaatea, kae sui ei nee
so stay Dxs then in Anp go Lapana away and replace Anp Erg
Malaki.

‘So [he] stays [in that position], Lapana goes away, and Malaki replaces
him.’

Few predictive patterns can be identified regarding the incidence of tense-aspect-
mood marker deletion.
The tense-aspect-mood marker which most frequently undergoes ‘discourse
governed’ deletion is the universal and nonpast marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1(a), (b), and
(d) below). Second, certain grammatical environments are particularly favourable
to deletion of the tense-aspect-mood marker. These include the presence of a negator
(cf. 1.4) or of certain aspectual adverbs like the inceptive faatoaa ‘just’ (cf.
2.1.3.3.2.1(e)). Deletion cannot take place under certain circumstances, such as when
a clitic pronoun is present (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5(a)). The deletion of the universal tense-
aspect-mood marker is conditioned by specific factors when it appears in certain
numeral expressions or quantifiers (cf. 2.1.6.2.2, 2.1.6.2.3, and 2.1.6.6.1).
As briefly discussed in 1.1.1.1(a) and 1.1.1.1(b), tense in reported speech does
not differ from the patterns described below. As illustrated in 1.1.2.5, there are no
sequence-of-tense constraints across superordinate and subordinate clauses. The
absence of formal tense marking in equational structures is discussed in 1.2.1.1.
2.1.3.2.1. Tense distinctions
Relatively few tense distinctions are made. There is a basic contrast between the
past tense on the one hand, marked with the tense marker ne, and the nonpast and
universal tense, marked with e. Two modal markers can also be used to mark the
future. There are no relative tenses.
(a) Universal
Universal tense can be expressed with the tense-aspect-mood marker e, which
otherwise denotes nonpast tense, and is the least marked and most frequent tense-
aspect-mood marker. It appears in clauses that denote situations characteristic of
all time, past, present, and future, or in which tense is not relevant or important:
(2443)
E mataku i agaaga, e mataku i kulii, e mataku i puusi.
Nps afraid at ghost Nps afraid at dog Nps afraid at cat
‘[He]’s afraid of ghosts, [he]’s afraid of dogs, [he]’s afraid of cats.’
Whatever its function, e is geminated to ee when the word that follows it has only
two morae.
Because it is the least marked tense category, e is used in several constructions
that are unmarked for tense, aspect, or mood, but must be marked for finiteness,
such as certain numerals (cf. 2.1.6.2.2 and 2.1.6.2.3) and quantifiers (cf. 2.1.6.6.1).
(b) Present
The tense-aspect-mood marker e also marks the present tense:
(2444)
E tonu koe.
Nps right you
‘You are right.’
(2445)
E tagi me e mataku i te kulii.
Nps cry because Nps afraid at the dog
‘[He]’s crying because [he]’s afraid of the dog.’
Hooper’s characterization of e in Tokelauan also describes Tuvaluan e very nicely,
and is worth quoting in full:
The use of e indicates that a certain situation holds at a given reference time.
The situation is presented without any reference to endpoints, or any implication

of endpoints. Moreover, e says nothing about whether the situation also held
prior to that reference time, or whether it will continue beyond the reference
time. These things are worked out on the basis of the meaning of the verb itself
and factors in the linguistic and discourse context. (Hooper 1993:145)
Two tense-aspect-mood markers associated principally with aspectual distinctions,
the inchoative koo (cf. 2.1.3.3.1(a)) and the continuous koi (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(d)) refer
frequently, but not obligatorily, to the present tense.
(c) Past
The past tense is most straightforwardly indicated by the tense-aspect-mood
marker ne:
(2446)
Te motu ko Niuooku ne pukegia nee Siaamani.
the islet Foc Niuoku Pst take+Trn Erg Germany
‘Niuoku Islet was taken by Germans.’
(2447)
Ko koe ne fiafia kee fano koe ki loto i faigaa mea kolaa.
Foc you Pst happy Sbj go you to middle in event those
‘You were the one who wanted to go to those events.’
The marker ne is optional in that, when the tense is unambiguously established in
the discourse or extralinguistic context, the universal marker e can be used to mark
past events:
(2448)
I aso konaa, e toko uke a taagata mo faafine e mmate i
in day those Nps Num many Cnt men and women Nps die in
masaki fakalaupaa.
illness malnutrition
‘In those days, many men and women died of malnutrition.’
[lit.: ‘In those days, there are many men and women who die of
malnutrition.’]
There is no formal means of marking tenses relative to a point in the past. Both the
pluperfect and the future-in-the-past are expressed with regular absolute tense-
aspect-mood markers:
(2449)
Ne iita mai kia aku me i au ne fano ki motu i te ao.
Pst angry Dxs to I because because I Pst go to islet in the day
‘They got angry at me because I had gone to the islet during the day.’
(2450)
Ne foki mai kkonei, kae koo fakailoa mai iaa ia kaa fano ki
Pst return Dxs to+here and Inc Cst+know Dxs Cmp he Fut go to
Fiiti.
Fiji
‘He came back here and announced that he would be going to Fiji.’
The past is not subdivided according to degrees of remoteness, and the same devices
can be used to mark either the distant past or the recent past. However, the aspect
marker koo, described in 2.1.3.3.1(a), frequently, but not obligatorily, refers to recently
initiated situations. There is a special negator for past situations, seki; for a
description, see 1.4(b). An unproductive prefix ana- appears in several adverbials
with past meaning (cf. 2.1.1.6.4).
(d) Future
The future can be expressed in a variety of ways. The least marked involves the
universal and nonpast tense-aspect-mood marker e, whose nonfuture uses are

described in (a) and (b) above. The second most frequent indicator of future tense
is the tense-aspect-mood marker kaa:
(2451)
Koutou kaa ssopo atu i te malaga a te vaka mai tua.
you-3 Inc get-on Dxs in the trip of the ship at back
‘You will be getting on the next trip by the ship.’
(2452)
Koo fai mai iaa ia kaa nofo i konei.
Inc say Dxs Cmp he Fut stay at here
‘He tells me that he’s going to stay here.’
The difference in meaning between e and kaa is subtle. First, e is always potentially
ambiguous between a future reading on the one hand, and a universal or present
reading on the other, while kaa can only mark future. Second, kaa has modal
connotations, which can vary in nature from context to context. In some cases, kaa
adds a shade of uncertainty and contingency to the clause, as illustrated by the
following contrast:
(2453)
Koe e fano maataeao.
you Nps go tomorrow
‘You’re leaving tomorrow.’
(2454)
Koe kaa fano maataeao.
you Fut go tomorrow
‘You’ll be leaving tomorrow [if everything goes well].’
In the second sentence, kaa implies that the speaker is probably not in full control of
the situation described by the clause, while the implication of the first example
with e is that the assertion is made out of a position of certainty. In other contexts,
kaa connotes greater certainty or inevitability than other constructions with which
it contrasts. For example, it contrasts with the precautionary-mood marker maa or
one of its allomorphs (cf. 2.1.3.4.11) in certain cases, such as the following:
(2455)
E ita iaa ia kaa fano ki te fale.
Nps displeased because he Fut go to the house
‘He doesn’t want to be sent home [but he is being sent home anyway].’
(2456)
E ita iaa ia maa fano ki te fale.
Nps displeased because he Prc go to the house
‘He doesn’t want to be sent home [and, as a result, whether he will be
sent home or not is uncertain].’
As witnessed by the glosses on the above sentences, kaa implies that the situation
which motivates the situation denoted by the superordinate clause is inevitable, in
contrast to the sentence with maa, in which the situation denoted by the subordinate
clause puts into question whether the situation denoted by the superordinate clause
will take place. Another semantic contrast between kaa and maa will be discussed
presently. The future marker kaa can also have optative or intentional connotations:
(2457)
Ne fai mai ma kaa taumafai ia kee feituuala ia ki tai.
Pst say Dxs Cmp Fut try he Sbj moiety he to seaward
‘He told me that he was going to try to join the oceanside village moiety.’
Elsewhere, kaa has functions other than the marking of tense, all of which conjure
contingency: it marks temporal sequencing (1.1.2.4.2.1(a)), temporal simultaneity
(1.1.2.4.2.1(a)), and nonimaginary conditionality (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.5 and 2.1.3.4.2).

The third tense-aspect-mood associated with future situations is maa (and its
allomorphs mana, mane, and mani; cf. 2.1.3.4.11), which, like kaa, carries modal
connotations in addition to being a tense marker:
(2458)
Te tamaliki maa too!
the child Prc fall
‘The child is about to fall down!’
As a future-tense marker, maa contrasts with both e and kaa in a straightforward
manner. Compare examples (2453) and (2454) above with the following:
(2459)
Koe maa fano maataeao.
you Prc go tomorrow
‘You might be leaving tomorrow [if you don’t do something to prevent
it].’
As shown in 2.1.3.4.11, the tense-aspect-mood marker is also a precautionary mood
marker. It indicates that the situation referred to by the clause is undesirable, and
implies that another situation should take place to prevent this undesirable situation
from taking place.
The allomorph maa of the future-precautionary marker is homophonous with,
and probably etymologically related to, an unproductive future prefix maa- (cf.
2.1.1.6.3). Unlike the tense-aspect-mood marker, maa- does not have alternative
forms. All roots to which it may be affixed can also function as verbs, and therefore
the compound lexemes are homophonous with temporal sequencing clauses with
a future-precautionary tense-aspect-mood marker of the type described in
(2460)
E fano maafiafi.
Nps go this-afternoon
‘[She] will leave this afternoon.’
(2461)
E fano maa afiafi.
Nps go when afternoon
‘[She] will leave when afternoon [comes].’
The analysis of maa- as an affix rather than an independent morpheme in most of
its manifestations is supported by the fact that, like most sentence-modifying
adverbs, maa-prefixed compounds can be moved to clause-initial position, while
temporal clauses with maa cannot precede the superordinate clause (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.1(a)):
(2462)
Maafiafi, e fano.
this-afternoon Nps go
‘This afternoon, [she] will leave.’
(2463)
* Maa afiafi, e fano.
when afternoon Nps go

(2464)

‘When afternoon [comes], [she] will leave.’

2.1.3.2.2. Tense in nonindicative moods and nonfinite forms
Clauses in the two nonindicative moods, subjunctive and imperative, are not
marked for tense. Indeed, the basic markers of these moods are
syntagmatically incompatible with tense markers (cf. 1.1.2.1.2 and 2.1.3.4.3
respectively). As shown in 2.1.3.4.2(d), there are two types of formal marker of
the conditional mood, preverbal markers and conjunctions. Two of the
preverbal markers are the same morphemes as the future-tense markers kaa
and maa, the third is the optative-mood marker moi, which is unmarked for
tense. None tolerates another marker of tense, aspect, or mood in the same
clause. Conditional conjunctions allow a full range of tense, aspect, and
semantically compatible mood categories in the clause in which they occur.
Nonfinite forms (i.e., verbs of o-subordinated clauses and nominalized
verbs) cannot be marked for tense, aspect, or mood with ordinary preverbal
markers, since these are dropped in the formation of the nonfinite forms. Of
course, time reference can always be marked with adverbial modifiers
whenever tense-aspect-mood markers are disallowed.

2.1.3.3. Aspect
As in all languages, aspect can be denoted in a number of ways, some more
grammaticalized than others. At the most grammaticalized end of the spectrum,
one finds tense-aspect-mood markers comparable to the markers described in 2.1.3.2,
whose sole or primary function is to mark aspect (or tense or mood depending on
the case). Second, aspect can be marked with verbs whose primary function is to
denote aspect. Typically, these verbs function as the superordinate verb in a complex
construction, to which the rest of the sentence is subordinated. Finally, the least
grammaticalized end of the spectrum is occupied by aspectual adverbs. Different
constructions are available for different aspectual categories, but the same aspectual
category may be expressed in more than one way. In some cases, the same word
may alternatively function as a tense-aspect-mood marker, a verb with aspectual
meaning, and an aspectual adverb. Certain words appear to have undergone or to
be undergoing category reassignment over time.
Among other constructions and categories that have aspectual meaning figure
the two nominalizing strategies described in 2.1.3.5; several valency decreasing
and increasing processes (cf. 2.1.3.1.2 and 2.1.3.1.3 respectively); and a number of
intensifying and downtoning adverbs. In the following discussion, the translations
of many morphemes with aspectual meaning that appear in interlinear glosses are
oversimplified for the sake of brevity and consistency.
2.1.3.3.1. Perfect aspect
The perfect aspect can be indicated in one of three ways. First, it may be expressed
with the aspect marker koo, which can also be used to mark a variety of other
aspectual categories. Second, it may be expressed with complex constructions, the
superordinate verb of which is marked with koo. Third, question structures and
clauses subordinated to a verb in the negative can be marked for the perfect aspect
with the aspect marker kai.
(a) Aspect marker koo
I describe the tense-aspect-mood marker koo as an inchoative aspect marker because
its primary function is to indicate that the situation denoted by the clause began in
the past (be it remote or recent) and is still of relevance at the present time or at the
temporal point of reference of the discourse:

constructions (cf. 2.1.3.3.1(b)) have strong terminative connotations. The end of a
situation can also be expressed lexically with two of the same verbs as are used in
oti-constructions, namely oti ‘finished’ and palele ‘depleted, finished’, and with a
nominalized clause as their argument:
(2533)

Verbs denoting terminative aspectual categories cannot be marked for perfect

subordinate verb, i.e., the combinations *koo oti ne oti and *koo palele ne palele are
ungrammatical. The combinations ?koo oti ne palele and ?koo palele ne oti are

(g) Iterative aspect
Several morphemes and one morphological process are associated with the marking

habitual aspect. Two processes, the postposed adverb saale and full reduplication
and repetition, can mark both iterative and noniterative habituality; all other
processes can only mark iterative habituality or nonhabitual iterativeness.

marks iterative aspect:

also denote noniterative habituality (cf. (c) above):

(j) Simultaneous aspect
Simultaneity is not marked as a special aspectual category. For a description of
constructions associated with temporal simultaneity, see 1.1.2.4.2.1(c).
(k) Telic aspect
There is no formal marking of telic aspect. However, many syntactic and
morphological processes produce structural variants which differ from one another
in terms of telic aspect. For example, some transitive verbs may be detransitivized
by not mentioning the direct object (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(b)), and the detransitivized version
is always less telic (i.e., less likely to denote telic situations) than the transitive
version. Similarly, verb forms that can govern either transitive or middle-case
marking (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(c)) are more telic in their transitive manifestations. The
stativizing prefix ma-, discussed in 2.1.3.1.2(e), and the prefix ma- that denotes
potentiality (cf. 2.1.3.4.7) both decrease the telic value of the situation denoted by
the verb to which they are affixed.
2.1.3.3.2.2. Possible combinations of categories There are both semantic and
morphological constraints on the combination of aspectual values. Semantic
constraints forbid the combination of inceptive, terminative, and semelfactive aspect
markers on the one hand with, on the other hand, continuous, iterative, progressive,
and habitual aspect markers. The perfect-aspect markers also cannot cooccur with
the continuous and progressive marker koi. Several other restrictions are noted in
the foregoing discussion. No other cooccurrence patterns are disallowed, as long
as morphological constraints do not apply. Morphological constraints forbid the
occurrence in the same clause of more than one tense-aspect-mood marker, and
forbid the occurrence of tense-aspect-mood markers in nonfinite clauses (cf. 2.1.3.5).
Tense, aspect, and mood categories that are not constrained by morphological factors
can freely cooccur with one another.
2.1.3.4. Mood
Attention is drawn to the remarks made in the introduction to sections on tense
and aspect (2.1.3.2 and 2.1.3.3 respectively), some of which are relevant to the
following discussion.
2.1.3.4.1. Indicative
There is no formal marking of the indicative mood. The indicative mood is denoted,
by default, by the absence of nonindicative mood marking.
2.1.3.4.2. Conditional
The conditional mood may be marked overtly in one of two mutually
exclusive ways: with mood markers identical in form and behaviour to tense
and aspect markers described in the previous sections; or with conditional
conjunctions morphologically related to the conditional-mood markers. As
discussed further in 1.1.2.4.2.5, the choice between these two strategies is
governed by two factors: whether the ‘if clause (i.e., the protasis) is preposed
or postposed to the ‘then’ clause (i.e., the apodosis); and whether
conditionality is imaginary or nonimaginary. I use the term ‘nonimaginary’ as
in 1.1.2.4.2.5(b-c), to denote situations that may have taken place, may be
taking place, or might take place, be they hypothetical or counterfactual, and
the term ‘imaginary’ to denote the opposite.

2.1.3.4.9. Evidentiality
There is no formal marking of evidentiality, i.e., of the nature of the speaker’s or
writer’s authority for making a particular statement. However, many of the
morphological, lexical, and syntactic strategies cross-referenced in 2.1.3.4.8 have
secondary evidential status. Among other morphological devices that have
evidential functions figure the following: the perfect-aspect marker koo (cf.
2.1.3.3.1(a)), the inceptive prefix paa- (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(e)), and the deictic adverb mai
(cf. 2.1.3.6.10(a)).
2.1.3.4.10. Hortatory
There is no formal marking of hortatory mood. Hortatory sentences are usually in
the indicative or imperative mood, or sometimes in the optative, as the following
example:

Hortatory mood can also be marked with the precautionary-mood marker maa (or
one of its allomorphs) when the situation has an inherently negative meaning; see

2.1.3.4.11. Precautionary (monitory)
The mood marker maa (and its allomorphs mana, mane, and mani) marks
precautionary mood, and is roughly equivalent in meaning (but not stylistic
markedness) to English ‘lest’ when it introduces a subordinate clause (cf. 1.4.6(a)):
(2613)
Koe naa saa pati maasei iaa koe maa maalaia.

‘Don’t use swear words, lest you be damned.’
It appears frequently in subordinate clauses of the type illustrated by the above
examples, although it may also appear in independent clauses, as illustrated in
2.1.3.2.1(d). All sentences in which maa or its allomorphs appear are interpreted as
referring to future events.
The various allomorphs of this marker have exactly the same meaning and
stylistic distribution. The forms maa on the one hand and mana, mane, and mani on
the other probably originate from different dialect areas, although all forms are
used in all dialects today: maa is probably the original Southern dialectal form,
while mana is reportedly a Northern form. The variation between mana and the less
common mane and mani provides a clue to the origin of the allomorphic variation.
The second syllable of the forms mana, mane, and mani probably originated as the
past tense marker, i.e., the morpheme ne in the Southern dialects and ni in the
Northern dialects (ne is also heard in the North and ni in the South, but infrequently

2.1.3.4.13. Consecutive
There is no formal marking of consecutive mood. Strategies used to indicate
sequentiality between situations include o-subordination (cf. 1.1.2.1.1), subjunctive

2.1.3.4.14. Contingent
There is no special category associated with the contingent mood. Many markers
of relative certainty (cf. 2.1.3.4.8) can also function as markers of contingency. See

2.1.3.4.15. Desiderative
The preposed adverb fia marks desiderative notions. It is productive in that it can
be preposed to any verb that denotes a semantically appropriate situation:
(2615)
Au e fia fesoasoani atu ki tau gaaluega.
I Nps want help Dxs to your work
‘I want to help you in your work.’
The desiderative adverb coalesces with the polysemic verb fai ‘do, make’, resulting
in the middle verb fiafai ‘desire, want’, which frequently has sexual or morally
negative connotations. That the two morphemes have coalesced into a separate
word is witnessed by the fact that fiafai undergoes number agreement with its subject,
which the base form fai does not undergo. The desiderative fia generally is not
preposed to verbs that already denote desiderative situations, such as manako ‘wish’,
loto ‘wish’, malie ‘agree to’, fina ‘rapacious for’, vale ‘crazy about’, and umiti ‘crave’
(although grammaticality judgements are split with manako and perhaps other verbs
in the list).

The adverb fia has a secondary function. Preposed to words denoting social
categories, it conveys the affectively charged meaning of ‘pretend (to be), act as,
imagine oneself (to be)’, usually in a derogatory manner:
(2616)
Koi fooliki fua, a koo fia tamataene!
still small just and Inc want young-man
‘[He]’s just a kid, and he’s trying to act like a young man!’
Compounds thus formed are noun-derived verbs (cf. 1.16.1), which can be
nominalized in turn.
The two functions of fia are closely related and potentially ambiguous. Given
the strongly behaviouristic manner in which intentionality, motivation, and
personhood are defined in Tuvaluan society (Besnier 1989b, 1990a, 1991), I am
tempted to see the polysemy of fia as a translation phenomenon, and to consider it
to have a unified meaning from an emic perspective. A similar analysis may be
applicable to the notions of ‘hunger’, ‘thirst’, and ‘sleepiness’, which can only be
translated as the compounds fia kai ‘want to eat, hungry’, fia ota ‘want to eat raw
food, hungry for raw food’, fia inu ‘want to drink, thirsty’, and fia moe ‘want to
sleep, sleepy’. According to the proposed analysis, fia kai does not have two
meanings, ‘hungry’ and ‘want to eat’, but rather a single meaning, because hunger
would be defined locally as the desire to eat.
The desiderative adverb is never modified by other adverbs, it never functions
as an independent lexeme, it can modify verbs of all valencies, and it does not
govern case marking or alter the valency of the sentence. Thus it has no verbal
properties. However, it is associated with interesting patterns of preference with
regard to the choice in ‘desirer’ among the various noun phrases in the clause.
When it modifies an intransitive verb, the ‘desirer’ must be the subject of the clause.
This is the case of (2615) and (2616). Thus an intransitive verb whose subject does
not denote a volitional entity cannot be modified by fia:
(2617)
Taku pausi koo (*fia) fano mo toku taina.
my suitcase Inc want go with my sibling
‘My brother (*wants to take)/took my suitcase.’
When fia modifies a transitive verb, several patterns obtain. If either the subject or
the direct object is the only noun phrase in the clause that denotes a volitional
entity, the feeling of desire is attributed to that entity:
(2618)
Au koo fia kai nee au te atu teenaa.
I Inc want eat Erg I the bonito that
‘I want to eat that bonito.’
(2619)
Ko ia loa koo fia fakassiu nee te vaiua.
Foc he indeed Inc want Cst+wet Erg the rain
‘He wants to be made wet by the rain.’
When the referents of either argument of the verb can be volitional, the desire is
attributed to the referent of the most topical noun phrase, which usually appears in
preverbal position. Typically, this noun phrase is the direct object:
(2620)
A tino koo fia lavea nee laatou te tagata saka.
Cnt person Inc want see Erg they-3 the man dance
‘The people want to see the dancer.’

2.1.3.4.16. Nearly realized
Nearly realized situations, whether desirable or not, can be marked in one of two
ways. First, the marker moi, identical to the mood marker found in optative clauses
(cf. 2.1.3.4.4) and imaginary conditions (cf. 2.1.3.4.2(c)), can denote either undesirable
or desirable nearly realized situations:
(2622)
Au moi fiti ki lalo!
I Opt fall-backwards to down
‘I almost fell backwards!’
(2623)
Moi maua nee ia tena pine i ttausaga nei.
Opt get Erg he his decoration in the+year this
‘He almost got a decoration this year.’
Second, nearly realized situations can be marked with the compounds toe itiiti, moi itiiti,
or moi toe itiiti, the first of which is the most common. The lexeme itiiti is a borrowing from
Samoan, where it means ‘small’; in Tuvaluan it only occurs in compounds with moi or toe
(although it also appears in the borrowed compounds tautala itiiti ‘cheeky, not know
one’s place in society’). The form moi is the optative or imaginary conditional marker; the
form toe is the adverb with the meaning of ‘again, last, remaining’, which can also have a
variety of other functions (cf. 1.11.1.3.5 and 1.16.4.3). Depending on the situation,
compounds of the form toe itiiti are either modal or aspectual, or both. They can function
as the first part of an additively coordinated construction with the sentence coordinator
kae (but not its allomorphs described in 1.3.1.1.2), the second part of which is the clause
that denotes the nearly realized situation:
(2624)
Toe itiiti kae ppaki ki loto a vakalele.
almost and crash to centre Cnt airplane
‘The airplanes almost crashed into one another.’
Alternatively, it can function as the superordinate verb of a complex construction,
to which the clause denoting the situation marked for nearly realized mood is
subordinated by apposition (cf. 1.1.2.1.5):
(2625)
Moi itiiti koo tupu ei ttaua tonu.
almost Inc happen Anp the+fight real
‘A real fight almost broke out over it.’
(2626)
Ttou moa toe itiiti koo ttoo.
our-3-i hen almost Inc lay
‘Our hen is about to lay [eggs].’
Compounds with itiiti function like verbs, although they do not take tense-aspect-
mood markers. They are equivalent in structure and meaning to constructions with
moo mea or muu mea (cf. 2.1.6.6.3(b)).

2.1.3.5. Finite and nonfinite forms
The only clear category of nonfinite verbs in the language are nominalized verbs.
Virtually all verbs in the language can undergo nominalization (see 1.15.1 for an
exception), including existential verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b)), negative existential verbs
(cf. 1.4(d)), predicative prepositional phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(c)), and, with some
qualifications, predicated possessive phrases (cf. 1.10.1.2). Nominalized verbs are
very frequent in natural discourse, and a broad range of constructions and processes
either require or favour nominalized verb forms.
Nominalized verbs come in two types, which are described in turn below: a
‘bare’ form, which is identical to that of the finite form of the verb; and a suffixed
form, which is derived by attaching the nominalizing suffix -Vga to the verb (which
may then undergo minor structural modifications). In both cases, the verb loses its
tense-aspect-mood markers, but it may keep any adverbial modifier, including those
with temporal, aspectual, and modal meaning, as well as negators:
(2627)
Au e ofo i te fui vau o te vaka.
I Nps surprised at the slow-to come of the ship
‘I am amazed by how late the ship is.’
(2628)
Te see lava te maalamalama i aso kolaa, nee?
the Neg enough the enlightenment in day those Tag
‘There was so little understanding in those days, right?’
Both types of nominalized verbs resemble nouns in their basic external morphology.
For example, they take articles, although they tend to occur mostly with the singular
definite article (cf. 2.1.1.8).
The syntactic characteristics of nominalization are described in 1.1.2.2.6 and
1.1.2.4.3, and its clausal morphology in 2.1.1.3.4. Subject-verb number agreement
in nominalized clauses is discussed in 2.1.3.6.6.

that of corresponding finite forms:

Bare nominalized forms are sometimes difficult to distinguish from lexically related
nouns and cognate nouns, because they often have the same form and are closely
related in meaning, as illustrated in Table 2.12. However, bare nominalized forms
of verbs must be distinguished from cognate nouns for several reasons. First, the
meaning of bare nominalized forms can be derived predictably from that of the
verb, while the meaning of cognate nouns is often idiosyncratically related to that
of the verb. Second, bare nominalized forms refer to situations, while cognate nouns
generally refer to objects or abstract entities. Third, cognate nouns are frequently
more specific in meaning than nominalized verbs. Fourth, bare nominalized forms
and cognate nouns often take different possessive modifiers; for example, the
arguments of the nominalized forms of asu ‘scoop, bail’ and tau ‘harvest’ are marked
for inalienable possession, following patterns regularly associated with
nominalization (cf. 2.1.1.3.4), but the corresponding cognate nouns can only be
possessed alienably (cf. 2.1.1.4.6).
Nominalized forms must also be distinguished from words that function as nouns
in their basic form but that can sometimes be used as verbs (cf. 1.16.1). For example,
pati ‘word’, kkano ‘flesh’, and ala ‘road’ can sometimes appear as verbs, with the
meaning of ‘say’, ‘related’, and ‘motivate’ respectively. As discussed in 1.16.1, several
criteria can be applied to such cases to show that the nominal use of these words is
unmarked and their verbal use marked. Clearly, no nominalization process is at
play here.
Bare nominalized forms refer to situations that are viewed as temporally
unbounded. The situations to which they refer are generally habitual, continuous,
progressive, durative, or iterative:
(2633)

nominalization from unsuffixed forms.

2.1.3.6. Agreement in person, number, and other categories
In the following discussion, I refer to verbs that agree in number with one of their
arguments as ‘agreeing verbs’. The term ‘plural’ refers to the number category
associated with nouns, rather than pronouns, and thus means ‘with more than one
referent’ (cf. 2.1.1.8); it includes both the dual and plural categories distinguished
in pronominal morphology (cf. 2.1.2.1.4).
2.1.3.6.1. Agreement with arguments of the verb
Agreement distinguishes different classes of verbs, each of which will be treated
separately here. Agreement is obligatory in some cases, and optional in others.
Optional agreement may become obligatory under certain conditions, discussed in
2.1.3.6.3 and 2.1.3.6.5.
First, most intransitive verbs agree in number with the subject. For this class of

2.1.3.6.4. Features targeted in agreement
The only feature targeted in agreement is number. For the purpose of agreement,
the dual-plural number distinction in pronouns is conflated into one category.
2.1.3.6.5. Factors affecting agreement
In several situations, syntactic number and semantic number conflict with one
another, and, when this is the case, agreement is based generally on semantic factors.
However, agreement with semantic plurality is sometimes optional.
(a) Agreement controlled by singular nouns with plural referents
Many nouns, both simple and compound, denoting plural entities (e.g., groups of
animate and inanimate entities, bodies of knowledge, uncountable entities) are
marked with singular articles (cf. 2.1.1.8.2). All such words are considered to be
either singular or plural for the purpose of verb agreement. Thus the following
alternatives obtain:
(2670)
Koo (k)kai te faagota.
Inc eat(+Agr) the sea-fauna
‘The fish are biting.’
(2671)
Te uaa niu koo see (o)ola nei.
the matters-relating-to-coconuts Inc Neg alive(+Agr) now.
‘The coconuts are not doing well.’

morphologically singular noun phrases with plural referents. If the noun phrase
includes a singular demonstrative, the verb may be marked for either singular or

As illustrated in 2.1.1.8.2, the meaning of verbs like malaku ‘(of many fruits or

metaphorically, agreement patterns vary across idiolects. In some idiolects, they
do not undergo agreement:

2.1.3.6.7. Switch reference
There is no switch-reference system.
2.1.3.6.8. Reflexive form of verbs
Reflexivity is not encoded in verb morphology. However, the intensifier eiloa and
its allomorphs, which function as reflexive markers, may modify the verb in reflexive
clauses; see 1.6 for discussion and illustrations.
2.1.3.6.9. Reciprocal form of verbs
Reciprocality can be marked on the verb with a circumfix of the form fe-X-(C)aki,
where X stands for the root of the verb and C is a consonant, taken from the same
list as the consonants that appear in the -(C)ia suffix (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(f)); usually, for
each verb root, the same consonant appears in the -(C)ia suffix and the reciprocal
circumfix. The syntactic characteristics of circumfixal reciprocality are discussed in
1.7.1.3 and 1.7.2–9; the effect of the circumfix on the valency of the verb is described
in 2.1.3.1.4.
The affix is made up of two unproductive affixes, a prefix fe- and a suffix -(C)aki.
The prefix fe- can be traced to a Proto-Polynesian prefix *fe- with pluralizing

fenuminumi ‘all tangled up’ (cf. numi ‘tangled’), and perhaps fekai ‘ferocious’ (cf. kai
‘eat’). The prefix is unproductive, and the meaning of prefixed forms usually cannot
be derived simply from that of the root forms.31
The suffix -(C)aki is a little more frequent across the lexicon, but it is also
unproductive. Reflecting a Proto-Polynesian morpheme *-(C)aki, which appears
to have given an instrumental focus to the verb, this suffix does not have a
generalizable function in contemporary Tuvaluan. In some forms, shades of its
former function as an instrumental marker remain; for example, taapuaki ‘worship’
(from tapu ‘sacred’), tuulaki ‘(of birds, etc.) use as a stand’ (from tuu ‘stand’), and
pikitaki ‘stuck with objects’ (from piki ‘stick’). However, the meaning of many
suffixed forms is derived from that of the root in arbitrary fashion. Witness alafaki
‘keep wake’ (cf. ala ‘(a)wake’), alofaki ‘beckon’ (cf. aalo ‘row’), akasaki ‘strive’
(perhaps from aka ‘kick’), and fatuaki ‘begin weaving’ (from fatu ‘compose’).
Occasionally, the suffixed and root forms (or a derived form) have essentially the
same meaning; for example, moeaki and fakamoemoe ‘hope’, fakatuanaki and
fakatuatua ‘have faith’. Some suffixed forms are nouns: such is the case of aofaki

2.1.3.6.10. Verbal deixis
Deixis is marked on the verb primarily with the help of a small set of adverbs,
cognates of which are found in all Polynesian languages, the semantics of which
has puzzled many scholars (e.g., Platt 1986 on Samoan). In Tuvaluan, two basic
binary semantic oppositions underlie the system, opposing on the one hand the
forms mai ‘towards the point of reference of the discourse’ (henceforth ‘hither’)
and atu ‘away from the point of reference of the discourse’ (henceforth ‘thither’);
and on the other hand aka ‘up’ and ifo ‘down’. As will be discussed in this section,
the translations provided here are expedient oversimplifications.
The deictic aka occupies a special place in this paradigm, in that it also functions
as a polite downtoner and thus can cooccur, in this function, with other deictics. (It
can also mean ‘other’, as discussed in 2.1.6.6.2(c).) In all other instances, only one
deictic per verb is allowed:
(2688)
Koo ttolo mai te fonu!
Inc crawl Dxs the turtle
‘A turtle is crawling up [to land]!’
(2689)
Kee faitau atu nee au te ueta i te ggana Ppaalagi.
Sbj read Dxs Erg I the weather-report in the language Westerner
‘Let me read out to you the weather report in English.’
Deictic adverbs are primarily associated with verbs of motion, verbs of
sending and receiving, verbs denoting sensory and perceptual categories,
verbs denoting evolutions in time, as well as communication verbs denoting
speech acts, acts of writing, acts of calling out, and so on (cf. 1.1.1.1(a) for
examples). However, they can also modify many other types of verbs, as will
be illustrated presently.
The four deictic adverbs exhibit a number of formal and distributional
idiosyncrasies. First, the deictic aka, an irregular reflex of Proto-Polynesian
*(h,s)ake, has an alternative, slightly archaic form ake (the regular reflex of the
protoform), used occasionally instead of aka (it is also the regular form of the
deictic in the Northern dialects).33 Second, one verb of motion, vau ‘come’ is
never modified by a deictic adverb, presumably because the action it denotes
is already inherently oriented in space. Yet vau follows the same semantic
principles as mai, and its meaning can be thought of as incorporating the
meaning of mai (it contrasts with fanatu ‘go thither’). The optional suppletive
plural forms of vau, namely mmai, aummai, and ommai (cf. 2.1.3.6.2), are
historically related to mai (although they are not synchronically derivable from
it), and are also distributionally incompatible with mai. In contrast, both aka
and ifo can modify verbs to which they are etymologically related, namely ake
‘reach land, beach oneself’, sake ‘slant, raise one’s foot into an elevated area, (of
a school of fish) beach oneself’, ifo ‘prostrate oneself, humble oneself’, and ssifo
‘slant down, lean down’:

the deictic adverb is generally sufficient and occurs without additional deictic

The following discussion first treats the meaning of mai and atu, which are
semantically more complex, before turning to aka and ifo. For a discussion of the
use of these deictics in comparative structures, see 1.8.1(a).
(a) Deictics mai ‘hither’ and atu ‘thither’
When they modify verbs of motion and related notions, mai and atu denote
respectively motion towards and away from the speaker or writer. In their most
unmarked usage, they take as point of reference the general area in which the speaker
or writer is located, particularly in opposition to the location of the interlocutor.
However, in some cases, the deictics appear to violate this generalization. For
example, in the first of the following, mai ‘hither’ modifies a verb denoting a speech
act that is clearly oriented towards the interlocutor, and not the speaker; in the
second example, atu ‘thither’ cooccurs with the prepositional phrase ki au ‘to me’
(i.e., ‘hither’):
(2695)
E fakasii mai kee fanatu koe.
Nps utter-interjection+Itj Dxs Sbj go you
‘[He] is whistling (hither) [to you] for you to come over.’
(2696)
Fakamuli kee fanatu ei koe ki au.
later Sbj go+Dxs Anp you to I
‘Later on, come and [see] me.’
These examples demonstrate that the deictic frame of reference can shift from the
speaker or writer onto the interlocutor. This shift is generally governed by non-
syntactic factors except in one context: when the speaker refers to motion by the
interlocutor towards the speaker, the frame of reference must be the interlocutor’s;
thus motion towards the speaker must be marked with atu rather than mai (and
with fano ‘go’ rather than vau ‘come’). This shift is obligatory in nonquoted and
directly quoted speech, and does not take place in indirectly quoted speech:
(2697)
Fai aka kia Semo kee tele mai mo te ulo lasi!
tell please to Semo Sbj run Dxs with the pot large
‘Tell Semo to bring (hither) the large cooking pot in a hurry!’
(2698)
Fai aka kia Semo, “Tele atu koe mo te ulo lasi!”
tell please to Semo run Dxs you with the pot large
‘Tell Semo [the following], “take (thither) the large cooking pot in a
hurry!”’

nor second-person entities are participants. In such cases, the speaker chooses the
participant with whom he or she identifies most closely as the deictic frame of
reference. The following example appears as the conclusion of a story about a man
who began delivering a church sermon, but then forgot what he was going to say:

2.1.3.6.12. Incorporation
Several elements of the clause may be verb-incorporated, yielding structures that
exhibit varying degrees of morphological ‘bonding’ between the verb and the
incorporated element: some incorporation processes result in compounds that
behave like single words when subjected to other morphological processes (e.g.,
nominalizing suffixation, transitivizing suffixation), while others output
morphologically more disjoint structures.
Not all processes described in this section would be described as ‘incorporation’
by other descriptivists. For example, Mithun (1984) describes the most basic type
of direct-object corporation as a process of derivational morphology, rather than as
a syntactic process, in contrast to ‘object stripping’ (Miner 1983). The following
describes and distinguishes between incorporation and stripping, which I call ‘tight’
and ‘loose’ incorporation respectively.
No incorporation process targets subjects, adjectives, or obliques other than those
described in (b) below.
(a) Incorporation of direct objects
What I call ‘direct-object incorporation’ is an optional process whereby the direct
object of a transitive verb ‘merges’ with the verb complex to form a single unit of

(2721)

The major semantic difference between incorporated and unincorporated direct
objects is that the former denote nonreferential, nonindividuated, and generic
entities. Thus proper nouns and personal pronouns (including indefinite and non-
specific pronouns) cannot undergo incorporation, since they denote individuated
entities. Incorporated direct objects cannot be modified by articles, article-like
modifiers, or relative clauses; many incorporated direct objects can, however, take
adjectives, as long as these are not too ‘heavy’ (in most idiolects, for example,
adjectives that take arguments are not allowed in that position):
(2725)

‘We frequently eat fresh fish.’
Coordinated direct objects can be verb-incorporated as long as they are of a
‘reasonable’ weight (in most cases, probably no more than two coordinated elements
are allowed):
(2726)
Taatou kaa kkai ika mo uu i motu.
we-3-i Inc eat+Agr fish and coconut-crab at islet
‘We’re going to eat fish and coconut crabs at the islets.’
Incorporated structures tend to denote durative, iterative, and atelic situations.
Indeed, these aspectual values commonly go hand in hand with the presence of
nonreferential, nonindividuated direct objects (Hopper and Thompson 1980). Verbs
with incorporated direct objects can be used as attributive adjectives:
(2727)

(2728)

‘You are a woman-deceiver.’

characteristics as unincorporated structures with definite plural direct objects, since
the latter are frequently case-marked with ø and take zero articles. However, plural

In theory, direct-object incorporation can apply to any transitive clause (except

it is subject to certain semantic constraints. Direct objects of certain verbs are more
likely to be incorporated than others; for example, the verb lagona ‘hear’ rarely
appear with an incorporated direct object:

Generally speaking, direct-object incorporation cannot apply when it refers to an

verb (see Chung 1978:185 for a similar analysis of direct-object incorporation in

contexts where direct-object incorporation does not apply, in that there are sentences,
like (2721) above, in which the direct object denotes an unaffected or incompletely
affected entity, but in which incorporation can apply. Furthermore, the restriction
concerns situations, rather than linguistic units. Indeed, it is possible to find contexts

(2734)

a preposition, in which ei has undergone incorporation:
(2774)
Teenaa te mea ne ita (i) ei.
that the thing Pst angry at Anp
‘That’s why [she] was angry.’
When incorporated, ei is ordered before verb-modifying adverbs, such as foki ‘also’:
(2775)
Koo maavvae ei foki kaaiga ttonu.
Inc split Anp also family blood
‘Blood relatives also break up over that.’
Because ei never coalesces with the verb, anaphoric-pronoun incorporation is only
a ‘loose’ incorporation phenomenon. For example, in contrast to postverbal adverbial
modifiers described in (c) above, ei does not coalesce with the verb when the latter
undergoes suffixed nominalization:

while others are sensitive to discourse factors. When its appearance is governed by
discourse factors, anaphoric-pronoun incorporation is never obligatory. In contrast,
certain syntactic uses of ei constrain its incorporation in one fashion or another; for
example, it must be incorporated in clefted interrogative-word constructions (cf.

relative clauses (cf. 1.1.2.3.5).
(e) Other processes akin to incorporation
Several processes result in constructions that bear some surface resemblance to
incorporated constructions, although they differ from the structures described in
this section. The adverbial quantifier katoa ‘all’ may float from noun phrases to
become a modifier of the verb (cf. 1.14.1), or may be raised from a noun phrase in a
subordinate clause to become a modifier of the verb of the main clause (cf. 1.14.2).
Like the anaphoric pronoun ei, katoa is never treated as forming a morphological
unit by either suffixed nominalization or suffixed transitivization:
(2779)
* te kaasanikatoaaga o niu
the tie-in-pair+all+Nom of coconut
(‘the process of tying all the coconuts together in pairs’)
(2780)
te kaasaniiga katoa o niu
the tie-in-pair+Nom all of coconut
These patterns, and the fact that katoa float and raising involve no change in the
form of the adverb, suggest that quantifier float and raising are not incorporating
processes.
A number of syntactic processes and morphemes described elsewhere in
this grammar resemble incorporation processes and incorporated elements, or
derive historically from incorporation processes: clitic pronouns (cf.
2.1.2.1.1.5), which can be viewed as subject pronouns that have undergone
incorporation into the verb complex; the universal or nonpast tense-aspect
marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1.1), which was historically a clitic third-person singular
pronoun form; and the transitive suffix -gina (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(c)), which derives
from an incorporated direct-object pronoun.

2.1.3.7. Serial verbs
The existence of verb serialization, or verb chains, is well attested among Oceanic
languages other than members of the Polynesian family (e.g., Foley and Olson
1985, Harrison 1984a). In contrast, no Polynesian language has so far been described
as having structures of this type, although Hooper (1993:239) suggests that they
exist in Tokelauan. No Tuvaluan structure can be unequivocally identified as verb
chains, but certain strings of verbs resemble verb chains. Such is the case, for
example, of the verbs fakasiga ‘[make oneself] fall’ and tagi ‘cry’ in the following:
(2781)
Ne fakasiga tagi ki vae o tena maatua kee fakamaagalo ia.
Pst Cst+fall cry to foot of his mother Sbj forgive he
‘[He] fell cry[ing] to his mother’s feet [for her] to forgive him.’
I have not encountered series consisting of more than two verbs, and, if indeed
these structures are examples of verb serialization, they are considerably more
modest in scope than verb series in languages that make productive use of them.
Paired verbs that resemble verb series are ordered according to a general principle,
to the effect that the most dynamic verb comes first, while the second verb generally
denotes a more backgrounded, atelic, and continuous situation. Many strings have
the status of more or less set idioms. In this category fall such series as mind mmae
‘urinate painfully’ (mimi ‘urinate’, mmae ‘hurt’), moe ssogo ‘wet one’s bed’ (moe ‘sleep’,
ssogo ‘smell of urine’), tagi too ‘(of a fowl) to cluck after laying an egg’ (tagi ‘cry’, too
‘lay [an egg]’), and fakalogo ssee ‘mishear’ (fakalogo ‘listen’, ssee ‘wrong’). In a few cases,
the first verb only occurs in serial constructions: fakamagii does not have any meaning
other than in the series fakamagii tagi ‘whine, cry softly’ (from tagi ‘cry’). The
verb fakamisi ‘think longingly’ appears in series with specialized meanings: fakamisi
kata ‘smile’, fakamisi alofa ‘harbour unexpressed feelings of empathy’ (from alofa ‘feel
empathy’), and fakamisi tagi, synonymous with fakamagii tagi.
Verbs in series cannot be separated by anything, and share the same tense-aspect-
mood marker. However, they need not share the same argument structure and
need not agree in valency. For example, tanu ‘bury’ and ola ‘alive’, kai ‘eat’ and
maluu ‘soft’, and fai ‘do’ and sao ‘get away’ in each of the following have both
different valencies and different subjects:
(2782)
Laatou ne tanu ola nee au.
they-3 Pst bury alive Erg I
‘I buried them alive.’
(2783)
Te loomatua e kai maluu ana masi.
the old-woman Nps eat soft her cabin-biscuits
‘The old woman dunks her cabin biscuits.’
(2784)
Maatou ne ssoko te fai ssao.
we-3-e Pst constant the do get-away+Agr
‘We had [a lot of fish] get away.’
In general, the argument structure of the entire clause follows the pattern associated
with the first verb in the series. However, some postverbal adverbs and prepositional
modifiers are clearly associated with the second verb:
(2785)
Au koo nofo masausau atu kiaa koe.
I Inc stay reminisce Dxs to you
‘I constantly think longingly about you.’
