When serialized verbs are agreeing verbs (cf. 2.1.3.6.1), several possibilities obtain.
If both verbs are agreeing verbs and the grammatical subject of the series refers to
the agent of both verbs, both verbs agree with it:
(2786)
E kkata vaallea.
Nps laugh+Agr stupid+Agr
‘[They] laugh stupidly.’
When both verbs are agreeing verbs but the subject does not refer to the agent of
both verbs, the first verb generally agrees with the subject, while agreement patterns
associated with the second verb are idiosyncratic. For example, in the same idiolect,
the verb maluu ‘soft’ does not agree with the subject in (2787) but does so obligatorily
in (2788) (the latter is to be compared with (2783)):
(2787)
A atu koo fai ssoko te kkai ma*(al)luu.
Cnt bonito Inc do constant the eat+Agr soft*(+Agr)
‘The bonitos keep nibbling [at the lure].’
(2788)
Loomaattua e kkai ma*(al)luu olotou masi.
old-women Nps eat soft*(+Agr) their-3 cabin-biscuit
‘The old women dunk their cabin biscuits.’
In no case do verbs in series agree with different arguments in the clause. Agreement
patterns vary across clauses, as well as across idiolects. In some situations, agreement
is optional within the same idiolect:
(2789)
Koo laku ta(at)tela nee ia ana gatu ki lalo!
Inc throw scattered(+Agr) Erg he his clothes to down
‘He is throwing his clothes all over the place!’
These constructions can be analysed in at least two alternative ways. First, they can
be considered to be compound verbs, and the formation of concatenated structures
can be considered to be part of derivational morphology. However, the productivity
of verb concatenation, and the fact that concatenated verbs behave autonomously
of one another with respect to agreement, suggest that the phenomenon differs
from other lexical compounding processes. Second, the second serialized element
could be understood to be an adverbial modifier of the first element. The fact that
the argument structure of the clause generally conforms to the syntax and semantics
of the first element supports this analysis. However, no adverb in the language
agrees with subjects, and the fact that both serialized elements can undergo
agreement militates against this analysis.
2.1.4. Adjectives
As discussed in 1.16.4, there are three classes of adjective: a productive category of
verbal adjectives; a less productive category of nominal adjectives; and a restricted
residual category of preposed adjectives. The following discussion concentrates on
the first two categories. None of the processes and categories overviewed in this
section apply to preposed adjectives, which can only function attributively, do not
undergo agreement, and cannot be marked for comparison or degrees of quality.
In addition to the three main adjective categories, one also finds verbal noun-
adjective compounds (cf. 2.2.6.3.3). They are a subcategory of verbal adjectives,
in that they resemble ordinary verbal adjectives in most respects. They differ
from other verbal adjectives with respect to agreement, and these differences are
described below.

2.1.4.1. Predicative and attributive adjectives
Both predicative and attributive adjectives are attested. From the perspective of the
category ‘adjective’, the attributive function is unmarked, since it is shared by all
words that have adjectival properties. Not all adjective categories can function as
predicates, and the ability to do so is one of the principal motivations for identifying
two main categories of adjectives.
All and only verbal adjectives can function as predicates, although some forms
are predicated more commonly than others. Following are a few contrastive
predicative-attributive pairs:
(2790)
Koo mmafa tena fesili.
Inc heavy her question
‘Her question is a difficult one.’
(2791)
tena fesili mmafa
her question heavy
‘her difficult question’
(2792)
Koo taaua te aso nei i maafaufau o tino.
Inc important the day this at mind of person
‘This is an important day in people’s thinking.’
(2793)
se aso taaua i maafaufau o tino
a day important at mind of person
‘an important day in people’s thinking’
(2794)
Konei omotou manu e tausi nee maatou.
these our-3-e animal Nps keep Erg we-3-e
‘These are the animals we keep.’
(2795)
omotou manu tausi konei
our-3-e animal keep these
‘these domestic animals of ours’
The internal morphology of verbal adjectives is the same whether they are used
predicatively or attributively. Members of the subcategory of verbal noun-adjective
compounds can also appear in either predicative or attributive contexts without
undergoing any formal changes:
(2796)
Ttamaliki teenaa ko ia loo koo pati matua.
the+child that Foc he indeed Inc word old
‘That child is verbally very mature.’
(2797)
ttamaliki pati matua
the+child word old
‘a verbally mature child’
(2798)
Ttoeaina teenaa koi mata taulekaleka faeloa.
the+old-man that still face handsome constantly
‘That old man still has a handsome face.’
(2799)
ttoeaina mata taulekaleka faeloa
the+old-man face handsome constantly
‘the old man with a handsome face’
When verbal adjectives (including verbal noun-adjective compounds) are used
predicatively, they are indistinguishable from regular verbs.

2.1.4.2. Absolute and contingent states
No distinction is made between absolute (permanent, normal) and contingent
(temporary, abnormal) states.
2.1.4.3. Noun-adjective agreement
2.1.4.3.1. Number agreement
Whenever an adjective agrees with a noun, the category upon which agreement is
based is number; adjectives take on a plural form formally identical to the form of
plural verbs (cf. 2.1.3.6.1). Adjective classes behave differently with regards to
agreement. The following discussion identifies three distinct patterns: one associated
with nominal adjectives; another with verbal adjectives; and a last pattern relevant
to the noun-adjective compound subclass of verbal adjectives, whose behaviour
with respect to agreement is complex enough to deserve separate treatment.
(a) Nominal adjectives
Nominal adjectives never agree with any feature of the noun they modify. Thus the
form of the nominal adjectives in the following is invariant regardless of whether
the modified noun is singular or plural:
(2803)
te tifa fatu
the plate stone
‘a porcelain plate’
(2804)
tifa fatu
plate stone
‘the porcelain plates’
This feature of nominal adjectives is particularly important in identifying the
derivation of adjectives from forms that can function as either nouns or verbs. For
example, the fact that the attributive adjective alofa does not agree with its plural
head noun in (2805) indicates that it is derived from the noun alofa ‘empathy’, while
agreement between the attributive adjective alofa and the plural noun in (2806)

(b) Verbal adjectives
When they function as predicates, verbal adjectives are not distinguishable from
regular intransitive verbs (cf. 1.16.4.1). Thus all agreement patterns described in

such a class.
An attributive adjective derived from an intransitive verb that has an agreement
form (cf. 2.1.3.6) agrees in number with the noun it modifies if that noun functions
as the subject of the adjective when the latter is predicative. For example, the form
of the attributive adjective valea ‘ignorant’ changes from (2807) to (2808) in the same
way that the form of the verb valea ‘ignorant’ changes from (2809) to (2810):
(2807)

‘an ignorant man’

‘ignorant men’

‘That man is just ignorant.’
(2810)

‘Those men are just ignorant.’

the verbal adjectives uli ‘black’ and loa ‘long’ undergo agreement in other

(c) Verbal noun-adjective compounds
Noun-adjective compounds that have been ‘recycled’ as adjectives form a subclass
of verbal adjectives (cf. 2.2.6.3.3), since they can all function as predicates. With
respect to agreement, several patterns can be distinguished, which apply to both
predicative uses of noun-adjective compounds and their attributive uses with head
nouns corresponding to the subject of predicative structures. Whether a particular
noun-adjective compound follows one or the other pattern is determined lexically.
According to one pattern, agreement is controlled ‘internally’, in the sense that the
adjective of the compound agrees with the noun within the compound. Such
compounds generally are always either singular or plural. For example, aso llasi
‘spend end-of-year holidays’ is always plural, and hence the adjective element in
the compound is always a plural form:
(2820)

‘an end-of-year feast’
[lit.: ‘a big-days feast’]

‘I’ll spend the end-of-year holidays at Nukufetau this year.’
[lit.: ‘I’ll big-days to Nukufetau this year.’]

element of the compound agrees with the subject of the predicate or the head noun.

2.1.4.3.2. Factors affecting agreement
As shown above, agreement is affected by the category in which the adjective falls.
The relative position of the noun and the adjective and whether or not the noun is
overtly expressed are not relevant factors, because the relative position of nouns
and attributive adjectives is fixed, barring a few marginal exceptions, and attributive
adjectives can only modify overt nouns.

2.1.4.3.3. Agreement and noun categories
Conflict between grammatical and semantic categories are resolved with both
predicative and attributive adjectives in a manner which is identical to that used to
resolve such conflicts with verb agreement; see 2.1.3.6.5 for discussion of the latter.
2.1.4.4. Comparison
Since nominal adjectives never denote gradable notions, comparison is only relevant
to verbal adjectives. Predicative verbal adjectives function exactly like regular verbs,
and the discussion of comparative structures in 1.8, of equative structures in 1.9,
and of superlatives in 1.8.7 apply to predicative verbal adjectives as much as to
regular verbs. (The latter category is not distinguished from the former in this
section, which include illustrations of regular verbs.)
The most natural way of expressing comparisons with attributive adjectives is
to turn them into predicative adjectives and then mark them for comparison. This
can be achieved least disruptively by turning the adjective into a relative clause.

Attributive adjectives can also be marked for superlative comparison, and the
same strategies are employed as those associated with predicative contexts (cf.
1.8.7). An intensifying adverb is postposed to the adjective, and a standard of
comparison can be expressed as a locatively marked prepositional modifier of
the noun phrase:
(2834)
A Vaitupu ko te fenua lasi eiloa i fenua o Tuuvalu.
Cnt Vaitupu Foc the island big indeed at island of Tuvalu
‘Vaitupu is the largest island of Tuvalu.’
No distinction is made between superlative comparisons that take as standard of
comparison other entities and comparisons that take as standard the same entity at
another location or another time. Only adjectives that modify nouns corresponding
to the subject of equivalent predicative adjectives can be marked for comparison.
Comparative constructions with other adjectives yield pragmatically unacceptable
results.
2.1.4.5. Degrees of quality
Degrees of quality are marked on predicative adjectives in the same fashion as any
other verb. Attributive adjectives can also be marked for degrees of quality with
the same intensifying and downtoning adverbs as are used with predicates.
Following is an example of attributive adjectives modified by intensifiers:
(2835)
Se tamaliki poto kkii.
a child intelligent very
‘[He’s] a very intelligent child.’
(2836)
ne pati tonu kkisi eiloa
some word right dead indeed
‘dead-right words indeed’
Although the superabundance adverb too ‘too’ is most idiomatic with predicates, it
is not ungrammatical as a modifier of attributive adjectives:
(2837)
Te tuulaga teenaa se tuulaga too faigataa moo te llei o tou olaga.
the status that a status too difficult Ben the good of your life
‘Where you find yourself is too difficult a position for it to be of any
good to your life.’
Adverbial downtoners of all types can modify attributive adjectives freely:
(2838)
Se mataaupu tai faigataa tena mea ne avaka.
a matter quite difficult his thing Pst bring+Dxs
‘What he brought up is quite a difficult matter.’
Degree of quality presumes gradability, and therefore adjectives that denote notions
that are not readily gradable cannot be modified by adverbials denoting degree of
quality. In this category fall verbal adjectives like muamua ‘first’ and numerals, as
well as all nominal adjectives. However, these adjectives can be modified by the
all-purpose intensifier eiloa and its allomorphs.

548
Morphology
2.1.4.6. Verbal morphology of predicative adjectives
Predicative adjectives are indistinguishable from regular verbs, as shown in 1.2.1.1.2
and in the above sections. Thus their morphology resembles that of a verb in every
respect.
2.1.5. Prepositions and case markers
As discussed in 1.16.5, prepositions are difficult to distinguish from case markers.
The following discussion therefore focuses on both categories. There are no
postpositions.
2.1.5.1. Inventory of prepositions and case markers
Like other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan has a comparatively small inventory of
forms that function as prepositions and case markers. For this reason, and because
most grammatical and semantic functions are encoded with prepositions and case
markers, each form has a broad range of functions, some of which are clearly related
to one another, while others are more loosely connected. The functions of all forms
are discussed at length in 2.1.1 and the extent to which they constitute a well defined
morphosyntactic class is discussed in 1.16.5. The following lists and cross-references
the various functions associated with each form. This description is necessarily
brief, and reference should be made to the relevant discussion for a fuller account
of the exact nature and range of each function. Furthermore, the categorization
provided here should not be taken to imply that each category is syntactically or
semantically distinct. Again, cases where this question is relevant are discussed in
the appropriate section.
The following overview covers morphologically simple prepositions, and only
treats overt forms, to the exclusion of ‘zero’ prepositional elements. Allomorphs,
where they exist, are not listed here. Forms that result from compounding or
derivation are discussed in 2.2.6.
(a) Case marker nee
The least multifunctional of all case markers, nee functions primarily as the ergative
case marker (2.1.1.2.2(a), (b), and (e)), as well as the marker of pseudoergative case
(2.1.3.1.3(d)).
(b) Case marker a
This case marker denotes either the absolutive case (2.1.1.2.1.1 and 2.1.1.2.4) or
contrastiveness (1.11.2.1.7), and often both at once. It is optional in most instances,
although it becomes obligatory or strongly preferred under certain circumstances,
particularly with the third-person singular pronoun or the interrogative word ai
‘who?’, and with nouns that lack an overt article (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1 and 2.1.2.6.1).
(c) Case marker ko
This case marker marks constituent focus (1.11.2.1.4) and subjects or predicates of
copular constructions (1.2.1.1.1(a) and 2.1.1.2.3). It also appears with object
complements (2.1.1.2.11) and qualification (2.1.1.4.31), and may mark a single noun
phrase or nominalized verb to emphasize the entire sentence (1.11.1.3.2–3). It is
often found in answers to yes-no questions (1.11.3).
(d) Preposition i
The primary function of i is to mark location at rest in space or time
(2.1.1.5.1(a) and 2.1.1.6.1), as well as nonlocal, local, and temporal source

middle objects (2.1.1.2.8(a)), objects of miscellaneous verbs (2.1.1.2.8(b)),
certain direct objects of nominalized verbs (2.1.1.3.4.5(d)), subjects of certain
experience clauses (2.1.1.2.1.2(b)), cause-target participants in cause-target

or parameters of equation in various equative constructions (1.9.1).

The primary meaning of ki is movement in space or time (2.1.1.5.1(b) and 2.1.1.6.1).
In some cases, it marks location at rest (2.1.1.5.1(a)). As a case marker, ki marks

2.1.5.2. Preposition-noun agreement
Prepositions do not systematically agree for any grammatical category with their
objects. However, the three most basic prepositions, namely i (location), ki
(direction), and mai (source), regardless of their grammatical or semantic function,
are obligatorily suffixed with a morpheme -aa or its allomorph -a when their
object falls into one of several categories. The long form of the suffix is used
when the following word consists of two morae or less, and the short form is
used elsewhere.
The suffix is required when the object of the preposition is a proper name with
a human referent, as illustrated in all examples provided so far. The suffix is generally
not used when the object of the preposition is a proper noun with a nonhuman
referent or a proper noun which is not a name. However, when a place name refers
to an entity of political import, and when this import is foregrounded in the situation
denoted by the sentence, the suffix must be used. Such is the case, for example,
when the place name refers to a nation or a government with volitional power,
which thus acquires anthropomorphic qualities:
(2839)
Falani ne takavale ia ai i ttaua teenaa?
France Pst defeated at who? at the+war that
‘Who defeated France in that war?’
(2840)
Teelaa laa, faipati Amelika kia Peletaania kee olo keaattea mo
then speak America to Britain Sbj go away from
Amelika.
America
‘So America spoke to Britain [and asked them] to leave America.’
The appropriate interrogative word in these contexts is the proper interrogative
word ai ‘who?’, as illustrated in and discussed in 2.1.2.6.1. The suffix is obligatory
with many pronouns (cf. 2.1.5.3) and with the interrogative word ai ‘who?’, whether
or not they refer to human or nonhuman entities (cf. 2.1.2.6.1). The suffix is also
obligatory when the object of the preposition is the name of a month (cf. 2.1.1.6.1).
It is optional with the numeral expression ttoko luaa ‘those two’ (cf. 2.1.6.5.1(a)) as
object. The suffix is optional when the object of the preposition is a proper name
marked with the group marker saa (or haa in the Nukulaelae dialect), which, as
discussed in 2.1.1.8.4–5, may be preposed to proper names and to a few other
nonproper noun phrases. For further discussion of -a(a), see 2.1.5.3.
2.1.5.3. Prepositions with pronominal objects
Prepositions do not combine morphologically with pronouns, although certain
unmarked usages of the anaphoric pronoun ei are equivalent to third-person
personal pronouns marked with the locative preposition i (cf. 2.1.2.1.7).
Two bound morphemes are associated with prepositions that have pronominal
objects. The first of these is the suffix -a(a), whose form and occurrence is discussed
in 2.1.5.2. The other bound morpheme of relevance is -te, which can also be suffixed
to prepositions with pronominal objects instead of -aa. This suffix differs from -aa
in several respects. First, it is archaic and is a strong index of linguistic conservatism.

It is much more current in the Northern dialects of Tuvaluan, and it also functions
as a regional dialect marker. Second, it can only appear when the object of the
preposition is a singular pronoun:
(2841)
Au ne fai atu kite koe kee saa vau koe.
I Pst say Dxs to you Sbj Neg come you
‘I told you not to come.’
Dual and plural pronouns cannot be marked with prepositions suffixed with -te.
Unlike -a(a), this suffix does not behave exceptionally with the first-person singular
personal pronoun. Third, the morpheme can be suffixed to any of the three
prepositions i, ki, and mai, but also, although much more rarely, to the prepositions
mo (accompaniment and miscellaneous objects), a (alienable possession), and o
(inalienable possession):
(2842)
Au koo ffiu mote koe!
I Inc tired with you
‘I am tired of you!’
The morpheme itself is rare enough in contemporary Tuvaluan, so that
occurrences of it with the three prepositions with which it appears less
commonly are extremely rare.
The two mutually exclusive morphemes -a(a) and -te must be analysed as suffixes,
rather than independent morphemes, because they are always treated by stress
placement as an integral part of the preposition. In contrast to their monomorphemic
equivalents, which are normally unstressed, the prepositions ia(a) and kia(a) receive
stress like regular words. (The preposition mai and its suffixed forms maia(a) are
stressed like regular words in all contexts.)
2.1.5.4. Prepositions and articles
Prepositions do not coalesce with articles to form prepositional articles. However,
when a single-mora preposition is followed by a single-mora article (e.g., the definite
singular article te, the indefinite singular article se, the indefinite plural article ne),
the preposition and the article are treated as a single-word unit for the purpose of
phonological stress assignment; hence stress falls on the preposition, which is the
penultimate syllable of the preposition-article string. Stress is indicated in the
following with acute accents:
(2843)
kí te úmu
to the cooking-hut
‘to the cooking hut’
(2844)
mó se kaafílo
with a fish-hook
‘with a fish-hook’
2.1.6. Numerals and quantifiers
Neither numerals nor quantifiers constitute a clearly recognizable morphosyntactic
category. In general, numerals behave like verbs. Quantifiers are drawn from a
variety of morphological classes. Numerals are discussed in 2.1.6.1–5, and
quantifiers in 2.1.6.6. For a discussion of quantifier float and quantifier raising,
two grammatical processes associated with the quantifier katoa ‘all’, see 1.14.1
and 1.14.2 respectively.

2.1.6.2. Cardinal numerals as predicates and attributes
All numeral forms used in counting (with the exception of toa ‘ten’) appear in

predicative and attributive positions. As predicates, numerals are indistinguishable
from predicative adjectives (cf. 2.1.4). As attributes, numerals may be either preposed
or postposed to the nouns they modify. In postposed position, they share many
features with relativized predicates; in preposed position, they lose most of their
verbal characteristics. In addition, some numerals can be used as adverbial modifiers
of verbs.
The following discussion of the structure of numerals, which focuses primarily
on ordinary numerals (i.e., numerals whose morphology is discussed in 2.1.6.1),
also applies to most specialized numerals (cf. 2.1.6.3), as the latter can also be used
either attributively, in either preposed or postposed position, or predicatively.
2.1.6.2.1. Predicative cardinal numerals
As predicates, numerals can be marked for any tense, aspect, or mood category,
and may be modified by any appropriate modifier:
(2857)
Vaitupu e lua ana ituuala.
Vaitupu Nps two its village-side
‘Vaitupu [has] two villages sides.’
(2858)
Koo iva nei ttou paala.
Inc nine now our-3-i kingfish
‘We[’ve caught] nine kingfish so far.‘
Like ordinary predicates, numerals can appear in all types of subordinate clause:
(2859)
Taumafai [kee afe au taalaa [e maua]].
try Sbj thousand your dollar Nps get
‘Try to earn one thousand dollars.’
Numerals used predicatively may undergo or govern any syntactic process
commonly associated with verbs. In particular, they may be nominalized, which is
the way in which ordinal constructions are formed (cf. 2.1.6.4).
When a predicative numeral is part of a measurement, the unit of measure usually
forms a verbal compound with the numeral, in which the unit comes last:
(2860)
E iva pauna te mmafa o te atu teenei.
Nps nine pound the weight of the bonito this
‘This bonito weighs nine pounds.’
If the numeral in a measurement is 1, the unit is marked with the singular definite
article te (or its allomorph t- or a singular definite possessive pronoun):
(2861)
Koo tasi nei toku tausaga i konei.
Inc one now my year at here
‘I’ve been here a year.’

the relative position of the numeral and the noun phrase it modifies.
Attributive cardinal numerals may be postposed to the nouns they modify.
Postposed numerals are marked with a morpheme e, which is homophonous with
the universal and nonpast tense-aspect-mood marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1), to which it is
very likely to be etymologically related. Under ordinary circumstances, this morpheme
cannot be deleted in postposed attributive cardinal constructions, a feature

denote the number of individuals involved in the event denoted by the verb:

as one’:

2.1.6.3. Specialized numerals
Tuvaluan has a relatively complex system of specialized numerals, used to count
animals, objects, and concepts of particular importance in Tuvaluan society and
culture. Native speakers recognize these numerals as a noteworthy area of language;
they are the subject of prescriptive discussions and are seen as an area of language
worth investigating. Yet there are idiolectal and dialectal variations in the form and
use of these numerals, particularly for the less common forms and in the formation
of complex expressions. Most of the data presented in this section were elicited on
Nukulaelae atoll, and differences in details may be encountered in other dialects of
Tuvaluan.
Specialized numerals are used in both cardinal and ordinal expressions, both in
counting and as attributes, and may be proposed or postposed like ordinary
numerals (cf. 2.1.6.2.3). Most are obligatory and in common usage in everyday
speech, and the system is by no means a prescriptively preserved system no longer
in common use. However, some forms (e.g., those associated with humans, bonitos,
reef fish, and coconuts) are more widely known and used than others (e.g., those
associated with birds, crabs, coconut-frond blinds, and footsteps). The following
excerpt from the transcript of an account of a fishing expedition illustrates the care

The form of some specialized numerals bears no resemblance to ordinary numerals
in contemporary Tuvaluan; such is the case, for example, of mattelau ‘one hundred
(reef fishes)’ and teaamoga ‘twenty (coconuts)’. However, most of these forms can
be related to either Proto-Polynesian reconstructions or words in contemporary
Tuvaluan whose meaning bears some relationship to the object being counted. Thus,
for instance, the Proto-Polynesian numeral *(te)lau is recognizable in the form
mattelau (the underlying form of the other morpheme in the word is mata, whose
literal meaning is ‘face, eye, front’), and teaamoga is undoubtedly related to the
noun aamoga ‘yoke used to carry a load of coconuts’, which is not surprising since
twenty coconuts is the load one can comfortably carry with a yoke. Many forms
have te as their first syllable (e.g., teaamoga, tekau, teaoa, tefua), which is a reflex of
the proto-article *te (the time depth of this article is subject to debate in Polynesian
comparative linguistics). However, it cannot be analysed as the contemporary
Tuvaluan singular definite article te (cf. 2.1.1.8.6) because the latter can modify
specialized numerals with te as their first syllable (in which case it is usually reduced
to t-; e.g., tteaamoga).
Other specialized forms are obtained by attaching a prefix or suffix to ordinary
numerals; for example, tolugapulupulu ‘thirty (coconuts)’ consists of the ordinary
numeral tolu ‘three’ and a suffix -gapulupulu, exclusively associated with counting
tens of coconuts. Another category consists of ordinary numerals modified by
classifier-like adverbial elements, most of which are preposed; an example is mata
lua ‘twenty (reef fish, swamp taro roots, taro roots, or gardenia flowers)’, in which
mata is probably related historically to mata ‘face, eye, front’, and lua is the
ordinary numeral ‘two’. These second and third types could thus be classified
under the rubric of ‘other derivatives of numerals’ (cf. 2.1.6.5). If a specialized
numeral system consists of a mixture of all three formal types, it is described in
this section, even though some of the specialized numerals are formed from
ordinary numerals. However, if a numeral system consists only of derived forms
(classifier-like elements or affixes), it is treated in section 2.1.6.5. The classifier-like

In general, specialized numerals have idiosyncratic forms. One category of
objects may thus be counted like a second category within a certain number
range, and like a third category within another number range. For example,
bonitos and bigeye tunas are counted by suffixing ordinary numerals with -gafua
in the range of 3 to 9, as are coconuts and birds. But the numeral referring to 20
tunas or bigeye bonitos is tekau, which is not used for any other object; and when
counting tens of such fish between 30 and 90, the adverb tino is preposed to
ordinary numerals (e.g., tino tolu ‘thirty (bonitos or bigeye tunas)’), a method also
used to count people and birds, but not coconuts (cf. tolugapulupu ‘thirty
(coconuts)’). Similarly, when counting bonitos in most idiolects, a different form is
used for the unit part of the numerals 12 and 22 (lua v. teaoa). Finally, certain
specialized numerals may be combined with ordinary numerals to form complex
numerals, while others can only be combined with other specialized numerals.
The form of specialized numerals presents a number of morphological (and
hence orthographic) problems. Which forms are to be considered bound
morphemes, and which are free morphemes? The restricted use of most
specialized numeral forms does not allow many of the substitutions and
permutations which one uses to answer this question in ordinary circumstances.
For the purpose of determining which morphemes are to be written as affixes and
which are to be written as separate words, I have used the following rule of
thumb: if a specialized numeral modifier can modify the interrogative word fia
‘how many’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.4(a)), this modifier is considered to be a free morpheme
and is written as a separate word. For example, tino ‘multiplicand by ten [for
humans]’ and mata ‘multiplicand by ten [for reef fish]’ can modify fia and are thus
considered to be independent words:
(2890)
Koo tino fia taatou?

‘How many tens of us are there?’
(2891)

ten how-many? your mullet
‘How many tens of mullets did you catch?’
In contrast, -gapulupulu ‘multiplicand by ten [for coconuts]’ cannot modify fia, and
thus it is written as a suffix.
In complex specialized numerals, one of two conjunctions, mo (cf. 1.3.1.3) and
maa, may appear between tens and units, hundreds and tens, and so on. The first of
these reduces to ma before words of more than two morae (this allomorphic variation
is not represented in the orthography used in this grammar). The distribution of
mo and maa overlaps to a certain extent. Both can be used in specialized numeral
expressions that function as verb or adjective, predicate or attribute:

2.1.6.4. Ordinal numerals
The same forms are used for cardinal and ordinal numerals. Both ordinary and
specialized forms can be used ordinally, although specialized forms are rarely
encountered as ordinal numerals in natural discourse. There are two ways of
constructing ordinal structures. See also 2.1.6.5.1(e) for the discussion of another
ordinal-like construction.
2.1.6.4.1. Nominalized numeral predicates as ordinal numerals
Ordinal numerals can be formed by nominalizing predicative numerals. The
numeral retains any adverb that may modify it as a predicate, and the construction
has all the characteristics of ordinary nominalized constructions (cf. 2.1.1.3.4 and
2.1.3.5). The quantified noun can be left unmarked for case, although it is more
commonly marked for inalienable possession with the possessive marker o, as are
subject arguments of many nominalized intransitive verbs:
(2930)
Ko te tolu teenei o aso o ttou maafutaga.
Foc the third this of day of our-3-i gathering
‘This is the third day that we have gathered together.’
(2931)
Koo faanau te toko lima o laa tama.
Inc born the Num five of their-2 child
‘Their fifth child was just born.’
Nominalized ordinal numerals function like ordinary noun phrases. They can be
marked for any case category and may fulfil any grammatical function commonly
associated with noun phrases.
2.1.6.4.2. Ordinal numerals marked with the preposition i
The second ordinal numeral construction is a nominalized form of the numeral
modified by the locative preposition i (cf. 2.1.1.5.1). The resulting prepositional
phrase modifies the noun being quantified:
(2932)
te tino i te toko tolu i te unu mua
the person at the Num three in the row front
‘the third person in the front row’
This construction derives from a postposed attributive cardinal-numeral
construction (cf. 2.1.6.2.2). For example, the ordinal phrase in the above example
derives from the following postposed attributive cardinal phrase:
(2933)

person Nps Num three
‘three people’
Ordinal-numeral structures marked with i do not differ in meaning from ordinal-
numeral structures described in 2.1.6.4.1. However, they are stylistically more formal,
and are preferred in idiomatically ‘fixed’ phrases like the following:
(2934)
te taua o te lalolagi i te lua

2.1.6.5. Other derivatives of numerals and related forms
Discussed here are modifiers of numerals that are not part of a specialized numeral
system (cf. 2.1.6.3) and lexemes frequently associated with numerals. Other
modifiers and affixes are discussed in 2.1.6.6. One preposed numeral modifier, hoko
‘exactly, even’, is found in the Nanumea and Nanumaga dialects of Northern
Tuvaluan, but does not have an equivalent in the Southern dialects.
2.1.6.5.1. Free modifiers of numerals
(a) Classifier-like toko for humans
As described in 2.1.6.3(a), the preposed classifier-like morpheme toko is obligatorily
preposed to ordinary numerals when they refer to humans. It appears in both
cardinal- and ordinal-numeral expressions, and with both preposed and postposed
numerals. The following illustrates its use with an ordinal numeral:
(2936)
te toeaina i te toko lua i te feituu ki tai
the old-man at the Num two at the side to lagoon
‘the second old man towards the lagoon’
It is optional with verbs like uke ‘many’, timomo ‘few’, and fia ‘how many’ (cf.
2.1.2.6.4(a)). When toko modifies a cardinal number in a postposed attributive
construction, the numeral morpheme e, which is ordinarily obligatory, becomes
optional (cf. 2.1.6.2.1).
When marked with toko, the numeral tasi ‘one’ may acquire the meaning of ‘by
oneself, independent(ly)’. Toko tasi can be used as either a regular numeral or an
adverb, and can refer to humans and nonhumans. Ordinary numerals between 2
and 9 preposed with toko may be used as independent nouns in an idiomatic
expression roughly translatable as ‘these/those N’. It is most common with lua
‘two’ and the last vowel of the numeral is usually (but not obligatorily) geminated
(cf. 2.1.1.12.1(b)). The expression ttoko luaa ‘those two’ behaves like a proper noun
in one respect, i.e., in the form of the more common prepositions when they take
the expression as object (cf. 2.1.5.2).
(b) Classifier-like tua and tao
The classifier-like morphemes tua and tao may be preposed to ordinary numerals
(usually between 1 and 9) or to the interrogative word fia ‘how many’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.4(a))
when counting or referring to a wide range of objects and concepts. All speakers
agree that tua (from Proto-Polynesian *tuqa ‘turn’) may be used for flat objects that
are commonly piled up (e.g., clothing, mats, roofing, waves) or for strands in sennit,
braiding, or rope:
(2937)

‘[She] is wearing four layers of clothing.’

2.1.6.6. Quantifiers
Quantifiers do not form a unified morphological category. Some are verbs, while
others are best described as adverbs, affixes, or articles. The following discussion is
organized by morphological category: quantifying verbs are covered in 2.1.6.6.1,
quantifying adverbs in 2.1.6.6.2, preposed noun modifiers in 2.1.6.6.3, and 2.1.6.6.4
describes the quantifier soo ‘any’, which is preposed to full noun phrases. For a
discussion of the numeral modifiers ta- and uta-, which have quantifier-like
properties, see 2.1.6.5.2(c), and for a description of nonreferential final-vowel
gemination, whose function overlaps with those of certain quantifiers, see 2.1.1.12.

2.1.6.6.3. Quantifying preposed noun modifiers
This section describes various quantifiers that are preposed to nouns. Some either
take the place of or combine with articles, while others occur between articles and
the head of the noun phrase.
(a) naai ‘a little, a few’
The preposed noun modifier naai denotes a small quantity or number, and usually
translates as ‘a little, a bit of, a few, a piece of’. It marks both uncountable and
countable nouns in the plural, which can be marked for indefiniteness with the
plural indefinite article ne or for definiteness with a zero article. There is no clear
difference in meaning between the two options:

(e) kau ‘group, multitude’
When preposed to the head of a noun phrase (usually singular), this morpheme
has a variety of meanings depending on the context. In its productive use as a
quantifier, it is preposed to a nominal descriptor of a type of person to denote a
group characterized by the descriptor. Thus preposing kau to toeaina ‘old man, elder’
yields te kau toeaina ‘(the) older men, (the) elders’. Nouns denoting islands or nations
are frequently modified by kau, e.g., te kau Saamoa ‘(the) Samoans’ and te kau
Nukufetau ‘Nukufetau (Islanders)’.

for example, te kau vvale ‘the drunks’ (from vale ‘drunk’) and te kau faagota ‘the

and the resulting string is always a noun. These characteristics suggest that kau is
the head noun.

2.1.7. ADVERBS
As discussed in 1.2.1.3.1.1, adverbs form a heterogeneous word class, and in many
cases there is a tendency for ‘adverbial’ notions to be expressed in the main verb of
the clause, rather than with adverbial modifiers. This feature is specially relevant
to the discussion of comparison and degree of quality in sections 2.1.7.1 and 2.1.7.2
respectively.

as an adverb in the following:

2.2. DERIVATIONAL MORPHOLOGY
Generally speaking, derivational morphology in Tuvaluan is relatively restricted,
a characteristic that is directly related to the propensity for words to appear in
diverse morphosyntactic frames, particularly nominal and verbal, without
undergoing any changes in their internal structure (cf. 1.16). Most structure-altering
morphological processes in the language have been described elsewhere in the
grammar. The following discussion cross-references these discussions and describes
morphological processes not covered elsewhere.
It is important to distinguish true derivational morphological processes, which
are productive and whose effect on meaning is predictable, from homophony, which
can be of two major types. First, two words can be homophonous because they
derive synchronically from the same root, even though one word is not derivable
from the other through a productive morphological process. Such is the case of
ttogi ‘pay’ and ‘price’, since the relationship between the meaning of the verb and
noun forms does not conform to any pattern at play elsewhere in the lexicon. Second,
‘chance’ homophony describes sets of genuinely unrelated words that are
nevertheless identical in form. An illustration is laa ‘sail’, laa ‘sun’, laa ‘their-2, they
[clitic]’, laa ‘letter L’, laa ‘musical note A’, laa ‘downtoning adverb’. Chance
homophony is common because the language has a restricted phonemic inventory
and a highly constraining phonotactic structure. One can also include in this category
forms that may have been historically related but can no longer be analysed as
such. For example, it is possible that motu ‘islet’ and motu ‘broken, discontinuous’
were related to one another in some manner at some stage in the history of the
language, since islets are often talked about as pieces of land ‘broken up’ by the
sea. However, these forms cannot be derived from one another synchronically, and

the fact that these two particular forms can be reconstructed for Proto-Polynesian
with both meanings indicate that if derivation is involved it must predate Proto-

Further problems are encountered in distinguishing derivational morphology
from compounding morphology. As traditionally defined, derivational morphology
produces new words by affixing bound morphemes to existing roots (and perhaps
modifying the internal form of existing roots), while compounding morphology
produces new words by juxtaposing free lexemes either linearly or hierarchically.
The distinction thus assumes that one can easily decide whether a particular
morpheme is bound or free. In Tuvaluan, this decision is not always simple. Take
for example the morpheme gaati, which means ‘coconut meat lining the inside wall
of the nut’ when used as a free morpheme. When preposed to certain lexemes, it
can also mean ‘empty X’ where X is the meaning of the lexeme, as in gaati vakalele
‘empty airplane’, gaati pookesi ‘empty box’, or metaphorically ‘worthless’ (e.g., gaati
taaofi ‘worthless opinion’). There is a clear metaphorical connection between the
meaning of gaati as a free lexeme and in compounds, but it is unclear whether the
two meanings are sufficiently different that two separate words should be posited,
one free and one bound, or whether they retain enough semantic similarity to posit
a single lexeme with two different meanings. In the first instance, the formation of
compounds with gaati is part of derivational morphology, while it is a compounding
process in the second instance.
In the following discussion, I take a conservative approach, and discuss only
processes that are unproblematically derivational in nature, thus relegating
compounding processes like those with gaati to a study of the lexicon. In 2.2.6.3, I
overview one compounding process that affects the internal structure of the
compounded elements, one compounding process that affects the morphological
classification of the compound, and one related aspect of word morphology, namely
collocationally restricted modifiers.
2.2.1. Nouns from other categories
2.2.1.1. Nouns from nouns
There are no productive derivational processes that create nouns from other nouns.
Among unproductive processes is a prefix gaa-, which can be attached to a closed
set of words, namely uta ‘land, bush’, tai ‘sea, lagoon’, loto ‘village’ (in its primary
meaning, ‘centre’), mua ‘public arena’ (in its primary meaning, ‘front’, and
metaphorically ‘front part of a village, where power resides’), and muli ‘private
arena’ (in its primary meaning, ‘backside’). The prefixed words fall into two semantic
categories: gaauta, gaatai, and gaaloto all mean ‘in the direction of X, around X’,
where X is the meaning of the unprefixed form; and gaamua and gaa-muli are strictly
speaking nouns but are rarely used unless prefixed with faka- ‘in the manner of (cf.
2.2.2.1.3), which transforms the words into adverbs or verbs with the specialized
meaning of ‘(act) for the interest of the community’ and ‘(act) for one’s own or
one’s family’s interest’. The forms gaauta, gaatai, and gaaloto only appear in
prepositional phrases, and they behave like local nouns, i.e., they are inherently
plural and do not take an article (cf. 2.1.1.8.2). There is little difference in meaning
between them and local uses of the equivalent unprefixed forms, although the
prefixed form is a little more vague:
(3042)
Koo fano ki (gaa)uta.

‘[He] went to(wards) the bush.’

fakatuagaene ‘cousin of opposite gender’ from tuagaene ‘sibling of opposite gender’)
and verbs denoting ‘related as an X’:
(3056)
Au e fakatuagaene ki ei.
I Nps in-manner-of+sibling to Anp
‘I am her cousin.’
For a discussion of the quirky behaviour of fakafa(a)fine ‘act feminine’ and fakata(a)gata
‘act masculine’, see 2.1.1.8.3.
Finally, faka- can turn certain nouns denoting institutions or abstract
concepts into verbs, verbal adjectives, and adverbs, but requires that a definite
singular article te appear before the noun. The result can roughly translate as
‘pertain(ing) to X’, where X is the meaning of the noun. Examples are faka-te-
maaloo ‘pertain to the government’, faka-te-fono-pule ‘pertain to the Island
Council’, faka-te-maneapa ‘pertain to the maneaba’ (i.e., the Council of Elders,
customs and traditions), faka-te-lalolagi ‘pertain to the sacred’ (cf. lalolagi
‘heaven’), in opposition to faka-te-foitino ‘pertain to the body’. With a few
nouns, the article is optional, with no precise effect on meaning, e.g., fakafenua
or faka-te-fenua ‘pertain to the island community’; none of the previous
examples can appear without an article.
2.2.2.1.4. mau ‘constantly, plentiful’
This morpheme can be preposed to verbs and nouns alike to derive verbs that
denote the prolonged nature of a situation, or the continuous presence or abundance
of something. Examples are: mau tino ‘always frequented by people’ derives from
tino ‘person’, mau uttanu ‘(of a person or place) with abundant germinated nuts’
from uttanu ‘germinated coconuts’, and mau masaki ‘sickly’ from masaki ‘ill’. One
compound, maumea ‘wealthy’, from mea ‘thing’, has been relexicalized. Mau is
occasionally used as a independent noun, verb, or adverb:

2.2.2.2. Verbs from verbs
Relevant to this discussion is the unproductive prefix ma- ‘capable of’ discussed in
2.1.3.4.7.
2.2.2.2.1. Approximative faka-
As shown in 2.1.3.1.3(a), the primary function of faka- is to form causative verbs, a
function which can be viewed as a derivational process. In addition, faka- can be
prefixed to verb roots and results in giving an approximative meaning to the word
(‘sort of, as if’). From gasuke ‘move’, for example, can be derived fakagasuke ‘sort of
move’, from tipa ‘take a step’ fakatipa ‘(look) as if one is taking a step’, and from
ppusa ‘blister(ed)’ fakappusa ‘on its way to blistering, look blistered’. Only verbs
that can take the causative faka- can be prefixed with this other meaning of faka-,
which suggests that the two functions of the prefix may be related.
The prefix faka- is also involved in deriving verbs in its multiplicative function
with numerals (cf. 2.1.6.5.2(a)).
2.2.2.2.2. -goofie ‘readily’ and -gataa ‘not readily’
The two suffixes -goofie and -gataa denote respectively the ease and difficulty with
which a situation is brought about, or the high and low incidence or frequency of a
situation. They may be attached to a wide variety of forms, although they are not
productive enough to be suffixed to borrowings. They may be suffixed to intransitive
verbs:
(3060)
Ko ia loo koo konaagoofie.
Foc he indeed Inc drunk+readily
‘He gets very easily drunk.’
(3061)
Seeai se tamaliki e kaugataa peelaa!
Neg a child Nps partake+not-readily thus
‘She’s the most disobedient of children!’
It may also be affixed to transitive verbs; however, the result is an intransitive verb,
which takes as its argument the direct object of the transitive verb from which the
verb is derived:
(3062)
Koe naa koo mateagataa i ou gatu konaa.
you that Inc recognize+not-readily in your clothing those
‘You are difficult to recognize in those clothes.’

The two suffixes thus follow an ergative-absolutive pattern, in which subjects of
intransitive verbs and direct objects form a unified category in opposition to subjects
of transitive verbs. The noun phrase that functions as the subject of a transitive
verb and as the experiencer of the suffixed form of the verb may be expressed as a
locatively marked oblique modifier of the suffixed verb:
(3063)
Te kao teenei koo inugataa i au.
the sour-toddy this Inc drink+not-readily at I
‘That sour toddy is nearly undrinkable to me.’
Some verbs acquire a specialized meaning when suffixed with either suffix. Such is
the case of kau ‘partake (in a group activity)’, which, when suffixed with -goofie or
-gataa, means ‘obedient’ and ‘disobedient’ respectively (e.g., (3061)). The unsuffixed
and suffixed forms are closer in meaning in Tuvaluan than in English, in that work
is almost always communal in Tuvaluan society (and hence involves ‘partaking’)
and because ‘obedience’ is mostly equated with one’s willingness to perform tasks
for the community. The form -gataa only can be suffixed directly onto the
unproductive past suffix ana- (cf. 2.1.1.6.4), and the result, anagataa, means ‘long
lasting’. Suffixing the polysemic verb fai ‘do, make’ gives rise to the forms faigoofie
and faigataa, with the general meaning of ‘easy’ and ‘difficult’ respectively which
can govern raising (cf. 1.1.2.7).
All forms in -gataa undergo subject-verb agreement controlled by the subject as
with other noncausative agreeing verbs. Agreement is marked by applying partial
internal reduplication to the suffix, which becomes -gaattaa. The verb root remains
unchanged, even if it has an agreement form (cf. 2.1.3.6.1). Thus inugataa ‘difficult
to drink’, which is derived from inu ‘drink’ (plural form, iinu), takes on an agreement
form inugaattaa. In contrast, -goofie does not have a plural form, and blocks subject-
verb agreement. Thus forms suffixed with -goofie are invariable.
The suffix -gataa is roughly equivalent in meaning to some uses of a preposed
verb-modifying adverb fui ‘not readily, slow in, difficult to’:
(3064)
Te ika teelaa e fui maua i koga konei.

‘That fish is rarely caught in these areas.’
This adverb does not affect the valency of the verb.
2.2.2.2.3. taka- ‘around, all over’
This relatively unproductive prefix can be attached to certain verbal roots to denote
circular movement or the indiscriminate repetition of the situation, not unlike
metaphorical uses of ‘around’ in English. For example, takatipa ‘stagger around’ is
derived from tipa ‘take a step’, takatuutuu ‘stand around’ from tuu ‘stand’, and
takafiatoa ‘go around acting defiantly’ from fia ‘pretend to be’ (cf. 2.1.3.4.15) and toa
‘courageous, warlike, defiant’. When it is prefixed to verbs that already denote
circular movement, taka- denotes repetition, emphasis, or both, as in takammio ‘twist
around’ from mmio ‘twist’, and takannimo ‘completely dizzy’, from nnimo ‘dizzy’.
The prefix also appears with roots that are not attested in unprefixed form in the
contemporary language, e.g., takafili ‘roll over’ (cf. Proto-Polynesian *fili ‘turn, roll’),
takapili ‘move around, (of the wind) shift direction’, and takalialia ‘have aversion,
disgusted’ (cf. fakalialia ‘demented’). The prefixed form and the root sometimes
have different, although not unrelated, meanings, as is the case of takaseesee ‘stagger
around’ from ssee ‘err’, and takavale ‘defeated’ from vale ‘unsocialized’ (which appears

2.2.2.2.4. Miscellaneous bound morphemes
Mention should be made of an unproductive set of prefixes that may have been
involved historically in the derivation of certain verbs from other verbs. These
morphemes are recognizable as the first element in certain words, and can take on
the forms ga-, pa-, or to-. Some prefixed forms are the stative equivalent of the
unprefixed form, which suggests that these prefixes may have been allomorphs of
the stativizing ma- (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(e)) at some point in the history of the language.
Possible examples include: galue ‘shake, oscillate’ from lue ‘shake’, galulu ‘tremble’
(cf. luuluu ‘shake’); gaofe ‘bent’ from ofe ‘bend, force’; pakini (also makini) ‘fast’, perhaps
related to kini ‘strike’; palele ‘run out’, perhaps related to lele ‘run’; patoo ‘produce
crashing sound’, perhaps related to too ‘fall’, tafiti ‘wrestle’, perhaps related to fiti
‘struggle’; tafuli ‘hurry along’, perhaps related to fuli ‘chase’; and tatoo ‘slope down’,
perhaps related to too ‘fall’.
2.2.2.3–4. Verbs from adjectives and adverbs
Verbal adjectives behave like regular verbs with respect to derivational morphology.
Verbs are not generally derived from adverbs, although the observations made in
1.2.1.3.1.1 regarding the propensity for adverbial notions to be expressed as verbs
are of relevance here.
2.2.2.5. Verbs from interjections
The multifunctional prefix faka- can be attached to a conventionalized rendition of
many interjections to denote ‘produce the interjection X’. By ‘conventionalized
rendition’ I mean that the interjection is phonological and suprasegmentally
regularized, i.e., its form is made to conform to the phonological structure of words
if it does not already do so, alternative forms are usually conflated into one standard
form, and it is stripped of exclamatory intonation. Thus io ‘all right, yes’ produces
fakaioio ‘to keep on agreeing by saying “io”’, while a whistle gives rise to fakasii
‘produce a whistle’:
(3065)
Seki fakataalofa mai ki au.
Neg utter-interjection+hello Dxs to I
‘[She] never said hello to me.’
(3066)
E fakasii mai kee fanatu koe.
Nps utter-interjection+Itj Dxs Sbj go you
‘[He] is whistling (hither) [to you] for you to come over.’
2.2.3. Adjectives from other categories
For the derivation of nominal adjectives from nouns and that of verbal adjectives
from verbs, see 1.16.4. Adjectives cannot be derived from adverbs.

2.2.6. Compounding
Sections 2.2.6.1 and 2.2.6.2 are concerned with prepositions, while 2.2.6.3 covers
compound morphology.
2.2.6.1. Complex prepositions
Complex prepositions form a heterogeneous class, loosely defined by the fact
that they take noun phrases as objects, they are syntagmatically incompatible
with other prepositions, and they are formed by compounding simple
prepositions or case markers with lexical elements. The following discussion
covers all prepositions considered to be complex or derived in this grammar;
other compounds in the language could also be considered to be complex
prepositions by another analyst.
2.2.6.1.1. Two prepositions
The only prepositions that can occur in sequence are the two prepositions denoting
nonlocal or local source, mai and i ‘from’ (cf. 2.1.1.4.2 and 2.1.1.5.1). The compound
mai i does not differ in meaning from either mai or i, although it tends to be more
characteristic of careful language. For examples of its use in various contexts, see
2.1.1.4.2 and 2.1.1.5.1.
2.2.6.1.2. Nominal formations
Complex local prepositions are made up of three elements. The first is a preposition,
which may be i for location at rest, ki for direction, and mai for source (see 2.1.1.5.1
for a more detailed characterization). The second is an unmarked noun in the plural,
from an inventory of so-called ‘local nouns’ provided in 2.1.1.5(c), or the particle
loo, which denotes object of comparison (cf. 2.1.1.2.6). The third is either the locative
preposition i or the inalienable possessive preposition o; no difference in meaning
is attached to the use of one or the other, although syntactic differences emerge in
certain contexts (cf. 1.2.1.1.3). Sentences and phrases with complex prepositions
are provided in 2.1.1.5(c) and throughout section 2.1.1.5.

Arguments for treating local nouns, i.e., the middle component of complex

as an independent word.
Local nouns may be modified by noun modifiers like ordinary nouns, although
only monolexemic modifiers are allowed, and only those with a more ‘grammatical’

local noun, also often occur as full prepositional phrases without a modifier. Such
instances can simply be analysed by treating the local noun as the object of the
preposition:

Among the local nouns, luga ‘top, up’ occupies a special place because it can appear

2.2.6.3. Compound morphology
Whether Tuvaluan has compounds is a complex question, because at first blush
most candidates resemble regular head-modifier structures. For example, the string
fulu mata ‘eyebrow’ could be taken as a compound, although in many respects fulu
‘hair’ behaves like the head of a noun phrase and mata ‘eye area’ as a nominal
adjective, and the morphological behaviour and structure of the string appear to be
no different from the morphological behaviour and structure of other strings made
up of a noun modified by a nominal adjective. Thus, according to this analysis, fulu
mata would deserve special consideration in a bilingual dictionary because its
translation into a foreign language such as English is not straightforwardly
retrievable from the structure of the Tuvaluan compound; however, but it would
not require special consideration in a monolingual dictionary.
Deciding whether a string constitutes a compound or an ordinary head and
modifier depends first on the extent to which the elements undergo formal changes,
second on the extent to which the string behaves like a single unit, and third on the
extent to which the meaning of the string is retrievable from the meaning of its
elements. The third criterion is the least reliable, both in Tuvaluan and
crosslinguistically. It works well in extreme cases, i.e., when the meaning of the
compound is very different or very similar to the sum of the meaning of its parts,
but does not work well in most cases, such as that of fulu mata ‘eyebrow’, as
arguments could be presented in support of either analysis.
The relevance of the first criterion to Tuvaluan morphology is limited by the fact
that, for the most part, no morphological changes occur in the formation of what
may turn out to be compounds (but see 2.2.6.3.2 for an exception). The second
criterion is the most useful. The string fulu mata, it turns out, behaves like a single
morphosyntactic unit, rather than a noun-modifier string, in several respects. In
1.2.5.3, I mention that a noun can only have one nominal adjective, one verbal
adjective, or one of both, and two verbal adjectives if one of them is a colour term.
In these respects, fulu mata behaves exactly like an ordinary noun:
(3076)
fulu mata lapa ‘plastic eyebrow’ (lapa ‘plastic’)
fulu mata loi ‘false eyebrow’ (loi ‘false’)
fulu mata uusi loi ‘dark-coloured false eyebrows’ (uusi ‘dark’)

compounding element is suffixed with a linking bound morpheme. Another,
covered in 2.2.6.3.3, generates verbs and verbal adjectives from noun-verb pairs.
Lastly, section 2.2.6.3.4 is concerned with collocational restrictions between certain

2.2.6.3.1. Noun-noun pairing with productive first element
Among the more systematic patterns of noun compounding emerges a pairing
mechanism involving two nominal lexemes, the first of which has a generic meaning
that refers commonly to a shape or other qualitative or quantitative feature. The
resulting compound denotes a unit of the referent of the second noun, a component
of it, or a specific manifestation of it. For example, the semi-productive lau, which
means ‘leaf’ as an independent lexeme, compounds with nouns referring to objects
that come in flat surfaces, leaves, or layers:
(3080)
lau gatu ‘yardage of cloth’ (gatu ‘cloth’)
lau pepa ‘sheet of paper’ (pepa ‘paper’)
lau kaapa ‘sheet of corrugated iron’ (kaapa ‘tin, corrugated iron’)

2.2.6.3.2. Noun compounds with linker -a-
The morpheme -a- functions as linking device between pairs of lexemes of different
types. The first element of such pairs can sometimes function as an independent
lexeme in other contexts without -a- and sometimes not, and the second element is
always attested elsewhere as an independent morpheme. The compound functions
as a noun, although with certain first elements it has peculiar characteristics, which
are described elsewhere (cf. 1.15.2).
I write the linker as an interfix because it clearly functions as a suffix to the first
element of the compound (for example, stress assignment treats -a- as an integral
part of the first element), but the suffixed first part cannot occur without the second
part of the compound. For example, the compound vaegaa ika ‘type of fish’ is made
up of vaega ‘type’, the linker -a-, and ika ‘fish’. While vaega does occur by itself as an
noun, vaegaa- never does without another noun following it, with which it forms a
compound. Furthermore, nothing can occur between the first and second elements
of compounds, except when the first element is tamaa- ‘tiny’, in which case a
diminutive intensifier lee can intervene between the two components of the
compound (cf. 1.4.7(g)). The other meaning of tamaa-, i.e., ‘young of’, does not allow
this intensifier.
Whether a particular compounding pattern takes a linker or not depends in
part on the phonological structure of the first element of the compound and in part
on the semantics of both the first element and of the entire compound. First, the
first element always ends in/a/. However, some compounds whose first element
ends in/a/do not take a linker, such as compounds with matua ‘prototypical’ as a
first element (e.g., matua pulaka ‘main part of the swamp taro corm’, as opposed to
a shoot, matua atu ‘prototypical bonito’, as opposed to a nonprototypical subspecies).
Second, the first element denotes a generic notion, such as a type, a particular aspect,
an instance, a component, or the evaluative assessment of an instance of the referent

while fuagaa- ‘seed of’ denotes a component of the referent of the noun that follows,
but *tamaa faivaa laakau ‘tiny superb plant’ is not because both tamaa- and faivaa-
‘superb’ denote evaluative assessments.
Many compounds have been relexicalized, in the sense that their meaning (either
primary or derived) is no longer retrievable in a straightforward manner from the
meaning of its parts:

‘front’)
fogaa tala ‘glans penis’ (fogaa- ‘top surface of’, tala ‘thorn’)
fatugaa ika ‘large school of deep-sea fish’ (ika ‘fish’)
The component fatugaa- is only found in two other compounds semantically
unrelated to the last compound, namely fatugaa lima ‘wrist’ and fatugaa vae ‘ankle’.
Similarly, fuagaa laakau ‘seed’ has a secondary meaning, ‘(medicinal) pill’, which is
obviously related metaphorically to its primary meaning. In addition, a significant
number of compounds that have the structure of such compounds are actually
borrowings from Samoan, where a similar process is at work. These compounds
have been borrowed as whole words, and I write them as single words. They should
not be analysed as compounds in Tuvaluan, even though their components often
resemble or are identical to compounding components in Tuvaluan. Such is the
case of mataaupu ‘lesson, subject’, tuulaafono ‘law’, taulaaitu ‘spirit medium, (pre-
Christian) priest’, and toogaalaa ‘sunset, west’.
Compounds with linkers can be classified roughly into three categories on the
basis of productivity and of the nature of the first element. In the first type fall
compounds whose first element is a nominal lexeme, with which compounding is
productive, in the sense that any semantically appropriate noun can function as
the second element. In this category fall compounds with tamaa- ‘young of, tiny’
from tama ‘child’ and vaegaa- ‘type of’ from vaega ‘type’ (in subsequent examples,
components are provided in parentheses only if the meaning of the compound
diverges significantly):
(3086)

tamaa tagata ‘tiny man’
tamaa paatulee ‘tiny battery’
vaegaa maaloo ‘type of government’
vaegaa manu ‘type of bird’

The first element does not necessarily occur as an independent lexeme or, if it does,
its meaning in the contemporary language is not always straightforwardly related
to the meaning it has in compounds. For example, tinaa- ‘basic instance of, prototype

opaque (however, reflexes of Proto-Polynesian *faiwa in other Polynesian languages
often denote prized activities and objects, e.g., Tongan faiva ‘traditional dance
performance’).
Some collocational restrictions are encountered. For example, fuaa- and fuagaa-
both compound with plant names, among others, and denote fruits and nuts. Some
plant names, such as mei ‘breadfruit’, can take either (fuaa mei or fuagaa mei ‘breadfruit

‘bunch’ (fui fala ‘pandanus nut’) also found in fui niu ‘bunch of coconuts together,
bunch of ten coconuts tied together by a human’.
In the second type of compounds, the first element is a nominal entity (i.e., a
noun, nominalized verb, or noun-like lexeme) that can only be compounded with
a restricted range of second elements. Frequently, the meaning of the compound is
idiosyncratically related to the meaning of its components. For example, alaa-, related
to ala ‘path, way’, is only found in the first two compounds below, muaa-, related to
mua ‘front’, in the next two, and lapalapaa- and gaugaa- do not have any meaning

alaa vaka ‘waterway’ (vaka ‘canoe, ship’)

gaugaa leo ‘intonation, accent’ (leo ‘voice’)

2.2.6.3.3. Verbal noun-adjective compounds
What I call ‘verbal noun-adjective compounds’ consist of a noun which denotes a
body part (e.g. gutu ‘mouth (area)’, mata ‘eye (area)’, lima ‘arm, hand’, vae ‘leg,
foot’), a centre of cognition or of emotion (e.g. loto ‘heart’, manava ‘breath’), or the
product of a mental or body function (e.g. leo ‘voice’, pati ‘word’), modified by an
adjective or verb denoting a quality or activity associated with the body part or
function denoted by the first element. The noun usually isn’t an argument of the
adjective or verb:
(3092)
leo saauaa ‘verbally brutal’ (saauaa ‘brutal’)
mata faanoanoa ‘sad looking’ (faanoanoa ‘sad’)

loto alofa ‘empathetic’ (alofa ‘feel empathy’)

These compounds tend to denote characterizing traits. For example, someone is
said to ppelo ‘lie’ if he or she is caught lying once, but someone who is gutu ppelo is
a habitual liar. The entire compound behaves like a verb or verbal adjective.
Although the types of first elements described above are the most common,
verbal noun-adjective compounds can be formed with other types of first elements.
In a nutshell, nouns that refer to any salient characteristic of an entity can function
as the first element, particularly if the second element is a numeral or the
interrogative word fia ‘how many?’ (e.g., manuao tila tolu ‘three-mast warship’, taa
tili ono ‘six-net fish-drive’).
Verbal noun-adjective compounds function like regular verbal adjectives, and
the characteristics of verbal adjectives discussed elsewhere all apply to them (cf.
1.2.2, 1.2.5.2.1, 1.16.4, and 2.1.4). In particular, they can function as either predicates
or attributes (cf. 2.1.4.1). The peculiar patterns of agreement associated with them
are discussed in 2.1.4.3.1(c). These compounds are often used to denote a
circumstance, quality, and manner (cf. 2.1.1.4.5). Colour terms often take the form
of verbal noun-adjective compounds (cf. 5.1.2).
2.2.6.3.4. Collocationally restricted modifiers
While not compounds in the strict sense of the term, certain pairs of adjectives and
modifiers are collocationally restricted, in the sense that the modifier only appears
with one adjective, or at most a handful of adjectives. In a number of such cases,
the modifier is an intensifier which can be used as or is related to a word that can be
used as an independent word with a meaning comparable to that of the adjective,
and is often a reduplicated form. Such is the case of gapelepele ‘to the brim’, which
can modify sua ‘(of the tide, etc.) full’ or ffonu ‘(of a container, etc.) full’,
morphologically related to apele or gapele ‘very full’. Alternatively, maligiligi, related

3.1. PHONOLOGICAL UNITS
Like most other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan has relatively few distinctive
phonological units in its phonemic inventory. However, both consonant and vowel
geminates are attested in the language, in contrast to most closely related languages,
in which only vowels can be geminated.

3.1.2.1. Nonsyllabics
The language has three plosives, no affricate, three or four fricatives depending on
the dialect, three nasals, and one liquid.
3.1.2.1.1. Plosives and affricates
The three plosives/p t k/are voiceless and, when ungeminated, unaspirated. In
their citation form, they are labio-labial, apico-alveolar, and dorso-velar respectively.
There is little variation in their place of articulation, although/k/is sometimes
realized as a dorso-uvular in casual speech. Also in casual contexts, all three plosives
may be slightly voiced, and occasionally emerge as voiceless or slightly voiced

3.1.2.1.3. Nasals
The three nasals are/m ng/, labio-labial, apico-dental, and dorso-velar voiced
segments respectively. No significant pattern of articulatory variation is associated
with these segments.
3.1.2.1.4. Liquids
The liquid, transcribed here as/l/, is a voiced lateral segment in the Funafuti,
Vaitupu, and Nukufetau dialects, and either a voiced lateral or a tap in the
Nukulaelae dialect. The variation between the two articulations in the latter is
governed by similar sociolinguistic patterns to those described for/h/in 3.1.2.1.2.
In addition, a following high front vowel tends to favour its realization as a tap.
3.1.2.1.5. Glides
There are no glides in the language, although unstressed vowels in certain vowel
sequences are realized as glides (cf. 3.3.2.4).
3.1.2.2. Syllabics
The only syllabic segments are vowels, which number five:/i e a o u/. These
segments are normally realized as cardinal vowels. There is very little variation in
phonetic realization, except that/e o/can be slightly lowered when a stressed/ a/
either precedes or follows.
3.1.2.3. Segments restricted to loanwords
No segment is restricted to loanwords. The form of all loanwords from Samoan and
Gilbertese have been adapted to conform to Tuvaluan phonology. English is the only
language from which new borrowings are currently being introduced into the
language. There is a certain amount of variation in the extent to which borrowings
from English are phonologically adapted to the phonological and phonotactic structure
of Tuvaluan. The more established and conventionalized the loanword is as a lexical
item of the language, the more likely its phonological structure will have been adapted.
Newer and less integrated loanwords may be pronounced differently by different
speakers, depending on their competence in English.
3.1.2.4. Segments restricted to particular word classes
The only pattern of restriction attested is that associated with the occurrence of/
h/in the Nukulaelae dialect (cf. 3.1.2.1.2).
3.2. PHONOTACTICS
Tuvaluan resembles most other Polynesian languages in allowing only open
syllables and disallowing consonant clusters. Vowel sequences, however, are
theoretically unrestricted.

3.2.1. Restrictions on consonants
Word-final consonants are not attested. Word-initial consonants are allowed, and
all consonants may occur in word-initial position.
3.2.2. Consonant clusters
There are no consonant clusters in any position, other than geminated consonants,
which can be analysed as sequences of identical consonants (cf. 3.4.4.1).
3.2.3. Restrictions on vowels
All five vowels and their geminate counterparts may occur in word-final, word-
initial, and word-medial positions. All vowels can also occur in sequence and all
possible sequences of two vowels are attested. Three-vowel clusters are less
frequent and not all possibilities are attested with equal frequency. For example,
/ aua/is a frequent cluster, but/aio/occurs only in a few words (e.g., maio ‘strut’,
aaioo ‘Island Executive Officer’, from English ‘I.E.O.’), and/eua/and/uau/are not
attested. No obvious pattern can predict which clusters are attested and which
are not. There are very few four-vowel clusters (e.g., taeao ‘morning’, aoao ‘lay
preacher’, a borrowing from Samoan, uaea ‘wire’, a borrowing from English) and
probably only two five-vowel clusters, eiauee and oiauee ‘interjection of sorrow or
pain’ (cf. 4.2).
3.2.4. Phonotactic structure of lexical morphemes
Morphemes and words have the same phonotactic structure, with the marginal
exception of a handful of exclamations (cf. 4.2) and morphemes whose phonological

sensitive to word-internal morpheme boundaries (e.g., vowel deletion in the
formation of geminate consonants, described in 3.4.4.1). The most common

3.2.5. Syllables
Syllables are not analytically relevant to the language, in that no phonological process
refers to the syllable structure of words.
3.2.6. Segmental harmony and other sequential restrictions
There is no vowel or consonant harmony in the language. The only restriction on
the sequencing of a consonant and vowel is the fact that the sequence/vu/is
unattested (other than in borrowed place names, e.g., Viti Levu ‘main island of
Fiji’), and that the sequence/vo/is found in only one lexeme, vvolu ‘(of one’s face)
red from exposure or intense emotion’ (cf. 5.1.2.2.4). Whether this word is a
borrowing or not is unknown. The restriction on the occurrence of/v/before back
vowels has a historical explanation: Tuvaluan/v/is a reflex of a Proto-Polynesian
glide *w, which normally disappeared before a back vowel, with which it shares
articulatory characteristics, in the development of the daughter languages of Proto-
Polynesian.
3.3. SUPRASEGMENTALS
Segment gemination is described in 3.3.1. Section 3.3.2 covers word stress. Section
3.3.4 provides information on intonation.
3.3.1. Length contrasts
Both vowels and consonants occur in geminated and ungeminated forms.
Geminated consonants are always the result of the deletion of an unstressed vowel
between two identical consonants (cf. 3.4.4.1). Segment gemination is affected by
certain morphological processes, as discussed in 3.4.1.3.
3.3.1.1–3. Vowels
Phonemically, geminated vowels count as two morae. The principal piece of
evidence in support of this analysis is stress assignment, which is most economically
accounted for by considering geminated vowels as being made up of two morae
(cf. 3.3.2.4). Phonetically, the articulation of geminated vowels is held for a longer

this articulation is always less than twice the duration of the articulation of an
ungeminated vowel. Other aspects of the phonetic quality of geminated vowels is

There is only one degree of gemination for vowels. If a morphological process
outputs a string of more than two identical vowels, the string is reduced to two
vocalic morae. Strings of more than two identical vocalic morae occur most

3.3.1.4–6. Liquids, nasals, and fricatives
When geminated, the articulation of the liquid/l/, the nasals/m n g/, and the

the corresponding ungeminated segments. In the Nukulaelae dialect, geminated/

ungeminated equivalent (cf. 3.1.2.1.4).
3.3.1.7. Plosives
Geminated plosives/p t k/are heavily aspirated.
3.3.2. Stress
3.3.2.1. Significance of stress
Stress is a significant feature, but it is predictable and thus not phonemic.
3.3.2.2. Phonetic correlates of stress
Stressed vowels are realized with greater intensity, on a higher pitch, and for a
longer duration than unstressed vowels. These correlates are most noticeable for
primary stress. Stress has no phonetic effect on consonants.
3.3.2.3. Stress levels
One can distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of stress. They have the
same basic phonetic effects on segments, with decreasing intensity. In fast speech,
the phonetic distinction between tertiarily stressed segments and unstressed
segments is not perceptible to the naked ear.
3.3.2.4. Position of stress
Stress position is regular, and its assignment applies uniformly to all words and
compounds. Stress assignment can be described most economically by making
reference to the moraic structure of the word, and by treating geminated vowels as
two morae.

3.4.2. Metathesis
Unlike certain languages of Eastern Oceania (see Besnier 1987 for an example),
Tuvaluan does not exhibit synchronically productive metathesis. A few lexemes
have undergone metathesis-like processes at some stage in the development of the
language, affecting either consonants or vowels. In some cases, diachronic metathesis
has taken place in some dialects but not in others. Examples are Southern Tuvaluan
kaipea ‘crab species’ (Northern Tuvaluan paikea, from *paqikea), Southern Tuvaluan
mmala ‘charcoal’ (Northern Tuvaluan malala, from *malala), and Niutao dialect ole
‘stink’ (other dialects elo, from *qelo). Such historical developments are not unusual
in Polynesian languages.
3.4.3. Coalescence and split
The only process of coalescence is that which follows the deletion of unstressed
vowels in the formation of geminated consonants, as described in 3.4.4.1.
3.4.4. Deletion and insertion
The only productive process of deletion or insertion is the deletion of vowels that
carry tertiary stress in certain environments.
3.4.4.1. Deletion processes
When two CV sequences in the base form of a word are identical and positioned so
that the second sequence receives primary stress, the vowel of the first sequence is
obligatorily deleted and the resulting cluster of two identical consonants is realized
as a geminated consonant (cf. 3.3.1.4–7). The following gives the base form followed
by the form following deletion and then a gloss:

Synchronic evidence for the structure of the base form comes from a number of

3.4.5. Reduplication
Reduplication is a ubiquitous feature of the language, used for many different
semantic purposes. It comes in two forms: full reduplication and partial
reduplication.
3.4.5.1. Full reduplication
Full reduplication can only apply to bimoraic roots. It consists in the doubling of
the root, the result being a single word; the following gives the reduplicated form
followed by the root and then a gloss:

iterative or repetitive version of the meaning of the root. Full reduplication applies
productively only to verbs, although many nouns are the result of diachronic full
reduplication.

reduplicated form. The following examples illustrate the fact that the root from

620
Phonology
Full reduplication must be distinguished from repetition. The former is a
morphophonological process, while the latter is better characterized as a discourse
process. Full reduplication of the verb fano ‘go’ yields the form fanofano, and repetition
outputs the string fano fano. These two processes are distinguished in several ways
(even though their outputs are frequently identical phonetically). First, fully
reduplicated forms are assigned stress as one lexeme, while repeated lexemes are
assigned stress independently of one another. Second, full reduplication can only
apply once, and thus can yield only two segmentally identical strings, while repetition
can apply iteratively. Strings of up to eight repeated forms of certain verbs (e.g. nofo
‘stay’, fano ‘go’, inu ‘drink’) are not uncommon. Third, only bimoraic roots can undergo
full reduplication (thus inuinu ‘drink iteratively’ is grammatical, but *matakumataku
‘iteratively afraid’ isn’t), while repetition is not thus constrained. The constraint on full
reduplication refers to the phonotactic structure of roots, and not lexemes; thus full
reduplication may apply to a bimorphemic root which only exists as a lexical item in
partially reduplicated form; for example, the simplest lexical manifestation of the root
*losi ‘accuse falsely’ is the partially reduplicated form llosi, which can reduplicate fully
as losilosi. Fourth, fully reduplicated forms can undergo certain morphological
processes, like partial internal reduplication to mark agreement (cf. 2.1.3.6.1) as single
lexemes (e.g., the plural form inuiinu ‘drink’), while repeated forms undergo
agreement separately. Reduplicated forms are written as one word throughout this
grammar, while repeated forms are written as separate words. For examples of the use
of both full reduplication and repetition for the purpose of marking various
imperfective aspectual categories, see 2.1.3.3.2.1(c) and (g).
3.4.5.2. Partial reduplication
Partial reduplication is ubiquitous and can have a variety of common functions,
most notably the marking of number agreement in verbs that allow such marking
(cf. 2.1.3.6). The following discussion distinguishes between reduplication in which
the reduplicated element can be treated as a prefix or suffix (‘external’ reduplication)
and reduplication in which the reduplicated element must be treated as an infix
(‘internal’ reduplication). The distinction is only relevant to words whose
unreduplicated form has more than three morae.

consonant, if there is one, by prefixing a copy of the string to the word. When the
