Ideophones and interjections
 
4.1. IDEOPHONES
As in most Oceanic languages, there are no ideophones in Tuvaluan. Some words,
particularly those referring to sound production, are clearly onomatopoeic: ggolo
‘snore’, guuguu ‘dumb, hum’, ggulu ‘growl, rumble’, kaa ‘bark’, kii ‘squeal’, kuuku-
kukuu ‘crow, cock-a-doodle-doo’, miaau or giaau ‘meow’, pakee ‘crack’, and patoo
‘produce a crashing sound’. Onomatopoeia that do not refer to sounds include
ppou ‘stink’ (iconic of the sound one makes when smelling a stench) and tuli ‘Pacific
golden plover, Pluvialis dominicus’.38 However, these terms are not ideophones
according to current working definitions of ideophones as words whose
phonological configuration denotes systematically some property of their referent,
such as smell, colour, or position (Schachter 1985:21).
4.2. INTERJECTIONS
The internal structure of most interjections follows regular phonological and
morphological patterns. However, interjections are frequently uttered with
intonational contours that are peculiar to them. For example, in the Nukulaelae
dialect, the vowels in taapaa ee, exclamation of surprise, are often prolonged for an
unusual period of time, particularly the first one, which is also commonly lowered,
and the intonation contour begins in the lowest range of the speaker’s voice and
ends with a falsetto. Some interjections or the peculiar intonation contours associated
with them in particular dialects function as well-known dialectal shibboleths and
are the subject of much inter-island teasing.

5.1. STRUCTURED SEMANTIC FIELD
S 5.1.1. Kinship terminology
The notion of ‘being related’ is most generally expressed with the word kaaiga
‘family’, which can function as a noun or as a noun-derived verb. The term kano
‘blood relation’, etymologically related to kkano ‘flesh’, is also used as either a noun
or a noun-derived verb. Alternatively, toto ‘blood’ and tino ‘body’ can have the
metaphorical meaning of ‘blood relation, related by blood’. The three terms kano,
toto, and tino refer only to blood relations to the exclusion of adoptive and affinal
relations. The term kaaiga is more encompassing.
The kinship term inventory is relatively small, and each kinship term covers a
broad range of referents. In the basic system, the most important semantic
parameters are generation and gender relative to ego (i.e., whether the referent is
of the same gender as ego or not). The seniority parameter, of importance to the
kinship terminology of other Polynesian societies, is not relevant in Tuvaluan. Terms
for siblings are their own converse, and so are several other terms. There are few
terms for affines.
All kinship terms and their affixed and modified forms can be used as nouns or
verbs. Following is a sample of uses of the term taina ‘sibling of same gender as ego’
and its modified forms, beginning with an example of a nominal use of the term:

5.1.1.4–6. By adoption, fosterage, and affiliation
Several types of adoption and fosterage are recognized in Tuvaluan society, all of
which supplement rather than replace blood kin ties. Adoption of all types is very
frequent, as in many other Polynesian societies, and plays an important role as an
adaptation strategy to often scant resources such as land, since the creation of
adoptive ties coupled with the maintenance of blood ties can increase an individual’s
access to land resources (Brady 1976, Koch 1963).
There are several ways of referring to adoptions that involve the creation of
fictive parent-child ties. The verb puke ‘take’ is the most common term. The terms
tausi ‘keep, take care’ and faagai ‘feed’ usually connote a fostering relationship,
often temporary, usually not legalized. All three terms are transitive verbs and take
as subject an expression referring to the parent and as direct object a reference to
the child:
(3141)

Malia Pst take Erg Moapi
‘Moapi adopted Malia.’
The same three terms can also modify tama ‘child’ attributively (e.g., tama faagai
‘foster child’). Often an individual past child-bearing age adopts a young child,
thus creating a fictive grandparent-grandchild relationship, which is referred to in
the same manner. A fourth word commonly used to refer to legalized adoption is

5.1.1.7. Terms for pairs of kin
The compounding element tau is preposed to certain kinship terms to denote pairs
of relatives related through the particular relationship denoted by the kinship term.
For example, the expression tau maatua, formed with maatua ‘mother’, refers to a
mother-and-son pair or mother-and-daughter pair. The individuals involved may
be of any age, and the relationship may be either by blood or adoption of any type.
The term is not applied in its literal sense to relatives who are not tonu ‘true’, e.g., to
a pair comprised of an aunt and niece or of a mother-in-law and son-in-law (see
further on for special terms referring to collateral relationships). The word tau is
historically related to numerous other terms denoting plurality or related notions
in Polynesian languages: in Tuvaluan, it appears as a numeral modifier for coconuts
tied up in bunches (cf. 2.1.6.5.1(c)) and as an adverb denoting habitual or continuous
aspect (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(c)-(d)).
Kinship terms that can form compounds with tau are terms that denote
relationships normally characterized by strong affective bonds and mutual alofa
‘empathy’, although the particular behaviour differs from one type of relationship
to the next. One finds the following inventory of forms:
(3145)

5.1.2.2. Nonbasic colour terms
Nonbasic colour terms fall into several categories: derived terms, i.e., monolexical
terms that are derived from or identical to a non-colour term and that refer to the
typical colour of the referent of the related or identical term (5.1.2.2.1); compound
terms (5.1.2.2.2); borrowed terms (5.1.2.2.3); and terms that are restricted to a limited
range of referents (5.1.2.2.4). Modifiers of colour terms are treated in 5.1.1.2.5.
5.1.2.2.1. Derived terms
The following derived colour terms can be used in all frames regularly associated
with colour terms, e.g., with lanu ‘colour’ optional but preferred:
(3153)
llega ‘deep yellow, reddish orange’, from lega ‘egg yolk’ (cf. Proto-
Polynesian *rega ‘turmeric’)
ffelo (Vaitupu dialect) ‘yellow’ (cf. felo ‘Malay custard apple, Ficus
tinctoria’)
Under this category fall descriptors of marking patterns, whose referents are not
considered colours in other societies, but which behave exactly like colour terms in
Tuvaluan. For example, they can modify the noun lanu ‘colour’ and frequently
form verbal noun-adjective compounds with it:
(3154)
pulepule ‘spotted, chequered, with a pattern of two or more colours’
(probably from pule ‘cowrie (shell), Cypraeidae species’, whose shell
is spotted)
selesele ‘striped’ (cf. sele ‘cut in strips’)
tasi ‘solid’ (literally, ‘one, same’)
tuuttutu ‘with polka-dots’ (probably duplicated form of tutu ‘cauterise’)
valevale ‘multicolour, polychrome’ (literally ‘any old way, variously’)

lanu alava ‘brownish grey’ (alava ‘coconut species that yields reddish

5.1.2.2.3. Borrowed terms
Many English colour terms are known and used, even by people with limited
proficiency in English. The extent to which the terms are adapted to the phonological
structure of Tuvaluan depends largely on the relative fluency of the speaker in
English; thus bilingual speakers often use the term green, thereby engaging in one-
word code-switching, while speaking Tuvaluan, while monolingual speakers of
Tuvaluan use the phonologically adapted version of the term, kulini. Following are
the most common borrowed terms in phonologically adapted form:

kaasimia ‘light purple, mauve’ (from cashmere)
kookoo ‘brown’ (from cocoa)
kulei ‘grey’
kulini ‘green’
oolenisi ‘orange’
palauni ‘brown’
piniki ‘pink’
puluu ‘blue’
violeti ‘purple, violet’
All borrowed terms can be used in noun-adjective compounds with lanu ‘colour’
(e.g., lanu kulini ‘green’).

refer to colour only in conjunction with other qualities. Many of these terms are
generally not used in noun-adjective compounds with lanu:

meamea ‘(of sunburnt skin) red’
mmelo ‘(of one’s face) red from exposure or intense emotion’ (cf. melo

ssulu ‘(of a ripe fruit, the moon, or drying leaves) brightly coloured,
usually bright yellow or bright brown’
ttea ‘(of a person) pale because of illness or intense emotion, (of a colour,

5.1.2.2.5. Colour term modifiers
Colour terms can be modified by a number of words. The intensifier kkii can modify
basic or nonbasic terms denoting warm colours to denote brightness (e.g., kkula kkii
‘bright red’) and terms denoting cool colour to denote darkness (e.g., puluu kkii
‘deep blue’). The adjective maalosi and mmafa, literally ‘healthy, strong’ and ‘heavy’,
both mean ‘deep, dark’ with colour terms (e.g., palauni mmafa ‘dark brown’, puluu
maalosi ‘deep blue’). The term kkefu, which means ‘blurred’ in its literal sense,
combines with uli ‘black, dark’ in a compound uli kkefu ‘(dark) grey’, or sometimes
just appears as kkefu. Lightness is denoted by either maamaa ‘light’ or mmaa ‘clean,
clear’ (e.g., kkula mmaa ‘light red’).
A number of collocationally restricted modifiers (cf. 2.2.6.3.4) can only modify
specific colour terms and no other word in the language:
(3158)

kkula mmii ‘bright red’ (or the reduplicated form miimmimi)
uli patoi(toi), uli tamumu, uli tokitoki ‘jet black’
uusi palailai ‘(of hair, vegetation) deep dark’
vvolu tokitoki, vvolu tukituki, vvolu patoi(toi) ‘(of complexion) very
flushed’
The collocational patterns associated with these modifiers are highly idiosyncratic.
For example, both tokitoki and tukituki can modify vvolu ‘flushed’, but only tokitoki
can cooccur with uli ‘black’.

in the terms mea inu ‘drink’, mea kiki ‘protein food’, and mea ota (or sometimes ota)

5.1.4.1. Cooking terminology
Several terms can denote the act of cooking in its general form, the most unmarked
of which is fakappaku ‘cook (any style)’, the causative form of ppaku ‘cooked’ (also
‘(of food or one’s flesh) burnt’). The latter term is the antonym of mmata ‘raw,
uncooked, undercooked’, and has a now obsolete synonym, mmoso. The latter term
only refers to cooked food, in contrast to the polysemic ppaku. The polysemic verb
fai ‘do, make’ can also be used as a transitive verb or with an incorporated object,
most commonly meakkai ‘food’. Lastly, the borrowing kuuka means ‘cook in Western
fashion’, where ‘Western fashion’ can refer to a method (e.g., in a pan over the
kerosene stove) or a style (e.g., in a stew). Of relevance is the term fakagaalue ‘prepare
(protein food) as a stew or a casserole’, the causative form of gaalue ‘work’, which
refers to cooking in a Western fashion.

tao ‘bake in an earth oven or a European-style oven’

These terms can be modified with adverbs or prepositional phrases to denote other

Basic cooking terms probably denote methods that were in use in pre-contact
days (i.e., prior to the mid-nineteenth century). Baking, which stands out as a
particularly basic and probably ancient method, was and is done in an underground
oven (umu) similar to those found throughout Polynesia, created by heating stones
in an open fire in a pit in the ground, placing the food wrapped in leaves over the
stones, covering the food wrappings with protective mats, woven leaves, or canvas,
and burying the entire oven. The oven is uncovered (pusa) after a period of one or
several hours, during which the food has cooked slowly à l’étouffade. While the
umu is only prepared on festive occasions or once a week in more Westernized
areas of Polynesia, it remains part of everyday cooking on the Outer Islands.

5.1.4.2. Eating terminology
The most basic verb referring to the act of ingesting food is kai ‘eat’. However,
when the ingested food is (mea) ota ‘raw protein food’ (fish, meat, or eggs), or certain
vegetables such as fern shoots or coconut shoots (but not uttanu ‘germinated coconut
kernel’, among others), the verb is ota, not kai. The act of eating other types of food
raw can be described as kai mmata (mmata ‘raw’), not ota. The phrase ota mmata
refers to the ingestion of meat or fish normatively not eaten raw, such as pork.
To refer to the ingestion of liquids, the verb is inu ‘drink’. Unlike its cognate in
Fijian, a related language, this term is not applied to the ingestion of juicy fruit or
